The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.

p.seg: 1.1 Jìn Píng Gōng asked Shī Kuàng:
"What is the Way of a ruler of men?"
He replied:
"The Way of a ruler of men
is to be pure, tranquil, and without action,
to focus on universal love,
and to strive to employ the worthy.
He widely opens his ears and eyes
to observe all quarters;
he does not stubbornly immerse himself in common customs
and is not constrained by those around him.
He has far-reaching vision in a vast manner
and stands independently in an extraordinary way.
He frequently examines and evaluates merits
to oversee his subordinates.
This is the conduct of a ruler of men."
Píng Gōng said:
"Excellent."
1.2 Qí Xuān Wáng said to Yǐn Wén:
"What are the affairs of a ruler of men like?"
Yǐn Wén replied:
"The affairs of a ruler of men
consist of non-action while being able to accommodate subordinates.
When affairs are few, they are easy to follow;
when laws are sparse, they are easy to comply with.
Therefore, the people do not incur guilt because of the administration.
The Great Way accommodates the masses;
Great Virtue accommodates subordinates.
When the sage acts little, the world is governed.
The Shū says:
'Wisdom makes a sage.'
The poets say:
'In Qí there were level paths,
may his descendants preserve them.'"
Xuān Wáng said:
"Excellent."
1.3 Chéng Wáng enfeoffed Bó Qín as the Gōng of Lǔ,
summoned him, and told him:
"Do you know the Way of being a superior to others?
Whoever occupies a noble position
must respect their subordinates.
Following virtue and offering admonitions,
you must open the gate for forthright speech.
Be frugal and tranquil to support them.
Do not intimidate those who offer counsel with your authority,
do not block their words,
collect their remarks broadly,
and then choose what is worthy of consideration.
To have culture without military power
is to have no means to overawe subordinates;
to have military power without culture
makes the people fear but not feel close to you.
When culture and military power are both practiced,
authority and virtue are established.
Once authority and virtue are established,
the people will be close and submissive.
Purity and integrity will reach the top,
while craftiness and flattery will be blocked below.
Those who give counsel will be able to come forward,
and loyalty and trustworthiness will be nurtured."
Bó Qín bowed twice, accepted the mandate, and took his leave.
1.4 Chén Líng Gōng acted perversely and spoke erratically.
Xiè Yě said:
"Chén will surely perish!
I have repeatedly admonished the ruler,
but the ruler does not listen to me and loses his dignity even more.
The transformation of subordinates by the superior
is like the wind blowing over the grass.
If an east wind blows, the grass leans to the west;
if a west wind blows, the grass leans to the east.
Wherever the wind comes from, the grass leans accordingly.
Therefore, the movements of a ruler of men cannot but be cautious.
If one plants a crooked tree,
how can one get a straight shadow?
For a ruler of men who does not straighten his conduct and does not respect his words,
there has never been one who could preserve the title of Sovereign King
or leave behind a manifest and glorious name.
The Yì says:
'The superior man remains in his room,
but when he sends forth his words,
if they are good,
then people from over a thousand lǐ away will respond to them;
how much more so those who are near!
He remains in his room,
but when he sends forth his words,
if they are not good,
then people from over a thousand lǐ away will oppose them;
how much more so those who are near!
Words issue from one's person and affect the people;
actions start from nearby and are seen from afar.
Words and actions
are the pivot and trigger of the superior man.
The release of the pivot and trigger
is the master of honor or disgrace.
Words and actions
are the means by which the superior man moves Heaven and Earth;
can one not be cautious!'
When Heaven and Earth move, the myriad things transform.
The Shī says:
'Be cautious in the words you utter,
be respectful in your dignity,
and let everything be mild and good.'
This is what it refers to.
Now the ruler is not cautious in these things but is self-indulgent;
if he does not perish, he will surely be assassinated."
Líng Gōng heard this,
and considering Xiè Yě's words to be seductive speech, he killed him.
Later, he was indeed assassinated by Zhēng Shū.
1.5 Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒng Zǐ:
"I have heard that a superior man does not play board games;
is this true?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied:
"It is true."
Āi Gōng said:
"Why does he not play board games?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied:
"Because they involve having two chariots."
Āi Gōng said:
"If there are two chariots,
then why not play?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied:
"Because it involves practicing an evil way together."
Āi Gōng was startled.
After a while,
he said:
"Is the superior man's hatred of the evil way as extreme as this?"
Kǒng Zǐ replied:
"If a superior man's hatred of the evil way cannot be extreme,
then his love for the good way cannot be extreme either;
if his love for the good way cannot be extreme,
then the common people's affection for him cannot be extreme either.
The Shī says:
'Before I saw my lord,
my heart was full of sorrow;
but since I have seen him,
and since I have met him,
my heart is indeed pleased.'
The Shī's love for the good way is extreme like this."
Āi Gōng said:
"Excellent!
I have heard that a superior man brings to fruition the beauty in others
and does not bring to fruition their evil.
Were it not for Kǒng Zǐ,
how would I have heard these words!"
1.6 Héjiān Xiàn Wáng said:
"Yáo centered his mind on the world
and turned his will toward the destitute people.
He felt the pain of the myriad clans suffering from crimes
and worried about the living beings not being successful.
Therefore, if one person was hungry,
he would say:
'It is I who have made them hungry.'
If one person was cold,
he would say:
'It is I who have made them cold.'
If one person committed a crime,
he would say:
'It is I who have led them into it.'
Benevolence was manifested and righteousness was established;
virtue was broad and transformation was wide.
Therefore, the people were encouraged without rewards
and the people were governed without punishments.
Leading with empathy and then teaching afterward—
this is the Way of Yáo."
During the time of Shùn,
the Yǒu Miáo Clan did not submit.
The reason they did not submit was that
the Dà Shān was to their south,
the Diàn Shān was to their north,
the waves of Dòngtíng were to their left,
and the waters of Pénglǐ were to their right.
Using these natural defenses,
they did not submit.
Yǔ wanted to attack them, but Shùn did not allow it,
saying:
"My instruction and teaching have not yet been exhausted."
He thoroughly carried out his instruction and teaching,
and the Yǒu Miáo Clan requested to submit.
When the world heard of this,
everyone found Yǔ's sense of righteousness to be lacking
and returned to the virtue of Shùn.
1.7 Zhōu Gōng occupied the position of the Son of Heaven,
spreading virtue and bestowing kindness,
becoming even more enlightened the further his influence reached.
The Shí'èr Mù,
three in each direction,
were sent out to recommend the people of distant regions.
Those who were cold and hungry and had neither clothes nor food,
those who had lawsuits but were deprived of their livelihoods,
and those of worthy talent who had not been recommended,
were reported to the Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven held court for their lords,
he would bow and invite them forward,
saying:
“Could it be that there is something not attained in my governance and instruction?
Why is it that among the people who are overseen, there are those who are cold and hungry and have neither clothes nor food,
those who have lawsuits but were deprived of their livelihoods,
and those of worthy talent who have not been recommended?”
When those lords returned,
they summoned the Dàfū of their states and informed them of the Son of Heaven’s words.
When the common people heard this,
they all rejoiced and said:
“This is truly the Son of Heaven!
How can he, dwelling in such depth and distance, see us so clearly?
How could he be deceived!”
Thus, the Mù were the means by which he opened the four gates,
clarified the vision of the four eyes,
and extended the hearing of the four ears.
Consequently, those nearby felt close to him,
and those far away felt at peace.
The Shī says:
“Gentle with the distant and kind to the near,
thus stabilizing our king.”
This refers to this!
1.8 Héjiān Xiàn Wáng said:
“Yǔ claimed that if the people have no food,
then I cannot command them;
if an achievement is completed but does not benefit the people,
then I cannot encourage them.
Therefore, he dredged the Hé to guide its flow,
channeled the Jiāng to connect its Jiǔ Pài,
and drained the Wǔ Hú to settle the Dōng Hǎi.
The people labored indeed,
but the reason they did not feel resentful or bitter
was that the achievement was completed and its benefits returned to the people.”
1.9 When Yǔ went out and saw a criminal,
he descended from his carriage to inquire and wept for him.
Those around him said:
“A criminal does not follow the Way,
and thus has come to this.
Why does the King grieve for him to such an extent?”
Yǔ said:
“The people of Yáo and Shùn
all took the hearts of Yáo and Shùn as their own hearts.
Now that I, of little virtue, am the ruler,
the people each take their own heart as their heart;
this is why I grieve for them.”
The Shū says:
“If the people have sins,
they lie upon me alone.”
1.10 The people of Yú and the people of Ruì sought a settlement to their dispute from Wén Wáng.
Upon entering Wén Wáng’s borders,
they saw that his common people yielded to one another as if they were Shìdàfū.
Upon entering the capital,
they saw that his Shìdàfū yielded to one another as if they were Gōngqīng.
The people of the two states said to each other:
“His common people yield to become Shìdàfū,
and his Shìdàfū yield to become Gōngqīng.
If so, then this ruler must also yield the world without dwelling in it.”
The people of the two states,
without even seeing Wén Wáng in person,
yielded the land they were disputing
to make it fallow land and returned home.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“How great!
The Way of Wén Wáng,
nothing could be added to it!
He transformed without moving,
and achieved without acting.
By being reverent, cautious, and respectful of himself, Yú and Ruì were naturally pacified.”
Therefore, the Shū says:
“Only the reverence and awe of Wén Wáng.”
This refers to this.
1.11 Chéng Wáng was in leisure with Táng Shù Yú.
He cut a paulownia leaf into the shape of a guī and gave it to Táng Shù Yú,
saying:
“I use this to enfeoff you.”
Táng Shù Yú was delighted
and informed Zhōu Gōng.
Zhōu Gōng requested an audience and asked:
“Did the Son of Heaven enfeoff Yú?”
Chéng Wáng said:
“I was just joking with Yú.”
Zhōu Gōng replied:
“I have heard that
the Son of Heaven does not speak in jest.
When the Son of Heaven speaks, the scribe records it,
the musician recites it,
and the scholars praise it.”
Thereupon, he finally enfeoffed Táng Shù Yú in Jìn.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn can be called good at persuasion;
with one praise, he made Chéng Wáng more cautious with his words,
clarified the righteousness of loving one's brother,
and strengthened the support for the royal house.
1.12 During the time of Yáo,
Shùn served as Sītú,
Xiè served as Sīmǎ,
Yǔ served as Sīkōng,
Hòu Jì took charge of the fields and crops,
Kuí served as Yuèzhèng,
Chuí served as Gōngshī,
Bó Yí served as Zhìzōng,
Gāoyáo served as Dàlǐ,
and Yì took charge of driving birds and beasts.
Yáo’s physical strength and skills
were not enough to perform even one of these tasks.
Yet Yáo was the ruler while these nine men were his ministers;
what was the reason?
Yáo understood the affairs of the nine offices
and had the nine men each undertake their tasks;
they were all equal to their responsibilities
and thus achieved the nine successes.
Yáo then completed his great achievement and ruled the world as king.
Therefore, knowing people
is the way of the ruler;
knowing tasks
is the way of the minister.
When the ruler’s way is to know people
and the minister’s way is to know tasks,
and they do not disrupt the ancient laws,
the world will be well-governed.
1.13 Tāng asked Yī Yǐn:
“As for the Sāngōng, Jiǔqīng, twenty-seven Dàfū, and eighty-one Yuánshì,
is there a way to know them?”
Yī Yǐn replied:
“In the past, Yáo knew men upon seeing them;
Shùn knew men after employing them;
Yǔ recommended men based on their success.
These three rulers' ways of recommending the worthy
were all different yet successful;
yet even they sometimes made mistakes.
How much more so if one has no laws or standards but relies only on oneself,
using people according to one's own whims;
there will surely be great failure.
Therefore, if the ruler has the ministers present their own abilities,
then not one in ten thousand will be missed.”
1.14 How does a king select the worthy?
A king obtains worthy talents to assist himself,
and only then is there order.
Even with the brilliance of Yáo and Shùn, if the ministers as limbs and trunk are not complete,
the ruler’s grace will not flow,
and the moisture of transformation will not reach the people.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler is on the throne,
he is cautious in selecting scholars
and diligent in seeking the worthy.
He establishes the four assistants to aid himself
and has the eminent to manage the offices.
He honors their rank
and increases their salaries.
The worthy are promoted to manifest their glory,
and the incompetent are dismissed to perform manual labor.
Thus, the ruler has no lingering worries,
those below have no evil intentions,
the various officials are capable of governing,
the ministers delight in their duties,
grace flows to all living beings,
and its moisture reaches even the plants and trees.
Long ago, Yú Shùn had Yǔ on his left and Gāoyáo on his right;
he did not even descend from the hall, yet the world was well-governed.
This is the effect of employing the capable.
1.15 Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng:
"Those who promote the worthy but still face danger and ruin,
why is this so?"
Tài Gōng said:
"To promote the worthy but not employ them
is to have the reputation of promoting the worthy without the reality of obtaining true worthies."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Where does the fault lie?"
Tài Gōng said:
"The fault lies in the ruler liking to employ those with minor virtues
and not obtaining true worthies."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"What is it like to like employing those with minor virtues?"
Tài Gōng said:
"The ruler likes to hear praise and does not detest slander;
he considers the unworthy as worthy,
the unvirtuous as virtuous,
the disloyal as loyal,
and the untrustworthy as trustworthy.
Such a ruler regards praise as merit
and defamation as crime;
those with merit are not rewarded,
and those with crimes are not punished;
those with many partisans advance,
and those with few partisans retreat.
Therefore, the many ministers clique together and obscure the worthy;
the various officials form factions and commit many wicked acts.
Loyal ministers die from slander though innocent,
and wicked ministers are rewarded for praise though without merit.
Thus the state faces danger and ruin."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent.
Today I have heard the truth about slander and praise."
1.16 Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng:
"If one obtains the worthy and respects scholars,
yet still cannot achieve order,
why is this so?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"Being unable to decide for oneself
and instead deciding based on what others say
is a disaster."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"What does it mean to decide based on what others say?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"Being unable to determine whom to dismiss
and dismissing based on what others say;
being unable to determine whom to recruit
and recruiting based on what others say;
being unable to determine what to do
and acting based on what others say;
being unable to determine what to punish
and punishing based on what others say;
being unable to determine what to reward
and rewarding based on what others say.
The worthy are not necessarily used,
the unworthy are not necessarily dismissed,
and scholars are not necessarily respected."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent.
How then is the state governed?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"The ruler hates hearing the truth about himself
but likes hearing the truth about others;
he hates hearing of his own evils
but likes hearing of the evils of others.
Therefore, the state cannot necessarily be ordered."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent."
1.17 Qí Huán Gōng questioned Nìng Qī, saying:
"Guǎn Zǐ is old this year.
If he should leave me and pass from this world,
I fear that laws and orders will not be carried out,
many people will lose their positions,
the common people will become resentful,
and the state will have many thieves and bandits.
How can I prevent wickedness and evil from arising
and ensure the people have sufficient food and clothing?"
Nìng Qī replied:
"The essence lies in obtaining the worthy and employing them."
Huán Gōng said:
"How does one obtain the worthy?"
Nìng Qī replied:
"Open the paths for them,
observe them and then use them,
honor their positions,
make their salaries generous,
and make their names prominent.
Then the scholars of the world
will move quickly and arrive in great numbers."
Huán Gōng said:
"I have already promoted worthy scholars and used them;
were it not for your presence here,
there would still be no scholars of exceptional talent from among the commoners
coming to my gate to seek an audience with me."
Nìng Qī replied:
"This is because your observation is not clear,
your promotion of them is not prominent,
your use of them is suspicious,
their offices are lowly,
and their salaries are meager.
Moreover, there are five obstructions as to why a state does not obtain scholars:
the ruler does not like scholars
and flatterers are by his side;
this is the first obstruction.
Those who speak of beneficial matters are never used;
this is the second obstruction.
There is blockage and concealment,
and one must rely on those close to the ruler to be noticed;
this is the third obstruction.
Legal cases are interrogated to the limit
so as to find fault using the law;
this is the fourth obstruction.
Those in charge act according to their own desires
and usurp the power and mandates of the state;
this is the fifth obstruction.
If you remove these five obstructions,
then heroes will all arise
and the worthy and wise will come to dwell.
If the five obstructions are not removed,
then above, the ruler is shielded from the circumstances of the officials and people,
and below, the path for worthy scholars is blocked.
Therefore, in the governance of an enlightened king or a sage ruler,
it is like the rivers and seas which reject nothing,
and thus they forever remain the masters of the hundred streams.
An enlightened king or a sage ruler tolerates everything,
and thus they enjoy peace, joy, and longevity.
Viewing it from this perspective,
those who bring peace to the ruler and benefit to the people are not limited to just one scholar."
Huán Gōng said:
"Excellent.
I shall record these five obstructions to serve as a foundation for my self-warning."
1.18 Qí Jǐng Gōng questioned Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"I wish to follow you and improve the governance of the state of Qí.
Is this possible?"
He replied:
"Yīng has heard
that a state must have a complete set of officials before its governance can be improved."
Jǐng Gōng changed countenance and was displeased,
saying:
"Though the state of Qí is small,
how could it not have a complete set of officials?"
He replied:
"This is not what I meant.
In the past, when the former ruler Huán Gōng was physically weary
and his speech and commands were insufficient,
then Xí Péng assisted him.
When those close to him made many mistakes
and punishments were not appropriate,
then Xián Zhāng assisted him.
When his private life was unrestrained
and those around him were cowed and fearful,
then Dōng Guō Yá assisted him.
When the fields were not cultivated
and the people were not at peace,
then Nìng Qī assisted him.
When military officers were lazy
and soldiers were idle,
then Wáng Zǐ Chéng Fù assisted him.
When virtue and righteousness were not appropriate
and faithful conduct was declining,
then Guǎn Zǐ assisted him.
The former ruler was able to use the strengths of others to supplement his own shortcomings,
and use the fullness of others to make up for his own deficiencies.
Therefore, his speech and commands reached far without being disobeyed,
and his troops were deployed against the guilty without being blunted.
For this reason, the feudal lords submitted to his virtue,
and the Son of Heaven sent him sacrificial meat.
Now your mistakes are many,
yet not a single scholar has let them be heard;
therefore, I say the officials are not complete."
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Excellent."
1.19 Jǐng Gōng said to Yàn Zǐ:
"I hear that Gāo Liáo associates with you;
I request to see him."
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Yīng has heard
that those who fight for territory
cannot achieve kingship;
those who serve for salary
cannot achieve good governance.
Although Gāo Liáo and Yīng have been like brothers for a long time,
he has never corrected Yīng's faults
nor filled Yīng's deficiencies.
He is merely a minister who serves for salary;
how could he be sufficient to assist the ruler?"
1.20 King Zhāo of Yān asked Guō Kuí:
"My territory is narrow and my people few;
the people of Qí have taken eight cities of Jì,
and the Xiōngnú gallop beneath Lóufán.
Because of my unworthiness,
I have inherited the ancestral temple,
yet I fear endangering the state.
Is there a way to preserve it?"
Guō Kuí said:
"There is,
but I fear Your Majesty cannot use it."
King Zhāo left his seat
and requested to hear it.
Guō Kuí said:
"The minister of an emperor
is a minister in name,
but in reality is a teacher.
The minister of a king
is a minister in name,
but in reality is a friend.
The minister of a hegemon
is a minister in name,
but in reality is a guest.
The minister of a state in peril
is a minister in name,
but in reality is a captive.
Now if Your Majesty faces east
and seeks ministers by commanding with your eyes and your tone,
then men with the talents of servants will arrive.
If you face south to hold court
and seek ministers without losing the etiquette of bowing and yielding,
then men with the talents of ministers will arrive.
If you face west and treat them with equal etiquette,
humbling yourself in your expression
and not using your position of power to seek ministers,
then men with the talents of friends will arrive.
If you face north and seek ministers with a restrained and hesitant manner,
then men with the talents of masters and teachers will arrive.
In this way, at best you can be a king,
and at least you can be a hegemon;
let Your Majesty choose among these."
The King of Yān said:
"I wish to learn but have no teacher."
Guō Kuí said:
"If Your Majesty truly wishes to promote the Way,
I, Kuí, ask to open the way for the scholars of the world."
Thereupon the King of Yān always placed Guō Kuí in the superior seat facing south.
After three years,
Sū Zǐ heard of it
and returned to Yān from Zhōu;
Zōu Yǎn heard of it
and returned to Yān from Qí;
Lè Yì heard of it
and returned to Yān from Zhào;
Qū Jǐng heard of it
and returned to Yān from Chǔ.
These four gentlemen all arrived,
and indeed, by means of a weak Yān, they annexed strong Qí.
Yān and Qí were not states of equal power or equal combatants;
the reason it happened thus
was the strength of these four gentlemen.
The *Shī* says:
"Numerous are the many scholars,
King Wén is thereby at peace."
This refers to this.
1.21 After King Zhuāng of Chǔ had subdued the Earl of Zhèng
and defeated the army of Jìn,
General Zǐ Zhòng spoke three times inappropriately.
King Zhuāng returned
and passed through the fief of Shēn Hóu.
Shēn Hóu presented a meal,
but it was noon and the King would not eat.
Shēn Hóu asked what his offense was.
King Zhuāng sighed deeply and said:
"I have heard:
if the ruler is a worthy ruler
and also has a teacher, he becomes a king;
if the ruler is an average ruler
and also has a teacher, he becomes a hegemon;
if the ruler is an inferior ruler
and his ministers are none as capable as the ruler, he perishes.
Now I am an inferior ruler,
and among the ministers there are none as capable as I,
so I fear perishing.
Furthermore, a generation is never without sages,
and a state is never without worthies.
If there are worthies in the world and I alone cannot find them,
then with a life such as mine,
what is the point of eating!"
Therefore King Zhuāng subdued great states in battle
and the feudal lords righteously followed him.
He was solemn, worried, and fearful;
he did not consider sage-like wisdom to reside in himself,
but regretted his own unworthiness
and thought of obtaining worthy assistants.
Forgetting his meal at noon,
he can truly be called an enlightened ruler.
1.22 An enlightened ruler has three fears:
first, occupying a high position and fearing not hearing his faults;
second, being successful and fearing arrogance;
third, hearing the ultimate words of the world and fearing being unable to practice them.
How do we know this is so?
Formerly, King Gǒujiàn of Yuè fought with the people of Wú,
greatly defeated them,
and annexed the Jiǔ Yí.
At that time,
the ruler stood facing south,
with three close ministers
and five distant ministers,
and ordered the ministers:
"He who hears my faults and does not report them, his crime is punishable."
This is occupying a high position and fearing not hearing his faults.
Formerly, Duke Wén of Jìn fought with the people of Chǔ,
greatly defeated them,
and burned their camp,
the fire not dying out for three days.
Duke Wén withdrew and had a worried expression.
An attendant said:
"Your Lordship greatly defeated Chǔ,
why do you have a worried expression now?"
Duke Wén said:
"I have heard that those who can find peace through victory in battle
are only sages.
As for those who win by deception,
they are never without danger;
that is why I am worried."
This is being successful and fearing arrogance.
Formerly, Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng;
he debated their words
and delighted in their principles.
On the morning of the first month,
he ordered the preparation of the great sacrifice
and presented it to the ancestors.
Duke Huán stood facing west,
and Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng stood facing east.
Duke Huán offered praise, saying:
"Since I have been able to listen to the words of these two gentlemen,
my eyes have become brighter
and my ears have become sharper.
I do not dare to keep this to myself
and wish to present them to my ancestors."
This is hearing the ultimate words of the world
and fearing being unable to practice them.
1.23 Duke Jǐng of Qí went out to hunt;
going up the mountain he saw a tiger,
and going down to the marsh he saw a snake.
When he returned,
he summoned Yàn Zǐ and asked him:
"Today I went out to hunt;
going up the mountain I saw a tiger,
and going down to the marsh I saw a snake.
Is this perhaps what is called an ill omen?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"A state has three ill omens,
but these are not among them.
To have worthies and not know them
is the first ill omen;
to know them and not use them
is the second ill omen;
to use them and not trust them
is the third ill omen.
What are called ill omens
are things such as these.
Now, going up the mountain and seeing a tiger—
that is the tiger's home;
going down to the marsh and seeing a snake—
that is the snake's den.
Going to the tiger's home
and the snake's den and seeing them,
how could that be an ill omen?"
1.24 King Zhuāng of Chǔ loved hunting.
A high official remonstrated:
"Jìn and Chǔ are rival states;
if Chǔ does not plot against Jìn,
Jìn will surely plot against Chǔ.
Is Your Majesty not perhaps too indulged in pleasure?"
The King said:
"I hunt in order to seek scholars.
Those who pierce tigers and leopards in the thickets,
by this I know their courage;
those who seize rhinoceroses and fight wild bulls,
by this I know their strength and power;
when the hunt is over and we divide the catch,
by this I know their benevolence.
By following this way,
I have obtained three scholars,
and the state of Chǔ is thereby at peace."
Therefore it is said:
"If one has the will, then there is nothing that is not a proper task,"
this refers to this.
1.25 During the time of Tāng, there was a great drought for seven years;
the Luò River cracked and the streams dried up,
the sand was scorched and the stones were melted.
Thereupon, he sent a person carrying a three-legged tripod to pray to the mountains and rivers,
teaching him to pray, saying:
"Is the government immoderate?
Are the people suffering?
Is bribery prevalent?
Are slanderers flourishing?
Are palaces being built excessively?
Are the entreaties of women influential?
Why has the lack of rain reached such an extreme!"
Before the words were finished, the sky rained heavily.
Therefore, Heaven's response to man
is like a shadow following a form
or an echo following a sound.
The Shī says:
"Offerings were made to those above and below,
there was no spirit that was not honored."
This speaks of the suffering of drought.
1.26 During the time of Tài Wù of Yīn,
a mulberry and a paper mulberry grew in the courtyard;
they sprouted at dusk,
and by dawn, they were as large as a hug.
The scribe requested to divine this in the temple of Tāng,
and Tài Wù followed his advice.
The diviner said:
"I have heard:
Auspicious signs
are the precursors of fortune;
if one sees an auspicious sign but acts without goodness,
then fortune will not arise.
Ominous signs
are the precursors of calamity;
if one sees an ominous sign but is able to act with goodness,
then calamity will not arrive."
Thereupon, he held court early and retired late,
inquired after the sick and condoled with the mourning;
after three days, the mulberry and paper mulberry vanished on their own.
1.27 Gāo Zōng
was Wǔ Dīng;
he was lofty and thus honored as an ancestor,
hence his title Gāo Zōng.
After Chéng Tāng,
the Way of the former kings fell into neglect,
and laws were violated.
A mulberry and a paper mulberry grew together in the court,
and in seven days, they were as large as a hug.
Wǔ Dīng summoned his minister and asked him about it.
His minister said:
"Although I know of it,
I may not speak;
ask Zǔ Jǐ."
Zǔ Jǐ said: "The mulberry and paper mulberry
are wild plants,
yet they grow in the court;
perhaps the state will perish?"
Wǔ Dīng was terrified,
corrected his person and cultivated his conduct,
reflecting on the government of the former kings.
He restored destroyed states,
continued extinguished lineages,
promoted secluded talents,
and clarified the way of caring for the elderly.
After three years,
sixteen states from among the Mán and Yí paid court through multiple translations.
This is what is meant by a ruler who preserves the perishing and continues the extinguished;
for this reason, he was lofty and respected.
1.28 When Sòng had a great flood,
the people of Lǔ condoled with them,
saying:
"Heaven has sent down excessive rain,
the valleys are full and overflowing,
extending even to your land,
thus worrying those in government;
our ruler has sent his servant to respectfully condole."
The people of Sòng responded, saying:
"I am not talented;
my fasting was not diligent,
the city walls were not repaired,
the people were employed at the wrong time;
Heaven has added calamity,
and also left your ruler with worry;
I humbly acknowledge the honor of your mission."
The Jūnzǐ heard this and said:
"The state of Sòng is nearly there!"
When asked:
"What do you mean?"
He said:
"In the past, Jié of Xià and Zhòu of Yīn would not take responsibility for their faults,
and their downfall was sudden;
Chéng Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ knew how to take responsibility for their faults,
and their rise was abrupt.
To have a fault and correct it
is the same as having no fault.
Therefore it is said:
They are nearly there!"
The people of Sòng heard this,
rose early and slept late,
held court early and retired late,
condoled with the dead and inquired after the sick,
and exerted their strength within the realm.
In three years,
the harvests were bountiful and the government was peaceful.
If the people of Sòng had not heard the words of the Jūnzǐ,
then the grain would not have been bountiful and the state would not have been at peace.
The Shī says:
"Greatly assist in the burden,
show me the manifestation of virtuous conduct."
This is what is meant.
1.29 Chǔ Zhāo Wáng was ill,
and it was divined, saying:
"The Hé is the cause of the curse."
The grandees requested to use the three animal sacrifices for it.
The King said:
"Stop.
In ancient times, the former kings divided the land and established territories;
sacrifices did not exceed the Wàng.
The Jiāng, Hàn, Suī, and Zhāng are the Wàng of Chǔ.
The arrival of calamity or fortune
does not come from beyond these.
Although I am without virtue,
the Hé is not something through which I have earned guilt."
He consequently did not sacrifice to it.
Zhòng Ní heard this and said:
"Zhāo Wáng can be said to know the Great Way;
is it not fitting that he did not lose his state!"
1.30 In the time of Chǔ Zhāo Wáng,
there was a cloud like a red bird
that flew flanking the sun
for three days.
Zhāo Wáng was troubled by it
and sent a person on a relay horse
eastward to ask the Grand Historian Zhōu Lí about it.
Zhōu Lí said:
"It will bring harm to the King's person,
but it can be averted using the Lìng Yǐn and Sī Mǎ."
The Lìng Yǐn and Sī Mǎ heard this,
stayed overnight to fast and bathe,
intending to offer their own persons in prayer.
The King said:
"Stop.
My presence in the state of Chǔ
is like the body having a chest and ribs;
the presence of the Lìng Yǐn and Sī Mǎ
is like the body having legs and arms.
If the chest and ribs have an illness,
and it is transferred to the legs and arms,
how does that remove it from the person?"
1.31 Zhū Wén Gōng divined about moving to Yì.
The scribe said:
"It is beneficial for the people but not beneficial for the ruler."
The ruler said:
"If it is beneficial for the people,
it is a benefit to me.
Heaven produces the common people and establishes a ruler for them
in order to benefit them.
Since the people will benefit,
I must certainly share in it."
An attendant said:
"Your life could be lengthened;
why does my lord not act accordingly?"
The ruler said:
"My mandate lies in shepherding the people;
the length or shortness of life
is a matter of time.
If the people benefit,
what could be more auspicious than that?"
He then moved to Yì.
1.32 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng, seeing that Heaven showed no portents and Earth produced no anomalies,
then prayed to the mountains and rivers, saying:
"Has Heaven perhaps forgotten me?"
This one was able to seek his faults through Heaven
and would certainly not reject remonstrance;
he did not forget danger while in safety,
and thus was able to complete his achievements as a hegemon to the end.
1.33 Tāng said:
“Medicinal food is first tasted by those of humble status,
and only then reaches those of noble status;
medicinal words are first presented to those of noble status,
and only then are heard by those of humble status.”
Therefore, for medicinal food to be tasted by the humble
before reaching the noble
is the rule of instruction;
for medicinal words to be presented to the noble
before being heard by the humble
is the Way.
Thus, if one makes others taste the food
before eating it oneself,
one’s gain of the flavor is great;
but if one makes others ‘taste’ the words
before hearing them oneself,
one’s gain of the words is small.
For this reason, an enlightened superior, regarding words,
must listen to them from others,
must hear them from others,
must select them from others,
must take them from others,
must gather them from others,
must store them from others,
and must act upon them from others.
Therefore, the Way is enlightened when taken through systematic methods,
becomes manifest when acted upon through systematic methods,
and is stored when applied to all things through systematic methods.
For this reason, those who seek the Way
do not use their eyes but their hearts;
those who take hold of the Way do not use their hands but their ears.
1.34 King Wén of Chǔ was ill,
and he told his Dàfū:
“Guǎn Ráo offends me with righteousness
and opposes me with ritual;
when I am with him, I am uneasy,
but when I do not see him, I do not miss him;
however, I have gained much from him.
You must certainly enfeoff him with a noble rank while I am still alive.
Shēn Hóu Bó encourages me in what I desire
and carries out what I enjoy before I even act;
when I am with him, I am at ease,
and when I do not see him, I miss him;
however, I have suffered losses because of him.
You must certainly dismiss him while I am still alive.”
The Dàfū gave their consent.
Thereupon, they enfeoffed Guǎn Ráo as a Dàfū,
and gave gifts to Shēn Hóu Bó and sent him away.
Shēn Hóu Bó was about to go to Zhèng.
The King said:
“You must be cautious!
As a person, you are not benevolent,
yet you desire to control the government of others.
Do not go to Lǔ, Wèi, Sòng, or Zhèng.”
He did not listen
and eventually went to Zhèng.
After three years, he obtained control of the government of Zhèng,
but five months later, the people of Zhèng killed him.
1.35 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ was traveling with Luán Jī
and was about to drown him in the river,
saying:
“I used to like music and women,
and Luán Jī brought them to me;
I used to like palaces, halls, and terraces,
and Luán Jī built them for me;
I used to like fine horses and good charioteering,
and Luán Jī sought them for me.
Now I have liked worthy scholars for six years,
yet Luán Jī has never introduced a single person.
This is to advance my faults and dismiss my goodness.”
1.36 Someone said to Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ:
“My Lord, why do you not change?”
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“Alright.”
Those on his left and right said:
“The Lord has committed no fault,
so why change?”
The Lord said:
“I said ‘Alright’
not because there was necessarily a fault,
but because I intend to seek it so as to encourage those who come to remonstrate.
If I reject him now,
that would be rejecting those who remonstrate;
if the remonstrators stop,
there will not be a day without my committing faults.”
1.37 Hán Wǔ Zǐ was hunting;
the beasts had already been gathered,
and the hunting chariots were assembled.
A messenger arrived to announce:
“The Duke of Jìn has died.”
Wǔ Zǐ said to Luán Huái Zǐ:
“You also know how I love hunting;
the beasts are already gathered,
and the hunting chariots are assembled.
May I finish the hunt before going to offer my condolences?”
Huái Zǐ replied:
“The fall of the Fàn clan
was because they had many who assisted their errors and few who opposed them.
Now, I am to you, my Lord,
one who assists.
Lěi is to you, my Lord,
one who opposes.
Why do you not ask Lěi?”
Wǔ Zǐ said:
“Yíng, do you wish to oppose me?
You have already opposed me,
so why is Lěi necessary?”
He then abandoned the hunt.
1.38 Shī Jīng was playing the zither
while Marquis Wén of Wèi rose to dance,
chanting:
“May my words never meet with opposition.”
Shī Jīng grabbed his zither and struck Marquis Wén with it;
he missed,
but hit the crown tassels,
shattering them.
Marquis Wén looked back and said to his attendants:
“As a subject, to strike his ruler—
what is the crime?”
The attendants said:
“The crime warrants being boiled alive.”
They dragged Shī Jīng down one step from the hall.
Shī Jīng said:
“May your subject be allowed one word before I die?”
Marquis Wén said:
“You may.”
Shī Jīng said:
“In the past, when Yáo and Shùn were rulers,
they only feared that their words would not be opposed;
when Jié and Zhòu were rulers,
they only feared that their words would be opposed.
Your subject was striking Jié and Zhòu,
not striking my Lord.”
Marquis Wén said:
“Release him,
for this is my own fault.
Hang the zither upon the city gate
to serve as a sign for me;
and do not repair the tassels,
to serve as a warning for me.”
1.39 Duke Jǐng of Qí was traveling in Lóu
when he heard that Yàn Zǐ had died.
The Duke took a courier carriage in plain mourning clothes and drove it himself,
and thinking it too slow,
he got down from the carriage and ran.
Realizing he was not as fast as the carriage,
he got back in.
By the time he reached the capital,
he had gotten down four times to run,
weeping as he went.
When he arrived,
he fell over the body and wailed:
“Master Dàfū, day and night you corrected me,
not missing even an inch.
I was still dissolute and did not reform,
and resentment and guilt accumulated heavily among the common people.
Now Heaven has brought disaster upon the state of Qí,
not visiting it upon me, but upon you.
The altars of the state of Qí are in peril,
and to whom shall the common people turn now!”
1.40 Seventeen years after Yàn Zǐ had passed away,
Duke Jǐng was drinking wine with various Dàfū.
The Duke shot an arrow and missed the target,
yet those in the hall shouted “Well done!”
as if with one voice.
The Duke changed color and sighed,
putting aside his bow and arrows.
Xuán Zhāng entered,
and the Duke said:
“Zhāng!
Since I lost Yàn Zǐ seventeen years ago,
I have never heard of my failings.
Now I shot and missed the target,
yet those shouting ‘Well done’ were as if with one voice.”
Xuán Zhāng replied:
“This is the unworthiness of these ministers.
Their wisdom is insufficient to recognize Your Lordship’s failings,
and their courage is insufficient to offend Your Lordship’s countenance.
However, there is one thing.
Your subject has heard it said:
"If the ruler likes something,
then the ministers will wear it;
if the ruler craves something,
then the ministers will eat it."
Now, the inchworm eats yellow and its body becomes yellow;
it eats green and its body becomes green.
Does the ruler still have the words of sycophants?
The Duke said:
"Good.
With today's words,
Xián Zhāng acts as the ruler,
and I act as the minister."
At this time, people from the sea brought in fish,
and the Duke bestowed fifty carriage-loads upon Xián Zhāng.
When Xián Zhāng returned,
the carriages of fish blocked the road;
he patted the hand of his driver and said:
"Those who sang 'Good!' earlier
all wanted to be like these fish.
In the past, Yàn Zǐ refused rewards to correct the ruler,
and thus his faults were not concealed.
Now the various ministers use flattery to seek profit,
so they present their pledges and sing 'Good!'
as if from a single mouth.
Now, the support I have given the ruler has not yet been seen by the masses,
yet I receive fish like these;
this is to turn against the righteousness of Yàn Zǐ and follow the desires of flattery."
He firmly refused the fish and did not accept them.
The gentleman said:
"The integrity of Xián Zhāng
was the legacy of Yàn Zǐ's conduct."
1.41 When Heaven gives birth to people,
it is surely not for the sake of the ruler;
when Heaven establishes a ruler,
it is surely not for the sake of the position.
Now, being a ruler of men,
to follow one's private desires and not care for one's people
is to not uphold the will of Heaven
and to forget why the position is suitable for service.
For one like this,
the Chūn Qiū does not grant him the status of a ruler and treats him as a barbarian.
The Earl of Zhèng (Zhèng Bó) hated one person and thus abandoned his entire army,
therefore there is the phrase, "Barbarians do not act as rulers."
If the ruler of men does not reflect upon himself with this,
and has already lost his true heart,
how would he know it?
Therefore it is said:
"One who possesses a state cannot but study the Chūn Qiū."
This is what it refers to.
1.42 A person of Qí assassinated their ruler.
Lǔ Xiāng Gōng grasped a halberd and rose up, saying:
"What minister would dare to kill his ruler?"
Shī Jù said:
"Now, the ruler of Qí was unable to govern them
and employed unworthy people;
he indulged the desires of one man
to oppress the nature of ten thousand men.
This is not the way to establish a ruler.
That his person died
was of his own making.
Now your lordship does not love the lives of ten thousand men
but is pained by the death of one man;
how is that not an error?
His ministers were already without the Way,
and their ruler was also not worth pitying."
1.43 Kǒng Zǐ said:
"Wén Wáng is like the 'first year,'
Wǔ Wáng is like 'spring of the king,'
Zhōu Gōng is like the 'first month.'
Wén Wáng had Wáng Jì as his father,
Tài Rèn as his mother,
Tài Sì as his consort,
Wǔ Wáng and Zhōu Gōng as his sons,
and Tài Diān and Hóng Yǎo as his ministers;
his foundation was beautiful.
Wǔ Wáng rectified his person to rectify his state,
and rectified his state to rectify the world.
He attacked the wayless
and punished the guilty;
with one movement, the world was rectified,
his deeds were correct.
When spring attains its season,
all things come to life;
when a ruler attains his Way,
all ten thousand people attain order.
Zhōu Gōng carried himself and the world followed him;
his sincerity was ultimate."
1.44 Those who honor the ruler and demean the minister
do so by using power to command them;
if the power is lost, then authority collapses.
Therefore, if the Son of Heaven loses the Way,
then the feudal lords become honored;
if the feudal lords lose their governance,
then the grandees rise up;
if the grandees lose their office,
then the common people flourish.
Viewing it from this,
it has never occurred that the superior does not lose
while the inferior gains.
1.45 Kǒng Zǐ said:
"If the Way of Xià had not perished,
the virtue of Shāng would not have arisen;
if the virtue of Shāng had not perished,
the virtue of Zhōu would not have arisen;
if the virtue of Zhōu had not perished,
the Chūn Qiū would not have been created.
Only after the Chūn Qiū was created did the gentleman know that the Way of Zhōu had perished."
Therefore, superiors and inferiors undermining each other
is like water and fire extinguishing each other.
A ruler of men cannot but examine this and not let his ministers become overly powerful;
this is for private houses to flourish while the public house is destroyed.
If the ruler of men does not examine this,
then the state will be in danger.
Guǎn Zǐ said:
"Authority cannot be placed in two places;
governance cannot come from two gates."
Therefore it is said:
"If the shin is larger than the thigh, it is difficult to walk;
if the fingers are larger than the arm, it is difficult to grasp."
If the root is small and the tip is large,
they cannot command each other.
1.46 Sī Chéng Zǐ Hǎn was Chancellor of Sòng
and said to the Ruler of Sòng:
"The danger or stability of the state,
and the order or chaos of the people,
lie in the ruler’s exercise of rewards and punishments.
When rewards are appropriate, worthy people are encouraged;
when punishments are correct, wicked people are stopped.
When rewards and punishments are not appropriate,
then worthy people are not encouraged,
and wicked people are not stopped.
The wicked and evil will form cliques,
deceiving those above and blinding the master
to compete for rank and emolument;
one must be cautious.
Now, rewards, gifts, yielding, and giving
are what people like;
let the ruler carry these out himself.
Punishments, penalties, and executions
are what people dislike;
I request that your minister take charge of them."
The Ruler said:
"Good.
You shall be in charge of the disliked,
and I will carry out the liked;
I know I will not be laughed at by the feudal lords."
Thereupon the Ruler of Sòng carried out rewards and gifts, while Zǐ Hǎn was given the administration of punishments and penalties.
The people of the state knew that the awe of punishment and execution
rested solely with Zǐ Hǎn;
the high ministers were close to him,
and the common people were attached to him.
Before a year had passed,
Zǐ Hǎn expelled his ruler and monopolized the government.
Therefore it is said:
"Do not have a weak ruler and a strong grandee."
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"Fish cannot leave the deep pool;
the sharp tools of a state
cannot be lent to others."
This is what it refers to.
2.1 The art of a minister
involves following orders and reporting back on their execution,
not daring to act solely on one’s own authority,
being righteous and not conforming blindly,
and not seeking status for its own sake.
He must definitely benefit the state
and must definitely be of assistance to the ruler;
thus, his own person is honored and his descendants preserve his legacy.
Therefore, the conduct of a minister includes the Six Positives (*Liù Zhèng*) and the Six Negatives (*Liù Xié*).
Practicing the Six Positives leads to glory,
while committing the Six Negatives leads to disgrace.
Indeed, glory and disgrace
are the gateways to disaster and fortune.
What are the Six Positives and the Six Negatives?
The Six Positives are:
First, when the sprouts of change have not yet moved
and signs have not yet appeared,
to clearly and uniquely perceive the omens of survival or ruin
and the essentials of gain or loss,
taking preventive measures before things occur
so that the ruler stands loftily in a position of manifest glory
and the whole world praises his filial piety—
one who acts like this is a *Shèngchén* (Sage Minister);
Second, to empty the mind and clarify one's intentions,
to promote the good and open the way for the Way,
to encourage the ruler through ritual and righteousness,
to explain long-term strategies to the ruler,
following along with his excellences
while correcting and saving him from his faults,
so that when success is achieved and tasks are established,
the credit for the good is attributed to the ruler
and he does not dare to boast of his own labors—
one who acts like this is a *Liángchén* (Good Minister);
Third, to humble one’s person and body,
rising early and retiring late,
tirelessly recommending the worthy,
frequently citing the deeds of antiquity
to inspire the ruler's intent,
hoping to be of some benefit
in order to bring peace to the state and its ancestral altars—
one who acts like this is a *Zhōngchén* (Loyal Minister);
Fourth, to observe clearly and see into the obscure,
perceiving success and failure,
preventing and remedying issues early,
guiding the ruler back to the right path,
closing the gaps
and cutting off the source of trouble,
turning disaster into fortune
so the ruler is ultimately without worry—
one who acts like this is a *Zhìchén* (Wise Minister);
Fifth, to uphold the statutes and honor the law,
performing the duties of his office,
declining salaries and refusing rewards,
not accepting gifts or bribes,
keeping his clothing neat and orderly,
and being frugal in food and drink—
one who acts like this is a *Zhēnchén* (Pure Minister);
Sixth, when the state is in confusion and chaos
and others do not offer remonstrance,
yet he dares to brave the ruler’s stern countenance,
speaking face-to-face of the ruler's faults,
not shrinking from execution,
so that through his death the state is at peace
and he does not regret his actions—
one who acts like this is a *Zhíchén* (Straightforward Minister).
These are the Six Positives.
The Six Negatives are:
First, to be content in office and greedy for salary,
managing for the benefit of one's private family
without attending to public affairs,
concealing his wisdom
and hiding his abilities,
while the ruler is starved for discourse
and thirsty for strategy,
yet he is still unwilling to give his full devotion,
complacently drifting along with the world,
looking around at those on his left and right—
one who acts like this is a *Jùchén* (Caretaker Minister);
Second, whatever the ruler says, he calls good,
and whatever the ruler does, he calls acceptable,
secretly seeking out what the ruler likes and presenting it
to gratify the ruler's eyes and ears,
ingratiating himself and compromising his character,
joining the ruler in pleasures
without regard for future harm—
one who acts like this is a *Yúchén* (Flattering Minister);
Third, to be internally crooked and dangerous
while appearing cautious on the outside,
using clever words and an ingratiating expression,
while also being jealous of the worthy in his heart,
emphasizing the virtues and hiding the faults of those he wishes to promote,
while emphasizing the mistakes and concealing the virtues of those he wishes to demote,
causing the ruler to act recklessly and grant excessive appointments,
making rewards and punishments inappropriate
and causing orders not to be carried out—
one who acts like this is a *Jiānchén* (Treacherous Minister);
Fourth, to have wisdom enough to embellish wrongs
and eloquence enough to carry out his persuasion,
turning words around and changing language to create elaborate arguments,
internally alienating the ruler from his own kin
and externally creating jealousy and chaos in the court—
one who acts like this is a *Chánchén* (Slandering Minister);
Fifth, to monopolize power and seize influence,
manipulating state affairs to make them seem heavy or light,
forming factions within his private gates to enrich his family,
further increasing his own power and prestige,
and arrogantly forging the ruler's commands to elevate himself—
one who acts like this is a *Zéichén* (Traitorous Minister);
Sixth, to flatter the ruler with evil
and plunge the ruler into unrighteousness,
forming cliques and conspiring
to obscure the ruler's clarity,
using eloquent and fine words when inside the court
but changing his speech once outside,
making no distinction between white and black
and leaving no gap between right and wrong,
waiting for the right moment to advance his agenda
and attaching himself accordingly,
causing the ruler's bad reputation to spread throughout the borders
and be heard by all neighbors—
one who acts like this is a *Wángguó zhī chén* (Minister Who Ruins the State).
These are the Six Negatives.
A worthy minister stays on the path of the Six Positives
and does not practice the arts of the Six Negatives;
thus, those above are at peace and those below are well-ordered;
in life, he is happy,
and in death, he is remembered with affection;
this is the art of the minister.
2.2 *Tāng* asked *Yī Yǐn*:
"How do the *Sāngōng*, *Jiǔqīng*, *Dàfū*, and *Lièshì* differ from one another?"
*Yī Yǐn* replied:
"As for the *Sāngōng*,
their wisdom reaches to the Great Way,
they respond to changes without reaching an end,
they are discerning about the nature of all things,
and they are conversant with the Way of Heaven.
Their words are sufficient to harmonize *Yīn* and *Yáng*,
correct the four seasons,
and regulate the wind and rain;
one who is like this
is elevated to be a *Sāngōng*.
Therefore, the affairs of the *Sāngōng*
constantly reside in the Way.
As for the *Jiǔqīng*,
they do not miss the four seasons,
they open canals and channels,
repair dikes and embankments,
plant trees,
and improve the five grains;
they are conversant with the principles of the earth (*dìlǐ*).
They know what can and cannot pass through,
and what can and cannot be beneficial;
one who is like this
is elevated to be a *Jiǔqīng*.
Therefore, the affairs of the *Jiǔqīng*
constantly reside in *Dé*.
As for the *Dàfū*,
they go out and come in among the people,
taking and giving in common benefit with the people;
they are conversant with human affairs,
their conduct is like following a plumb line,
they do not cause harm through their speech,
and when they speak to the world,
it does not bring harm to themselves;
they keep the mountain passes and bridges open
and keep the treasuries and storehouses full;
one who is like this
is elevated to be a *Dàfū*.
Therefore, the affairs of the *Dàfū*
constantly reside in *Rén*.
As for the *Lièshì*,
they know righteousness and do not lose their heart,
they perform deeds without monopolizing the rewards,
they are loyal and upright in strong remonstrance without being treacherous,
they cast aside private interest to establish the public good and their words follow the standards of the law;
one who is like this
is elevated to be a *Lièshì*.
Therefore, the affairs of the *Lièshì*
constantly reside in *Yì*.
Thus, when the Way, *Dé*, *Rén*, and *Yì* are established, the world is correct.
In all these four cases,
an enlightened king treats them as ministers but does not treat them as subordinates. "
*Tāng* said:
"What does 'treats them as ministers but not as subordinates' mean?"
*Yī Yǐn* replied:
"There are four whom a ruler does not address as subordinates:
paternal uncles
are treated as ministers but not addressed as subordinates;
elder brothers
are treated as ministers but not addressed as subordinates;
the ministers of former kings
are treated as ministers but not addressed as subordinates;
and scholars of great virtue
are treated as ministers but not addressed as subordinates.
This is what is called the Great Accord (*Dàshùn*)."
2.3 Tāng asked Yī Yǐn:
“In ancient times, why were the Sān Gōng, Jiǔ Qīng, Dà Fū, and Liè Shì established?”
Yī Yǐn replied:
“The Sān Gōng
are for coordinating the five matters;
the Jiǔ Qīng
are for coordinating with the Sān Gōng;
the Dà Fū
are for coordinating with the Jiǔ Qīng;
the Liè Shì
are for coordinating with the Dà Fū.
Thus, there is coordination upon coordination;
this is called the Shì Zōng.
If the Shì Zōng is not lost,
the internal and external will be as one.”
2.4 Zǐ Gòng asked Kǒng Zǐ:
“Among the ministers of today, who is worthy?”
Kǒng Zǐ said:
“I do not know yet.
In the past,
Qí had Bào Shū,
and Zhèng had Zǐ Pí;
they were worthy men.”
Zǐ Gòng said:
“Is it then that Qí had no Guǎn Zhòng
and Zhèng had no Zǐ Chǎn?”
Kǒng Zǐ said:
“Cì,
you only know one side,
but do not know the other.
Have you heard that recommending the worthy makes one worthy,
or that exerting one's effort makes one worthy?”
Zǐ Gòng said:
“Recommending the worthy makes one worthy.”
Kǒng Zǐ said:
“Indeed.
I have heard of Bào Shū recommending Guǎn Zhòng;
I have heard of Zǐ Pí recommending Zǐ Chǎn.
I have not heard of Guǎn Zhòng or Zǐ Chǎn having recommended anyone.”
2.5 Wèi Wén Hóu was about to appoint a Xiàng.
He summoned Lǐ Kè and asked him,
saying:
“I am going to appoint a Xiàng,
choosing between Jì Chéng Zǐ and Zhái Chù.
Which one is it appropriate for me to appoint?”
Lǐ Kè said:
“I have heard
that the lowly do not counsel the noble,
outsiders do not counsel those within,
and the distant do not counsel the close.
I am distant and lowly;
I do not dare to receive your command.”
Wén Hóu said:
“This is an affair of state;
I wish to face the matter with you, so do not decline.”
Lǐ Kè said:
“It is because my Lord does not observe closely;
the answer can be known.
In nobility, look at whom they recommend;
in wealth, look at whom they give to;
in poverty, look at what they do not take;
in hardship, look at what they do not do.
Observing from this,
it can be known.”
Wén Hóu said:
“You may retire.
My Xiàng is decided.”
Lǐ Kè went out
and met Zhái Huáng.
Zhái Huáng asked:
“I heard the Lord asked you about the Xiàng;
who, after all, will it be?”
Lǐ Kè said:
“Jì Chéng Zǐ will be it.”
Zhái Huáng changed color in displeasure and said:
“I am disappointed in you.”
Lǐ Kè said:
“Why are you so suddenly disappointed in me?
When you spoke of me to your Lord,
was it to form a clique with me to seek high office?
When the Lord asked me about the Xiàng,
I replied:
‘It is because my Lord does not observe closely.
In nobility, look at whom they recommend;
in wealth, look at whom they give to;
in poverty, look at what they do not take;
in hardship, look at what they do not do.
Observing from this,
it can be known.’
The Lord said:
‘You may retire.
My Xiàng is decided.’
By this, I know Jì Chéng Zǐ will be the Xiàng.”
Zhái Huáng said unhappily:
“Why should I not be the Xiàng?
The Governor of Xī Hé
was appointed by me;
the Nèi Shǐ who handles matters
was appointed by me.
When the King wanted to attack Zhòng Shān,
I recommended Lè Yáng;
when there was no official to govern it,
I recommended you;
when there was no one to tutor his son,
I recommended Qū Hóu Fù.
How am I inferior to Jì Chéng Zǐ?”
Lǐ Kè said:
“You are not as good as Jì Chéng Zǐ.
Jì Chéng Zǐ received a fief of a thousand zhōng;
nine-tenths he spent on those outside and one-tenth on his own household,
using it to engage the scholars of the world.
Thus, to the east, he obtained Bǔ Zǐ Xià, Tián Zǐ Fāng, and Duàn Gàn Mù.
Those whom he recommended
are teachers to the ruler.
Those whom you recommended
are merely talents for ministers.”
Zhái Huáng was startled and ashamed, saying:
“I was wrong in my response to you;
I beg to cultivate myself and then learn from you.”
Before he had finished speaking,
the attendants announced that Jì Chéng Zǐ had been appointed as Xiàng.
Thereupon, Zhái Huáng fell silent and changed expression,
feeling internal shame,
and did not dare go out for three months.
2.6 The Lìng Yǐn of Chǔ died.
Jǐng Gōng met Chéng Gōng Qián and said:
“To whom will the post of Lìng Yǐn go?”
Chéng Gōng Qián said:
“Probably to Qū Chūn?”
Jǐng Gōng said angrily:
“The people of the state think it will go to me.”
Chéng Gōng Qián said:
“Your resources are few,
while Qū Chūn’s resources are many.
By the standards of duty, he has taken on the greatest worries of the world,
yet you treat him as a mere friend.
The singing crane and the straw dog have very little knowledge,
yet you toy with them.
Chī Yí Zǐ Pí attends daily upon Qū Chūn,
and Sǔn Pō is his friend.
The wisdom of these two men
is enough to serve as Lìng Yǐn,
yet they do not dare monopolize their own wisdom but entrust it to Qū Chūn.
Therefore, I say:
‘Will the government not go to Qū Chūn?’”
2.7 Tián Zǐfāng was crossing the Xīhé
to visit Zhái Huáng.
Zhái Huáng was riding in a grand chariot
with a flowery canopy
and golden bridles;
the floor mats were secured with weights.
Of such
teams of four horses, there were eighty.
Zǐfāng watched him from afar
and suspected him to be a sovereign.
The road was narrow,
so he got down and waited by the side of his chariot.
When Zhái Huáng arrived and saw Zǐfāng,
he got down from his chariot and hurried toward him,
casting himself downwind,
and said:
"It is Chù."
Tián Zǐfāng said:
"Is it you!
Previously when I watched you from afar,
I suspected you were a sovereign.
Now that you have arrived, you are but a subject.
How did you come to reach this state?"
Zhái Huáng replied:
"These are all things the Lord bestowed upon his servant;
having accumulated them for thirty years,
they have thus reached this level.
At a time of leisure,
I was making an offering in the open wilds
when I happened to meet you, Sir."
Zǐfāng said:
"Why has the Lord bestowed such a wealth of chariots and carriages upon you?"
Zhái Huáng replied:
"In the past, Xīhé had no defender;
I recommended Wú Qǐ, and the regions beyond Xīhé became peaceful.
Yè had no magistrate;
I recommended Xīmén Bào, and Wèi had no trouble from Zhào.
Suānzǎo had no magistrate;
I recommended Běimén Kě, and Wèi had no worry from Qí.
Wèi wished to attack Zhōngshān;
I recommended Lè Yáng, and Zhōngshān was captured.
Wèi had no official to govern it;
I recommended Lǐ Kè, and the state of Wèi became well-ordered.
Because I recommended these five great officers,
my rank and salary were doubled,
and for this reason I have reached this state."
Zǐfāng said:
"Very well,
you should exert yourself!
The position of Chancellor of the state of Wèi
will not pass you by for another."
Zhái Huáng replied:
"Among the Lord’s younger brothers by the same mother, there is Gōngsūn Jìchéng,
who recommended Zǐxià and the Lord took him as a teacher;
he recommended Duàngàn Mù and the Lord took him as a friend;
he recommended you, Sir, and the Lord respects you.
Those whom he recommended are teachers, friends, and those held in respect.
Those whom I recommended
are all officials who maintain their duties and salaries.
How could I reach the position of Chancellor of the state of Wèi?"
Zǐfāng said:
"I have heard that one who is worthy is worthy,
and one who can recommend the worthy is also worthy.
All five you recommended are worthy;
you should exert yourself,
and you will surely be next."
2.8 King Wēi of Qí was traveling at Yáotái,
when Chénghóu Qìng came to report matters,
followed by a very large number of chariots and riders in formation.
The King watched him from afar
and said to his attendants:
"Who is the one coming?"
The attendants said:
"It is Chénghóu Qìng."
The King said:
"The state is extremely poor,
so why does he go out with such splendor?"
The attendants said:
"Those who give to others have a way to hold them accountable;
those who receive from others have a way to exchange for it.
Your Majesty should try asking for his explanation."
Chénghóu Qìng arrived,
presented himself and said:
"It is Jì."
The King did not respond.
He said again:
"It is Jì."
The King did not respond.
He said again:
"It is Jì."
The King said:
"The state is extremely poor,
so why do you go out with such splendor?"
Chénghóu Qìng said:
"Forgive my capital offense,
and allow your servant to state his explanation."
The King said:
"Granted."
He replied:
"Jì recommended Tián Jūzǐ for Xīhé, and Qín and Liáng became weak;
Jì recommended Tián Jiězǐ for Nánchéng, and the people of Chǔ brought silks and brocades to pay court;
Jì recommended Qián Zhuózǐ for Míngzhōu, and the people of Yān provided livestock,
and the people of Zhào provided grain;
Jì recommended Tián Zhòngshǒuzǐ for Jímò, and Qí became fully sufficient;
Jì recommended Běiguō Diāobózǐ as a Great Officer, and the nine branches of the royal clan became more intimate,
while the people became wealthier.
Having recommended these several fine men,
Your Majesty may simply rest your head and sleep;
why worry about the state being poor?"
2.9 Duke Mù of Qín sent a merchant to transport salt to Wèi.
He levied it from various merchants.
A merchant bought Bǎilǐ Xī for the price of five black ram skins
and had him drive a cart to Qín.
Duke Mù of Qín inspected the salt
and saw that Bǎilǐ Xī’s oxen were fat.
He said:
"The load was heavy, the road was long, and the terrain was treacherous,
so why are the oxen fat?"
He replied:
"Your servant fed and watered them at the proper times
and used them without violence.
When there was a dangerous spot,
I personally preceded or followed them;
therefore they are fat."
Duke Mù knew he was a man of noble character.
He ordered the officials to prepare a bath, clothes, and a cap, and sat with him.
The Duke was greatly pleased.
On another day, he discussed politics with Gōngsūn Zhī.
Gōngsūn Zhī was very uneasy
and said:
"Your Majesty’s ears and eyes are sharp,
and your thoughts are careful and discerning.
Could it be that Your Majesty has found a sage?"
The Duke said:
"Indeed.
I am pleased with the words of that man Xī;
he is like a sage."
Gōngsūn Zhī then returned home, took a goose to offer congratulations,
and said:
"Your Majesty has gained a minister for the altars of grain and soil;
I dare to congratulate you on the fortune of the state."
The Duke did not decline
and received it with two bows.
The next day,
Gōngsūn Zhī then resigned from his position as High Minister to yield it to Bǎilǐ Xī,
saying:
"The state of Qín is in a remote location,
and the people are rustic, ignorant, and without knowledge;
this is the root of danger and ruin.
I know myself that I am not sufficient to occupy a superior position,
and I ask to yield it to him."
The Duke did not permit it.
Gōngsūn Zhī said:
"That Your Majesty has gained a sage minister for the state without using a guest counselor
is Your Majesty’s blessing.
That I see a worthy man and yield to him
is my blessing.
Now that Your Majesty has already received your blessing,
yet you make me lose my blessing,
is that acceptable?
I request to complete the resignation."
The Duke did not permit it.
Gōngsūn Zhī said:
"For me to be unworthy and yet occupy a high position
means Your Majesty has lost the proper order.
Being unworthy and losing order
is my fault.
Promoting the worthy and demoting the unworthy
is Your Majesty’s wisdom.
If I now occupy the position,
it would nullify Your Majesty’s virtue and go against my own conduct;
I shall flee."
The Duke then accepted it.
Thus Bǎilǐ Xī became the High Minister to govern the state,
and Gōngsūn Zhī became the Secondary Minister to assist him.
2.10 Viscount Jiǎn of Zhào was traveling from Jìnyáng to Hándān.
He stopped in the middle of the road.
An officer in charge of the chariots came forward to ask:
"Why has my lord stopped?"
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
"Dǒng Ānyú is behind."
An officer said:
"This is a matter concerning the three armies;
why does my lord delay the three armies for the sake of one man?"
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
"Very well."
He drove a hundred paces and stopped again.
The officer was about to come forward and remonstrate,
when Dǒng Ānyú arrived just then.
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
"The road from Qín that connects with the state of Jìn,
I forgot to order people to block it."
Dǒng Ānyú said:
"This is why I stayed behind."
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
"The precious jades of the office,
I forgot to order people to load them."
He replied:
"This is why I stayed behind."
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
"The Xíngrén Zhú Guò is of advanced age,
and his words have never failed to be a model for the state of Jìn;
in my departure, I forgot to order people to bid him farewell and present gifts."
He replied:
"This is why I stayed behind."
Jiǎn Zhǔ can be said to have reflected inwardly and known others outwardly!
Therefore, his person was at ease and his state was secure.
The Yùshǐ Dàfū Zhōu Chāng said:
"If a ruler of men could truly be like Zhào Jiǎn Zhǔ,
the court would not be in danger."
2.11 Yàn Zǐ was attending Jǐng Gōng,
and the morning was cold.
The Duke said:
"Please bring in hot food."
He replied:
"Yīng is not Your Lordship’s kitchen servant;
I dare to decline."
The Duke said:
"Please bring in fur robes."
He replied:
"Yīng is not Your Lordship’s official of the fields and marshes;
I dare to decline."
The Duke said:
"Then what is the Master to me?"
He replied:
"I am a minister of the altars of soil and grain."
The Duke said:
"What is meant by a minister of the altars of soil and grain?"
He replied:
"A minister of the altars of soil and grain
is able to establish the state,
distinguish the appropriateness of those above and below,
ensuring they obtain their proper principles;
regulate the order of the hundred officials,
ensuring they obtain their proper places;
and formulate diplomatic rhetoric
that can be distributed to the four quarters."
From this time onward,
if the ruler did not act according to ritual,
he would not see Yàn Zǐ.
2.12 The Marquis of Qí asked Yàn Zǐ:
"When a loyal minister serves his ruler,
what is it like?"
He replied:
"If there is disaster, he does not die for him;
if the ruler goes into exile, he does not see him off."
The ruler said:
"I divide land to enfeoff him,
and grant him rank to make him noble;
yet if the ruler has disaster and he does not die,
and if the ruler goes into exile and he does not see him off,
can he be called loyal?"
He replied:
"If his words are used,
the ruler will have no disaster throughout his life,
so why should the minister die?
If his remonstrance is followed,
the ruler will not go into exile throughout his life,
so why should the minister see him off?
If his words are not used
and he dies when disaster strikes,
that is to die in vain;
if his remonstrance is not followed
and he sees the ruler off into exile,
that is to act hypocritically.
Therefore, a loyal minister is one who can offer goodness to his ruler,
and cannot fall into disaster together with his ruler."
2.13 Yàn Zǐ went to court,
riding in a broken carriage
and driving a weak horse.
Jǐng Gōng saw him and said:
"Alas,
is the Master's salary so meager?
Why do you ride in such an extremely unattractive manner!"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Relying on my Lord's gifts,
I have been able to provide for my three clans, and my friends throughout the state are all able to live.
I have warm clothes and enough food;
a broken carriage and a weak horse
to serve my person
are sufficient for me."
When Yàn Zǐ left,
the Duke sent Liángqiū Jù to present him with a grand carriage and a team of horses;
three times he returned them and would not accept.
The Duke was not pleased.
He quickly summoned Yàn Zǐ.
When Yàn Zǐ arrived,
the Duke said:
"If the Master does not accept them,
I too will not ride mine."
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"My Lord has me oversee the various officials;
I limit my maintenance in clothing, food, and drink
to set an example for the people of the state of Qí,
yet I still fear they will be extravagant and disregard their conduct.
Now if there is a grand carriage and a team of horses,
and my Lord rides them above,
and I also ride them below,
then the people will lack righteousness;
if they are extravagant in their clothing and food and disregard their conduct,
I will have no way to forbid it."
He then declined and would not accept.
2.14 Jǐng Gōng was drinking wine,
and Chén Huánzǐ was in attendance.
Seeing Yànzǐ from afar,
he spoke again to the Duke, saying:
"Please impose a penalty cup on Yànzǐ."
The Duke said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"Yànzǐ wears clothes of black hemp,
a coat of deer skin,
drives a carriage with a simple frame,
and harnesses a poor horse to come to court.
This is to conceal the gifts of the ruler."
The Duke said:
"Granted."
The cupbearer presented the goblet and stepped forward,
saying:
"The ruler orders you to drink this penalty cup."
Yànzǐ asked:
"For what reason?"
Chén Huánzǐ said:
"The ruler has granted you the rank of a high official to honor your person,
and favored you with a million in wealth to enrich your family.
Among the various ministers, no one’s rank is more honorable than yours,
and no one’s stipend is more generous than yours.
Now you wear clothes of black hemp,
a coat of deer skin,
drive a carriage with a simple frame,
and harness a poor horse to come to court.
This is to conceal the gifts of the ruler,
and therefore we impose the penalty cup on you."
Yànzǐ left his mat and said:
"May I explain after I drink,
or should I explain before I drink?"
The Duke said:
"Explain first, then drink."
Yànzǐ said:
"The ruler granted me the rank of a high official to make my person distinguished.
I, Yīng, did not dare to accept it for the sake of distinction,
but rather to carry out the ruler’s commands.
He favored me with a million in wealth
to enrich my family.
I, Yīng, did not dare to accept it for the sake of wealth,
but rather to manifest the ruler’s generosity.
I have heard that under the wise rulers of old,
if a minister received generous gifts but did not look after his kin and countrymen,
then he was faulted;
if he faced his duties and maintained his office
but was not equal to his responsibilities,
then he was faulted.
If among the ruler’s domestic servants
or the minister’s fathers and brothers,
there were those dispersed in the wild or the countryside,
this would be my crime.
If among the ruler’s external servants
or those under the minister’s charge,
there were those wandering or lost in the four directions,
this would be my crime.
If the weapons and armor were not complete
or the war chariots were not maintained,
this would be my crime.
As for coming to court with a worn carriage and a poor horse,
I think this is not my crime.
Furthermore, using the ruler’s gifts,
among my father’s kin, none is without a carriage to ride;
among my mother’s kin, none is lacking in food or clothing;
among my wife’s kin, none suffers from cold or hunger.
Among the neglected scholars of the state, several hundred households wait for me to provide before they light their fires.
Is doing this concealing the ruler’s gifts,
or is it making the ruler’s gifts manifest?"
The Duke said:
"Well said!
Impose the penalty cup on Wúyǔ for me instead."
2.15 Yànzǐ was just eating
when the ruler’s messenger arrived.
He shared his food and ate with him,
but the messenger was not full, and Yànzǐ was not full either.
The messenger returned
and told Jǐng Gōng about it.
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Alas!
That the Master’s family
is poor to such an extent!
I did not know it;
this is my fault."
He ordered the officials to grant Yànzǐ a district of a thousand households.
Yànzǐ bowed twice and declined,
saying:
"My family is not poor.
Because of the ruler’s gifts,
my bounty covers three generations of kin
and extends to my friends,
and I use it to assist the common people.
The ruler’s gifts are already generous!
My family is not poor.
I have heard that
to take generously from the ruler
and give generously to others
is to act as the ruler in the ruler’s stead;
a loyal minister does not do this.
To take generously from the ruler and store it away
is to keep it in baskets and chests;
a benevolent person does not do this.
To take generously from the ruler and have nowhere to bestow it,
so that when one dies the wealth passes to others,
a wise person does not do this.
I have heard that for one who is a minister,
to promote the ruler's affairs is considered loyalty,
and to restrain oneself when retired is considered integrity.
Cloth of eight shēn
and a single vessel of food
are enough!"
The messenger returned three times,
but in the end Yànzǐ declined and would not accept.
2.16 Chén Chéngzǐ asked Chīyí Zipí:
"What do you take as a constant?"
He replied:
"If the ruler dies, I do not die;
if the ruler flees into exile, I do not go into exile."
Chén Chéngzǐ said:
"In that case, what do you take as a constant?"
He replied:
"Leaving before death can occur,
and leaving before exile can occur—
then how could there be any death or exile?"
2.17 Following orders to benefit the ruler is called compliance.
Following orders to distress the ruler is called flattery.
Opposing orders to benefit the ruler is called loyalty.
Opposing orders to distress the ruler is called rebellion.
When the ruler has faults
and one does not remonstrate or contend,
it will endanger the state
and bring down the altars of the soil and grain.
To be able to speak one's mind fully to the ruler,
staying if the advice is used,
and leaving if it is not used,
is called Remonstrance.
If advice being used means one may live,
and not being used means one must die,
it is called Contention.
To be able to combine wisdom and unite strength,
leading the subordinates to together forcefully correct the ruler,
so that even if the ruler is uneasy,
he cannot but listen,
thereby resolving the great troubles of the state
and removing the great harms of the state,
resulting in the honoring of the ruler and the stability of the state—
this is called Assistance.
To be able to withstand the ruler’s commands,
reverse the ruler’s actions,
and take hold of the ruler’s authority
in order to secure the state from danger,
remove the lord’s disgrace,
and conduct campaigns sufficient to achieve great benefit for the state—
this is called Rectification.
Therefore, people who provide Remonstrance, Contention, Assistance, and Rectification
are the ministers of the soil and grain.
An enlightened ruler treats them with honor and ritual,
while a dark ruler regards them as his own enemies.
Thus, those whom an enlightened ruler rewards
are those whom a dark ruler executes.
An enlightened ruler loves to ask questions;
a dark ruler loves to act alone.
An enlightened ruler promotes the worthy and employs the capable to enjoy their achievements;
a dark ruler fears the worthy and envies the capable, thereby destroying his own legacy.
Punishing his loyal ones and rewarding his enemies—
this is called the ultimate darkness,
and it is why Jié and Zhòu perished.
The Classic of Poetry says:
"None was willing to listen to this,
and so the Great Mandate was overturned."
