This is what it refers to.
2.18 Jiǎn Zǐ had ministers named Yǐn Chuò and Shè Jué.
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Jué loves me;
when he remonstrates with me, it is never in front of the crowd.
Chuò does not love me;
when he remonstrates with me, it must be in front of the crowd."
Yǐn Chuò said:
"Jué loves to protect the ruler's reputation,
but he does not love to correct the ruler’s faults.
I love to correct the ruler’s faults,
but I do not love to protect the ruler’s reputation."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A gentleman indeed is Yǐn Chuò!
He criticizes to the face and does not flatter to the face."
2.19 Gāo Liáo served under Yàn Zǐ;
after three years, he was without fault.
Yàn Zǐ dismissed him,
and his attendants remonstrated, saying:
"Gāo Liáo has served the Master for three years;
you have never even granted him a rank or title, and now you dismiss him—
can this be righteous?"
Yàn Zǐ said:
"I, Yīng,
am a narrow and humble person;
only through the four dimensions of support can I be made straight.
Now, this man has served me for three years,
yet he has never once corrected my errors;
this is why I dismissed him."
2.20 Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"I, Cì, am a subordinate to others,
but I do not yet know the way of being a subordinate."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"As for one who is a subordinate to others,
is he not like the earth?
Plant in it, and the five grains grow there;
dig into it, and sweet springs emerge;
plants and trees are planted there;
birds and beasts are raised there;
the living stand upon it,
and the dead enter into it;
it performs many services but does not speak of them.
One who is a subordinate to others,
is indeed like the earth!"
2.21 Sūn Qīng said:
"The young serving the old,
the lowly serving the noble,
and the unworthy serving the worthy—
these are the universal principles of the world.
If there are those who are noble but cannot lead others,
or are lowly but are ashamed to be subordinates,
this is the heart of a treacherous person.
If the person does not abandon a treacherous heart
and their conduct does not abandon a treacherous path,
yet they seek to be praised by the masses,
is that not indeed difficult?"
2.22 Gōngshū Wénzǐ asked Shǐ Sǒu, saying:
"Wǔzǐ Shèng has served Zhào Jiǎnzǐ for a long time,
and his favor has not slackened;
why is this?"
Shǐ Sǒu said:
"Wǔzǐ Shèng is broadly learned and highly capable, yet his position is lowly.
When the ruler is close and familiar with him,
he exerts himself to be quick and humble;
when the ruler overlooks and distances him,
he remains respectful and without an expression of resentment.
Inside, he joins in planning for the state;
outside, his favor is not displayed.
When the ruler grants him a salary,
he knows when it is sufficient and declines;
therefore, he is able to endure for a long time."
2.23 The Tài Shì says:
"Those who cling to subordinates and deceive their superiors shall die;
those who cling to superiors and deceive their subordinates shall be punished.
Those who participate in the governance of the state but are of no benefit to the people shall retire;
those in high positions who cannot promote the worthy shall be expelled.
This is how the good are encouraged and the evil are dismissed."
Thus, the Chuán says:
"One who harms the good is a destroyer of the state;
one who obscures the good is a slanderer of the state;
one who accuses the innocent
is a thief of the state."
2.24 The Wáng Zhì says:
"Those who make false use of ghosts and spirits, times and days, or turtle and yarrow divination to confuse the masses
shall be put to death."
2.25 Zǐlù was the magistrate of Pú.
To prepare for water disasters,
he worked with the people in the spring to repair the ditches and canals.
Because the work was tedious and bitter for the people,
he gave each person a basket of food and a jar of drink.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this
and sent Zǐgòng to stop it.
Zǐlù was indignant and displeased;
he went to see the Master and said:
"I, Yóu, because violent rains were approaching
and I feared a water disaster,
therefore worked with the people to repair the ditches and canals to prepare for it.
Since many of the people were lacking in food,
I gave each person a basket of food and a jar of drink.
Yet the Master sent Cì to stop it.
Why is this?
The Master is stopping Yóu from practicing benevolence.
If the Master teaches through benevolence but forbids its practice,
I, Yóu, cannot accept this."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If you thought the people were starving,
why did you not inform the ruler,
so that he could open the granaries to provide for them?
Instead, by feeding them with your private resources,
you made it so that the ruler's kindness was not known
while your own virtue and righteousness were displayed.
If you stop quickly, it will be fine;
otherwise, the time before you receive punishment will not be long!"
Zǐlù was convinced at heart and withdrew.
3.1 Kǒngzǐ said:
"The gentleman applies himself to the root;
once the root is established, the Way is born."
If the root is not upright, the branches will surely be crooked;
if the beginning is not flourishing, the end will surely decline.
The Shī says:
"The plains and marshes have been leveled,
the spring waters are clear."
When the root is established, the Way is born.
According to the principles of the Chūnqiū,
one who has a righteous spring will have no chaotic autumn;
one who has a righteous ruler will have no endangered state.
The Yì says:
"Establish the root and the myriad principles will be managed;
if one loses it by a hair's breadth,
the error will be by a thousand miles."
For this reason, the gentleman values establishing the root and regards the setting of the beginning as important.
3.2 Wèiwǔ Hóu asked Wú Zǐ about the First Year.
Wú Zǐ replied:
"It means that the ruler of a state must be cautious about the beginning."
"How is one cautious about the beginning?"
He said:
"Rectify it."
"How does one rectify it?"
He said:
"Enlighten wisdom.
If wisdom is not enlightened, how can one see what is righteous?
Hear much and choose from it—
this is the means to enlighten wisdom.
Therefore, in ancient times, when a ruler began to hear of governance,
every Great Officer offered a word,
every Scholar was granted an audience,
commoners who requested an interview were surely admitted,
members of the ducal clan who asked questions were surely answered,
and those coming from the four directions were not rejected.
This can be called being unobscured.
The distribution of salary surely reached all;
the use of punishment was surely accurate;
the ruler's heart was surely benevolent,
thinking of the people's benefit
and removing the people's harm.
This can be called not losing the masses.
The ruler's person was surely upright;
close ministers were surely selected;
Great Officers did not hold concurrent offices;
those who held the handle of power over the people were not from a single clan.
This can be called not concentrating power.
These are all the intent of the Chūnqiū and the root of the First Year."
3.3 Kǒngzǐ said:
"There are six roots to conducting one's person.
Once the root is established,
then one can be a gentleman.
In establishing the person, there is righteousness, but filial piety is the root;
in observing mourning, there is ritual, but grief is the root;
in battle formations, there are ranks, but courage is the root;
in governing the state, there is order, but ability is the root;
in dwelling in the state, there is ritual, but succession is the root;
in producing wealth, there is timing, but labor is the root.
If the established root is not firm,
do not strive for flourishing branches;
if relatives are not pleased,
do not strive for external relations;
if affairs have no end or beginning,
do not strive for many undertakings;
if what is heard and remembered is not spoken of,
do not strive for much talk;
if those nearby are not pleased,
do not strive for those far away.
Therefore, returning to the root and cultivating what is near
is the Way of the gentleman."
3.4 Of everything
Heaven produces and
Earth nourishes,
none is more noble than humanity. Of the ways of humanity, none is greater than the intimacy between father and son
and the righteousness between ruler and minister.
The way of a father is sageliness,
and the way of a son is benevolence;
the way of a ruler is righteousness,
and the way of a minister is loyalty.
In a virtuous father’s relation to his son,
he uses compassion and kindness to give him life,
and uses instruction and admonition to bring him to completion.
He cultivates his sense of righteousness,
conceals his flaws,
regulates his conduct according to the seasons,
and is cautious in what he bestows.
When a son is seven years old or older,
the father selects an enlightened teacher for him
and chooses good friends,
not allowing him to see evil,
gradually imbuing him with goodness from a young age
to transform him early.
Therefore, when a virtuous son serves his parents,
in his speech and presentation of words,
his responses do not offend their ears;
in his movements and pace,
his appearance and demeanor do not offend their eyes;
in humbling his body and debasing himself, he does not offend their hearts.
The gentleman serves his parents to accumulate virtue.
The son
is the root of the parents;
there is nothing he should push back against or refuse to follow.
Those who push back and do not follow commands
are only those who would harm their parents.
Therefore, whatever brings peace to the parents,
the son provides it all.
When a virtuous minister serves his ruler,
from the day he accepts office,
he regards the lord as his father,
the state as his home,
and the scholars as his brothers.
Therefore, if there is anything that can bring peace to the state and benefit to the people,
he does not avoid its difficulties
and does not fear its labor
in order to fulfill his righteousness.
Thus his ruler also assists him
to fulfill his virtue.
The ruler, the minister, and the common people
take each other as their foundation,
like a circle without end.
The Master also said:
“Of human conduct, none is greater than filial piety.”
When filial conduct is perfected within,
a fine reputation is spread without.
This is called building upon the foundation,
and the blossoms will naturally flourish.
The ruler takes the minister as his foundation,
the minister takes the ruler as his foundation,
the father takes the son as his foundation,
the son takes the father as his foundation;
for those who abandon their foundation,
the blossoms will wither.
3.5 *Zǐlù* said:
“One who carries a heavy burden and travels a long distance
does not choose the ground on which to rest;
one whose family is poor and whose parents are old
does not choose the salary before taking office.
Formerly, when I, *Yóu*, served my two parents,
I often ate the fruit of pigweed and pulse
and carried rice for my parents from over a hundred *lǐ* away.
After my parents passed away,
I traveled south to *Chǔ*,
followed by a hundred chariots,
with ten thousand *zhōng* of grain accumulated.
I sit upon layered cushions
and eat from a row of tripods,
but I wish I could again eat pigweed and pulse and carry rice for my parents,
yet that time can never be regained.
A dried fish hanging on a rope—
how long before it is moth-eaten?
The lifespan of two parents
is as fleeting as a shadow passing through a gap.
Plants and trees wish to grow,
but the frost and dew do not permit it;
the virtuous person wishes to provide nourishment,
but the two parents do not wait.”
Therefore it is said:
“When the family is poor and the parents are old,
one does not choose the salary before taking office.”
3.6 *Bóqín* and *Kāng Shū Fēng* went to pay court to King *Chéng*,
and saw *Zhōu Gōng*.
Three times they saw him, and three times they were beaten with a rod.
*Kāng Shū* had a look of alarm
and said to *Bóqín*:
“There is a certain *Shāng Zǐ*,
who is a worthy man;
let us go see him together.”
*Kāng Shū Fēng* and *Bóqín* saw *Shāng Zǐ* and said:
“We individuals,
for days now, have gone to pay court to King *Chéng*
and saw *Zhōu Gōng*.
Three times we saw him and three times we were beaten;
what is the explanation for this?”
*Shāng Zǐ* said:
“Why do you two not go together to look at the south side of the *Nánshān* mountains?
There is a tree there
named the *Qiáo*.”
The two of them went to look at the south side of the *Nánshān* mountains,
saw the *Qiáo*,
which was lofty, fruiting, and looking upward.
They returned and reported this to *Shāng Zǐ*.
*Shāng Zǐ* said:
“The *Qiáo*
is the way of the father.”
*Shāng Zǐ* said:
“Why do you two not go together to look at the north side of the *Nánshān* mountains?
There is a tree there named the *Zǐ*.”
The two of them went to look at the north side of the *Nánshān* mountains,
saw the *Zǐ*,
which was bountiful, fruiting, and bowing downward.
They returned and reported this to *Shāng Zǐ*.
*Shāng Zǐ* said:
“The *Zǐ*
is the way of the son.”
The next day, the two of them
saw *Zhōu Gōng*.
Upon entering the gate, they hurried forward;
upon ascending the hall, they knelt.
*Zhōu Gōng* stroked their heads,
comforted them and gave them food,
saying:
“Where did you encounter a gentleman?”
The two replied:
“We saw *Shāng Zǐ*.”
*Zhōu Gōng* said:
“A gentleman indeed
is *Shāng Zǐ*!”
3.7 *Zēng Zǐ* was weeding melons and accidentally cut a root.
*Zēng Xī* was enraged,
took a large staff and struck him.
*Zēng Zǐ* fell to the ground.
After a while, he regained consciousness,
sprang up,
and came forward, saying:
“Earlier, I, *Shēn*, committed an offense against you, Great One.
You used your strength to instruct me;
I hope you are not unwell from the effort?”
He retired to his room, played the zither and sang,
wanting to let *Zēng Xī* hear his singing
so he would know he was at peace.
When *Kǒng Zǐ* heard of this,
he told his disciples:
“If *Shēn* comes,
do not let him in.”
*Zēng Zǐ*, believing himself to be without fault,
sent someone to apologize to *Kǒng Zǐ*.
*Kǒng Zǐ* said:
“Have you heard that *Gǔsǒu* had a son named *Shùn*?
When *Shùn* served his father,
when he was sought for service,
he was never not by his side;
but when his father sought to kill him,
he could never be found.
He stayed for a small switch,
but he fled from a large club,
so as to escape violent rage.
Now you have abandoned your body to wait for violent rage;
you stood there and did not leave.
Had you been killed, you would have embroiled your father in unrighteousness.
What unfiliality could be greater than this?
Are you not a subject of the Son of Heaven?
If one kills a subject of the Son of Heaven,
what is the crime?”
Even with a talent like *Zēng Zǐ*’s,
and being a student in the school of *Kǒng Zǐ*,
he had a fault and did not know it.
How difficult it is to abide by righteousness!
3.8 Hán Bóyú had a fault,
and his mother caned him.
He wept.
His mother asked him, saying:
“On other days when I caned you,
I never saw you weep.
Why do you weep today?”
He replied:
“On other days when Yú committed an offense,
the caning was always painful.
Now my mother’s strength has declined
and the caning cannot cause me pain;
this is why I weep.”
Therefore it is said:
When parents are angry with them,
if it does not arise in their thoughts
and is not seen in their expression,
and they deeply accept their punishment
so as to be pitiable,
this is superior.
When parents are angry with them,
if it does not arise in their thoughts
and is not seen in their expression,
this is the next best.
When parents are angry with them,
if it arises in their thoughts
and is seen in their expression,
this is inferior.
3.9 That adults possess virtue
and youths have achievements
is the teaching of the *Dà Xué*.
Prohibition at the time before an act has occurred is called prevention.
Teaching according to when the student is receptive is called timeliness.
Mutual observation of goodness is called polishing.
Learning that does not skip over stages and is applied sequentially is called orderly.
If prohibition comes only after an act has occurred,
then it meets resistance and cannot be overcome.
If one studies only after the proper time has passed,
then even with diligent effort, success is difficult.
If teaching is applied haphazardly and not in order,
then it results in disorder and lack of governance.
If one studies alone without friends,
then one is isolated and ill-informed.
Therefore it is said:
There is the bright *Bìyōng*,
there is the worthy *Pàngōng*.
In the fields and villages they travel together,
numerous and dignified,
following one another while holding ritual gifts,
gathering in clans for cultural learning.
3.10 Shào Gōng of Zhōu was nineteen years old
when he saw what was right and underwent the capping ceremony;
once capped, one can serve as a regional leader or a feudal lord.
When a person is in the time of childhood and ignorance,
if they do not seek a teacher to correct their foundation,
they have no way to establish their character or preserve their nature.
Those who are young are certainly foolish,
and those who are foolish act recklessly.
If those who are foolish act recklessly,
they cannot protect themselves.
Mèngzǐ said:
“Everyone knows to use food to cure hunger,
but no one knows to use learning to cure foolishness.”
Therefore, youths of good potential
must be diligent in study and inquiry
to cultivate their nature.
If people today could truly hone their talents,
purify their own spiritual intelligence,
observe the responses of things,
understand the essentials of the Way,
observe the beginnings and ends of matters,
view the realm beyond boundaries,
wander freely within the infinite,
roam beyond the mundane world,
standing tall and independent,
and transcending the world,
then this is where the supreme sages let their spirits roam.
However, people of later ages
cannot reside in leisure and meditate,
play the *qín* and read books,
look back and observe high antiquity,
befriend worthy great officers,
study and discuss,
and daily find contentment in themselves.
They keep worldly affairs at a distance,
distinguish clearly between benefit and harm,
calculate gains and losses,
and observe fortune and misfortune.
They establish righteousness and set standards
to serve as models,
exhaustively pursuing the root and the branches,
and investigating the reality of things.
In death, they leave a legacy;
in life, they have an honored name;
these are all things that talented people can achieve.
Yet those who are unable to do so
are lazy and negligent
because they have too many idle days.
Thus they lose their foundation and have no reputation.
Truly, learning
is the foundation for honoring one's name and establishing one’s character.
When appearances and forms are equal,
the one who adorns their appearance is favored;
when inner quality and nature are of the same kind,
the one who studies is wise.
Therefore, whetstones and polishing tools are not metal,
but they can sharpen metal;
the *Shī* and *Shū* stand set apart,
and are not me,
but they can sharpen the mind.
Scholars who inquire and seek,
rising day and night,
sharpen their inner selves and increase their knowledge to distinguish principles.
Therefore, in personal conduct they are complete,
and in establishing themselves they are not in danger.
If a scholar wishes to be deeply enlightened and broadly observant to leave a glorious name
yet does not like the way of inquiry and seeking,
this is like cutting the root of wisdom and blocking the source of wisdom;
how can they establish themselves!
Even though the *Qíjì* horse is fast,
if it does not encounter Bó Lè,
it will not reach a thousand *lǐ*.
Even though the *Gānjiàng* sword is sharp,
without human effort it cannot cut by itself.
Even though the *Wūhào* bow is excellent,
without being placed in a frame,
it cannot be used.
Even though a person’s talent is high,
if they do not devote themselves to learning,
they cannot become a sage.
When water accumulates to form a river,
then flood-dragons are born there.
When earth accumulates to form a mountain,
then *yùzhāng* trees grow there.
When learning accumulates to form a sage,
then wealth, honor, and prestige arrive.
A robe worth a thousand pieces of gold
is not made from the skin of a single fox.
The rafters of a terrace or temple
are not the branches of a single tree.
The laws of the former kings
are not the wisdom of a single scholar.
Therefore it is said:
Inquiry is the foundation of wisdom,
and reflection is the path of wisdom.
The *Zhōngyōng* says:
“To be fond of asking is close to wisdom,
to practice with effort is close to benevolence,
to know shame is close to courage.”
Of those who accumulated the small to become great,
was it not only Zhòngní!
Learning is the means by which one reverses feelings, regulates nature, and fulfills talent.
Staying close to the worthy and inquiring
is the means to grow virtue;
discussing and joining with friends
is the means to improve one another.
The *Shī* says:
“As if cutting, as if filing;
as if carving, as if polishing.”
This is what it means.
3.11 Now, clearing the land and cultivating grain
to nourish the living and send off the dead,
sharpening metal and stone and mixing herbal medicines to treat illnesses and suffering,
knowing how to construct houses to avoid the heat and rain,
and building terraces and pavilions to avoid dampness.
At home, one knows to cherish one’s kin;
abroad, one knows to honor one’s lord.
Internally, there is the distinction between men and women;
externally, there is the relationship between friends.
These are the moral teachings of the *Shèng Rén*.
The *Rú Zhě* received them and passed them down
to instruct and admonish later generations.
Now, the wicked people of these latter days
conversely criticize the *Rú Zhě*,
saying:
“What is the use of being a *Rú*?”
For people like this,
they have lost sight of the fundamentals.
It is like eating grain and wearing silk
yet criticizing the farmers and weavers;
riding in boats and carriages,
finding comfort and ease in them,
yet criticizing the craftsmen;
eating from pots and steamers,
relying on them for survival,
yet criticizing the potters and smiths.
These words contradict their feelings, and these actions are blind to their hearts.
For people like this,
they are not close to their own flesh and blood,
and they do not befriend refined scholars.
These are the abandoned people of the Three Dynasties,
whom a lord of men does not pardon.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
“Throw him to the hyenas and tigers;
even the hyenas and tigers will not eat him.
Throw him to the northern regions;
the northern regions will not receive him.
Throw him to *Yǒu Hào*.”
This is what is meant.
3.12 *Mèngzǐ* said:
“People know to fertilize their fields,
but no one knows to fertilize their heart.”
Fertilizing a field is nothing more than benefiting the sprouts and obtaining grain.
Fertilizing the heart is easy to practice,
and allows one to obtain what they desire.
What is meant by fertilizing the heart?
It is to be broadly learned and widely informed.
What is meant by being easy to practice?
It is to unify one’s nature and stop excessive desires.
3.13 *Zǐsī* said:
“Learning is that which increases talent;
a whetstone is that which sharpens a blade.
I once dwelt in solitude and thought deeply,
but it was not as effective as the swiftness of learning.
I once stood on tiptoe to gaze afar,
but it was not as effective as the broad view from climbing a high place.
Therefore, when calling out downwind,
the sound does not become more urgent, yet those who hear are many;
when beckoning from a hill,
the arm does not become longer, yet those who see are far away.”
Thus, fish rely on water,
birds rely on the wind,
and plants rely on the seasons.
3.14 *Kǒngzǐ* said:
“That which allows one to speak with another all day without fatigue
is surely learning!
One’s physical body may not be worth looking at,
one’s courage and strength may not be worth fearing,
one’s ancestors may not be worth praising,
and one’s clan and surname may not be worth mentioning;
yet, the reason one can be heard of in all four directions and be illustrious among the feudal lords
is surely learning!
The *Shī* says:
‘Neither erring nor forgetting,
follow the old regulations.’
This refers to learning.”
3.15 *Kǒngzǐ* said:
a *jūn zǐ* cannot go without learning,
and in meeting others, he cannot go without adornment.
Without adornment, there is no root;
without a root, there is a loss of principle;
loss of principle leads to a lack of loyalty;
lack of loyalty leads to a loss of ritual;
loss of ritual leads to an inability to establish oneself.
Now, that which shines from afar
is adornment;
that which becomes clearer as one draws near
is learning.
It is like a stagnant pond;
when rainwater pours into it,
reeds and rushes grow there.
Viewing it from above,
one knows it is not a spring.”
3.16 *Gōnghùzǐ* said:
“Those who possess a state cannot go without studying the *Chūn Qiū*.
Those born to honor
become arrogant;
those born to wealth
become haughty.
For those born to wealth and honor
to also have a mirror for reflection and be self-attained,
they are rare!
The *Chūn Qiū*
is the mirror of a state.
Within the *Chūn Qiū*,
thirty-six rulers were assassinated,
fifty-two states were destroyed,
and many feudal lords fled in haste
and could not preserve their altars of soil and grain;
none of these failed to show signs beforehand which they then followed to their end.”
3.17 *Jìn Píng Gōng* asked *Shī Kuàng*:
“I am seventy years of age
and wish to learn, but I fear it is already too late.”
*Shī Kuàng* said:
“If it is late,
why not light a candle?”
*Píng Gōng* said:
“How can a subject play a joke on his lord?”
*Shī Kuàng* said:
“How would a blind subject dare joke with his lord?
I have heard that
to love learning when young
is like the sun rising;
to love learning in one’s prime
is like the light of the midday sun;
to love learning when old
is like the brilliance of a lit candle.
To be old and not learn
is to be in darkness like walking at night.
Between the brilliance of a lit candle
and walking in darkness, which is better?”
*Píng Gōng* said:
“Excellent!”
3.18 *Héjiān Xiàn Wáng* said:
“*Tāng* said that learning the Way of the sage kings
is like the sun;
sitting quietly and thinking alone
is like a fire.
Now, discarding the study of the Way of the sage kings
is like discarding the light of the sun;
why then think alone
like the light of a fire?
One can see small things,
but it cannot be used for great wisdom.
Only through learning and inquiry can one broaden their illustrious virtue and wisdom.”
3.19 *Liángqiū Jù* said to *Yànzǐ*:
“Until I die, I will never catch up to you, Master!”
*Yànzǐ* said:
“I, *Yīng*, have heard:
He who acts often succeeds;
he who walks often arrives.
I am no different from other people;
I simply act constantly without stopping
and walk constantly without resting.
That is why it is difficult to catch up.”
3.20 *Nìng Yuè*
was a commoner from *Zhōngmóu*.
Toiling under the labor of plowing and sowing,
he said to his friend:
“What can I do to escape this suffering?”
His friend said:
“Nothing is as good as learning;
after thirty years of learning, you can achieve success.”
*Nìng Yuè* said:
“I ask to do it in fifteen years.
When others rest,
I will not dare to rest;
when others sleep,
I will not dare to sleep.”
After fifteen years of learning, *Zhōu Wēi Gōng* took him as a teacher.
Now, a runner may be fast,
but if he stops after two *lǐ*;
and a walker may be slow,
but if he does not stop for a hundred *lǐ*.
Given *Nìng Yuè*’s talent and his long persistence without stopping,
that he became a teacher to feudal lords,
was it not appropriate!
3.21 Kǒngzǐ said to Zǐlù:
"What do you like?"
Zǐlù said:
"I like the long sword."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"That is not what I am asking.
I mean that if you add study to your abilities,
how could anyone reach your level?"
Zǐlù said:
"Is study also beneficial?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Generally, if a ruler lacks ministers who remonstrate, he will lose the proper way of government;
if a scholar lacks friends who instruct him, he will lose the clarity of what he hears.
When driving a wild horse, one does not release the whip;
when handling a bow, it is not returned to the press-frame.
Wood becomes straight when subjected to the marking line;
a person becomes a sage when accepting remonstrance.
If one accepts learning and values questioning,
who would not achieve success smoothly?
To destroy benevolence and hate scholars
is to draw near to punishment.
A gentleman cannot do without learning."
Zǐlù said:
"On the southern mountains there is bamboo;
it grows straight by itself without being bent.
If cut and used as an arrow,
it can pierce through rhinoceros-hide.
What need is there for learning?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If it is notched and feathered,
and its head is sharpened and polished,
will it not penetrate even deeper?"
Zǐlù bowed twice and said:
"I respectfully accept your teaching!"
3.22 Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"I request to set aside ancient learning
and act according to my own intentions;
is this acceptable?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is not.
In the past, a son of the Dōngyí admired the righteousness of the Zhūxià.
He had a daughter,
and when her husband died,
he took a private son-in-law for her within the household,
and she never remarried.
Not remarrying is indeed not remarrying,
but this was not in accordance with the righteousness of chastity.
A younger brother in Cāngwú
married a wife who was beautiful,
and he requested to exchange her with his elder brother.
Loyal he may have been,
but this was not in accordance with ritual propriety.
Now you wish to set aside ancient learning and act according to your own intentions;
how do you know that your intentions will not take the wrong as right and the right as wrong?
If one does not follow the proper beginning,
even if one wishes to regret it later,
it will be difficult!"
3.23 A thick wall on a weak foundation
may not necessarily collapse,
but when the floodwaters arrive,
it will surely be the first to be destroyed;
a tree with shallow roots,
where the root ball is not deep,
may not necessarily fall,
but when a whirlwind rises
and a rainstorm arrives,
it will surely be the first to be uprooted.
If a gentleman dwells in a state
but does not exalt benevolence and righteousness
and does not honor worthy ministers,
the state may not necessarily perish,
but once there is an extraordinary disaster,
when chariots race and people flee,
and misfortune arrives in an instant,
then he begins to worry with a parched throat and scorched lips,
sighing to heaven,
hoping that heaven might save him—
is this not difficult?
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If one is not cautious in the beginning,
and regrets it afterward,
even though there is regret, it is to no avail."
The *Shī* says:
"Sobbing and weeping,
what use is a sigh now?"
This means that by not first correcting the root, one brings about sorrow in the end.
3.24 Yú Jūn asked Pénchéng Zǐ,
saying:
"Nowadays, craftsmen become skillful over time,
but physical beauty fades as one ages.
If a person, before reaching the peak of their prime,
increasingly accumulates the arts of the mind and technical skills
to prepare for the time when their beauty begins to fade.
Beauty will surely be exhausted before old age,
but wisdom and schemes are no different from the time of youth.
When the beauty that could be loved
is elegantly coming to an end,
in this vast world, where can one entrust a body of no ability?
Therefore, those who have skills
do not burden their person and have never perished,
while beauty cannot flourish forever."
3.25 Qí Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What does a king value most?"
He said:
"Value Heaven."
Huán Gōng looked up at the sky.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"What is called 'Heaven'
is not the vast and blue sky.
One who rules over people
takes the common people as Heaven.
If the people are with him, he is secure;
if they assist him, he is strong;
if they oppose him, he is in danger;
if they turn their backs on him, he perishes."
The *Shī* says:
"If people are not good,
they will resent each other in every direction."
That the people resent their superiors
and yet the state does not eventually perish
has never happened.
3.26 Héjiān Xiàn Wáng said:
"Guǎn Zǐ stated: 'When the granaries are full,
the people know ritual and moderation;
when food and clothing are sufficient,
they know honor and shame.'
Grain is
that by which the state flourishes,
by which men and women look fine,
by which ritual and righteousness are practiced,
and by which the people's hearts are at peace.
In the *Shàngshū*, the 'Five Blessings' start with wealth.
When Zǐgòng asked about governing,
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Enrich them.'
Once they are enriched,
then teach them.
This is the root of governing a state."
3.27 Wén Gōng met Jiù Jì,
whose ancestral temple was adjacent to the west wall.
Gōng said:
"Who is it that lives to the west?"
He replied:
"It is your old servant."
Gōng said:
"Expand your residence to the west."
He replied:
"My loyalty
is not as strong as the labor of the old servants;
their wall is broken and they do not rebuild it."
Gōng asked:
"Why not rebuild it?"
He replied:
"A single day not spent farming
means a hundred days without food."
Gōng went out and told this to his driver.
The driver bowed his head to the crossbar of the carriage and said:
"The *Lǚxíng* says:
'When one man has cause for celebration,
the millions of people rely on it.'
Your brilliance
is the fortune of all your ministers."
Thereupon he issued an order to the state:
"Do not indulge in building palaces and houses
so as to interfere with people's residences;
let the building of walls follow the seasons,
and do not take away from the work of agriculture."
3.28 King Gòng of Chǔ had many favored sons,
and the position of the heir apparent was not fixed.
Qū Jiàn said:
“Chǔ will surely have much disorder.
If a single rabbit runs down the street,
ten thousand people will chase it;
but if one person catches it,
the ten thousand will no longer run.
When the allocation of status is not yet fixed,
then a single rabbit running
causes ten thousand people to be in turmoil;
when the allocation is already fixed,
even a greedy person knows when to stop.
Now Chǔ has many favored sons,
yet there is no designated primary heir;
disorder will arise from this.
For the heir apparent
is the foundation of the state
and the hope of the common people.
Since the state has no foundation
and the people's hopes are disappointed,
its root is severed.
When the root is severed, there is disruption and disorder,
just like the running rabbit.”
King Gòng heard this
and established King Kāng as the crown prince.
Afterward, there were still the disorders of Lìngyǐn Wéi and Gōngzǐ Qìjí.
3.29 Duke Xiāng of Jìn died,
and the successor was young.
Zhào Xuānzǐ acted as prime minister
and said to the grandees:
“To establish a young ruler
is to fear many difficulties;
I request to establish Yōng.
Yōng is older
and is currently abroad in Qín.
Qín is great,
and it is sufficient to serve as support.”
Jiǎ Jì said:
“It is not as good as establishing Gōngzǐ Lè.
Lè is favored in the state;
the late ruler loved him and sent him to serve in Dí.
Dí is also sufficient to serve as support.”
Mù Yíng held the crown prince and cried out in the court, saying:
“What was the crime of the late ruler?
What is the crime of his successor?
Do you discard the legitimate heir and not establish him,
while seeking a ruler from abroad?”
She left the court
and, holding him, went to see Zhào Xuānzǐ,
saying:
“You loathe difficulties,
and therefore wish to establish an older ruler.
But if an older ruler is established and the young heir grows up,
then the difficulties will truly arrive.”
Zhào Xuānzǐ was troubled by this
and subsequently established the crown prince.
3.30 Zhào Jiǎnzi made Xiāngzǐ his successor.
Dǒng Ānyú said:
“Wúxù has no talent;
now you make him the successor,
why?”
Jiǎnzi said:
“Because as a person, he is capable of enduring humiliation for the sake of the altars of the soil and grain.”
On another day,
Zhì Bó was drinking with Xiāngzǐ and poured wine over Xiāngzǐ’s head.
The grandees requested to kill him.
Xiāngzǐ said:
“When the late ruler established me,
he said I ‘could endure humiliation for the sake of the altars of the soil and grain’;
did he say I should be able to stab people?”
After ten months passed,
Zhì Bó besieged Xiāngzǐ at Jìnyáng.
Xiāngzǐ dispersed his ranks and struck him,
greatly defeating Zhì Bó,
and lacquered his skull to use as a drinking vessel.
4.1 Among the gentlemen who have courage and are resolute in their actions,
if they do not use these to establish their integrity and practice righteousness,
but instead die recklessly for no good name,
is it not painful!
There are gentlemen who sacrifice their lives to achieve benevolence
and face harm to establish righteousness;
they rely on principles of integrity and do not deliberate when facing death.
Therefore, they can die while their names flow to future generations.
Without courageous decisiveness,
who could carry this out?
4.2 Zi Lù said:
“One who cannot find sweetness in toil and hardship,
who cannot be tranquil in poverty,
and who cannot think lightly of death
but yet says ‘I can practice righteousness,’
I do not believe him.”
In the past, Shēn Bāoxū stood in the court of Qín for seven days and seven nights,
weeping without stopping his voice,
and thereby preserved Chǔ.
If he could not endure toil and hardship,
how could he have done this?
Zéngzǐ wore cloth garments and coarse padded robes that were not even whole,
and did not eat his fill of dregs and husks or soups of pigweed and pulse;
yet when righteousness did not align, he declined the position of high minister.
If he were not tranquil in poverty,
how could he have done this?
Bǐ Gàn was about to die, yet his remonstrance became even more loyal;
Bó Yí and Shū Qí died of hunger at Shǒuyáng, yet their will became even more manifest.
If they did not think lightly of death,
how could they have done this?
Therefore, if a gentleman wishes to establish righteousness and practice the Way,
he must act regardless of whether it is difficult or easy;
to establish himself and make his name known,
he must succeed without regard for benefit or harm.
The Shī says:
“That gentleman there
is great and sincere.”
If one is not an excellent, sincere, refined, and motivated gentleman,
who could carry this out!
4.3 Prince Bǐ Gàn sacrificed his life to achieve his loyalty;
Wěi Shēng sacrificed his life to achieve his trustworthiness;
Bó Yí and Shū Qí sacrificed their lives to achieve their integrity.
These four men
were all accomplished gentlemen of the world.
Did they not love their lives?
They believed that if righteousness is not established
and their names are not manifest,
that is the shame of a gentleman.
Therefore, they sacrificed their lives to fulfill their conduct.
From this perspective,
low status and poverty
are not the shame of a gentleman.
What a gentleman is ashamed of is:
when the world praises loyalty, he is not included;
when they praise trustworthiness, he is not included;
and when they praise integrity, he is not included.
If these three qualities reside in one’s person,
one’s name will be passed down to future generations,
coexisting with the sun and moon without ceasing.
Even in a world without the Way,
it cannot be defiled.
Thus, it is not that they loved death and hated life,
nor that they hated wealth and honor or enjoyed poverty and low status.
If it proceeds from the Way
and follows its principles,
and honor and wealth come to them,
a gentleman would not decline them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“If wealth could be sought,
though I had to be a servant holding a whip,
I would do it.
If it cannot be sought,
I will follow what I love.”
This is the conduct of a great sage.
The Shī says:
“My heart is not a stone,
it cannot be turned;
my heart is not a mat,
it cannot be rolled up.”
This means not losing oneself.
If one can avoid losing oneself,
then one can help to overcome difficulties.
This is why the gentleman surpasses the multitude.
4.4 Chǔ attacked Chén;
the West Gate of Chén was burned,
so they made the surrendered people repair it.
Kǒngzǐ passed by
but did not salute by leaning on the crossbar of his carriage.
Zi Lù said:
“According to the rites,
when passing three people, one should descend from the carriage;
when passing two, one should salute by leaning on the crossbar.
Now the number of people repairing the gate of Chén is many;
why does the Master not salute?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Qiū has heard
that to be unaware when the state is perishing
is not wise;
to know but not to struggle
is not loyal;
to be loyal but not to die for it
is not to have integrity.
Now the people repairing the gate of Chén cannot perform even one of these;
therefore, Qiū does not salute them.”
4.5 Kǒngzǐ saw Duke Jǐng of Qí;
Duke Jǐng offered him Lǐnqiū as a means of support.
Kǒngzǐ declined and would not receive it.
After leaving, he said to his disciples:
“I have heard that a gentleman should receive a salary based on merit.
Now I have advised Duke Jǐng,
but Duke Jǐng has not yet practiced it,
yet he grants me Lǐnqiū.
His failure to understand Qiū is indeed extreme.”
He then declined it and departed.
4.6 Zēng Zǐ wore ragged clothes while plowing.
The Lǔ Jūn sent someone to bestow a fief upon him,
saying,
"Please use this to mend your clothes."
Zēng Zǐ did not accept it.
The messenger returned repeatedly,
yet he still did not accept it.
The messenger said,
"Xiān Shēng, it is not that you sought it from others;
someone is offering it to you,
so why not accept it?"
Zēng Zǐ said,
"I have heard that
those who receive from others fear others,
and those who give to others are arrogant toward others.
Even if you have a gift for me
and are not arrogant toward me,
can I fail to fear you?"
In the end, he did not accept it.
Kǒng Zǐ heard of this and said,
"The words of Shēn
are sufficient to preserve his integrity."
4.7 Zǐ Sī lived in Wèi.
His hemp robe had no outer lining,
and in twenty days he had only nine meals.
Tián Zǐ Fāng heard of this
and sent someone to give him a white fox fur coat.
Fearing he would not accept it,
he therefore told him:
"I lent it to someone
and then forgot about it;
when I give something to someone,
it is like throwing it away."
Zǐ Sī declined and would not accept it.
Tián Zǐ Fāng said,
"I have it and you do not;
for what reason do you not accept it?"
Zǐ Sī said,
"I, Jí, have heard that
giving recklessly is not as good as casting things away into ditches and ravines.
Although I, Jí, am poor,
I cannot bear to treat my own person as a ditch or ravine;
therefore, I dare not accept it."
4.8 Sòng Xiāng Gōng Zī Fù was the Tài Zǐ of Huán Gōng.
Huán Gōng had a son by a later wife named Gōng Zǐ Mù Yí,
and the Gōng loved him.
Because the Gōng loved him, Zī Fù
wished to establish him as the heir.
He requested of the Gōng, saying,
"Please allow Mù Yí to be established,
and I will serve as his Xiàng and elder brother to assist him."
The Gōng said,
"For what reason?"
He replied,
"My maternal uncle is in Wèi
and loves me;
if I am eventually established, I will not be able to go there,
and my tracks will be cut off from Wèi,
which would be turning my back on my mother.
Furthermore, I know myself that I am not worthy to be placed above Mù Yí."
The Gōng did not permit it.
He requested it of the Gōng forcefully,
and the Gōng permitted it,
intending to establish Gōng Zǐ Mù Yí.
Mù Yí declined, saying,
"When the elder brother is established and the younger brother is below him,
that is the righteous way;
if now the younger brother is established and the elder brother is below him,
it is unrighteous.
If you make Mù Yí do what is unrighteous,
Mù Yí will flee."
He then fled to Wèi,
and Zī Fù followed him.
Three years later,
Huán Gōng fell ill
and sent someone to summon Zī Fù,
saying,
"If you do not come,
it will cause me to die of sorrow."
Zī Fù then returned,
and the Gōng again established him as Tài Zǐ,
after which Mù Yí returned.
4.9 Lí Jī of Jìn slandered Tài Zǐ Shēn Shēng to Xiàn Gōng,
and Xiàn Gōng intended to kill him.
Gōng Zǐ Chóng Ěr said to Shēn Shēng,
"The one who did this
is not you; it is not your fault.
Why do you not go forward and defend yourself?
If you defend yourself,
you will surely be cleared of guilt."
Shēn Shēng said,
"I cannot.
If I defend myself,
Lí Jī will surely be found guilty.
My lord is old;
without Lí Jī, he cannot rest peacefully on his mat
or find flavor in his food.
How could I cause my lord to end his days in resentment?"
Chóng Ěr said,
"If you will not defend yourself,
then it would be better to leave quickly."
Shēn Shēng said,
"I cannot.
To leave and escape death
is to cast blame upon my lord.
To make a father’s faults manifest
and seek a good reputation among the Zhū Hóu—
who would be willing to admit me?
Inside, I would be distressed by my kin;
outside, I would be distressed by my flight.
This would double the evil against me.
I have heard that
loyalty does not expose the lord,
wisdom does not double wrongdoing,
and courage does not flee from death.
Such being the case,
I will face it with my own person."
He then fell upon his sword and died.
The Jūn Zǐ heard of this and said,
"It was heaven's mandate indeed,
O Shì Zǐ!"
The *Shī* says,
"Ornate and elegant,
forming this shell-patterned brocade.
Those who slander others
have truly gone too far."
4.10 In the time of Jìn Xiàn Gōng,
there was an officer named Hú Tū
who was the Fù to Tài Zǐ Shēn Shēng.
The Gōng established Lí Jī as his Fū Rén,
and the state was filled with many worries.
Hú Tū claimed illness and did not go out.
In the sixth year,
Xiàn Gōng executed the Tài Zǐ because of the slanders.
As the Tài Zǐ was about to die,
he sent someone to say to Hú Tū,
"My lord is old,
and the state is in many difficulties.
If the Fù would come out once to assist my lord,
I, Shēn Shēng, will receive this favor and die without resentment."
He bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and died.
Hú Tū then returned to serve Xiàn Gōng.
Three years later,
Xiàn Gōng died.
Hú Tū took his leave of the Zhū Dà Fū, saying,
"I, Tū, received the command of the Tài Zǐ,
and now the matter is finished.
Rather than living long in a chaotic world,
it is better to die and report to the Tài Zǐ."
He then returned home and committed suicide.
4.11 Chǔ Píng Wáng sent Fèn Yáng to kill Tài Zǐ Jiàn.
Before he arrived, Fèn Yáng sent a messenger to let him go,
and the Tài Zǐ fled to Sòng.
The Wáng summoned Fèn Yáng.
Fèn Yáng had the people of Chéng Fù arrest him to arrive before the Wáng.
The Wáng said,
"The words came out of my mouth
and entered your ears;
who told Jiàn?"
He replied,
"I told him.
The Wáng originally commanded me, saying,
'Serve Jiàn as you serve me.'
I am untalented
and could not be of two minds.
I upheld the initial command until the end,
so I sent him away.
Afterward, I regretted it,
but it was too late."
The Wáng said,
"How is it
that you dare to come here?"
He replied,
"To be sent and fail the command,
and then to be summoned and not come,
would be a double fault.
If I fled, there would be nowhere for me to take refuge."
The Wáng then pardoned him.
4.12 Duke Líng of Jìn was tyrannical,
and Zhào Xuānzǐ repeatedly remonstrated with him.
Duke Líng was distressed by this
and sent Chú Zhī Mí to assassinate him.
Chú Zhī Mí went there at dawn,
and the door to the bedchamber was already open.
Xuānzǐ was in full ceremonial dress, about to attend court;
as it was still early,
he sat and dozed.
Zhī Mí withdrew
and sighed, saying:
"Not forgetting reverence and respect,
he is truly a master of the people!
To assassinate a master of the people
is disloyal;
to abandon the ruler's command
is untrustworthy.
Having committed either of these,
it is better to die!"
He then struck a locust tree and died.
4.13 Among the people of Qí, there was a man named Zǐ Lán Zǐ,
who served Bái Gōng Shèng.
Shèng was about to start a rebellion,
so he told Zǐ Lán Zǐ:
"I am going to carry out a great undertaking in the state,
and I wish for you to join me."
Zǐ Lán Zǐ said:
"For me to serve you and yet join you in killing the lord
would be to assist you in unrighteousness;
but to fear trouble and desert you
would be to flee from you in your time of difficulty.
Therefore, I will not join you in killing the lord,
so as to fulfill my righteousness,
but I shall cut my throat in the courtyard
so as to fulfill my conduct."
4.14 In Chǔ, there was a gentleman named Shēn Míng,
who lived at home and cared for his father;
his filial piety was known throughout the state of Chǔ.
The King wished to appoint him as Chancellor,
but Shēn Míng declined and would not accept.
His father said:
"The King wishes to make you Chancellor;
why do you say you will not accept?"
Shēn Míng replied:
"To set aside being a filial son to my father to become a loyal minister to the King—
why should I?"
His father said:
"If it allows you to have a salary from the state
and a position at court,
you will be happy and I shall be without worry.
I wish for you to be Chancellor."
Shēn Míng said:
"I obey."
He then entered the court,
and the King of Chǔ accordingly appointed him Chancellor.
After he had served there for three years,
Bái Gōng caused a rebellion,
killing Lìngyǐn Zǐxī and Sīmǎ Zǐqī.
Shēn Míng was about to go and die for the cause.
His father stopped him, saying:
"To abandon your father and die,
can that be permissible?"
Shēn Míng said:
"I have heard that for those who serve as officials,
their persons belong to the ruler while their salaries belong to their parents.
Now that I have left you to serve the ruler,
can I not die in his hour of need?"
He then took his leave and went,
subsequently surrounding the rebels with troops.
Bái Gōng said to Shí Qǐ:
"Shēn Míng
is a courageous warrior of the world.
Now he surrounds me with troops;
what shall I do about him?"
Shí Qǐ said:
"Shēn Míng
is a filial son of the world.
You should go and seize his father with soldiers.
When Shēn Míng hears of it, he will surely come,
and then you can speak with him."
Bái Gōng said:
"Good."
He then went and took the father,
holding him with soldiers,
and sent someone to tell Shēn Míng:
"If you are with me,
I will divide the state of Chǔ with you;
if you are not with me,
your father shall die."
Shēn Míng shed tears and responded:
"At first I was my father's filial son,
but now I am my lord's loyal minister.
I have heard
that he who eats another's food dies for his affairs,
and he who receives another's salary exhausts his ability.
Now I can no longer be a filial son to my father,
for I am a loyal minister to the lord;
how can I preserve my own person?"
He took up the drumsticks and beat the drum,
eventually killing Bái Gōng,
and his father also died.
The King rewarded him with a hundred catties of gold.
Shēn Míng said:
"To eat the lord's food
but avoid the lord's difficulties
is not being a loyal minister;
to stabilize the lord's state
but cause the death of one's father
is not being a filial son.
Reputation cannot be established in two ways,
and conduct cannot be perfected on both sides.
If I were to live like this,
with what face could I stand before the world?"
He then committed suicide.
4.15 Duke Zhuāng of Qí was about to attack Jǔ
and selected the guests for the five chariots,
but Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu alone were not included,
so they returned home and would not eat.
Their mother said:
"If you live without righteousness
and die without a name,
then even if you were on the five chariots,
who would not laugh at you?
If you live with righteousness
and die with a name,
then the guests of the five chariots
will all be beneath you."
They hurried to eat and then departed.
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu shared a chariot,
attending Duke Zhuāng and arriving at Jǔ.
The people of Jǔ met them.
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu dismounted to fight
and captured three hundred armored heads.
Duke Zhuāng stopped them, saying:
"You two stop!
I will share the state of Qí with you."
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu said:
"The Lord chose the guests of the five chariots,
yet Zhōu and Liáng were not among them;
this was to belittle our courage.
Now that we face the enemy and wade into danger,
to stop us with profit
is to stain our conduct.
Penetrating deep and killing many
is the duty of a subject;
the profits of the state of Qí
are not for us to know."
They then advanced to fight,
breaking the army and smashing the formations;
the three armies did not dare withstand them.
Upon reaching the walls of Jǔ,
the people of Jǔ placed hot coals on the ground.
The two men stood for a while,
unable to enter.
Xíhóu Zhòng, serving as the attendant on the right, said:
"I have heard that the gentlemen of old who braved calamities and waded into danger
would see their purpose through to the end regardless of external things.
Come,
I will provide a bridge for you."
Xíhóu Zhòng leaned on his shield and lay down upon the coals;
the two men stepped over him and entered.
They looked back and wept for him.
Huá Zhōu sighed afterward,
and Qǐ Liáng said:
"Are you without courage?
Why do you weep for so long?"
Huá Zhōu said:
"How could I be without courage!
It is because his courage was equal to ours,
yet he died before me;
therefore I grieve for him."
The people of Jǔ said:
"Do not die!
We will share the state of Jǔ with you."
Qǐ Liáng and Huá Zhōu said:
"To leave one's state and defect to the enemy
is not being a loyal minister;
to desert one's superior to receive gifts
is not upright conduct.
Furthermore, to make a promise at cockcrow
and forget it by midday
is not being trustworthy.
Penetrating deep and killing many
is the duty of a subject;
the profits of the state of Jǔ
are not for us to know."
They then advanced to fight,
killed twenty-seven people and died.
When Qǐ Liáng's wife heard of it, she wept;
the wall collapsed because of it, and the corner crumbled.
This is not why it was raised.
4.16 When the Yuè army arrived at Qí,
Yōngmén Zǐdí requested to die for the state.
The King of Qí said:
"The sound of drums and bells has not been heard,
arrows and stones have not yet crossed,
and long weapons have not yet met.
Why are you so set on dying?
Is this the ritual of a minister?"
Yōngmén Zǐdí replied:
"I have heard
that in the past, a former king was hunting in a park.
The left wheel-hub squeaked,
and the chariot attendant on the right requested to die for it.
The king said:
'Why would you die?'
The chariot attendant replied:
'Because its squeaking disturbed my lord.'
The king said:
'The squeaking of the left hub
is the fault of the craftsman.
What business do you have with it?'
The chariot attendant replied:
'I did not see the craftsman's chariot;
I only saw its squeaking disturbing my lord.'
He then slit his throat and died.
Did this happen?"
The King of Qí said:
"It did."
Yōngmén Zǐdí said:
"Now the Yuè army has arrived,
and its disturbance to my lord,
is it any less than that of the left hub?
If a chariot attendant could die for a left hub,
how can I alone not die for the Yuè army?"
He then slit his throat and died.
On that day,
the people of Yuè withdrew their army and retreated seventy lǐ,
saying:
"If the King of Qí has a minister equal to Yōngmén Zǐdí,
it would likely cause the altars of the state of Yuè to lack blood sacrifices."
They then withdrew their army and returned.
The King of Qí buried Yōngmén Zǐdí with the rites of a shàng qīng.
4.17 The people of Chǔ were about to battle the people of Wú.
The Chǔ troops were few while the Wú troops were many.
The Chǔ general Zǐnáng said:
"If I attack this state, I will surely be defeated.
To disgrace the king and lose territory
is something a loyal minister cannot bear to do."
Without reporting to the king,
he withdrew the troops and retreated.
When he reached the outskirts of the capital,
he sent someone to report to the king, saying:
"I request death."
The king said:
"The retreat of the great officer
was intended for benefit,
and now it is indeed beneficial.
The great officer shall not die."
Zǐnáng said:
"If those who retreat are without guilt,
then in later generations, those who serve as ministers
will all follow my example of retreating and incur a reputation for acting disadvantageously.
If it is like this, the state of Chǔ will eventually become the weakest in the world.
I request death."
He withdrew and fell upon his sword.
The king said:
"Since it is indeed so,
I ask to fulfill the great officer's righteousness."
He then prepared a paulownia coffin three inches thick,
placed an axe and a block upon it,
and paraded it through the state.
4.18 Sòng Kāng Gōng attacked Ā
and slaughtered Shànfù.
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"Initially I did not know myself;
I thought that if I were in a state of a thousand chariots, then a state of ten thousand chariots would not dare attack it,
and if I were in a state of ten thousand chariots, then the world would not dare plot against it.
Now I, Zhào, am in Ā,
yet Sòng slaughters Shànfù.
This means that I, Zhào, have no way to establish myself.
I will go to punish the King of Sòng."
Zhào then entered Sòng,
but for three months he could not see him.
Someone said:
"Why not use the opportunity provided by an envoy from a neighboring state to see him?"
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"I cannot.
If I use a neighboring state's envoy to assassinate him,
then envoys of future generations will not be trusted,
and the reliability of those carrying credentials will not be used.
Everyone will say,
'It was Zhào who caused this.'
I cannot do it."
Someone said:
"Why not use the ministers to recommend a scholar living in retirement to assassinate him?"
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"I cannot.
If I use the ministers to recommend a scholar living in retirement to assassinate him,
then the loyal ministers of future generations will not be trusted,
and persuasive scholars will not be looked upon.
Everyone will say,
'It was Zhào who caused this.'
I cannot do it.
I have heard that of the scholars of old,
when angry they thought of reason,
and in danger they did not forget righteousness.
I must surely correct my conduct to seek it."
After a full year,
Sòng Kāng Gōng died of illness.
Chénggōng Zhào said:
"An honorable man does not disgrace his name,
and a man of faith does not neglect his conduct.
Now I was in Ā,
and Sòng slaughtered Shànfù;
this is a disgraced name.
I set about to punish the King of Sòng,
but for a full year I did not succeed;
this is neglected conduct.
If I live like this,
with what face can I see the scholars of the world?"
He then stood on the summit of Péng Shān until he withered away.
4.19 Fó Xì used the county of Zhōngmóu to rebel.
He offered cities for salaries and cooking cauldrons,
saying:
"Those who side with me shall receive a city,
and those who do not side with me shall be boiled."
The scholars of Zhōngmóu all sided with him.
Tián Jī, a young man from the north of the city, was the only one to arrive late.
He lifted his robes and was about to enter the cauldron,
saying:
"I, Jī, have heard
that for a righteous man, even if carriages and caps are in front of him,
he will not mount them if it is not righteous;
even if axes and halberds are behind him,
he will not avoid a righteous death."
He then lifted his robes and was about to enter the cauldron,
but Fó Xì waved him away and stopped him.
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ attacked Zhōngmóu,
captured it and took it.
In assessing those who had merit,
he began with Tián Jī.
Tián Jī said:
"I have heard that an honorable man does not shame others.
If I were to receive the reward for Zhōngmóu in this way,
then the scholars of Zhōngmóu would be ashamed for the rest of their lives."
He then carried his mother on his back
and moved south to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ held his righteousness in high regard
and treated him as a sīmǎ.
4.20 Qí Cuī Zhù assassinated Zhuāng Gōng.
Xíng Kuài-kuì was on a mission to Jìn and was returning
when his servant asked,
“Cuī Zhù has assassinated Zhuāng Gōng;
what will you do?”
Xíng Kuài-kuì said,
“Drive on!
I shall enter and die to repay my lord.”
The servant said,
“That your lord lacked the Way
was something that among the neighboring Zhūhóu,
there were none who had not heard.
For a gentleman like you to die for him,
is that not difficult?”
Xíng Kuài-kuì said,
“True,
you speak well,
yet it is also too late.
Had you spoken to me earlier,
I could have remonstrated with him.
If my remonstrances were not heard,
I could have left.
Now, having neither remonstrated
nor left,
I have heard that he who eats another’s stipend dies for his affairs.
Since I have already eaten the stipend of a chaotic ruler,
how can I now seek a well-governed ruler to die for?”
He then drove the carriage in and died.
The servant said,
“If people have a chaotic ruler
and yet others will die for him,
I have a well-governed superior;
can I do anything less than die?”
He then tied the reins and slit his own throat upon the carriage.
When the gentleman heard of this, he said,
“Xíng Kuài-kuì may be said to have maintained his integrity and died for righteousness.
Death is
what people find difficult;
as for the death of the servant,
although it may not have fully accorded with righteousness,
it nevertheless possessed the intent of a man of purpose.”
The Shī says,
“Morning and night without ceasing,
to serve the One Man.”
This refers to Xíng Shēng.
Mèngzǐ says,
“The brave man does not forget that he may lose his head.”
This refers to the servant.
4.21 Yān Zhāo Wáng sent Lè Yì to attack Qí,
and Mǐn Wáng fled.
When the Yān forces first entered Qí,
they heard that Wáng Chù of Gài Yì was a worthy man.
An order was issued to the army:
“Within thirty lǐ of Gài Yì,
do not enter,”
because of Wáng Chù.
Soon after, someone was sent to say to Wáng Chù,
“The people of Qí highly regard your righteousness.
I wish to make you a general
and enfeoff you with ten thousand households.”
Wáng Chù firmly declined the men of Yān.
The men of Yān said,
“If you do not comply,
I will lead the three armies and massacre Gài Yì.”
Wáng Chù said,
“A loyal minister does not serve two lords;
a chaste woman does not change her husband.
The King of Qí did not listen to my remonstrances,
so I retired to farm in the fields.
Now that the state is broken and lost,
I cannot preserve it;
if I am now coerced by military force to become your general,
this would be helping Jié to do violence.
Rather than living without righteousness,
it is certainly better to be boiled alive.”
He then hung himself from a tree branch,
threw himself down, broke his neck, and died.
When the displaced Dàfū of Qí heard of this, they said,
“Wáng Chù
was a commoner,
yet his sense of righteousness was such that he would not turn his back on Qí to face Yān.
How much more so should those who hold office and eat a stipend!”
They then gathered together and went to Jǔ,
sought out the various princes,
and established Xiāng Wáng.
4.22 Zuǒ Rú was friends with Dù Bó;
both served Zhōu Xuān Wáng.
Xuān Wáng was about to kill Dù Bó,
though it was not for any crime.
Zuǒ Rú contested this with the King,
repeating his argument nine times,
but the King would not grant it.
The King said,
“To separate from your lord and favor your friend—
that is you.”
Zuǒ Rú replied,
“I have heard that
if the lord’s way is right and the friend’s is contrary,
then one follows the lord to punish the friend;
if the friend’s way is right and the lord’s is contrary,
then one follows the friend to oppose the lord.”
The King was enraged and said,
“Change your words and you shall live;
do not change your words and you shall die.”
Zuǒ Rú replied,
“I have heard that the gentlemen of old did not twist righteousness to escape death,
nor did they change their words to seek life.
Therefore, I can make clear the King’s error
by dying for Dù Bó’s lack of guilt.”
The King killed Dù Bó,
and Zuǒ Rú died for him.
4.23 Jǔ Mù Gōng had a minister named Zhū Lì-fù,
who served Mù Gōng
but was not recognized by him.
In winter he lived in the mountains and forests,
eating acorns and chestnuts;
in summer he lived on the islands and marshes,
eating water chestnuts and lotus roots.
When Mù Gōng died in a time of crisis,
Zhū Lì-fù was about to go and die for him.
His friend said,
“You served the lord and were not recognized;
now that the lord is in crisis
and you go to die for him,
would that not be improper?”
Zhū Lì-fù said,
“Previously I thought the lord did not know me.
Now, if the lord dies and I do not die,
that would prove indeed that he did not know me.
I will go and die for him
to stimulate all those in the world who do not know their ministers.”
He then went and died for him.
4.24 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng was hunting at Yúnmèng,
shot a pheasant,
and caught it.
Shēn Gōng Zǐ-bèi attacked and seized it from him.
The King was going to kill him,
but a Dàfū remonstrated, saying,
“Zǐ-bèi is a man who respects himself;
there must be a reason for him to fight for the King’s pheasant.
May the King please investigate it.”
Before three months had passed,
Zǐ-bèi fell ill and died.
At the Battle of Bì,
Chǔ won a great victory over Jìn.
Upon returning, rewards for merit were being given.
Shēn Gōng Zǐ-bèi’s younger brother stepped forward and requested a reward from the King, saying,
“When a person has merit,
they are rewarded at the foot of the carriage.”
The King said,
“What do you mean?”
He replied,
“My elder brother read an ancient record that said:
‘He who shoots a pheasant,
before three months pass,
must die.’
My elder brother
fought to get it
and thus died prematurely.”
The King ordered the Píng Fǔ to be opened and the record checked,
and it was indeed found in the records.
He then gave him a generous reward.
5.1 The Sage's relationship to the people of the world,
is it not like that of an infant?
He feeds those who are hungry,
clothes those who are cold,
nourishes and cares for them,
rears and raises them,
fearing only that they might not reach maturity.
The *Shī* says:
"Bushy is the sweet pear tree,
do not lop it, do not fell it,
for it is where Zhào Bó halted."
The *Chuán* says:
"Those from Shǎn to the east
were governed by Zhōu Gōng;
those from Shǎn to the west
were governed by Zhào Gōng."
While Zhào Gōng was performing his official duties,
it was the time for tending silkworms and mulberries;
not wishing to disrupt the people's work,
he did not enter the towns
but stayed under a sweet pear tree to hear and adjudicate cases.
The people between Shǎn
all found their proper place,
and therefore later generations remembered and sang of him.
Because they thought well of him, they spoke of him;
when speaking was not enough,
they sighed and lamented;
when sighing and lamenting were not enough,
they sang and chanted.
The poet feels and then thinks,
thinks and then accumulates,
accumulates and then becomes full,
becomes full and then expresses it,
and the expression follows its proper path to reach its rightful place.
The common people sighed at his beauty and offered their respect.
If even the sweet pear tree was not felled,
how could government and education fail to be implemented?
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the poem 'Gān Táng',
I see the respect due to an ancestral temple.
Great indeed!
Thinking of the person,
one must love his tree;
honoring the person,
one must respect his position.
To bring peace and order to the myriad things—
how close this is to the Way of the ancient Sages!"
5.2 The virtuous teaching of a humane person
truly stems from compassion within,
sincerity in the heart,
and a mind that cannot stop itself.
Therefore, his governing of the world
is like rescuing a drowning person.
Seeing the strong bullying the weak in the world,
the many oppressing the few,
the young and orphaned exposed and naked,
the dead, wounded, and those bound as captives,
he cannot bear it to be so.
For this reason, Kǒngzǐ visited seventy-two rulers,
hoping that the Way might be put into practice once so he could apply his virtue,
to allow the people to live in full nourishment,
the commoners to be settled on their land,
the myriad things to be harmonious and prosperous,
and each to enjoy its natural end.
Ultimately, he did not find such an encounter,
so he wept upon seeing the Lín,
grieving that the Way was not practiced
and virtuous grace did not reach all.
Thereupon he retired to compose the *Chūnqiū*,
clarifying the Way of the Uncrowned King
to show to later generations.
His desire to bestow his kindness
was never interrupted or forgotten;
thus, the kings of a hundred generations honor him,
and men of purpose take him as a model.
They recite his writings.
Handed down to the present without ceasing,
it is because his virtue reached them.
The *Shī* says:
"Galloping and driving fast,
everywhere I go I consult and plan."
This is what it means.
5.3 Sage kings spread virtue and bestow kindness,
not to seek reward from the common people;
they perform the suburban sacrifices, the Dì sacrifice, and the seasonal ancestral rites,
not to seek reward from the ghosts and gods.
The mountains reach their height and clouds and rain arise there;
the waters reach their depth and scaly dragons are born there;
the gentleman achieves his Way and blessings and emoluments return to him.
For those who have hidden virtue,
there must be manifest reward;
for those who have secret deeds,
there must be a clear reputation.
In ancient times, when ditches and dikes were not maintained,
water caused harm to the people.
Yǔ cut through Lóngmén,
opened up Yīquè,
and leveled and regulated the water and land,
allowing the people to live on dry ground.
When the people were not harmonious
and the five ranks of relations were not compliant,
Xiè taught the righteousness of lord and minister,
the affection between father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
and the order between elder and younger.
When the fields and wilds were not cultivated
and the people's food was insufficient,
Hòu Jì taught them
to open up the land and clear the weeds,
to fertilize the soil and plant grain,
causing the common people's households to be provided for and every person to be satisfied.
Therefore, among the descendants of these three lords,
there were none who did not become kings,
because they had hidden virtue.
When the Zhōu house declined
and ritual and righteousness were discarded,
Kǒngzǐ used the Way of the Three Dynasties
to guide later generations;
that his lineage continues to the present day without ceasing
is because he had secret deeds.
5.4 The *Zhōu Sòng* says:
"In the year of plenty, there is much millet and rice,
and also high granaries,
by millions and billions.
Making wine and sweet spirits,
we offer them to our male and female ancestors,
to fulfill all the rituals
and bring down blessings in abundance."
The *Lǐjì* says:
"If the superior sacrificial animal is lost, then use the inferior one;
if the inferior one is lost, then the sacrifice lacks its full offerings."
This is because any deficiency causes unhappiness.
Thus, the Sage's relation to the world
is like being in a single hall.
Suppose there are people filling the hall and drinking wine,
but there is one person alone and despondent, facing a corner and weeping;
then everyone in the hall will be unhappy because of it.
The Sage's relation to the world
is like being in a single hall:
if there is even one person who has not found his place,
then the filial son would not dare to present his offerings.
5.5 Wèi Wǔhóu was floating down the Xīhé.
In midstream,
he looked back and said to Wú Qǐ:
"How beautiful!
The strength of these rivers and mountains
is the treasure of the state of Wèi."
Wú Qǐ replied:
"It lies in virtue, not in strategic obstacles.
Formerly, the Sānmiáo clan had Dòngtíng to their left and Pénglí to their right,
but because they did not cultivate virtue and righteousness, Yǔ destroyed them.
The dwelling of Xià Jié
had the Hé and Jì to the left and Tàihuà to the right,
Yīquè was to its south,
and Yángcháng to its north;
but because his governance was not humane, Tāng exiled him.
The state of Yīn Zhòu
had Mèngmén to its left and Tàiháng to its right,
Chángshān was to its north,
and the Dàhé flowed to its south;
but because his governance was not virtuous, Wǔ Wáng attacked him.
Looking at it from this,
it lies in virtue, not in strategic obstacles.
If you, my lord, do not cultivate virtue,
everyone in this boat will become an enemy state."
Wǔhóu said:
"Well said."
5.6 When Wǔ Wáng conquered Yīn,
he summoned Tài Gōng and asked:
"What shall be done with their officials and people?"
Tài Gōng replied:
"I have heard that if one loves a person,
one even loves the crows on his roof;
if one hates a person,
one even loathes his servants.
Kill all the enemies
so that none remain—
how would that be?"
The King said:
"That is not acceptable."
Tài Gōng left,
and Shào Gōng entered.
The King said:
"What should be done?"
Shào Gōng replied:
"Kill those who are guilty,
and let those who are innocent live—
how would that be?"
The King said:
"That is not acceptable."
Shào Gōng left,
and Zhōu Gōng entered.
The King said:
"What should be done?"
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Let each person live in their own dwelling
and farm their own fields.
Do not change the old for the new;
treat only the benevolent as kin.
If the common people commit faults,
let the responsibility lie with me alone."
Wǔ Wáng said:
"How vast and great is the way to pacify the world!"
The reason why scholars and gentlemen are valued
is because of their benevolence and virtue.
5.7 Kǒngzǐ said:
"To live in a neighborhood of benevolence is beautiful.
If one chooses not to dwell in benevolence,
how can one be considered wise?"
A person of benevolence must practice reciprocity before acting.
To perform one unrighteous deed
or to kill one innocent person,
even if it leads to obtaining a high office or a great position,
a benevolent person would not do it.
A person of great benevolence
extends love from those who are near to those who are far.
When there is disharmony,
one sacrifices small benevolence to achieve great benevolence.
Great benevolence
reaches the Four Seas;
small benevolence
stops at one's wife and children.
Wives and children
use their cleverness to seek profit,
use a woman’s affection to soothe,
disguise their inner feelings,
and embellish their falsehoods;
who can tell if they are not genuine?
Although one may enjoy honor for a time,
scholars and gentlemen consider it a great disgrace.
Therefore, Gòng Gōng, Huān Dòu, Fú Lǐ, and Dèng Xī,
were not lacking in intelligence or knowledge;
however, the reason they were executed by the Sage Kings
was that they lacked virtue and sought profit improperly.
Shù Diāo and Yì Yá mutilated their bodies or killed their sons to seek profit,
and eventually became rebels in Qí.
Therefore, if ministers are not benevolent,
the chaos of usurpation and assassination arises;
if ministers are benevolent,
the state is well-governed and the ruler is honored.
An enlightened ruler observes this,
and the ancestral temple remains in great peace.
If even ministers should value benevolence,
how much more so for the ruler of men?
Thus Jié and Zhòu lost the world through lack of benevolence,
while Tāng and Wǔ gained the lands of the seas by accumulating virtue.
For this reason, Sage Kings value virtue and strive to practice it.
《Mèngzǐ》 says:
"Extending one's kindness is enough to reach the Four Seas;
not extending one's kindness is not even enough to protect one's wife and children.
The reason why the ancients greatly surpassed others was for no other reason than this:
they were good at extending what they had."
5.8 Yàn Zǐ was serving wine to Jǐng Gōng,
and ordered that the vessels must be new.
The household steward said:
"Our resources are insufficient;
I request to collect taxes from the people."
Yàn Zǐ said:
"Stop!
Joy is something shared by both superiors and subordinates.
Thus the Son of Heaven shares it with the world,
the feudal lords share it with those within their borders,
and from the grand masters down, each shares it with their colleagues;
there is no such thing as solitary joy.
Now if the superior enjoys his pleasure
while the subordinates suffer from the expense,
this is solitary joy.
It is not acceptable."
5.9 Qí Huán Gōng led a northern expedition against the Shān Róng tribe,
and his path took him through Yān.
The ruler of Yān welcomed him and saw him off beyond the border.
Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"According to ritual, when feudal lords welcome one another,
do they go beyond the border?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Unless it is for the Son of Heaven, they do not go beyond the border."
Huán Gōng said:
"In that case, the ruler of Yān has committed a breach of ritual out of fear.
It would be unprincipled of me
to cause the ruler of Yān to violate ritual."
He then carved off the land that the ruler of Yān had reached
and gave it to the ruler of Yān.
When the feudal lords heard of this,
they all paid court to Qí.
The 《Shī》 says:
"Be peaceful and reverent in your position,
and love those who are upright;
the spirits will hear of it,
and grant you great blessings."
This is what is meant by that.
5.10 Jǐng Gōng was reaching for a sparrow chick;
the chick was weak,
so he put it back.
Yàn Zǐ heard of this
and without waiting, he entered to see him.
The Duke was perspiring and looked apprehensive.
Yàn Zǐ said:
"What was my Lord doing?"
Jǐng Gōng said:
"I was reaching for a sparrow chick;
the chick was weak,
so I put it back."
Yàn Zǐ stepped back, faced north, bowed twice, and congratulated him, saying:
"My Lord possesses the way of the Sage Kings!"
Jǐng Gōng said:
"I was only reaching for a sparrow chick,
and since it was weak,
I put it back.
How does that correspond to the way of the Sage Kings?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"My Lord reached for a sparrow chick,
and because it was weak,
you put it back—
this is a concern for the young and vulnerable.
My Lord’s benevolence and love
even extend to birds and beasts;
how much more so then for people?
This is the way of the Sage Kings."
5.11 Jǐng Gōng saw an infant begging on the road.
The Duke said:
"Does this child have nowhere to go?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Since my Lord is here,
why should anyone have nowhere to go?
Have the officials care for him,
and let the matter be reported immediately."
5.12 Jǐng Gōng was traveling in the Shòu Gōng palace
and saw an elderly man carrying firewood who had the look of hunger.
The Duke felt pity for him
and with a sigh ordered the officials to care for him.
Yàn Zǐ said:
"I have heard
that to delight in the worthy and pity the unworthy
is the foundation of guarding the state.
Now my Lord loves the elderly,
and your kindness reaches everywhere;
this is the foundation of governing the state."
The Duke smiled,
having a look of joy.
Yàn Zǐ said:
"A Sage King, seeing the worthy, takes delight in their worthiness;
seeing the unworthy, he pities their lack of worth.
Now I request that those old and weak who are not cared for,
and those widowers and widows who have no homes,
be evaluated and provided with regular support."
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, the elderly and the weak had care,
and the widowers and widows had homes.
5.13 When Huán Gōng went to Pínglíng,
he saw a commoner who was elderly and supporting himself.
The Duke asked him the reason,
and he replied:
“I have nine sons,
but my family is poor and has no means to provide them with wives.
I have sent them out as hired laborers, and they have not yet returned.”
Huán Gōng took five of his female attendants and gave them as wives.
Guǎn Zhòng entered to see him and said:
“Is your Grace’s bestowal of kindness not too small?”
The Duke asked:
“Why so?”
He replied:
“If your Grace waits until you see someone before bestowing kindness,
then there will be few in the state of Qí who have wives.”
The Duke said:
“What should be done?”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“Order that men of the state marry at twenty
and women marry at fifteen.”
5.14 When the Emperor Xiào Xuān first ascended the throne,
Lù Wēnshū, a minor official of the Court of Justice, submitted a memorial
speaking on valuing virtue and slowing punishments.
His words said:
“When Your Majesty first ascended the supreme position,
tallying with the mandate of Heaven,
