you should correct the mistakes of previous generations,
rectify the lineage you have received,
cleanse the cumbersome regulations,
remove the suffering of the people,
preserve those who are perishing and continue those whose lines are severed,
to respond to the virtue of Heaven,
which would be a great fortune for the world.
I have heard that in the past Qín had ten faults,
and one of them still remains,
which is the officials who manage the prisons.
Formerly in the time of Qín,
they destroyed literature and learning,
favored military prowess,
belittled men of benevolence and righteousness,
and honored officials who managed the prisons.
Upright words were called slander,
and pointing out faults was called deceptive speech.
Therefore, gentlemen in formal robes were not employed in the world,
the earnest words of loyal and good men were pent up in their chests,
while sounds of praise and flattery filled the ears daily.
Empty beauty intoxicated the heart,
while real calamities were obscured and blocked.
This is why Qín lost the world.
Now, all within the seas rely on Your Majesty’s deep grace;
there is no danger of war,
nor the suffering of hunger and cold.
Fathers and sons, husbands and wives work together to secure their homes;
the world is very fortunate.
However, the reason great peace is not yet harmonized
is that the prisons are in chaos.
Now, prisons
are the great fate of the world;
those who die cannot be brought back to life,
and those who are severed cannot be reattached.
The Book of History says:
‘Rather than kill the innocent,
it is better to fail to follow the standard.’
Today’s prison officials are not like this;
superiors and subordinates drive each other,
taking harshness as brilliance.
Those who are severe gain a public reputation,
while those who are fair suffer many later troubles.
Therefore, prison officials all desire to condemn to death;
it is not that they hate people,
but that their way of securing themselves lies in the death of others.
Consequently, the blood of the dead flows in the markets,
those subjected to punishment stand shoulder to shoulder,
and the number of those sentenced to death is counted in the tens of thousands annually;
this is what grieves the sages.
That great peace is not yet harmonized
is entirely because of this.
It is human nature to be happy with life when at peace
and to think of death when in pain.
Under the beating of the rod,
what confession can they not obtain?
Thus, when prisoners cannot bear the pain,
they fabricate false words to satisfy the officials;
and when the officials who manage them find this advantageous,
they guide them to make it clear.
Fearing the memorial might be rejected by superiors,
they refine and manipulate it to ensure it is thorough.
When the indictment is complete,
even if Gāo Yáo heard it,
he would still think the death penalty was more than deserved.
Why?
Because those who refined it are many,
and the crime composed in writing is clear.
Thus prison officials specialize in being deep and harsh;
they are cruel and destructive without limit,
acting shiftily for the moment,
and ignoring the troubles of the state.
These are the great thieves of the age.
Thus the proverb says:
‘If you draw a prison on the ground,
consider not entering it;
if you carve an official from wood,
do not hope to confront him.’
These are all expressions of resentment against the officials’ style,
and words of grief and pain.
Therefore, among the troubles of the world,
none is deeper than the prisons;
for ruining laws and disturbing governance,
and for separating relatives and blocking the Way,
none is worse than the officials who manage the prisons.
This is what I meant by the one fault that still remains.
I have heard that if the eggs in a bird’s nest are not destroyed,
then the fènghuáng will gather there;
if the crime of slander is not punished,
then good words will be presented.
Thus the Traditions say:
‘Mountains and marshes hide diseases,
rivers and lakes accept filth,
fine jade conceals flaws,
and the ruler of a state tolerates insults;
this is the Way of Heaven.’
Risking death, I bring this to your attention.
I wish Your Majesty would examine slander,
listen to earnest words,
open the mouths of those in the world,
broaden the path for admonishment,
correct this one fault of the fallen Qín,
follow the excellent virtue of Wén and Wǔ,
reduce legal regulations,
relax punishments,
and abolish troublesome prison matters.
Then the wind of great peace can rise in the world,
blessings and harmony will be enjoyed,
lasting as long as Heaven without end,
and the world will be very fortunate.”
The memorial was submitted,
and the Emperor approved of it.
Later, he eventually became the Grand Governor of Línhuái.
5.15 In spring, Jìn Píng Gōng was building a terrace.
Shū Xiàng said:
“It is not permissible.
In ancient times, the sage kings valued virtue and strove to bestow it;
they relaxed punishments and prioritized the people’s farming seasons.
Now, to build a terrace in spring
is to take away the people’s time.
If virtue is not bestowed, the people will not return;
if punishments are not relaxed, the common people will be sorrowful.
To employ people who have not returned,
to use commoners who are sorrowful and resentful,
and furthermore to take away their farming time
is to double their exhaustion.
Now, in shepherding the common people,
to nurture them while doubling their exhaustion
is surely not the way to stabilize their lives and ensure their survival,
or to be called a ruler of men in later generations!”
Píng Gōng said:
“Good.”
He then ceased the labor on the terrace.
5.16 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ was building a terrace in Hándān in spring.
The rain fell without ceasing.
He said to his attendants:
“Can we not hurry the sowing?”
Yǐn Duó replied:
“The public business is urgent,
so they have set aside their seeds and hung them on the terrace.
Even if they wanted to hurry the sowing,
they could not do so.”
Jiǎn Zǐ was startled;
he then abandoned the terrace and ceased the labor,
saying:
“I considered the terrace urgent,
but it is not as urgent as the people’s needs.
Because the people did not have to build the terrace,
they will know of my love.”
5.17 Zhōngháng Xiàn Zǐ was about to attack Zhèng.
Fàn Wén Zǐ said:
“It is not permissible.
Even if you achieve your aims in Zhèng,
the feudal lords will resent us,
and worries will surely grow.”
Xì Zhì then said:
“To obtain Zhèng
is to annex a state.
Annexing states makes one a king.
Do kings truly have many worries?”
Wén Zǐ said:
“A king flourishes in his virtue and those from afar return to him;
therefore he has no worries.
Now we have little virtue yet achieve the feats of a king;
therefore we have many worries.
Now, have you ever seen someone with no land but desiring wealth and joy?”
5.18 Jì Kāng Zǐ said to Zǐ Yóu:
"Does a person of benevolence love others?"
Zǐ Yóu said:
"Yes."
"Do others also love them?"
Zǐ Yóu said:
"Yes."
Kāng Zǐ said:
"When Zǐ Chǎn died,
the people of Zhèng
—the men discarded their jade rings and pendants,
the women discarded their pearl earrings,
couples wailed in the alleys,
and for three months the sound of flutes and zithers was not heard.
At the death of Zhòng Ní,
I did not hear of the state of Lǔ loving the Master in such a way.
Why is that?"
Zǐ Yóu said:
"Comparing Zǐ Chǎn to the Master
is perhaps like comparing irrigation water to rain from heaven.
Where irrigation water reaches, there is life;
where it does not reach, there is death.
But as for the lives of these people,
they must depend on timely rain.
Once they have been given life,
none recognize the love in its gift.
Therefore I say:
Is comparing Zǐ Chǎn to the Master
not like comparing irrigation water to rain from heaven?"
5.19 Zhōng Háng Mù Zǐ besieged Gǔ.
A person from Gǔ offered to rebel and hand over the city,
but he would not permit it.
The military officers said:
"The soldiers would not have to toil,
and we could obtain the city.
For what reason do you not accept it?"
He said:
"Having someone rebel with their city for me
is what I most detest.
If a person comes to me with a city,
why should I alone be fond of it?
To reward what I most detest
is to lose the standard of reward.
What then of that which I am fond of?
If I do not reward it,
that is to lose trustworthiness;
how then could I show myself to the people?"
The people of Gǔ again requested to surrender.
He sent someone to observe them;
their people still had food,
so he did not listen.
When the people of Gǔ reported their food was exhausted and their strength spent,
only then did he take it.
After conquering Gǔ, he returned,
without executing a single person.
5.20 When Kǒng Zǐ went to Chǔ,
a fisherman offered a fish that was very large;
Kǒng Zǐ would not accept it.
The fisherman said:
"The weather is hot and the market is far;
if I try to sell it and it does not sell,
I would think to throw it away on a dung heap.
It is better to offer it to a gentleman."
Kǒng Zǐ bowed twice and accepted it.
He had his disciples sweep the area, intending to sacrifice it.
The disciples said:
"That person was going to throw it away,
yet now the Master is going to sacrifice it;
why?"
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"I have heard
that one who strives to be generous and does not let surplus wealth rot
is a sage.
Now that I have received a sage’s gift,
can I not perform a sacrifice?"
5.21 Zhèng attacked Sòng,
and the people of Sòng were about to battle them.
Huà Yuán slaughtered sheep to feed the soldiers,
but his charioteer Yáng Zhēn was not included.
When it came to the battle,
Yáng Zhēn said:
"Regarding the mutton broth of the other day,
you were the one in charge;
regarding the affairs of today,
I am the one in charge."
He galloped with Huà Yuán into the Zhèng army,
and the people of Sòng were soundly defeated.
5.22 The King of Chǔ asked Zhuāng Xīn:
"What is the conduct of a gentleman
like?"
Zhuāng Xīn replied:
"At home he does not build high walls,
yet no one can harm him;
traveling he does not follow a guard,
yet no one can commit violence against him.
This is the conduct of a gentleman."
The King of Chǔ asked again:
"What is the wealth of a gentleman
like?"
He replied:
"The wealth of a gentleman
is to lend to others
without claiming virtue
and without demanding repayment.
When he provides food and drink to others,
he does not use them
and does not press them into labor.
Relatives love him,
the common people speak well of him,
and even the unworthy serve him,
all desiring for him to have a long and happy life without suffering misfortune.
This is the wealth of a gentleman."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Excellent."
5.23 The Chancellor and Marquis of Xī Píng, Yú Dìng Guó,
was a man of Xià Pī in Dōng Hǎi.
His father was known as Yú Gōng.
He served as a legal official and decisive officer in the county prison,
deciding cases and balancing the law,
and there was never anyone who suffered a grievance.
Those in the commandery who fell foul of the laws,
when their cases were decided by Yú Gōng,
none dared to hide the facts.
The people of Dōng Hǎi Commandery established a shrine for Yú Gōng during his lifetime,
naming it the Shrine of Yú Gōng.
In Dōng Hǎi there was a filial woman;
she had no children
and was widowed young,
yet she cared for her mother-in-law very diligently.
Her mother-in-law wanted her to remarry,
but she never would.
Her mother-in-law told the neighbors:
"This filial woman cares for me very diligently.
I pity her for having no children and remaining a widow for a long time.
I am old
and a burden to the young and vigorous;
what can be done?"
Later, the mother-in-law hanged herself and died.
The daughter of the mother-in-law told the officials:
"The woman killed my mother."
The officials arrested the filial woman.
The filial woman denied killing her mother-in-law.
The officials intended to use harsh torture,
so the filial woman falsely confessed.
When the completed case was sent up to the higher office,
Yú Gōng believed that she had cared for her mother-in-law for ten years and was known for her filial piety,
so she could not have killed her mother-in-law.
The Grand Administrator would not listen.
Even after arguing several times, Yú Gōng could not prevail,
so Yú Gōng resigned from his post, claiming illness.
The Grand Administrator ultimately executed the filial woman.
For three years, the commandery suffered a parched drought.
When a later Grand Administrator arrived,
he sought the cause through divination.
Yú Gōng said:
"The filial woman should not have died.
The previous Grand Administrator forced her execution,
and the fault must lie there."
Thereupon, a bull was slaughtered to sacrifice at the filial woman's grave;
the Grand Administrator and everyone below him went there in person.
Heavens immediately sent a great rain,
and the year's harvest was abundant.
Because of this, the people of the commandery respected and honored Yú Gōng even more.
When Yú Gōng was building his house,
he said to the craftsmen:
"Make a high gate for me.
In my handling of cases, I have never caused anyone a grievance;
my descendants will surely have those who are enfeoffed as marquises.
Make it wide enough to accommodate a high-canopied carriage drawn by four horses."
When it came to his son,
he was indeed enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xī Píng.
5.24 Mèng Jiǎn Zǐ served as prime minister of Liáng
and annexed Wèi.
Having committed a crime, he fled to Qí.
Guǎn Zhòng welcomed him and asked,
“When you were prime minister of Liáng and annexed Wèi,
how many followers did you have at your gate?”
Mèng Jiǎn Zǐ said,
“I had more than three thousand followers at my gate.”
Guǎn Zhòng asked,
“With how many people have you come now?”
He replied,
“I have come with three people.”
Guǎn Zhòng asked,
“Why is this?”
He replied,
“One person’s father died and he had no means to bury him,
so I buried him for him.
One person’s mother died and she had no means to be buried,
so I also buried her for him.
One person’s brother was in prison,
and I secured his release.
This is why I was able to come with these three people.”
Guǎn Zhòng boarded his carriage and said,
“Alas!
I will surely meet with destitution!
I cannot breeze upon people like the spring wind;
I cannot rain upon people like the summer rain.
I will surely meet with destitution!”
5.25 It is the nature of all people
that none do not desire to make their virtue good.
Yet, those who cannot practice good virtue
are ruined by profit.
Therefore, a Jūnzǐ is ashamed to speak of profit and fame.
If even speaking of profit and fame is shameful,
how much more so for one who lives to seek profit?
The Son of Heaven of Zhōu sent Jiāfù and Máobó to seek carriages and gold from the feudal lords;
the *Chūnqiū* criticizes this.
Therefore, if the Son of Heaven loves profit, the feudal lords will be greedy.
If the feudal lords are greedy, the grand masters will be base.
If the grand masters are base, the commoners will be thieves.
The transformation of inferiors by superiors
is like the wind bending the grass.
Therefore, those who are rulers
should clearly value virtue and despise profit to lead the inferiors.
Even so, if the inferiors do evil,
it still cannot be stopped.
Now, Yǐn Gōng was greedy for profit and personally fished on the Jì River
and performed the eight-row dance;
using this to transform the people of the state,
how could the people not neglect righteousness?
Neglecting righteousness and indulging their desires,
disasters will arise and subordinates will become depraved.
Therefore, in his fifth year, it was first recorded “locusts,”
meaning that disasters were about to arise
and the state was about to fall into chaos.
5.26 Sūn Qīng said:
“Now, those who fight
are those who forget their own lives,
forget their kin,
and forget their ruler.
Acting on a momentary anger to fight,
causing lifelong calamity,
and yet they still do it;
this is forgetting one’s life.
Their household is dispersed,
and their relatives are executed;
and yet they still do it;
this is forgetting one’s kin.
It is what the ruler and superiors detest
and what the penal laws strictly forbid;
and yet they violate them;
this is forgetting one’s ruler.
Now, even birds and beasts know to stay near their parents
and do not forget their kin.
If a person forgets their life,
internally forgets their kin,
and above forgets their ruler,
then they are not as benevolent as birds and beasts.
All those who fight
think they are right
and others are wrong.
If oneself is truly right
and the other is truly wrong,
then one is a Jūnzǐ and the other is a Xiǎorén.
For a Jūnzǐ to harm and be harmed by a Xiǎorén,
is what people call using white fox fur to patch dog or sheep skin,
or smearing oneself with charcoal;
is this not excessive?
Do they think it is wise?
Then there is no greater folly.
Do they think it is profitable?
Then there is no greater harm.
Do they think it is honorable?
Then there is no greater disgrace.
Why do people fight?
What is the reason?
Is it because they are like the mad, deluded, or diseased?
No, it is not.
They have human faces and many shared likes and dislikes.
People who fight
are truly foolish, deluded, and have lost the Way.”
The *Shījīng* says:
“Shouting and calling out,
they turn day into night.”
This refers to the conduct of fighting.
5.27 Zi Lù held a sword.
Kǒngzǐ asked,
“Yóu,
what use is this?”
Zi Lù said,
“One who was good in ancient times
certainly used it to be good;
one who was not good in ancient times
certainly used it for self-defense.”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“A Jūnzǐ takes loyalty as his substance
and benevolence as his defense.
Without leaving his small dwelling,
he is heard of a thousand *lǐ* away.
One who is not good is transformed by loyalty;
the violent and rebellious are surrounded by benevolence.
Why must one hold a sword?”
Zi Lù said,
“I, Yóu,
request to lift my robes and serve you, Master.”
5.28 Lè Yáng was a general for Wèi Wén Hóu
to attack Zhōngshān.
His son was in Zhōngshān at the time.
The people of Zhōngshān hung his son to show Lè Yáng.
Lè Yáng did not let his resolve falter
and attacked even more urgently.
Zhōngshān then boiled his son and sent him the broth.
Lè Yáng ate a whole bowl of it.
Zhōngshān saw his sincerity
and could not bear to fight him further,
and so they surrendered.
Consequently, he expanded the territory for Wén Hóu.
Wén Hóu rewarded his achievement but doubted his heart.
Mèng Sūn went hunting and caught a fawn.
He ordered Qín Xībā to take it back.
Its mother followed, crying out.
Qín Xībā could not bear it
and released the fawn to its mother.
Mèng Sūn was angry and banished Qín Xībā.
After one year,
he summoned him to be the tutor for his son.
The attendants said,
“Qín Xībā committed a crime against you,
yet now you make him your son’s tutor.
Why?”
Mèng Sūn said,
“If he could not bear the suffering of a single fawn,
how could he bear to harm my son?”
Therefore it is said:
Clever deception is not as good as clumsy sincerity.
Lè Yáng was doubted despite his achievement,
while Qín Xībā was more trusted despite his crime,
because of benevolence and the lack thereof.
5.29 Zhì Bó returned from Wèi,
and the Three Ministers held a banquet at Lántái.
Zhì Xiāngzǐ teased Hán Kāngzǐ and insulted Duàn Guī.
Zhì Guǒ heard of this,
and cautioned him, saying:
"If the master does not prepare for trouble,
trouble will surely arrive."
Zhì Xiāngzǐ replied:
"Trouble will be dictated by me.
If I do not create trouble,
who would dare to start it?"
Zhì Guǒ replied:
"It is otherwise.
The Xì clan had the trouble at Chēyuán;
the Zhào clan had the slander of Mèng Jī;
the Luán clan had the accusation of Shū Qí;
the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans had the trouble at Hányě.
These are all known to you, master.
The *Xià Shū* says:
'If one person makes three mistakes,
is resentment only found in the open?
One must plan for what is not yet visible.'
The *Zhōu Shū* says:
'Resentment does not lie in greatness,
nor does it lie in smallness.'
A superior man can be diligent in small matters,
thus he has no great calamities.
Now, in a single plan, the master has shamed a lord and his minister,
and yet you do not prepare,
saying,
'They dare not start trouble.'
Is this not unacceptable?
Alas!
One must not fail to be fearful;
even gnats, ants, bees, and scorpions
can all harm people,
how much more so a lord and his minister?"
Zhì Xiāngzǐ did not listen.
Five years after this,
there was the crisis at Jìnyáng,
and Duàn Guī turned against him and killed Zhì Bó in the army,
subsequently exterminating the Zhì clan.
5.30 Zhì Xiāngzǐ built a beautiful house,
and Shì Zhuó visited him in the evening.
Zhì Bó said:
"The house is truly beautiful!"
Shì Zhuó replied:
"Beautiful it indeed is,
but your servant also feels fear."
Zhì Bó said:
"What is there to fear?"
He replied:
"I serve my lord by holding the brush.
The records say:
'High mountains with deep springs
do not grow grass or trees;
in land of pines and cypresses,
the soil is not fertile.'
Now that the woodwork excels people,
I fear it will not put the people at ease."
Three years after the house was completed,
the Zhì clan perished.
6.1 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Virtue is not lonely;
it must have neighbors."
Now, those who bestow virtue value not being self-righteous about it;
those who receive kindness value certain repayment.
Therefore, a minister labors diligently for the lord without seeking reward;
the lord maintains his bounty to shepherd subordinates without priding himself on his virtue.
Thus the *Yì* says:
"To labor without resentment,
to have merit without being self-righteous about one's virtue,
is the height of generosity."
When lord and minister interact,
they connect through the ways of the market:
the lord suspends salary to wait for the minister,
and the minister exhausts his strength to repay the lord.
When it comes to a minister having unpredictable merit,
then the master adds to it with heavy rewards;
if the master has extraordinary kindness,
then the minister must face death to return it.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the north, there is a beast
whose name is the Jué;
its front legs are like a mouse's,
and its hind legs are like a rabbit's.
This beast
greatly loves the Qióngqióng and Jùxū;
when it finds sweet grass,
it must chew it and leave it for the Qióngqióng and Jùxū.
When the Qióngqióng and Jùxū see someone coming,
they must carry the Jué on their backs and flee.
It is not that the Jué by nature loves the Qióngqióng and Jùxū,
but because it borrows their legs;
those two beasts
also do not by nature love the Jué,
but because it finds sweet grass and leaves it for them.
If even birds, beasts, and insects know how to rely on each other for mutual repayment,
how much more so should scholars and superior men who wish to establish fame and profit in the world?"
If a minister does not return the lord's kindness
and instead recklessly manages his private interests,
it is the source of calamity.
If a lord cannot reward a minister's merit
and shrinks from distributing rewards,
it is also the foundation of disorder.
The sources and foundations of calamity and disorder
arise from not repaying kindness.
6.2 Zhào Xiāngzǐ was besieged at Jìnyáng.
When the siege was lifted,
he rewarded five ministers who had merit.
Gāo Hè had no merit but received the highest reward,
and all five men were angry.
Zhāng Mèngtán said to Xiāngzǐ:
"In Jìnyáng,
Gāo Hè had no great merit;
now you give him the highest reward,
why?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"When I was in the midst of distress,
the one who did not lose the etiquette between minister and lord
was only Gāo Hè.
Although you all have merit,
you were all arrogant.
For me to give Gāo Hè the highest reward,
is it not also acceptable?"
Zhòngní heard this and said:
"Zhào Xiāngzǐ can be called one who is good at rewarding scholars;
by rewarding one man,
among those who are ministers in the world,
none will dare lose the etiquette between lord and minister."
6.3 When Jìn Wéngōng was in exile,
Táo Shūhú followed him.
When Wéngōng returned to his state,
he distributed rewards three times but did not reach Táo Shūhú.
Táo Shūhú saw Jiù Fàn and said:
"I followed my lord into exile for thirteen years;
my face became dark and withered,
and my hands and feet became calloused.
Now that the lord has returned to his state
and has distributed rewards three times without reaching me,
could it be that the lord has forgotten me?
Or do I have some great fault?
Please try to speak to the lord for me."
Jiù Fàn spoke of it to Wéngōng.
Wéngōng said:
"Alas,
how could I forget this man!
Those who are lofty, brilliant, and most worthy,
whose virtuous conduct is complete and sincere,
who sustained me with the Way
and persuaded me with benevolence,
who refined my conduct
and illuminated my name,
making me a complete person—
I consider them for the highest reward.
Those who restrained me with ritual,
cautioned me with righteousness,
protected and supported me,
preventing me from doing wrong,
and who frequently led me to the gates of worthy men—
I consider them for the next reward.
As for those who were brave, strong, and powerful,
who stood in front when trouble was in front
and stood behind when trouble was behind,
delivering me from within calamities and troubles—
I consider them for the next level.
Moreover, have you alone not heard?
Those who die for a person are not as good as those who preserve a person's life;
those who die for an exile are not as good as those who preserve an exile's state.
After the three distributions of rewards,
the men of hard labor come next.
Among the men of hard labor,
this man is indeed the foremost.
How would I dare forget him?"
Zhōu Nèishǐ Shù Xīng heard of this and said:
"Will Wéngōng not become a hegemon!
In ancient times, the sage kings put virtue first and strength second;
Wéngōng has surely met this standard!"
The *Shī* says:
"Follow the rituals without transgressing."
This refers to this.
6.4 Jìn Wén Gōng entered his state;
he reached the Hé.
He ordered the disposal of the ritual bamboo and wooden vessels, and the mats and rugs;
those whose complexions were sallow and dark, and whose hands and feet were calloused,
were to stay behind.
Jiù Fàn heard this
and wept in the middle of the night.
Wén Gōng said:
"I have been in exile for nineteen years,
and now I am about to return to my state.
You, Master, do not rejoice but instead weep;
why is this?
Is it that you do not wish for me to return to my state?"
He replied:
"The ritual vessels and the mats and rugs
were what were used for your service, yet you discard them;
those whose complexions are sallow and dark
and whose hands and feet are calloused
are those who bore the labor and hardship, yet you put them all behind.
I have heard that if a ruler of a state obscures the scholars,
he will have no way to obtain loyal ministers;
if a Dà Fū obscures those with whom he traveled,
he will have no way to obtain loyal friends.
Now that we have reached the state,
I am among those to be obscured;
I cannot overcome my grief,
and therefore I weep."
Wén Gōng said:
"If disaster, fortune, profit, or harm
are not shared with the Jiù family,
may the clear water bear witness."
He invoked a curse,
then submerged a jade disc and made a covenant.
6.5 Jiè Zǐ Tuī said:
"Of the nine sons of Xiàn Gōng,
only the Lord remains.
Heaven has not yet cut off Jìn,
so it must have a ruler.
As for the one who presides over the sacrifices of Jìn,
who could it be but the Lord!
For these few gentlemen
to consider it their own effort
—is that not deceitful?"
When Wén Gōng ascended the throne,
the rewards did not reach Tuī.
Tuī's mother said:
"Why not also seek it?"
Tuī said:
"To find fault with others and then imitate them
is a crime even more severe.
Furthermore, I have uttered words of resentment;
I will not eat his food."
His mother said:
"At least let him know of it."
Tuī said:
"Words
are the adornment of the person.
Since I am about to go into hiding,
what use is adornment?"
His mother said:
"If you can be like this,
I will go into hiding together with you."
Until their deaths, they were never seen again.
Tuī's followers pitied him,
so they hung a writing on the palace gate that said:
"There was a dragon, soaring and grand,
who for a time lost its place.
Five snakes followed it,
wandering throughout the world.
The dragon was hungry and had no food;
one snake cut its own thigh.
The dragon has returned to its abyss
and is at peace in its territory.
Four snakes have entered their holes,
each having a place.
One snake has no hole
and cries out in the open wilds."
Wén Gōng went out,
saw the writing, and said:
"Alas!
This is Jiè Zǐ Tuī.
I was just preoccupied with the Royal House
and had not yet planned for his merit."
He sent people to summon him,
but he was gone.
He then sought his whereabouts
and heard that he had entered the mountains of Miánshàng.
Thereupon, Wén Gōng marked the mountains of Miánshàng and enfeoffed them,
making them the fields of Jiè Tuī,
and called them Mount Jiè.
6.6 When Jìn Wén Gōng went into exile
and traveled throughout the world,
Zhōu Zhī Qiáo left Yú and followed him.
When Wén Gōng returned to his state,
he chose those who could be ennobled and ennobled them,
and chose those who could receive a stipend and gave them stipends,
but only Zhōu Zhī Qiáo was not included.
Wén Gōng poured wine for the various Dà Fū.
When they were merry with wine,
Wén Gōng said:
"Why do you gentlemen not compose a poem for me?"
Zhōu Zhī Qiáo stepped forward and said:
"A superior man composes a poem;
a lowly man asks to present his words.
The words say:
'There was a dragon, soaring and grand,
who for a time lost its place.
One snake followed it,
wandering throughout the world.
The dragon has returned to its abyss
and is peaceful in its place.
One snake is withered and dry,
alone not finding its place.'"
Wén Gōng was startled and said:
"Do you desire a noble rank?
Please wait for the appointed time tomorrow morning.
Do you desire a stipend?
I shall command the lǐn rén now."
Zhōu Zhī Qiáo said:
"To receive a reward after asking for it
is what an incorruptible person does not accept;
to achieve fame through exhaustive speech
is what a humane person does not do.
Now, the sky naturally forms clouds
and copiously sends down rain,
then the sprouts and grass spring up,
and nothing can stop them.
Now, to grant a favor to one person because of that person's words
is like raining upon a single clod of earth;
the earth will not produce anything from it."
He then descended the steps and left.
Wén Gōng sought him but could not find him;
for the rest of his life, he recited the poem Fǔ Tián.
6.7 Bǐng Jí performed acts of hidden virtue for Xiào Xuān Huáng Dì when the Emperor was of low status.
When Xiào Xuān Huáng Dì ascended the throne,
no one knew of this,
and Jí also did not speak of it.
Jí was promoted from Senior Clerk to the Dà Jiàng Jūn until he reached the position of Yù Shǐ Dà Fū.
When Xuān Dì heard of his deeds,
he was about to enfeoff him.
It happened that Jí was very ill;
the Emperor was about to send someone to invest him with the sash and enfeoff him
while he was still alive.
The Emperor was worried that Jí would not recover from his illness.
The Tài Zǐ Tài Fù, Xiàhóu Shèng, said:
"He will not die yet.
I have heard that
one who has hidden virtue will surely enjoy its happiness
and it will extend to his descendants.
Now he has not yet obtained its happiness and is very ill;
this is not his fatal illness."
Later, his illness indeed recovered.
He was enfeoffed as the Bóyáng Hóu
and ultimately enjoyed that happiness.
6.8 Wèi Wén Hóu attacked Zhōngshān,
with Lè Yáng as the general.
Having already captured Zhōngshān,
he returned to report to Wèi Wén Hóu,
with an expression of pride in his merit.
Wèi Wén Hóu commanded the Master of Documents:
"Take the documents presented by the various ministers and guests
and bring them forward."
The Master of Documents lifted two chests and brought them forward,
ordering the general to look at them.
They were all documents about the difficulties of attacking Zhōngshān.
The general stepped back and withdrew,
then faced north and bowed twice, saying:
"The capture of Zhōngshān
was not due to my strength,
but was the merit of my Lord."
6.9 After Píngyuán Jūn had returned to Zhào,
Chǔ sent Chūnshēn Jūn to lead troops to rescue Zhào,
and Xìnlíng Jūn of Wèi also forged orders to seize Jìn Bǐ’s army and went to rescue Zhào,
but neither had arrived yet.
Qín urgently besieged Hándān,
and Hándān was in such peril that it was about to surrender.
Píngyuán Jūn was distressed by this.
Lǐ Tán, the son of an official at the Hándān guesthouse, said to Píngyuán Jūn:
“Are you not worried about the fall of Zhào?”
Píngyuán Jūn said:
“If Zhào falls, then I, Shèng, will be a captive.
How could I not be worried?”
Lǐ Tán said:
“The people of Hándān
are burning bones for fuel and exchanging children to eat them;
it can be said they are in extreme hardship.
Yet your inner palace houses women by the hundreds,
your wives and concubines wear fine silks and gauzes,
and your kitchen has surplus fine grain and meat.
The people are exhausted and the soldiers’ resources are spent;
some sharpen wood to make spears and halberds,
while your vessels, bells, and chimes remain as they were.
If you allow Qín to destroy Zhào,
how could you keep all this?
If Zhào is preserved,
why should you worry about having nothing?
If you truly can order your ladies and those below them to be organized among the soldiers,
share the work and labor,
and distribute everything your household possesses to feast the soldiers.
While they are in danger and suffering,
it is easy to show them kindness.”
Thereupon, Píngyuán Jūn followed his plan,
and three thousand brave men
all went out to face death,
following Lǐ Tán to charge the Qín army.
The Qín army was pushed back thirty lǐ.
It also happened that the reinforcements from Chǔ and Wèi arrived,
and the Qín army finally withdrew.
Lǐ Tán died,
and his father was enfeoffed as Lǐ Hóu.
6.10 Qín Miù Gōng once went out and lost his fine horse.
He went to search for it himself
and saw that people had already killed his horse
and were just then sharing its meat.
Miù Gōng said to them:
“This was my fine horse.”
Everyone stood up in fear.
Miù Gōng said:
“I have heard that for those who eat the meat of a fine horse without drinking wine,
it kills them.”
He then gave them wine to drink one by one.
Those who had killed the horse all left in shame.
After three years had passed,
Jìn attacked Qín Miù Gōng
and surrounded him.
The people who had previously eaten the horse meat said to each other:
“We can go out and face death
to repay the kindness of eating the horse and receiving the wine.”
They then broke through the siege,
and Miù Gōng was finally able to escape the difficulty,
defeated Jìn,
and captured Huì Gōng to return home.
This is an instance of virtue going out and blessings returning.
6.11 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng bestowed wine upon his ministers.
At dusk, as they were merry with wine,
the lamps and candles went out.
Then there was someone who pulled at a beautiful lady’s clothes.
The lady reached out and snapped off his cap tassel
and told the Wáng:
“Just now the candles went out,
and someone pulled at my clothes.
I reached out and got his cap tassel and hold it now.
Quickly have the fires brought up
to see who has the broken tassel.”
The Wáng said:
“I gave people wine
and caused them to lose their manners through drunkenness.
How could I wish to display a woman’s chastity yet humiliate a soldier?”
He then ordered those around him:
“Today, those drinking with me
who do not snap off their cap tassels are not having fun.”
The ministers, more than a hundred of them,
all snapped off their cap tassels before the fires were brought up,
and they finally finished the festivities in joy.
After two years had passed,
Jìn and Chǔ fought a battle.
There was a minister who was always in the front,
engaging five times and capturing five heads before pushing back the enemy,
and they finally achieved victory.
Zhuāng Wáng marveled at this and asked:
“My virtue is meager,
and I have never treated you differently;
for what reason do you face death without hesitation like this?”
He replied:
“I deserved to die.
Previously, when drunk, I lost my manners,
and the Wáng showed restraint, not exposing or executing me.
I never dared to let that hidden kindness
go without an obvious repayment to the Wáng.
I have always wished for my liver and brains to be smeared on the ground
and to use my neck’s blood to wash away the enemy for a long time.
I am the one who snapped off his tassel that night.”
Consequently, they repelled the Jìn army,
and Chǔ was able to become strong.
This shows that those who have hidden virtue will surely receive manifest reward.
6.12 Zhào Xuān Mèng was going to the capital of Jiàng
when he saw under a shaded mulberry tree a starving man lying down, unable to move.
Xuān Mèng stopped his carriage and prepared a meal for him,
personally putting it in his mouth to feed him.
The starving man swallowed twice and was then able to see.
Xuān Mèng asked:
“Why are you as hungry as this?”
He replied:
“I was an official in Jiàng,
but on my way home my provisions ran out.
I was ashamed to go begging and hated to take things for myself,
which is why I came to this state.”
Xuān Mèng gave him a pot of meal and two slices of dried meat.
The man bowed twice and kowtowed to receive them,
but did not dare to eat them.
When asked for the reason,
he replied:
“Just now when I ate, it was delicious.
I have an old mother,
and I wish to offer this to her.”
Xuān Mèng said:
“You eat this;
I will give you more.”
He then prepared another basket of food for him,
gave him two bundles of dried meat and a hundred coins,
and then left for Jiàng.
After three years,
Jìn Líng Gōng wished to kill Xuān Mèng,
so he stationed hidden soldiers in a room
and summoned Xuān Mèng to drink wine.
Xuān Mèng realized this
and left halfway through the drinking.
Líng Gōng ordered the soldiers in the room to quickly pursue and kill him.
One person pursued quickly
and reached Xuān Mèng first.
Seeing Xuān Mèng’s face,
he said:
“Alas,
it truly is you!
Please let me turn back and die for you.”
Xuān Mèng said:
“What is your name?”
The man ran back
and replied:
“Why ask for my name?
I am that starving man from under the mulberry tree.”
He went back to fight and died.
Xuān Mèng was able to survive.
This is what is meant by virtue and kindness.
Therefore, if you show kindness to a jūnzǐ,
the jūnzǐ will bring you blessings;
if you show kindness to a xiǎorén,
the xiǎorén will exhaust his strength for you.
If virtue to one man can save one’s life,
how much more so if kindness is placed upon ten thousand people?
Thus it is said:
“Virtue is never too small,
and resentment is never too insignificant.”
How can one not cultivate virtue and remove resentment,
and strive to benefit others?
When benefits go out, blessings return;
when resentment goes out, calamity comes.
That which is formed within responds without;
one cannot but be cautious.
This is what the Shū refers to as “virtue is never small.”
The Shī says:
“Valiant and martial is the warrior,
the shield and wall of the gōng and hóu.”
“Numerous are the many men of service,
by whom Wén Wáng enjoyed tranquility.”
How can a ruler of men not strive to love his men of service?
6.13 In the time of Xiào Jǐng,
Wú and Chǔ rebelled.
Yuán Àng, in his capacity as Tàicháng, was sent as an envoy to Wú.
Wú Wáng wanted to make him a general,
but he would not agree.
Wú Wáng intended to kill him
and sent a Dūwèi with five hundred men to surround and guard Yuán Àng in his camp.
When Àng had previously served as the Chancellor of Wú,
a Cóngshǐ had an illicit affair with Àng’s handmaid.
Àng knew of this,
but did not leak the secret
and treated him as before.
Someone told the Cóngshǐ,
saying, "The Lord knows of your affair with the handmaid."
The Cóngshǐ was terrified and fled toward home.
Àng chased after him personally,
and then bestowed the handmaid upon him as a gift,
and he returned to serve as his Cóngshǐ again.
When Àng was sent as an envoy to Wú
and found himself surrounded,
that Cóngshǐ happened to be the Xiào Sīmǎ guarding Àng.
At night, he led Àng up and said:
"You can leave now;
Wú Wáng plans to execute you at dawn."
Àng did not believe him and asked:
"Who are you, sir?"
The Sīmǎ said:
"I am your former Cóngshǐ who stole the handmaid."
Àng then respectfully thanked him and said:
"You have parents;
I am not worth involving you in trouble."
The Sīmǎ said:
"If you go,
I will also flee;
I will hide my parents elsewhere.
What have you to worry about!"
He then used a knife to slit the tent,
and led Àng out along a path through the drunken soldiers.
They then parted ways and left.
Àng subsequently returned to report to the Emperor.
6.14 Zhì Bó fought with Zhào Xiāngzǐ at the foot of Jìnyáng and died.
Zhì Bó’s minister, Yù Ràng, was furious;
his intense spirit was able to move the heart of Xiāngzǐ.
He then lacquered his body to change his form
and swallowed charcoal to change his voice.
When Xiāngzǐ was about to go out,
Yù Ràng feigned being a corpse
and lay under a bridge.
The four-horse carriage was startled
and would not proceed.
Xiāngzǐ’s heart was moved;
he sent a messenger to look under the bridge
and found Yù Ràng.
Xiāngzǐ valued his righteousness
and did not kill him.
Later, Yù Ràng again committed a crime to incur punishment,
and wearing the crimson clothes of a convict, he entered to repair the palace.
Xiāngzǐ’s heart was moved,
so he said:
"It must be Yù Ràng."
Xiāngzǐ seized and questioned him, saying:
"You first served Zhōngháng Jūn.
When Zhì Bó killed Zhōngháng Jūn,
you were unable to die for him,
but instead turned back to serve Zhì Bó.
Now that I have killed Zhì Bó,
you lacquer your body to become a leper
and swallow charcoal to become a mute,
desiring to kill me.
How is this different from your previous conduct?"
Yù Ràng said:
"Zhōngháng Jūn treated me as one of the common crowd,
so I served him as one of the common crowd.
Zhì Bó treated me as a Cháoshì,
so I acted as a Cháoshì for his use."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"This is not righteous,
but you are a man of courage."
He then placed himself in the carriage depot
and for three days let no food or drink enter his mouth
in order to show ritual respect to Yù Ràng.
Yù Ràng, knowing his own purpose was understood,
then committed suicide.
6.15 Jìn expelled the clan of Luán Yíng
and ordered that any of his retainers who dared follow him would die.
His retainer was named Xīn Yú,
and he followed him.
The officials caught him and were about to kill him.
The Lord said:
"I ordered you not to follow;
why did you dare to follow?"
Xīn Yú replied:
"I have heard that for those who have served a family for three generations, the head is their ruler;
for those who have served for two generations, the head is their master.
One serves a ruler with death
and serves a master with diligence,
because their favors were many.
Now I have been a subordinate to the Luán clan for three generations
and have received many of their favors.
How could I dare fear death and forget the grace of three generations?"
The Lord of Jìn released him.
6.16 The grandfather of Liúhóu Zhāng Liáng was Kāidì,
who was chancellor to Hán Zhāo Wáng, Xuānhuì Wáng, and Xiāng’āi Wáng.
His father, Píng, was chancellor to Lí Wáng and Dàohuì Wáng.
Píng died in the twenty-third year of Dàohuì Wáng.
Twenty years after his death,
Qín destroyed Hán.
Liáng was young
and had not yet served Hán as an official.
When Hán was crushed,
Liáng had three hundred family servants.
When his brother died he did not bury him,
but used all his family wealth to seek an assassin to kill the King of Qín
to take revenge for Hán,
because his grandfather and father had been chancellors of Hán for five generations.
He then studied the rites in Huáiyáng,
went east to see Cānghǎi Jūn,
and found a strongman,
for whom he made an iron mallet weighing one hundred and twenty catties.
When Qín Huángdì traveled east,
Liáng and the guest launched a surprise attack on Qín Huángdì at Bólàngshā,
but by mistake, they hit a secondary carriage.
Qín Huángdì was furious
and conducted a great search throughout the world,
offering a bounty for capture very urgently.
Liáng changed his name,
fled, and hid himself deeply.
Later, he finally followed the Hàn to take revenge on Qín.
6.17 When Bào Shū died,
Guǎn Zhòng lifted his lapel and wailed for him,
his tears falling like rain.
His followers said:
"He was not your ruler, minister, father, or son;
is there an explanation for this?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This is not something you would know.
I once engaged in trade with Bào Zǐ in Nányáng.
Three times I was humiliated in the market,
but Bào Zǐ did not consider me a coward,
for he knew I wished to distinguish myself.
Bào Zǐ once went with me to present a proposal to a king,
but three times we were not heard,
yet Bào Zǐ did not consider me unworthy,
for he knew I had not met an enlightened ruler.
Bào Zǐ once shared wealth and goods with me;
I took three parts more for myself,
but Bào Zǐ did not consider me greedy,
for he knew I was short of funds.
Those who gave me life were my parents;
the one who knew me was Bào Zǐ.
A scholar will die for one who knows him,
so how much more should he mourn for him?"
6.18 Zhào Dùn of Jìn recommended Hán Jué,
and the Lord of Jìn appointed him as the Commandant of the Central Army.
When Zhào Dùn died,
his son Shuò succeeded him as a High Official.
In the third year of Jǐng Gōng,
Zhào Shuò served as a general of Jìn.
Shuò took the elder sister of Chéng Gōng as his wife.
The Grand Master Túàn Gǔ wanted to exterminate the Zhào clan.
Earlier,
when Zhào Dùn was alive,
he dreamed that Shūdài was clutching his waist and weeping,
very sadly;
after a while he laughed,
clapped his hands, and sang.
Dùn consulted a diviner,
and the omen indicated that things would be severed at first but good later.
The scribe of Zhào cited the divination saying:
"This is very bad,
but it will not affect your lordship's person,
reaching only your lordship's son;
yet it is also your lordship's fault.
By the generation of your son Zhào Shuò, the family will decline further."
Túàn Gǔ
was first favored by Líng Gōng,
and by the time of Jìn Jǐng Gōng, Gǔ became the Minister of Justice;
about to cause trouble,
he pursued the assassin of Líng Gōng to implicate Zhào Dùn,
and announced to all the generals:
"Zhào Chuān assassinated Líng Gōng.
Although Dùn did not know of it,
he is still the primary culprit.
When a subject kills his lord,
and his descendants are in court,
how can the crime be punished?
I request to execute them."
Hán Jué said:
"Líng Gōng encountered the assassin
while Zhào Dùn was away.
Our former lord considered him guiltless,
and thus did not execute him.
Now you all intend to execute his descendants;
this is not the intent of the former lord but rather an arbitrary execution.
Arbitrary execution is called chaos.
For a subject to have such a major undertaking without the lord hearing of it
is to have no lord."
Túàn Gǔ did not listen.
Jué told Zhào Shuò to flee quickly.
Zhào Shuò refused,
saying:
"If you can ensure that the sacrifices of Zhào are not cut off,
I, Shuò, shall die without regret."
Hán Jué promised
and claimed illness, not going out.
Gǔ, without asking permission, arbitrarily led the generals to attack the Zhào clan at Xià Gōng,
killing Zhào Shuò, Zhào Tóng, Zhào Kuò, and Zhào Yīngqí,
exterminating their entire clan.
Shuò's wife, the sister of Chéng Gōng,
was pregnant;
she fled to the ducal palace to hide.
Later she gave birth to a boy
and nursed him.
Shuò's guest Chéng Yīng took the child and hid in the mountains.
Fifteen years passed.
Jìn Jǐng Gōng fell ill.
He performed a divination,
which said:
"The descendants of Dà Yè who did not succeed are causing a curse."
Jǐng Gōng asked Hán Jué.
Hán Jué knew the Zhào orphan was alive,
so he said:
"Among the descendants of Dà Yè whose sacrifices have been cut off in Jìn,
is it not the Zhào clan?
From Zhòngyǎn onwards, they all have the surname Yíng.
Zhòngyǎn had a human face and a bird's beak;
he descended to assist the Emperor Dàwù of Yīn,
and up to the Son of Heaven of Zhōu,
all had bright virtue.
Down to the unprincipled reigns of Yōu and Lì,
Shūdài left Zhōu for Jìn
to serve the former lord Wén Hóu.
Down to Chéng Gōng,
generations performed meritorious service,
and their sacrifices were never cut off.
Now in the time of my lord, only the Zhào clan has been extinguished;
the people of the state mourn them.
Therefore it appeared on the tortoise shells and stalks.
May your lordship consider this."
Jǐng Gōng asked:
"Does Zhào still have any descendants?"
Hán Jué replied truthfully with the details.
Thereupon Jǐng Gōng plotted with Hán Jué to establish the Zhào orphan,
summoning him and hiding him in the palace.
When the generals entered to inquire about the illness,
Jǐng Gōng used Hán Jué's troops to threaten the generals and showed them the Zhào orphan.
The orphan's name was Wǔ.
The generals had no choice
but to say:
"In the disaster at Xià Gōng formerly,
Túàn Gǔ caused it,
forging the lord's command
to order the officials.
Otherwise,
who would have dared to cause such trouble!
Were it not for your lordship's illness,
we officials would have surely requested to establish a Zhào successor.
Now that your lordship has given the order,
it is the wish of us officials."
Thereupon they summoned Zhào Wǔ and Chéng Yīng to pay respects to all the generals.
The generals then returned with Chéng Yīng and Zhào Wǔ to attack Túàn Gǔ,
exterminating his clan.
They restored Zhào Wǔ's lands and towns as before.
Therefore, how can a person be without kindness?
If one bestows kindness here,
one receives a return there.
Without Chéng Yīng, the Zhào orphan would not have been saved;
without Hán Jué, the Zhào successor would not have been restored.
Hán Jué can be said to have not forgotten kindness.
6.19 Qú Bóyù committed an offense against the Lord of Wèi
and fled to Jìn.
Among the Grand Masters of Jìn was one Mùmén Zǐgāo;
Qú Bóyù stayed at his house.
After two years,
the Lord of Wèi pardoned his crime and he returned.
Mùmén Zǐgāo sent his son to escort him to the border.
Qú Bóyù said:
"The son of the rustic man may return home now."
Later, Mùmén Zǐgāo committed an offense against the Lord of Jìn
and went to Qú Bóyù.
Bóyù spoke to the Lord of Wèi, saying:
"The worthy Grand Master of Jìn, Mùmén Zǐgāo, has committed an offense against the Lord of Jìn;
I wish for your lordship to treat him with ritual courtesy."
Thereupon the Lord of Wèi welcomed him in the outskirts
and eventually made him a High Official.
6.20 Běiguō Sāo went to the gate to see Yàn Zǐ and said:
"I secretly admire your righteousness
and wish to beg for the means to support my mother."
Yàn Zǐ sent someone to share grain from the granary and gold from the treasury and gave them to him.
He declined the gold but accepted the grain.
Some time later,
Yàn Zǐ fell under suspicion by Jǐng Gōng
and fled.
Běiguō Zǐ summoned his friend and told him:
"I admire Yàn Zǐ's righteousness
and once begged for the means to support my mother from him.
I have heard it said:
'When support reaches one's parents,
one must take upon oneself their difficulties.'
Now Yàn Zǐ has fallen under suspicion;
I will use my death to clear his name."
He then went to the ducal court
and said to the official in charge of petitions:
"Yàn Zǐ
is a worthy man of the world.
If he leaves the State of Qí now,
the State of Qí will surely be invaded.
Since it is certain that the state will be seen to be invaded,
it is better to die first.
I request to cut my throat to clear Yàn Zǐ's name."
He stepped back
and then committed suicide.
When the Duke heard of this,
he was greatly shocked,
mounted a carriage to personally pursue Yàn Zǐ,
reached him at the outskirts of the capital,
and requested that he return.
Yàn Zǐ had no choice but to return.
When he heard that Běiguō Zǐ had cleared his name with his death,
he sighed deeply and said:
"I, Yīng, am unworthy;
my offenses are certainly what they were,
yet a scholar used his life to clarify my name.
How tragic!"
6.21 Wú Chìshì was sent as an envoy to Zhìshì,
and requested passage through Wèi.
Nìng Wénzǐ prepared three hundred sets of hemp and fine linen cloth,
intending to present them to him.
Dàfū Bào said:
“Although Wú is a great state,
our territories do not border one another.
Having granted them passage,
we have shown sufficient respect;
why offer further gifts?”
Nìng Wénzǐ did not listen,
and eventually delivered them.
Wú Chìshì arrived at Zhìshì;
after finishing his business,
he was about to return to Wú.
Zhì Bó ordered boats to be built into a bridge.
Wú Chìshì said:
“I have heard that
when the Tiānzǐ crosses a river,
boats are built into a bridge;
for Zhūhóu, boats are lashed together for a bridge;
for Dàfū, boats are parallel.
Parallel boats
are the duty of a Chén.
Moreover, this excessive respect
must have a reason.”
He sent someone to observe,
and found that there were troops following behind,
intending to launch a surprise attack on Wèi.
Wú Chìshì said:
“Wèi granted us passage
and gave me generous gifts;
if I see their peril and do not inform them,
I would be conspiring against them.”
He claimed illness and stayed behind,
sending someone to warn Wèi.
The people of Wèi went on alert;
when Zhì Bó heard of this,
he desisted.
6.22 Chǔ and Wèi met at Jìnyáng,
intending to attack Qí.
The Qí Wáng was distressed by this
and sent someone to summon Chúnyú Kūn, saying:
“Chǔ and Wèi are plotting to attack Qí;
I wish for the Master to share in my worry.”
Chúnyú Kūn laughed loudly and did not respond.
The Wáng asked him again,
and again he laughed loudly and did not respond.
Three times he was asked and three times he laughed without responding.
The Wáng flushed with anger and said:
“Does the Master treat my state as a joke?”
Chúnyú Kūn replied:
“I would not dare to treat the Wáng’s state as a joke.
I was laughing at my neighbor’s sacrifice for the fields;
with a small basket of rice and a single crucian carp,
his prayer said:
‘From the low-lying and uneven fields,
may I obtain a hundred wagons of grain;
may the crab-mounds be suitable for grain.’
I was laughing because what he offered in sacrifice was so little,
while what he sought was so much.”
The Wáng said:
“Good.”
He bestowed upon him a thousand pieces of gold
and a hundred chariots,
and appointed him as a Shàngqīng.
6.23 Yáng Hǔ fell into disfavor in Wèi
and went north to see Jiǎn Zǐ, saying:
“From this time forward,
I will never again cultivate people.”
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“Why is that?”
Yáng Hǔ replied:
“Among those in my hall,
more than half are those I cultivated;
among the officials in the court,
those I established
are also more than half;
among the soldiers on the borders,
those I established
are also more than half.
Now, those in the hall
personally alienate me from the ruler;
the officials in the court
personally endanger me through the law;
and the soldiers on the borders
personally threaten me with weapons.”
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“Only the worthy are able to repay kindness,
while the unworthy cannot.
Those who plant peaches and plums
can rest in their shade in summer
and eat the fruit in autumn.
Those who plant caltrops
find no rest in the summer
and only get their thorns in the autumn.
Now, those whom you cultivated
are caltrops,
not peaches and plums.
From this time forward,
select those you wish to cultivate,
and do not choose them only after they have already been cultivated.”
6.24 Dōnglǘ Zǐ was once wealthy and noble but later became a beggar.
Someone asked him,
saying:
“Why has Your Excellency come to this?”
He said:
“I know that I served as Xiàng for six or seven years,
yet I never ennobled a single person;
I was twice wealthy with thirty million coins,
yet I never enriched a single person.
I did not know that the faults of a scholar's career would turn out like this.”
Kǒng Zǐ said:
“Things are difficult.
Whether small or large, few or many,
each has its resentments and dislikes.
This is the logic of fate.
That a person achieves success
depends on what they borrow from the outside.”
6.25 Wèi Wénhóu was speaking with Tián Zǐfāng,
and there were two young servants wearing blue and white clothes attending before the ruler.
Zǐfāng said:
“Are these the ruler’s favored sons?”
Wénhóu said:
“No,
their father died in battle,
and these are his young orphans;
I have taken them in.”
Zǐfāng said:
“I thought the ruler’s murderous heart was already sufficient,
but now it is even greater.
While the ruler dotes on these children,
whose father are you going to kill next?”
Wénhóu said sorrowfully:
“I have received your instruction.”
From then on,
military force was no longer used.
6.26 Wú Qǐ became a general of Wèi,
attacking Zhōngshān.
Among the soldiers, there was one who suffered from a festering boil;
Wú Zǐ himself sucked out its pus.
The soldier's mother wept for him.
A bystander said:
“The General treats your son in this way;
why do you still weep?”
She replied:
“Wú Zǐ sucked the wound of this boy's father,
and he was killed in the battle of Zhùshuǐ,
dying without ever turning back.
Now he is sucking the son's wound again;
how can I know in what battle this boy will die?
For this reason I cry for him.”
6.27 When Qí Yìgōng was a prince,
he had a dispute over land with the father of Bǐng Chù and did not win.
When he ascended the throne,
he dug up the father and cut off his feet,
then made Chù his groom;
he also seized the wife of Yōng Zhī
and made Zhī his chariot guard.
The Gōng was traveling at Shēn Chí,
and the two were bathing in the pool.
Chù struck Zhī with a whip,
and Zhī was angry.
Chù said:
“A man takes your wife and you do not dare to be angry;
if I strike you once,
how does it hurt you?”
Zhī said:
“How does that compare with someone who has his father's feet cut off and yet feels no distress?”
They then plotted to kill the Gōng
and placed his body in a bamboo grove.
6.28 The people of Chǔ presented a soft-shelled turtle to Zhèng Líng Gōng.
Gōngzǐ Jiā saw it.
Gōngzǐ Sòng’s index finger twitched,
and he said to Gōngzǐ Jiā:
“On other days when I was like this,
I always tasted a rare delicacy.”
When the turtle was served to the Grand Officers,
the Duke summoned Gōngzǐ Sòng but did not give him any.
Gōngzǐ Sòng was enraged,
dipped his finger into the cauldron,
tasted it, and left.
The Duke was enraged
and wished to kill him.
Gōngzǐ Sòng plotted with Gōngzǐ Jiā to strike first,
and they eventually assassinated Líng Gōng.
Zǐxià said:
“The *Chūnqiū* records instances of rulers not acting like rulers,
ministers not acting like ministers,
fathers not acting like fathers,
and sons not acting like sons.
This is not the result of a single day;
it reaches this point through a gradual process.”
7.1 Governance has three grades:
the governance of a King
transforms the people;
the governance of a Hegemon
awes them;
the governance of a Strongman
coerces them.
Now, each of these three has its application,
but transformation is the most valuable.
If transformation does not change them, then one awes them;
if awing them does not change them, then one coerces them;
if coercing them does not change them, then one punishes them.
As for reaching the point of punishment,
this is not what a King values.
Therefore, a Sage King prioritizes moral virtue and education and puts punishments and penalties last;
he establishes honor and shame and clarifies prohibitions and restraints;
he upholds the regulations of ritual and righteousness to show them the way,
and disdains the flaws of goods and profit to change them.
He cultivates what is near and regulates what is internal,
corrects the rituals of the threshold and the loom,
and unifies the relations between spouses;
then those below will all admire the honor of ritual and righteousness
and loathe the shame of greed and disorder.
That which brings this about
is the result of transformation.
7.2 Jì Sūn asked Kǒngzǐ:
“What if I were to kill those without the Way
to approach those with the Way?
How would that be?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“In your governance,
why use killing?
If you desire good, the people will be good.
The virtue of the gentleman is like the wind,
and the virtue of the petty person is like the grass.
When the wind blows over the grass, it must bend.”
This means clarifying transformation and nothing more.
7.3 Governing a state has two mechanisms:
punishment and virtue.
A King esteems virtue and is sparing with punishment;
a Hegemon employs both punishment and virtue;
a strong state puts punishment first and virtue last.
Punishment and virtue
are the means by which transformation arises.
Virtue
nurtures the good and advances those who are deficient;
punishment
chastises the wicked and prohibits those who would follow.
Therefore, the height of moral transformation reaches the level of rewards,
and the extremity of punishment and penalty reaches the level of execution.
Execution and rewards
are the means to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy
and to rank those with merit and those without merit.
Therefore, execution and rewards cannot be handled erratically;
if they are handled erratically, then good and evil will be thrown into disorder.
If there is merit but no reward, then the good will not be encouraged;
if there is fault but no execution, then the wicked will not be afraid.
If the good are not encouraged and the wicked are not afraid, yet one can still implement transformation throughout the world—
I have never heard of such a thing.
The *Shū* says:
“Exert all effort in rewards and punishments.”
This is what it means.
7.4 When the water is turbid, the fish are distressed;
when orders are harsh, the people are in disorder.
When a city wall is too steep, it will surely collapse;
when a riverbank is too high, it will surely give way.
Therefore, governing a state is like stringing a lute:
if the large strings are too tight, the small strings will snap.
Thus it is said:
“One who uses a tight rein and bit
is not a driver for a thousand *lǐ*.”
A sound with form
carries no further than a hundred *lǐ*;
a sound without form
extends to the four seas.
Therefore, one whose salary exceeds his merit will suffer loss;
one whose reputation exceeds his reality will be diminished.
When character and conduct harmonize and reputation corresponds to them,
then misfortune and fortune do not arrive in vain.
The *Shī* says:
“Why does he stay there?
There must be someone with him.
Why has he been there so long?
There must be a reason for it.”
This is what it means.
7.5 Gōngshū Wénzǐ served as the Lìngyǐn of Chǔ.
For three years,
none of the people dared to enter the court.
Gōngshūzǐ saw him and said:
“It is severe indeed.”
Wénzǐ said:
“The severity of the court—
can it be said to hinder the governance of the state?”
Gōngshūzǐ said:
“If things are severe, those below will be mute;
if those below are mute, those above will be deaf.
If the deaf and the mute cannot communicate,
how can the state be governed?
I have heard that
following the needle and thread completes the curtains;
combining pints and pecks fills the granaries;
and joining small streams forms the rivers and seas.
An enlightened ruler
may have commands that he receives but does not carry out,
but he never has anything he refuses to receive.”
7.6 Wèi Líng Gōng said to Kǒngzǐ:
“Someone told me
that for one who governs a state, if he is cautious within the ancestral temple hall,
then the state will be well-governed.
Is this possible?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“It is possible.
Those who love others will be loved by others;
those who hate others will be hated by others.
One who knows how to find this in himself
also knows how to find it in others.
What is meant by ‘knowing the world without leaving one’s small room’
is knowing how to reflect upon oneself.”
7.7 Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ about governing the people.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Be as fearful and cautious as if using a rotten rope to drive a galloping horse.”
Zǐgòng said:
“Why should one be so afraid?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“In a country where all are reached by the ruler's influence, they are all people;
if you lead them with the Way, they are my subjects;
if you do not lead them with the Way, they are my enemies.
How can one not be afraid?”
7.8 Qí Huán Gōng said to Guǎn Zhòng:
“I wish to undertake affairs in the state
as clearly as the sun and moon,
so that even the simple men and women all say they are good.
Is this possible?”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“It is possible,
but it is not the Way of the Sages.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Why is that?”
He replied:
“A short rope cannot be used to draw from a deep well; one with meager knowledge cannot be given the words of a Sage.
A kind person can be spoken with to distinguish things;
a wise person can be spoken with to distinguish the boundless;
a Sage can be spoken with to distinguish the divine and luminous.
What the Sages do
is not what the common people can reach.
If the people perceive the ruler to be only ten times as great as themselves,
they will still contend with him
and say:
‘He is not as good as I am.’
If they perceive him to be a hundred times as great,
they will criticize his faults.
If they perceive him to be a thousand times as great,
then who would not believe in him?
Therefore, the people cannot be managed by poking and prodding them;
they can be joined together and shepherded.
They cannot be treated with violence and killed;
they can be directed and summoned.
The masses cannot be persuaded house by house;
they can be raised up and shown the way.”
7.9 Wèi Líng Gōng asked Shǐ Qiú,
“What is the priority of governance?”
He replied,
“The Dàlǐ is the priority.
If court cases are not decided fairly,
the dead cannot be brought back to life,
and those who are severed cannot be rejoined.
Therefore it is said:
The Dàlǐ is the priority.”
Shortly thereafter,
Zǐlù saw the Gōng.
The Gōng told him the words of Shǐ Qiú.
Zǐlù said,
“The Sīmǎ is the priority.
When two states have difficulties
and two armies face each other,
the Sīmǎ wields the drumsticks to command them.
If a single battle is not appropriately handled,
the dead number in the tens of thousands.
To consider killing people as wrong,
yet this also results in killing many people.
Therefore it is said:
The Sīmǎ is the priority.”
Shortly thereafter,
Zǐgòng entered to see him.
The Gōng told him the words of the two men.
Zǐgòng said,
“How narrow-minded!
Formerly, Yǔ fought with the Yǒuhù Shì,
and after three deployments they did not submit.
Yǔ then cultivated education for one year,
and the Yǒuhù Shì requested to submit.
Therefore it is said:
if one removes the causes of the people’s litigation,
what court cases would be heard?
If weapons and armor are not deployed,
what drums would be sounded?
Therefore it is said:
education is the priority.”
7.10 Qí Huán Gōng went out to hunt.
While chasing a deer, he ran into a mountain valley
and met an old man whom he questioned,
saying,
“What valley is this?”
He replied,
“It is Yú Gōng’s Valley.”
Huán Gōng said,
“For what reason?”
He replied,
“It is named after your servant.”
Huán Gōng said,
“Looking at your appearance today,
you are not a foolish person.
Why is it named after the Gōng?”
He replied,
“May your servant explain it.
Your servant formerly raised a cow;
it gave birth to a calf which grew up,
so I sold it and bought a colt.
A youth said,
‘A cow cannot give birth to a horse.’
He then took the colt and left.
The neighbors heard of this
and considered your servant to be foolish,
so they named this valley Yú Gōng’s Valley.”
Huán Gōng said,
“The Gōng is indeed foolish!
For what reason did you give it to him?”
Huán Gōng then returned.
At court the next day,
he told Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng straightened his lapel, bowed twice, and said,
“This is the folly of Yíwú.
If Yáo were above
and Gāoyáo were the judge,
how could there be one who takes another’s colt?
If there were one who saw such violence as this old man did,
he would surely not have given it up.
This Gōng knew that the legal system was not upright,
and so he gave it away.
I request to withdraw and cultivate governance.”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“Disciples, remember this:
Huán Gōng
was a Bà ruler;
Guǎn Zhòng
was a worthy assistant.
Even they still took wisdom to be folly;
how much more so for those who do not reach the level of Huán Gōng and Guǎn Zhòng!”
7.11 In Lǔ, there were a father and son suing each other.
Kāngzǐ said,
“Kill them.”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“They cannot yet be killed.
It has been long since the people have known that lawsuits between fathers and sons are not good!
This is the fault of those above.
If those above followed the Dào,
such people would disappear.”
Kāngzǐ said,
“Governing the people takes filial piety as the root.
Now, to kill one person to punish unfiliality,
is that not also acceptable?”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“To execute them for being unfilial
is to cruelly kill the innocent.
When the Sānjūn suffer a great defeat,
they cannot be executed;
when court cases are not well-ordered,
punishments cannot be applied.
If those above set forth teachings and are the first to submit to them,
then the common people will follow like the wind.
If one does not follow them in personal conduct,
and only afterward waits to use punishments,
then the people will know crime.
A wall of one rèn
is something people cannot leap over;
but a mountain of a hundred rèn
is where children climb and play,
because the slope is gradual.
Now, this gradual decay of benevolence and righteousness has lasted a long time!
Can one say that the people will not overstep?
The Shī says:
‘Cause the people not to be led astray.’
In the past,
the Jūnzǐ guided his common people and did not let them go astray.
Therefore his majesty was stern but did not reach severity,
and punishments were set aside and not used.”
Thereupon, when the litigants heard this,
they requested to have no lawsuit.
7.12 Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ about governance.
Kǒngzǐ replied,
“Governance consists in making the people wealthy and long-lived.”
Āi Gōng said,
“What do you mean?”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“If taxes and levies are light, then the people will be wealthy.
If there are few duties, they will keep far from crime.
If they keep far from crime, then the people will be long-lived.”
The Gōng said,
“If it were like this, then I would be poor.”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“The Shī says:
‘The happy and easy-going Jūnzǐ,
is the parent of the people.’
I have never seen a child who is wealthy while the parents are poor.”
7.13 Wén Wáng asked Lǚ Wàng,
“How should one govern the world?”
He replied,
“A kingdom of a true king enriches the people;
a kingdom of a Bà enriches the Shì;
a kingdom that barely survives enriches the Dàfū;
a kingdom that has lost the Dào enriches its granaries and treasuries.
This is called ‘overflowing at the top and leaking at the bottom.’”
Wén Wáng said,
“Good.”
The reply was,
“Letting a good deed stay overnight is unlucky.”
That same day,
he opened his granaries and treasuries to relieve the widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless.
7.14 Wǔ Wáng asked Tàigōng,
“What is the way to govern the state?”
Tàigōng replied,
“The way to govern the state
is simply to love the people.”
He asked,
“How does one love the people?”
He replied,
“Benefit them and do not harm them;
complete them and do not ruin them;
give them life and do not kill them;
give to them and do not take from them;
make them happy and do not make them suffer;
make them joyful and do not make them angry.
This is the way to govern the state
and the righteousness of employing the people;
it is simply to love them.
If the people lose their livelihoods,
then you harm them.
If the farmers miss their seasons,
then you ruin them.
If for those who are guilty you make their punishments heavy,
then you kill them.
If you impose heavy taxes and levies,
then you take from them.
If you have many labor services to exhaust the people’s strength,
then you make them suffer.
If you toil and harass them,
then you make them angry.
Therefore, one who is good at governing the state
treats the people with the love of a parent for a child,
or an elder brother for a younger brother;
hearing of their hunger and cold, he feels sorrow for them;
seeing their toil and hardship, he feels grief for them.”
7.15 Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng:
“How does a worthy ruler govern the state?”
He replied:
“In a worthy ruler’s governance of the state,
his administration is fair,
his officials are not harsh,
his tax collection is moderate,
his personal expenditures are meager,
and he does not harm public law for private benefit.
Rewards are not bestowed upon those without merit,
and punishments are not applied to those without guilt;
he does not reward out of joy,
nor does he execute out of anger.
Those who harm the people are considered guilty,
and those who advance the worthy and promote the overlooked are rewarded.
The inner palace is not in disorder,
and the requests of palace women are not heeded.
Above, there is no depravity or wickedness;
below, there is no secret harm.
He does not build palaces to waste wealth,
nor does he frequent observation towers and ponds to weary the people,
nor does he use ornate carvings and engravings to gratify his ears and eyes.
Within the government offices, there are no stores of rotting grain,
and within the state, there are no wandering or starving people.
This is a worthy ruler’s governance of the state.”
Wǔ Wáng said:
“Excellent!”
7.16 Wǔ Wáng asked Tài Gōng:
“Regarding those who govern a state and frequently change the laws and decrees,
why is this?”
Tài Gōng said:
“Those who govern a state and frequently change the laws and decrees
do not treat the law as the law,
but treat what they personally like as the law.
Therefore, when a decree is issued, disorder arises;
when there is disorder, they change the law again.
This is why their laws and decrees are frequently changed.”
7.17 Chéng Wáng asked Yǐn Yì about governance:
“What virtue should I practice
so that the people may be close to their superior?”
He replied:
“Employ them according to the seasons and treat them with respect and compliance;
be loyal and love them;
and issue decrees with trust and do not go back on your word.”
The King said:
“To what extent should this be maintained?”
He replied:
“As if approaching a deep abyss,
or treading on thin ice.”
The King said:
“How fearful!”
He replied:
“Between heaven and earth,
and within the four seas,
if you treat them well, they are your subjects;
if you treat them poorly, they are your enemies.
Formerly, the ministers of Xià and Yīn
turned against and became enemies of Jié and Zhòu, while becoming subjects of Tāng and Wǔ;
the people of Sùshā
attacked their own ruler and turned to Shénnóng Shì.
This is something you clearly know;
how could you not be fearful?”
7.18 Zhòngní met with the Sòng Jūn.
Sòng Jūn asked Zhòngní:
“I wish to possess the state for a long time;
I wish to secure the loyalty of the various cities;
I wish to make the people peaceful and without confusion;
I wish to make the scholar-officials exhaust their strength;
I wish to make the sun and moon follow their seasons;
I wish to make sages come of their own accord;
and I wish to make the government offices well-ordered.
How should I do this?”
Zhòngní replied:
“Rulers of a thousand chariots
and lords of ten thousand chariots
who have questioned me, Qiū, are many,
but none have ever asked me for methods such as those you have asked.
However, all of them can be achieved.
I, Qiū, have heard:
when two rulers are close to each other, they will possess their states for a long time;
when the lord is kind and the ministers are loyal, the various cities will be secured;
if you do not kill the innocent
and do not release the guilty,
then the people will not be confused;
if you increase the salaries and rewards of scholar-officials, they will exhaust their strength;
if you honor Heaven and respect the spirits, then the sun and moon will follow their seasons;
if you are good at applying punishments and penalties, then sages will come of their own accord;
and if you honor the worthy and employ the capable, then the government offices will be well-ordered.”
Sòng Jūn said:
“How could it be otherwise!”
7.19 Zǐgòng said:
“Shè Gōng asked about governance from the Master,
and the Master said:
‘Governance lies in making those nearby content and those far away come.’
Lǔ Āi Gōng asked about governance from the Master,
and the Master said:
‘Governance lies in knowing your ministers.’
Qí Jǐng Gōng asked about governance from the Master,
and the Master said:
‘Governance lies in being frugal in expenditures.’
Three lords asked about governance from the Master,
and the Master’s responses were different;
is it that governance varies?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Now, the land of Jīng is broad but its cities are narrow,
and the people have the intention of leaving;
therefore I said:
‘Governance lies in making those nearby content and those far away come.’
Āi Gōng had three ministers
who internally formed cliques to delude their lord
and externally blocked and distanced the regional lords and guests
to obscure his clarity;
therefore I said:
‘Governance lies in knowing your ministers.’
Qí Jǐng Gōng was extravagant with his towers and pavilions
and excessive with his gardens and parks,
the pleasures of the five senses never ceasing,
and in a single morning, he granted estates of a hundred chariots to three people;
therefore I said:
‘Governance lies in being frugal in expenditures.’
These three things
are governance.
Does the Shī not say:
‘Disorder and separation bring distress,
where shall they find a place to go?’
This expresses sorrow over the separation and dispersal that lead to disorder.
‘They do not fulfill their duties,
but are only a distress to the King.’
This expresses sorrow over treacherous ministers obscuring their lord and leading to disorder.
‘They spread chaos and despise resources,
never showing kindness to our people.’
This expresses sorrow over extravagance and lack of restraint leading to disorder.
If you observe what these three were seeking,
would governance not be the same for them?”
7.20 Gōngyí Xiū was the chancellor of Lǔ.
When the Lord of Lǔ died,
his attendants requested to close the gates.
Gōngyí Xiū said:
“Stop!
I do not tax the ponds and depths,
I do not levy duties on Méng Shān,
I do not issue harsh decrees,
and I have already closed my heart;
why close the gates?”
7.21 Zǐchǎn was the chancellor of Zhèng.
Jiǎn Gōng said to Zǐchǎn:
“Do not let internal administration go out,
and do not let external administration come in.
If robes and furs are not beautiful,
if carriages and horses are not adorned,
and if sons and daughters are not elegant,
that is my shame.
If the state is not well-ordered
and the borders are not secure,
that is your shame, sir.”
Zǐchǎn was the chancellor of Zhèng
until the end of Jiǎn Gōng’s life;
internally there was no disorder in the capital,
and externally there were no troubles from the regional lords.
In Zǐchǎn’s administration of governance,
he selected the capable and employed them.
Féng Jiǎnzǐ was good at making decisions.
Zǐ Tàishū was good at resolving matters and was refined.
Gōngsūn Huī knew the affairs of the four neighboring states
and could distinguish the clans and surnames of their grand masters;
he could adapt instantly
and was also good at diplomacy.
Bì Chén was good at planning;
if he planned in the countryside, he succeeded,
but if he planned in the city, he did not.
When there were matters to attend to, they would take Bì Chén in a carriage
and go with him to the countryside
to have him plan what was feasible or not,
then they would tell Féng Jiǎnzǐ to make the decision,
have Gōngsūn Huī handle the diplomacy,
and when finalized,
it would be given to Zǐ Tàishū to carry out
and respond to the guests.
For this reason, they rarely failed in their affairs.
7.22 Dǒng Ānyú governed Jìnyáng,
and asked Jiǎn Lǎo about governance.
Jiǎn Lǎo said:
"The first is loyalty,
the second is trustworthiness,
and the third is daring."
Dǒng Ānyú asked:
"To whom should I be loyal?"
[Jiǎn Lǎo] said:
"Be loyal to your lord."
[Dǒng Ānyú] asked:
