"In what should I be trustworthy?"
[Jiǎn Lǎo] said:
"Be trustworthy toward orders."
[Dǒng Ānyú] asked:
"In what should I be daring?"
[Jiǎn Lǎo] said:
"Be daring against those who are not good."
Dǒng Ānyú said:
"These three things are sufficient!"
7.23 Wèi Wénhóu sent Xīmén Bào to go and govern Yè,
and told him:
"You must complete achievements, establish a reputation, and spread righteousness."
[Xīmén] Bào said:
"I venture to ask: regarding completing achievements, establishing a reputation, and spreading righteousness,
how should I do it?"
Wénhóu said:
"You go now.
There is no town that does not have worthy heroes and those who are eloquent and broad in knowledge;
there is no town that does not have those who like to publicize the faults of others and conceal their goodness.
When you go, you must inquire after the worthy heroes
and thereby be close to them;
as for those who are eloquent and broad in knowledge,
take them as your teachers;
inquire after those who like to publicize the faults of others
and conceal their goodness,
and thereby observe them.
You cannot act based solely on what you hear.
Indeed, hearing with the ears
is not as good as seeing with the eyes;
seeing with the eyes
is not as good as treading with the feet;
treading with the feet
is not as good as discerning with the hands.
When a person first enters office,
it is like entering a dark room;
over time it becomes increasingly bright.
When it is bright, then there is governance;
when there is governance, then things are carried out."
7.24 Mì Zǐjiàn governed Shànfù;
he played the sounding qín
and did not leave the hall,
yet Shànfù was well-governed.
Wūmǎ Qī also governed Shànfù;
he went out when the stars were up
and returned when the stars were up,
resting neither day nor night,
personally attending to everything,
and Shànfù was also well-governed.
Wūmǎ Qī asked Mì Zǐjiàn for the reason.
Mì Zǐjiàn said:
"My way is called employing people;
your way is called employing effort.
One who employs effort is naturally weary;
one who employs people is naturally at ease."
People said:
"Mì Zǐjiàn is indeed a gentleman;
he eases his four limbs,
preserves his ears and eyes,
and calms his mind and spirit, yet the various officials are governed;
he simply employs his methods.
Wūmǎ Qī is not so;
he exhausts his nature and affairs,
and wearies himself with teaching and instructing.
Although there is governance,
it has not yet reached the ultimate state."
7.25 Kǒngzǐ said to Mì Zǐjiàn:
"You govern Shànfù and the masses are pleased;
tell Qiū how you do it."
[Mì Zǐjiàn] said:
"I, Bùqí, treat the fathers of others as my own father,
treat the sons of others as my own son,
care for the orphans, and mourn for the deceased."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Good,
but these are small virtues;
the common people will attach to you,
but it is not yet enough."
[Mì Zǐjiàn] said:
"I, Bùqí,
have three men whom I serve as fathers,
five men whom I serve as brothers,
and eleven men whom I treat as friends."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Serving three men as fathers
can teach filial piety;
serving five men as brothers
can teach fraternal respect;
having eleven friends
can teach learning.
These are middle-level virtues;
the middle people will attach to you,
but it is not yet enough."
[Mì Zǐjiàn] said:
"In this land, there are five people among the populace who are worthier than I, Bùqí.
I, Bùqí, serve them,
and they all teach me the arts of governance."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The desire for what is great
lies right here.
In the past, Yáo and Shùn purified and made subtle their persons
to listen to and observe the world,
and they strove to attract worthy men.
Indeed, promoting the worthy
is the source of a hundred blessings
and the master of spiritual clarity.
What a pity!
The area Bùqí governs is small;
if the area Bùqí governed were large,
he would be a successor to Yáo and Shùn."
7.26 Mì Zǐjiàn became the Magistrate of Shànfù
and took his leave of Fūzǐ.
Fūzǐ said:
"Do not meet people only to reject them,
and do not promise something based on mere expectation.
To promise is to lose your integrity;
to reject is to be blocked off.
Be like a high mountain or a deep abyss:
looking up, its height cannot be reached;
measuring it, its depth cannot be fathomed."
Zǐjiàn said:
"Excellent,
how would I dare not accept your command!"
7.27 Mì Zǐjiàn became the Magistrate of Shànfù
and visited Yáng Zhòu.
He said:
"Do you have anything to give me as a parting gift?"
Yáng Zhòu said:
"I was of humble status when young
and do not know the art of governing the people,
but I have two ways of fishing
that I would like to give you."
Zǐjiàn said:
"What are the ways of fishing?"
Yáng Zhòu said:
"When casting the line and setting the bait,
the one that rushes to swallow it is the yángqiáo;
as a fish, it is thin and not delicious.
The one that seems to be there and yet not there,
and seems to eat and yet not eat, is the fáng;
as a fish, it is broad and has a rich flavor."
Mì Zǐjiàn said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, before he even reached Shànfù,
those with caps and carriages who came to meet him
crowded the road.
Zǐjiàn said:
"Drive the carriage on,
drive the carriage on!
Those whom Yáng Zhòu called the yángqiáo have arrived."
When he reached Shànfù,
he requested the elders and those who were respected and worthy and governed Shànfù together with them.
7.28 Kǒngzi had a nephew named Kǒng Miè,
who together with Mì Zǐjiàn both served as officials.
Kǒngzi went to visit Kǒng Miè and asked him:
"Since you became an official,
what have you gained and what have you lost?"
Kǒng Miè said:
"Since I became an official, I have gained nothing,
but there are three things I have lost.
They are:
Royal duties are like a succession of attacks,
so when can I find time to practice what I have learned?
Because of this, my learning cannot be clarified;
this is the first loss.
My salary is small;
the gruel is not enough to provide for my relatives;
because of this, my relatives have become more distant;
this is the second loss.
Public business is frequent and urgent;
I cannot go to mourn the dead or visit the sick;
because of this, my friends have become more distant;
this is the third loss."
Kǒngzi was not pleased
and then went to see Zǐjiàn, saying:
"Since you became an official,
what have you gained and what have you lost?"
Zǐjiàn said:
"Since I became an official,
I have lost nothing,
but there are three things I have gained:
The texts I formerly recited,
I now carry out and practice;
thus my learning becomes daily more clear;
this is the first gain.
Although my salary is small,
the gruel is enough to provide for my relatives;
because of this, my relatives have become closer;
this is the second gain.
Although public business is urgent,
I work hard at night to mourn the dead and visit the sick;
because of this, my friends have become closer;
this is the third gain."
Kǒngzi said of Zǐjiàn:
"A gentleman indeed is such a person!
A gentleman indeed is such a person!
If Lǔ had no gentlemen,
where could he have acquired such qualities?"
7.29 Yàn Zǐ governed Dōng’ē.
After three years,
Jǐng Gōng summoned him and rebuked him, saying:
"I thought you were capable,
and so I had you govern Dōng’ē.
Now you have governed it into chaos.
Retire and examine yourself;
I shall impose a great punishment upon you."
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"I request to change my way and alter my conduct to govern Dōng’ē.
If in three years it is not governed,
I request to die for it."
Jǐng Gōng granted this.
Thereupon, in the following year at the annual accounting,
Jǐng Gōng met him and congratulated him, saying:
"Very good!
Your governance of Dōng’ē."
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"In the past when I governed Dōng’ē,
requests for favors were not carried out
and bribes did not arrive.
The fish in the ponds and marshes
were used to benefit the poor people.
At that time,
the people had no hunger,
yet you, on the contrary, blamed me.
Now in my recent governance of Dōng’ē,
requests for favors are carried out,
bribes arrive,
I collect taxes in unison,
internalize little into the granaries,
and facilitate the affairs of those close to you.
The fish in the ponds and marshes
enter the houses of the powerful.
At this time,
more than half of the people are starving,
yet you, on the contrary, meet and congratulate me.
I am stupid and cannot again govern Dōng’ē.
I wish to beg for my old bones
to clear the path for a worthy person."
He bowed twice and stepped aside.
Jǐng Gōng then descended from his mat and apologized to him, saying:
"You must continue to govern Dōng’ē.
Dōng’ē
is your Dōng’ē;
I shall no longer interfere with it."
7.30 Zǐlù governed Pú.
He appeared before Kǒngzi and said:
"I, Yóu, wish to receive your teaching."
Kǒngzi said:
"In Pú there are many strong men,
and it is also difficult to govern.
However, I will tell you:
Be respectful and reverent,
and you can manage the brave.
Be lenient and upright,
and you can embrace the masses.
Be respectful and pure,
and you can be close to those above."
7.31 Zǐgòng became the Magistrate of Xìnyáng.
When he took his leave of Kǒngzi to go,
Kǒngzi said:
"Exert yourself and follow the order of things;
follow the seasons of Heaven.
Do not usurp, do not attack;
do not be violent, do not be a thief."
Zǐgòng said:
"I, Cì, have served the gentleman since I was young;
can a gentleman truly be a thief?"
Kǒngzi said:
"To use the unworthy to attack the worthy—
this is called 'usurping.'
To use the worthy to attack the unworthy—
this is called 'attacking.'
To be lax in one's orders
yet urgent in one's punishments—
this is called 'violence.'
To take the good of others and make it one's own—
this is called 'theft.'
As for the 'theft' of a gentleman,
must it necessarily involve wealth or currency?
I have heard it said:
Those who know how to be officials
uphold the law to benefit the people;
those who do not know how to be officials
pervert the law to infringe upon the people;
these are all sources from which resentment arises.
In approaching office, nothing is better than impartiality;
in approaching wealth, nothing is better than integrity.
The defense of integrity and impartiality
cannot be attacked.
To hide the good of others
is called obscuring the worthy.
To publicize the evil of others
is to be a petty person.
To not teach each other internally but slander each other externally
is to be unworthy of intimacy.
Speaking of the good of others
brings gain and no injury;
speaking of the evil of others
brings no gain and causes injury.
Therefore, a gentleman is cautious in his speech.
Do not put yourself first and others last.
Choose your words before speaking them;
let your mouth be like your ear."
7.32 Yáng Zhū saw the King of Liáng.
He spoke of governing the world as if turning it in the palm of one's hand.
The King of Liáng said:
"You have one wife and one concubine whom you cannot manage,
and a garden of three mǔ that you cannot weed.
Yet you speak of governing the world as if turning it in your palm—
why is that?"
Yáng Zhū said:
"I have those faults, but
have you not seen a shepherd?
With a flock of a hundred sheep,
if you have a five-foot-tall boy carrying a staff follow them,
they go east if he wishes them to go east,
and west if he wishes them to go west.
If you were to make Yáo pull one sheep
and Shùn carry a staff to follow it,
that would be the beginning of chaos.
I have heard it said:
A fish that can swallow a boat does not swim in a shallow pond;
a swan that flies high does not land on a muddy pool.
Why is that?
Because their will is extremely far-reaching.
The Huángzhōng and Dàlǚ bells
cannot be used to accompany a dance of complex music.
Why is that?
Because their sound is sparse and grand.
One who will govern what is great does not manage what is small;
one who achieves great success does not fret over small trifles.
This is what is meant."
7.33 Jǐng Chā was the Prime Minister of Zhèng.
There was a person of Zhèng who waded across a river in winter;
when he came out, his shins were cold.
Later, Jǐng Chā passed by him,
got down from his carriage, took him aboard,
and covered him with his upper garment.
Shūxiàng heard of this and said:
"Jǐng Zǐ acts as the state's prime minister—
is he not indeed narrow-minded?
I have heard that when a good official is in place,
within three months the ditches and canals are repaired,
and by the tenth month the fords and bridges are completed.
Even the six kinds of livestock do not get their feet wet;
how much less so the people?"
7.34 Wèi Wén Hóu asked Lǐ Kè:
“How should one govern a state?”
He replied:
“I have heard that the way to govern a state is
to provide food for those who labor and stipends for those with merit,
to employ those with ability and ensure rewards are certainly carried out,
and to ensure punishments are certainly appropriate.”
Wén Hóu said:
“My rewards and punishments are all appropriate, yet the people do not support me.
Why is this?”
He replied:
“Is it perhaps because the state has dissolute people?
I have heard it said:
Strip the dissolute people of their stipends
to attract scholars from the four directions.
If a father has merit and receives a stipend,
but his son has no merit yet eats of it;
when going out, he rides in carriages and on horses,
wearing fine furs,
considering them glorious;
when staying in, he cultivates the sounds of flutes, zithers, bells, and stones,
and finds peace in the pleasures of his wives and children,
thereby throwing the teachings of the village into disorder.
For those like this, strip them of their stipends to attract scholars from the four directions.
This is what is meant by ‘stripping the dissolute people.’”
7.35 Qí Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
“What is to be feared in governing a state?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“Fear the shrine rats.”
Huán Gōng said:
“What do you mean?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“Now, a shrine is made by binding wood together and coating it with mud.
Rats take advantage of this to take shelter there.
If you try to smoke them out, you fear burning the wood.
If you try to drown them with water, you fear ruining the mud coating.
The reason these rats cannot be killed
is because of the shrine.
A state also has shrine rats;
these are the people to the left and right of the sovereign.
Internally, they conceal good and evil from the ruler above;
externally, they sell their power and influence to the common people.
If you do not execute them, they cause disorder;
if you do execute them, they are protected and supported by the sovereign,
who holds them close to his heart.
These are the shrine rats of the state.
There was once a man who sold wine.
His vessels were very clean and pure,
and his shop sign was very long,
yet his wine turned sour and did not sell.
He asked the people of the neighborhood for the reason.
A neighbor said:
‘Your dog is fierce.
When people carry their vessels and enter,
intending to buy your wine,
the dog meets them and bites them.
This is the reason why the wine is sour and does not sell.’
A state also has fierce dogs;
these are the officials in charge of affairs.
When there are scholars of the Way and its arts
who wish to enlighten the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
those in charge of affairs meet them and bite at them.
These are the fierce dogs of the state.
If those to the left and right are shrine rats
and those in charge of affairs are fierce dogs,
then scholars of the Way and its arts will not be employed.
This is what is to be feared in governing a state.”
7.36 The Marquis of Qí asked Yàn Zǐ:
“What is to be feared in conducting government?”
He replied:
“Fear the failure to distinguish between good and evil.”
The Duke said:
“How can one examine this?”
He replied:
“By carefully selecting those to your left and right.
If those to the left and right are good, then the hundred officials will each find their proper place,
and good and evil will be distinguished.”
Kǒng Zǐ heard this and said:
“These words are indeed trustworthy!
If good words are advanced,
then there is no way for the not-good to enter.
If good words are not advanced,
then there is no way for the good to enter.”
7.37 The ruler of Fù Gǎo came to the court of Qí.
Huán Gōng asked him about governing the people.
The ruler of Fù Gǎo did not reply,
but instead wiped his mouth,
held his collar,
and pressed his hand to his heart.
Huán Gōng said:
“Do you share the sweet and bitter, the hunger and cold with the people!
He considers me a sage,
so he uses no words to make me understand.”
Consequently, he rewarded him with a thousand pieces of gold.
7.38 During the time of Jìn Wén Gōng,
a man of the Dí people offered the skins of a great fox and a patterned leopard.
Wén Gōng sighed deeply and said:
“What crime did the great fox and the patterned leopard commit?
It is because of their skins that they are guilty.”
The high official Luán Zhī said:
“If land is vast but not level,
and wealth is accumulated but not distributed,
is that not also the ‘crime’ of the fox and leopard?”
Wén Gōng said:
“Excellent!
Explain it.”
Luán Zhī said:
“If land is vast but not level,
people will level it;
if wealth is accumulated but not distributed,
people will fight for it.”
Thereupon, he divided the land to distribute to the people
and dispersed the wealth to relieve the poor.
7.39 Jìn Wén Hóu asked about government from Jiù Fàn.
Jiù Fàn replied:
“Dividing cooked meat is not as good as dividing raw meat;
dividing raw meat is not as good as dividing land.
If you cut it up to divide among the people and increase their ranks and stipends,
then the superior gains land and the people know wealth,
and if the superior loses land, the people know poverty.
What the ancients called gathering an army and going to war,
this must be what it means.”
7.40 Jìn Hóu asked Shì Wén Bó:
“On the first day of the third month,
there was a solar eclipse.
I am confused by my studies.
What the Shī calls ‘That sun is eclipsed,
how is it not bad?’—
what does it mean?”
He replied:
“It refers to an unkind government.
If the state has no proper government
and does not employ the good,
then it brings upon itself the blame of the calamities of the sun and moon.
Therefore, government cannot but be cautious.
There are only three aspects to government:
First,
follow the people;
second,
choose the right people;
third,
follow the seasons.”
7.41 Yán Líng Jì Zǐ was traveling in Jìn.
Upon entering its border,
he said:
“Alas,
what a tyrannical state!”
Upon entering its capital,
he said:
“Alas,
how the strength of this state is exhausted!”
Standing in its court,
he said:
“Alas,
what a disordered state!”
His followers said:
“Master, it has not been long since you entered the border of Jìn.
Why are you so certain in naming these things?”
Yán Líng Jì Zǐ said:
“Indeed.
When I entered its border,
I saw the fields were overgrown and neglected,
yet the taxes were high and rising;
because of this, I knew its government was tyrannical.
When I entered its capital,
the new houses were poorly made while the old houses were beautiful,
and the new walls were low while the old walls were high;
because of this, I knew the strength of the people was exhausted.
When I stood in its court,
the ruler could see yet did not inquire of his subordinates,
and his ministers were fond of boasting but did not offer remonstrance to those above;
because of this, I knew its state was in disorder.”
7.42 The reason why Qí is not as good as Lǔ is that
the worthiness of Tàigōng
was not as great as that of Bóqín.
Bóqín and Tàigōng both received their enfeoffments and each went to his state.
After three years,
Tàigōng came to court.
Zhōugōng asked him:
"Why was the governance so rapid?"
He replied:
"I honored the worthy,
putting the distant before the kin,
and putting righteousness before benevolence."
These are the traces of a hegemon.
Zhōugōng said:
"Tàigōng’s bounty will reach for five generations."
After five years,
Bóqín came to court.
Zhōugōng asked him:
"Why was the governance so difficult?"
He replied:
"I loved my kin,
putting the internal before the external,
and putting benevolence before righteousness."
These are the traces of a king.
Zhōugōng said:
"Lǔ’s bounty will reach for ten generations."
Therefore, that Lǔ has the traces of a king
is due to its benevolence and generosity;
that Qí has the traces of a hegemon
is due to its martial administration.
The reason why Qí is not as good as Lǔ
is that the worthiness of Tàigōng
was not as great as that of Bóqín.
7.43 Duke Jǐng liked women who dressed in men’s attire,
and all the people in the country followed suit.
The Duke sent officials to ban it,
saying:
"For women who dress in men’s attire,
tear their clothes
and cut their sashes."
Tearing clothes and cutting sashes could be seen everywhere, yet the practice did not stop.
Yànzǐ had an audience.
The Duke said:
"I sent officials to ban women dressing in men’s attire,
tearing their clothes
and cutting their sashes,
yet they are seen everywhere and do not stop.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"Your Lordship allows them to wear it within the palace
but bans it outside.
This is like hanging a cow’s head at the gate
while trying to sell horse meat.
If Your Lordship would make those within not wear it,
then no one outside would dare to do so."
The Duke said:
"Excellent."
He made those within the palace not wear it,
and before the month had turned,
no one in the country wore it anymore.
7.44 The people of Qí very much liked to strike each other's wheel hubs for sport,
and they would not stop despite bans.
Yànzǐ was concerned about this,
so he prepared a new carriage and fine horses.
When he went out and struck others' hubs,
he said:
"Striking hubs is inauspicious.
Is it that my sacrifices are not in order
or that my daily life is not respectful?"
He stepped down from the carriage,
abandoned it, and left.
Only then did the people of the country stop doing it.
Therefore it is said:
"If you ban something with regulations
but do not lead by personal example,
the people will not be willing to stop.
Therefore, to transform their hearts, nothing is better than teaching."
7.45 In the laws of the state of Lǔ,
if people of Lǔ ransomed male or female slaves from the feudal lords,
they were to receive gold from the treasury.
Zǐgòng ransomed someone from the feudal lords but returned the gold.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
"Cì has made a mistake!
When a sage undertakes an action,
it can change the winds and transform the customs,
and the teaching can be applied to the common people;
it is not merely to suit his own conduct.
Now, in the state of Lǔ, the wealthy are few and the poor are many.
If one receives gold for a ransom
and it is considered a lack of integrity,
then if one does not receive it,
later no one will ransom anyone again.
From now on,
the people of Lǔ will no longer ransom people."
Kǒngzǐ can be said to have understood transformation.
Thus Lǎozǐ said:
"To see the small is called clarity."
7.46 Kǒngzǐ went to see Jì Kāngzǐ.
Kāngzǐ was not pleased,
yet Kǒngzǐ saw him again.
Zǎi Yǔ said:
"I heard from the Master:
'If the kings and dukes do not summon you,
do not act.'
Now, your sightings of the Sīkòu have been not a few."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the state of Lǔ, the days of people using their numbers to oppress each other
and using weapons to commit violence against each other
have been long,
yet the officials do not govern.
What summons could be greater than this?"
The people of Lǔ heard this and said:
"When a sage is about to govern,
can he not first apply the punishments to himself?"
From then on,
there were no disputants in the state.
Kǒngzǐ said to his disciples:
"Even ten lǐ away from a mountain,
the sound of the cicadas
still persists.
In government affairs, nothing is like facing them."
7.47 In the ancient customs of Lǔ,
the neighborhoods of Túlǐ,
the netting of Luómén,
and the fishing of Huómén
uniquely attained ritual propriety.
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ praised them.
In the neighborhoods of Túlǐ,
the wealthy families provided for the poor;
in the netting of Luómén,
those with relatives took more,
and those without relatives took less;
in the fishing of Huómén,
those with relatives took the large fish,
and those without relatives took the small ones.
7.48 The Chūnqiū says:
When the four classes of people are equal, the kingly way flourishes and the common people are at peace.
The so-called four classes
are the scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
7.49 When the way of marriage is abandoned,
then the way of men and women is perverted,
and the path of licentiousness arises.
8.1 A ruler who desires to govern the world and pass down a glorious name
must honor the worthy and humble himself before scholars.
The Yì says:
"To humble oneself from above to those below,
that way is greatly bright."
It also says:
"To use one's nobility to humble oneself before the lowly
is to greatly win the people."
When an enlightened king extends virtue and humbles himself to those below,
he will embrace those far away and bring those near.
If a court has no worthy men,
it is like a swan without wings;
even if it has the vision of a thousand lǐ,
it still cannot reach the place where its heart desires to go.
Therefore, those who travel the rivers and seas rely on boats;
those who reach distant roads rely on carriages;
those who wish to be hegemons or kings rely on the worthy.
Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Shàng, Guǎn Yíwú, and Bǎilǐ Xī
were the boats and carriages of hegemons and kings.
To set aside fathers, brothers, sons, and grandsons
was not to distance them;
to employ cooks, fishermen, enemies, and slaves
was not to favor them.
The way to sustain the state and establish merit and fame
cannot be otherwise.
It is like a master carpenter building a palace;
he measures the size to know the timber,
and compares the work to know the number of people.
Therefore, when Lǚ Shàng was recruited, the world knew Shāng was about to perish and Zhōu would become king;
when Guǎn Yíwú and Bǎilǐ Xī were employed, the world knew Qí and Qín would certainly become hegemons.
How could they be merely boats and carriages!
Indeed, achieving the status of king or hegemon certainly depends on people,
and the destruction of states and ruin of families also certainly depends on people.
Jié used Yǒu Shēn,
Zhòu used È Lái,
Sòng used Táng Yāng,
Qí used Sū Qín,
Qín used Zhào Gāo,
and the world knew they would perish.
To desire success without the right people
is like wanting the night to be long on the day of the summer solstice,
or aiming at the sky to shoot fish and wanting the shot to be accurate.
Even Shùn and Yǔ would still be troubled,
how much more so for a common ruler!
8.2 In the time of the Chūnqiū,
the Tiānzǐ was weak,
and the Zhūhóu governed by force.
They all rebelled and did not attend court;
the many oppressed the few,
and the strong coerced the weak.
The Nán Yí and Běi Dí invaded each other,
and the existence of Zhōngguó hung by a thread.
Huán Gōng then employed Guǎn Zhòng, Bào Shū, Xí Péng, Bīn Xūwú, and Níng Qī.
Three times he preserved perishing states,
and once he continued severed lineages.
He saved Zhōngguó,
drove back the Róng and Dí,
and finally intimidated the Jīng and Mán,
thereby honoring the Zhōu Shì
and becoming the Hegemon over the Zhūhóu.
Jìn Wén Gōng employed Jiù Fàn, Xiān Zhěn, and Yáng Chǔfù.
He strengthened Zhōngguó,
defeated the powerful Chǔ,
assembled the Zhūhóu,
paid court to the Tiānzǐ,
and brought glory to the Zhōu Shì.
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng employed Sūnshū Áo, Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn, and Jiāngjūn Zǐzhòng.
He campaigned against Chén and made Zhèng submit.
He defeated the powerful Jìn
and was without match under Heaven.
Qín Mù Gōng employed Bǎilǐ Zǐ, Jiǎn Shū Zǐ, Wángzǐ Liào, and Yóu Yú.
He possessed Yōng Zhōu
and drove back and defeated the Western Róng.
Wú employed Yánzhōu Lái Jìzǐ,
annexed Jì Zhōu,
and displayed its might at Jīfù.
Zhèng Xī Gōng was as wealthy as a state of a thousand chariots
and as noble as a Zhūhóu,
but his administration of righteousness did not follow the hearts of the people,
and he was assassinated by his ministers
because he did not first obtain worthy men.
By the time of Jiǎn Gōng, he employed Zǐchǎn, Bì Chén, Shìshū, and Xíngrén Zǐyǔ.
Traitorous ministers were removed,
upright ministers were promoted,
they fended off the powerful Chǔ,
and joined with Zhōngguó.
The state was peaceful
for more than twenty years,
without the trouble of the powerful Chǔ.
Thus, when Yú had Gōngzhī Qí,
Jìn Xiàn Gōng could not sleep all night because of it.
When Chǔ had Zǐyù and Déchén,
Wén Gōng sat on the edge of his mat because of them.
So far-reaching is the ability of worthy men to avert disaster and repel enemies!
Now, Sòng Xiāng Gōng did not use the words of Gōngzǐ Mùyí,
and suffered great humiliation from Chǔ.
Cáo did not use the remonstrance of Xī Fùjī,
and was defeated and died at the hands of the Róng.
Therefore, the essential point for maintaining the five beginnings
and the root of order or chaos
lies in examining oneself and appointing the worthy.
For a state, appointing the worthy leads to good fortune,
while appointing the unworthy leads to disaster.
If one examines past generations and looks at past events,
the necessity of this is as certain as matching two halves of a tally;
this is something that those who are rulers of men cannot fail to be cautious about.
When a state is in confusion and chaos, good ministers appear;
when the state of Lǔ was in great chaos,
the worthiness of Jì Yǒu appeared.
When Xī Gōng ascended the throne and employed Jìzǐ,
the state of Lǔ was peaceful
and without worries within or without
for twenty-one years of administration.
After the death of Jìzǐ,
Zhù attacked its south,
and Qí invaded its north.
Lǔ could not overcome these troubles
and was about to beg for an army from Chǔ
just to preserve itself.
Thus, the Commentary says:
“The rise of trouble
must start from here.”
Gōngzǐ Mǎi could not be sent to guard Wèi,
and Gōngzǐ Suì did not obey the ruler’s command but went to Jìn on his own authority.
Internally, they were encroached upon by ministers,
and externally, they were distressed by military chaos;
such is the trouble of weakness.
The nature of Xī Gōng
was not that he was constantly worthy for the first twenty-one years
and then gradually changed to being unworthy afterward;
this was the benefit of Jìzǐ’s presence
and the loss caused by his absence.
Now, obtaining the worthy or losing the worthy—
the evidence of its benefit and loss is like this,
yet rulers are negligent in what they employ;
this is truly distressing.
If one’s wisdom is insufficient to recognize the worthy,
there is nothing to be done;
but if one’s wisdom can recognize them but one’s strength cannot decide,
and one hesitates and does not employ them,
then at the worst, death and destruction follow,
and at the least, chaos and ruin.
This is truly lamentable.
Did Sòng Shāng Gōng not know the worthiness of Kǒng Fù?
How did he know that if Kǒng Fù died, he himself would surely die,
and so he hurried to save him?
That he hurried to save him
shows that he knew his worthiness.
Did Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng not know the worthiness of Jìzǐ?
How did he know, when he was ill and about to die, to summon Jìzǐ and entrust him with the state’s administration?
That he entrusted him with the state’s administration
shows that he knew his worthiness.
These two rulers’ wisdom was able to see the worthy, yet both were unable to employ them earlier;
thus, Sòng Shāng Gōng was killed,
and Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng had his succession usurped.
If Sòng Shāng Gōng had employed Kǒng Fù earlier,
and Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng had used Jìzǐ from the beginning,
they would have brought peace to neighboring states,
let alone preserved themselves!
8.3 Zōu Zǐ spoke to Liáng Wáng, saying:
“Yī Yǐn was formerly a servant of the Yǒu Shīn Shì.
Tāng appointed him as one of the Sāngōng,
and the world was governed in Great Peace.
Guǎn Zhòng was formerly a petty thief from Chéngyīn,
an ordinary man of the world,
but Qí Huán Gōng obtained him and made him his Zhòngfù.
Bǎilǐ Xī begged for food on the road
and was sold for the price of five sheepskins,
but Qín Mù Gōng entrusted him with the government.
Níng Qī was formerly a man who drove carts;
he beat the yoke and sang songs on the road of Kāng,
and Huán Gōng entrusted him with the state.
Sīmǎ Xǐ had his feet amputated in Sòng,
yet he eventually became the Chancellor of Zhōngshān.
Fàn Suī had his ribs broken and his teeth knocked out in Wèi,
and afterward became the Yìng Hóu.
Tàigōng Wàng was formerly a husband cast out by an old woman,
a butcher's assistant in Cháogē,
and a lodging-house servant who welcomed guests at Jíjīn.
At the age of seventy, he became the Chancellor of Zhōu,
and at ninety, he was enfeoffed in Qí.
Thus, the Shī says:
‘The creeping vines
are in the open fields;
if a skilled craftsman finds them,
he makes them into fine linen,
but if a skilled craftsman does not find them,
they wither and die in the field.’
If these seven gentlemen had not encountered enlightened rulers and sage lords,
they would have almost lived as beggars
and withered and died in the midst of the fields,
just like the creeping vines.”
8.4 The subtlest movements of eyebrows and eyelashes
are manifest in one’s expression upon contact;
the wind of voices and sounds
is felt and moves the heart.
Níng Qī struck the horns of an ox and sang a song in the Shāng mode,
and Huán Gōng heard it and promoted him.
Bào Lóng knelt on a stone to climb a mountain,
and Kǒngzǐ got down from his carriage for him.
When Yáo and Shùn met each other,
they did not wait for the shadow of the mulberry tree to move;
when Wén Wáng promoted Tàigōng,
it did not take a long time.
Therefore, when sages and worthies meet,
they become close without waiting for time to pass.
When capable men see each other,
they know each other without waiting for a trial.
Thus, when scholars meet,
it is not necessarily by facing wealth and dividing goods together that one knows their integrity;
it is not necessarily by facing hardship and wading through danger together that one knows their courage.
By the way they handle affairs and make decisions,
their courage is known;
by the way they take and give with yielding,
their integrity is known.
Therefore, seeing a tiger’s tail, one knows it is larger than a leopard;
seeing an elephant’s tusk, one knows it is larger than an ox.
When one part is seen, all a hundred parts are known.
Looking at it from this perspective,
by what is seen, one can predict what has not yet happened;
by observing small details,
it is indeed enough to know the overall substance.
8.5 Yǔ ruled as king by means of Xià,
while Jié perished by means of Xià;
Tāng ruled as king by means of Yīn,
while Zhòu perished by means of Yīn.
Hélú, by means of Wú, was victorious in battle and matchless throughout the world,
but Fūchāi was captured by Yuè;
Wéngōng achieved hegemony by means of Jìnguó, but Lìgōng was assassinated in the Jùlì Palace;
Wēiwáng made Qí strong throughout the world, but Mǐnwáng was assassinated at Miàoliáng;
Mùgōng gained fame and noble title by means of Qín, but Èrshì was coerced at Wàngyí.
The ways in which they were monarchs were the same,
but their achievements and legacies were unequal;
this was because those they employed were different.
Therefore, Chéngwáng received the feudal lords in court while still in swaddling clothes,
because Zhōugōng handled the affairs of state;
Zhào Wǔlíngwáng was fifty years old but starved at Shāqiū,
because he employed Lǐ Duì.
Qí Huángōng obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
assembled the feudal lords nine times,
and unified the world;
when he lost Guǎn Zhòng
and employed Shù Diāo and Yì Yá,
he died and was not buried,
becoming a laughingstock of the world.
Within the life of a single person,
both honor and disgrace were experienced,
all depending on those he employed.
Thus, Wèi had Gōngzǐ Wújì and regained its lost territory.
Zhào employed Lìn Xiāngrú and the Qín army dared not come out.
Yānlíng employed Táng Suī and the state stood independent.
Chǔ had Shēn Bāoxū and Zhāowáng returned to his throne.
Qí had Tián Dān,
and Xiāngwáng regained his state.
From this perspective,
there has never been a case where a state without worthy assistants and talented scholars could succeed and establish a name, or secure safety and continue a broken lineage.
Such a thing has never existed.
Therefore, a state should not strive for size but for winning the hearts of the people;
assistants should not be many but should be worthy and talented.
To those who win the hearts of the people, the people go;
to those who have worthy assistants, the scholars flock.
Wénwáng requested the abolition of the punishment of the roasting pillar and the Yīn people followed him;
Tāng removed three sides of the hunting nets and the Xià people followed him;
Yuèwáng did not destroy the old graves and the Wú people submitted,
because what they did was in accord with the hearts of the people.
Thus, when sounds are the same, they resonate even in different places;
when virtues match, people become close even before meeting.
When worthy men stand in the court,
then the heroes of the world
will follow one another and hasten to them.
How do we know this is so?
It is said:
Guǎn Zhòng
was an enemy to Huángōng,
but Bào Shū considered him worthier than himself and recommended him as prime minister;
he spoke seventy times before he was finally listened to,
eventually making Huángōng set aside his desire for revenge and entrust him with the affairs of the state.
That Huángōng could sit with hands folded and do nothing while receiving the feudal lords in court
was due to the strength of Bào Shū.
The reason Guǎn Zhòng fled north to Huángōng without fear for his own safety
was that he shared the same sound with Bào Shū.
Zhòu killed Wángzǐ Bǐgān and Jīzǐ let down his hair and feigned madness;
Chén Línggōng killed Xiè Yě and Dèng Yuán left Chén
with his clan;
from then on,
Yīn was annexed by Zhōu,
and Chén perished by Chǔ,
because they killed Bǐgān and Xiè Yě and lost Jīzǐ and Dèng Yuán.
Yān Zhāowáng obtained Guō Wěi,
and Zōu Yǎn and Yuè Yì arrived from Qí and Zhào,
while Sū Zǐ and Qū Jǐng arrived from Zhōu and Chǔ;
they then raised troops and attacked Qí,
cornering Mǐnwáng in Jǔ.
If Yān measured its territory and counted its population,
it was not equal to Qí;
yet the reason it could carry out its will to this extent
was that it obtained scholars.
Therefore, there is no state in constant safety
and no people in constant order;
if they obtain the worthy, they will be safe and prosperous,
but if they lose them, they will face danger and ruin.
From antiquity to the present,
it has never been otherwise.
A clear mirror is that which reflects the form;
the past is that which allows us to know the present.
Now, if one knows to hate the reasons for danger and ruin in the past
but does not strive to follow the tracks of safety and prosperity,
it is no different from running backward while trying to catch up to the person in front.
Tàigōng knew this,
so he raised the descendants of Wēizǐ
and built a mound over the tomb of Bǐgān.
If a Sage's treatment of the dead
is as generous as this,
how much more so for those living in the present age?
Thus, his not losing them can be clearly recognized.
8.6 Qí Jǐnggōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Qín Mùgōng's state was small and located in a remote area, yet he achieved hegemony;
why?"
He replied:
"Though his state was small, his will was great;
though his location was remote, his government was balanced.
His appointments were decisive,
his plans were harmonious,
and his orders were not negligent.
He personally promoted the Wǔgǔ Dàfū from among the captives,
spoke with him,
and after three days entrusted him with the government.
By using such an approach,
even ruling as king would be possible;
being a hegemon is but a small thing."
8.7 Someone said:
"Would you say Huángōng was benevolent and righteous?
He killed his brother to take the throne;
that is not benevolent and righteous.
Would you say Huángōng was respectful and frugal?
He rode in the same carriage with a woman
and sped through the town;
that is not respectful and frugal.
Would you say Huángōng was clean and pure?
Within his inner quarters,
there were no marriageable women left;
that is not clean and pure.
These three behaviors
are those of a ruler who loses his state and his throne;
yet Huángōng possessed them all.
By obtaining Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng,
he assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unified the world,
made them all pay court to the Zhōu house,
and became the leader of the Five Hegemons,
all because he obtained worthy assistants.
When he lost Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng
and employed Shù Diāo and Yì Yá,
he died and was not buried,
and maggots crawled out of his door.
In the person of one man,
why were both honor and disgrace applied?
It was because those he employed were different.
From this perspective,
the employment of assistants is an urgent matter."
8.8 Zhōugōng Dàn was a scholar from a humble home;
those he humbled himself before numbered seventy,
and the scholars of the world all came.
Yànzǐ shared food and clothing with a hundred people,
and the scholars of the world also came.
Zhòngní cultivated the Way
and arranged the cultural patterns,
and the scholars of the world also came.
Bóyá Zǐ played the zither,
and his friend Zhōng Zǐqī listened.
While he was playing the zither with his mind on Tàishān,
Zhōng Zǐqī said:
"How wonderful is your zither playing!
It is lofty like Tàishān."
After a short while,
when his mind was on flowing water,
Zhōng Zǐqī said again:
"How wonderful is your zither playing!
It is vast like flowing water."
When Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bóyá smashed his zither and cut the strings,
never playing the zither again for the rest of his life,
believing that in the world there was no one worthy for whom to play the zither.
It is not only with the zither that it is like this;
it is the same with worthy men.
Although there may be worthy men, if there is no way to receive them,
by what means can they exhaust their loyalty?
A Jì steed does not reach a thousand lǐ by itself;
it waits for Bólè and only then arrives.
8.9 Zhōu Wēi Gōng asked Nìng Zǐ:
“Is there a way to select scholars?”
He replied:
“There is.
Advance those in distress,
preserve those who have fled,
and raise up those who have been cast aside;
then scholars from all directions will arrive from all sides.
If those in distress are not advanced,
those who have fled are not preserved,
and those cast aside are not raised up,
then scholars from all directions will rebel from all sides.
Even if city walls are firm, they cannot defend themselves;
even if weapons are sharp, they cannot protect themselves;
if one gains scholars and then loses them,
there must be a reason.
When scholars stay, the ruler is honored;
when scholars leave, the ruler is debased.”
Zhōu Wēi Gōng said:
“Are scholars really of such singular importance?”
He replied:
“Has My Lord not heard of Chǔ?
The King had scholars named Chǔ Xī Xū and Qiū Fù Kè;
the King intended to kill them,
so they fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn employed them,
and this led to the Battle of Chéngpú.
There was also a scholar named Miáo Bèn Huáng;
the King intended to kill him,
so he fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn employed him,
and this led to the Battle of Yānlíng.
There was also a scholar named Shàng Jiě Yú;
the King intended to kill him,
so he fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn employed them,
and this led to the Battle of Liǎngtáng.
There was also a scholar named Wǔ Zǐ Xū;
the King killed his father and brother,
so he fled to Wú.
Hélǘ employed him,
and he then raised an army and raided Yǐng.
Thus, even though Chǔ had greatly offended the rulers of Liáng, Zhèng, Sòng, and Wèi,
it had not yet reached such a state.
These four instances of offending its scholars
thrice exposed the bones of its people
and once lost its state.
From this perspective,
if scholars stay, the state survives;
if scholars leave, the state perishes.
Wǔ Zǐ Xū was angry and destroyed it;
Shēn Bāo Xū was angry and preserved it;
how can scholars not be valued!”
8.10 Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
“What kind of person should be selected?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“Do not select those who are opinionated,
do not select those who are overbearing,
and do not select those who are glib.”
Āi Gōng said:
“What do you mean?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The opinionated are very glib and sharp,
they cannot be fully utilized;
the overbearing will surely want to dominate others,
they cannot be taken as a model;
the glib are mostly deceitful and lack sincerity,
for fear they will not prove true afterward.
Only after the bow and arrow are harmonized and tuned does one seek to hit the target;
only after a horse is honest, willing, and obedient does one seek its fine talent;
a person must be loyal, trustworthy, serious, and substantial,
and only then should one seek their knowledge and ability.
If today there is a person who is not loyal, trustworthy, serious, and substantial, but has much knowledge and ability,
such a person is like a wolf or a jackal,
and one cannot let them near one's person.
Therefore, first prioritize those who are sincere in benevolence and trustworthiness,
and then grow close to them.
Once they have knowledge and ability,
then employ them.
Thus it is said:
Be close to the benevolent and employ the capable.
In the method of selecting people,
observe their words and examine their actions.
Words
are what express the heart and release the emotions.
Scholars capable of action
will surely be capable of speech.
Therefore, first observe their words and then measure their actions.
By measuring their actions by their words,
even if there are treacherous or lawless people,
they will have no way to hide their true nature.”
Āi Gōng said:
“Excellent.”
8.11 When Zhōu Gōng held the position of the Son of Heaven for seven years,
among the scholars in commoner's clothes,
those he visited as teachers while holding a gift were ten;
those he visited as friends were twelve;
those from poor alleys and thatched houses whom he visited first were forty-nine;
those who frequently offered good advice were one hundred;
those who taught scholars were one thousand;
and those who served in the court were ten thousand.
At this time,
if Zhōu Gōng had been arrogant and stingy,
then the worthy scholars of the world who arrived would have been few.
Even if some had arrived,
they would surely have been greedy people who merely drew a salary without merit.
Ministers who merely draw a salary
cannot preserve their ruler.
8.12 Qí Huán Gōng set up courtyard torches for scholars who wished to see him,
but for a whole year, no scholars arrived.
Then, a rustic man from the eastern countryside came to see him with the art of multiplication tables;
Huán Gōng said:
“Are multiplication tables enough to grant an audience?”
The rustic man replied:
“I do not believe multiplication tables are enough to grant an audience.
I heard that My Lord set up courtyard torches to wait for scholars,
but for a whole year, no scholars arrived.
The reason why scholars do not arrive
is because My Lord
is a worthy ruler of the world,
and scholars from all directions all consider themselves, by comparison, as not measuring up to My Lord,
so they do not come.
Now, multiplication tables are a meager skill,
yet if My Lord still treats me with ritual,
how much more so for those worthier than someone with multiplication tables?
Tài Shān does not reject soil and stones,
and the rivers and seas do not turn away small streams;
this is how they achieve their greatness.
The Poetry says:
‘The ancient people had a saying:
Consult even with those who gather grass and firewood.’
This speaks of broad consultation.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Excellent.”
He then treated him with ritual,
and within a month,
scholars from all directions came together, hand in hand.
The Poetry says:
“From the hall to the foundation,
from the sheep to the oxen.”
This speaks of moving from the inner to the outer,
and from the small to the large.
8.13 Qí Jǐng Gōng attacked Sòng.
Arriving at the Qí Dī embankment,
he climbed high to look out,
sighed deeply and lamented:
“In the past, my late ancestor Huán Gōng had eight hundred chariots and became hegemon over the feudal lords.
Today, I have three thousand chariots yet dare not remain here for long;
could it be because I have no Guǎn Zhòng?”
Xián Zhāng replied:
“I have heard that
when the water is vast, the fish are large;
when the ruler is enlightened, the ministers are loyal.
In the past, there was a Huán Gōng,
so there was a Guǎn Zhòng.
If Huán Gōng were here today,
then the ministers beneath his carriage
would all be Guǎn Zhòngs.”
8.14 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ was traveling on the Xī Hé and enjoyed it;
he sighed and said:
“How can I find worthy scholars to dwell with me?”
Gǔ Sāng, a boatman, knelt and replied:
“Pearls and jade have no feet,
yet they can come from thousands of miles away
because people like them.
Now, scholars have feet but do not come;
is this not because my Lord does not like them?”
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“I have a thousand guests at my gates;
if there is not enough for the morning meal,
in the evening I collect the market taxes;
if there is not enough for the evening meal,
in the morning I collect the market taxes.
Can I still be said not to like scholars?”
The boatman Gǔ Sāng replied:
“The swan flies high and soars far,
relying on its six primary wing feathers.
The hair on its back
and the down on its belly
are not even an inch in length;
if a handful is plucked away,
its flight will not become lower for it;
if a handful is added,
its flight will not become higher for it.
I do not know if the thousand guests at your gates
have the use of six primary wing feathers,
or if they are all just hair and down.”
8.15 King Xuān of Qí was sitting,
and Chúnyú Kūn was in attendance.
King Xuān said:
"What does the Master think I am fond of?"
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"In ancient times there were four things liked,
and Your Majesty likes three of them."
King Xuān said:
"How do the things liked in ancient times
compare with those I like?"
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"In ancient times they liked horses,
and Your Majesty also likes horses;
in ancient times they liked fine flavors,
and Your Majesty also likes fine flavors;
in ancient times they liked beauty,
and Your Majesty also likes beauty;
in ancient times they liked scholars,
but Your Majesty alone does not like scholars."
King Xuān said:
"It is just that there are no scholars in the state;
if there were, I would also be pleased with them."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"In ancient times there were Huáliú and Qíjì,
which no longer exist today,
yet Your Majesty selects from the crowd,
so Your Majesty likes horses.
In ancient times there were the fetuses of leopards and elephants,
which no longer exist today,
yet Your Majesty selects from the crowd,
so Your Majesty likes fine flavors.
In ancient times there were Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī,
which no longer exist today,
yet Your Majesty selects from the crowd,
so Your Majesty likes beauty.
If Your Majesty must wait for scholars like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng before liking them,
then scholars like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng
would also not like Your Majesty."
King Xuān was silent and had nothing with which to respond.
8.16 The Ruler of Wèi asked Tián Ràng, saying:
"I have granted fiefs totaling a thousand lǐ of land;
rewards given have exhausted the silks of the treasury,
yet scholars do not come;
why is this?"
Tián Ràng replied:
"Your Majesty's rewards
cannot be reached through merit;
Your Majesty's punishments
cannot be avoided through reason.
This is like raising a stick and calling a dog,
or drawing a bow and praying for a chicken!
Even if there is fragrant bait, you cannot attract them,
because harm to them is certain."
8.17 Zōng Wèi was Chancellor of Qí;
meeting with expulsion,
he ceased his duties and returned to his residence,
where he summoned the Gate Commander Tián Ráo and twenty-seven others and questioned them.
He said:
"Are there any among you scholars and officials who can go with me to the feudal lords?"
Tián Ráo and the others all prostrated and did not answer.
Zōng Wèi said:
"Why are scholars and officials so easy to obtain but so difficult to use?"
Ráo replied:
"It is not that scholars and officials are difficult to use;
it is that you, my lord, are unable to use them."
Zōng Wèi said:
"What do you mean by being unable to use scholars and officials?"
Tián Ráo replied:
"If there is rotting meat in the kitchen, then there will be no retainers willing to die at the gate.
Now, three sheng of millet is insufficient for the scholars,
yet your lordship's geese and ducks have surplus grain;
fine white silk and embroidered fabrics,
magnificent halls and balustrades,
are left to be ruined by wind and rain while scholars do not even get a hem for their robes;
pears and chestnuts from the orchard,
the women of the inner palace pick and throw at each other while scholars do not even get a single taste.
Furthermore, wealth
is what your lordship considers light;
death
is what a scholar considers heavy.
If your lordship cannot use the wealth you consider light
but wish to make scholars give up their lives which they consider heavy,
is that not difficult indeed!"
Thereupon Zōng Wèi had a look of shame on his face;
he paced back and forth, moved from his seat and apologized, saying:
"This is the fault of Wèi."
8.18 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Among the rulers of the present time, who is virtuous?"
He replied:
"Duke Líng of Wèi."
The Duke said:
"I have heard
that within his private chambers,
there is no distinction between aunts and sisters."
He replied:
"I observe his court;
I have not observed between his halls and stairs.
Duke Líng's younger brother is named Prince Qūmóu;
his wisdom is sufficient to govern a state of a thousand chariots,
and his trustworthiness is sufficient to defend it,
and Duke Líng loves him.
There is also a scholar named Wáng Lín;
whenever there is a worthy person in the state,
he surely recommends and employs them,
with none failing to attain office;
if they cannot attain office,
he retires and shares his stipend with them,
and Duke Líng respects him.
There is also a scholar named Qìng Zú;
when there are great affairs in the state, he steps forward and manages them,
with none failing to succeed,
and Duke Líng is pleased with him.
When Shǐ Qiú left Wèi,
Duke Líng stayed in a guest house for three months,
and did not use the zither or lute,
waiting for Shǐ Qiú's return before he himself returned;
this is how I know he is virtuous."
8.19 Jièzǐ Tuī at the age of fifteen became Chancellor of Jīng.
Zhòngní heard of this
and sent someone to observe him.
Upon returning,
he said:
"There are twenty-five talented scholars below the gallery,
and twenty-five elders in the hall."
Zhòngní said:
"Combining the wisdom of twenty-five people,
it is wiser than Tāng and Wǔ;
combining the strength of twenty-five people,
it is stronger than Péngzǔ;
using this to govern the world,
surely he will escape calamity!"
8.20 Kǒngzǐ was sitting at leisure,
and let out a sigh, saying:
"If Tóngdī Bóhuá had not died,
the world would surely be settled!"
Zǐlù said:
"I wish to hear what kind of person he was."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In his youth,
he was quick-witted and loved learning;
in his prime,
he was brave and unyielding;
in his old age,
he possessed the Way and could humble himself before others."
Zǐlù said:
"In his youth,
being quick-witted and loving learning is fine;
in his prime,
being brave and unyielding is fine.
But if one possesses the Way, why should he humble himself before others?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, you do not understand.
I have heard
that using the many to attack the few, nothing is not destroyed;
using the noble to humble oneself before the low, nothing is not gained.
In the past,
Zhōugōng Dàn managed the government of the world,
yet he humbled himself before seventy scholars;
was it because he lacked the Way?
It was because he wished to gain scholars.
One who possesses the Way and can humble himself before the scholars of the world,
is he not a gentleman!"
8.21 Wèi Wén Hóu was rushing from Zhōngshān to Ānyì.
Tián Zǐfāng was behind him.
Tàizǐ Jī encountered him;
he descended from his carriage and hurried forward,
but Zǐfāng remained seated in his carriage as before.
He said to the Prince:
"For my sake, please ask the Lord to wait for me at Cháogē."
The Prince was displeased
and subsequently said to Zǐfāng:
"I do not know—is it the poor and lowly who are arrogant toward others,
or the wealthy and noble who are arrogant toward others?"
Zǐfāng said:
"The poor and lowly are arrogant toward others.
How would the wealthy and noble dare to be arrogant toward others?
If a ruler of men is arrogant toward others, he will lose his state;
I have never seen one who waits until his state is lost.
If a Grand Officer is arrogant toward others, he will lose his house;
I have never seen one who waits until his house is lost.
If the poor and lowly do not find fulfillment,
they simply put on their sandals and depart.
Where could they go and not find poverty and lowliness?
The poor and lowly are arrogant toward others;
how would the wealthy and noble dare to be arrogant toward others?"
The Prince reached Wén Hóu
and recounted Tián Zǐfāng’s words.
Wén Hóu sighed and said:
"Were it not for my son,
how would I have heard the words of a worthy man?
I humbled myself before Zǐfāng in my conduct
and succeeded in befriending him.
Since I befriended Zǐfāng,
ruler and ministers have become more intimate,
and the common people have become more attached.
Thus I have achieved the merit of befriending scholars.
I wanted to attack Zhōngshān,
and I used military force to humble Lè Yáng;
in three years, Zhōngshān was presented to me.
Thus I have achieved the merit of befriending military force.
The reason I have not advanced a little further than this
is that I have not yet seen anyone who uses wisdom to be arrogant toward me.
If I could find someone who is arrogant toward me with wisdom,
would I not reach the level of the men of old?"
8.22 Jìn Wén Hóu was walking and ascending through a tunnel.
The Grand Officers all supported him,
but Suí Huì did not support him.
Wén Hóu said:
"Huì,
for one who is a minister to be callous toward his ruler,
what is his crime?"
He replied:
"His crime is heavier than death."
Wén Hóu said:
"What is meant by 'heavier than death'?"
He replied:
"He himself dies,
and his wife and children are executed with him."
Suí Huì said:
"Why does the Lord only ask about a minister being callous toward his ruler,
and not ask about a ruler being callous toward his ministers?"
Wén Hóu said:
"For a ruler to be callous toward his ministers,
what is his crime?"
Suí Huì replied:
"When a ruler is callous toward his ministers,
wise men will not plan for him,
eloquent men will not speak for him,
benevolent men will not act for him,
and brave men will not die for him."
Wén Hóu took hold of the hand-strap and descended from the carriage;
he apologized to the Grand Officers, saying:
"I have an ailment in my waist and thighs;
I hope you gentlemen do not blame me."
8.23 The Qí General Tián Kuì was going out to take command.
Zhāng Shēng saw him off in the suburbs and said:
"In the past, Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
but he washed his ears and would not accept;
does the General know this?"
He said:
"Yes,
so it was,
I know it."
"Bó Yí and Shú Qí declined the positions of feudal lords and would not take them;
does the General know this?"
He said:
"Yes,
so it was,
I know it."
"Yúlìng Zhòngzǐ declined the position of the Three Ducal Ministers to be a hired laborer
and water gardens for others;
does the General know this?"
He said:
"Yes,
so it was,
I know it."
"Zhì Guò left his ruler and younger brother,
changed his name,
and became one of the common people;
does the General know this?"
He said:
"Yes,
so it was,
I know it."
"Sūnshū Áo three times left the post of Chancellor without regret;
does the General know this?"
He said:
"Yes,
so it was,
I know it."
"These five Great Men
renounced such fame and were truly ashamed of it.
Now the General is about to wield the power of an entire state,
beating drums and holding banners,
wearing armor and holding sharp weapons,
commanding an army of a hundred thousand,
and wielding the power of execution;
be careful not to use what scholars are ashamed of to be arrogant toward scholars."
Tián Kuì said:
"Today you gentlemen have all performed the Zǔdào for me
with wine and dried meat,
but you alone, Sir, teach me the Great Way of the Sages.
I have respectfully heard your command."
8.24 Wèi Wén Hóu visited Duàn Gànmù;
he stood until exhausted and did not dare rest.
When he saw Zhái Huáng,
he sat cross-legged in the hall while speaking with him.
Zhái Huáng was displeased.
Wén Hóu said:
"If I offer Duàn Gànmù an office, he will not consent;
if I offer him a salary, he will not accept.
Now as for you, if you want an office, you reach the rank of Chancellor;
if you want a salary, you reach the rank of High Minister.
Since you have accepted my rewards
and yet demand my etiquette,
is that not a difficult request?"
8.25 Kǒngzǐ went to Tán
and encountered Chéng Zǐ on the road.
They tilted their carriage canopies and spoke all day.
After a while,
he looked at Zǐlù and said:
"Take a bundle of silk
to present to the gentleman."
Zǐlù did not answer.
After another while,
he looked again and said:
"Take a bundle of silk
to present to the gentleman."
Zǐlù replied with annoyance:
"I have heard that
if a scholar meets someone without an intermediary,
or if a woman marries without a matchmaker,
a gentleman does not go along with it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu,
does the Shī not say?
'In the wild there is creeping grass,
the falling dew is heavy.
There is a beautiful person,
clear-eyed and fine.
We met by chance,
just as I desired.'
Now Chéng Zǐ is a worthy scholar of the world;
if I do not present him with a gift now,
I may never see him again in my life.
In matters of great virtue, one must not cross the boundaries,
but in matters of small virtue, one may go in and out."
8.26 Qí Huán Gōng ordered Guǎn Zhòng to govern the state.
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"The lowly cannot oversee the noble."
Huán Gōng made him a High Minister,
but the state was not yet well-governed.
Huán Gōng said:
"For what reason?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"The poor cannot command the wealthy."
Huán Gōng gave him the market taxes of the state of Qí for one year,
but the state was still not well-governed.
Huán Gōng said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"The distant cannot control the kin."
Huán Gōng appointed him as Zhòngfù.
The state of Qí became greatly peaceful and subsequently dominated the world.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"With Guǎn Zhòng’s worthiness,
if he had not obtained these three powers,
he could not have enabled his ruler to face south and become a hegemon."
8.27 Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng, saying:
“I wish to let my wine goblets rot in wine
and my meat rot on the sacrificial stands.
Will this not harm my hegemony?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“This is merely a failure to prioritize what is noble.
Yet it will not harm your hegemony.”
Huán Gōng asked:
“What then harms hegemony?”
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
“Not knowing the worthy
harms hegemony;
knowing them but not using them
harms hegemony;
using them but not entrusting them with responsibility
harms hegemony;
entrusting them but not trusting them
harms hegemony;
trusting them but then allowing petty men to interfere with them
harms hegemony.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Excellent.”
8.28 When the people of Lǔ attacked Bì,
Zéng Zǐ took his leave of the Lord of Bì, saying:
“I request to depart,
and will return only after the invaders have withdrawn.
For now, please do not let dogs or pigs enter my dwelling.”
The Lord of Bì said:
“As for my treatment of you, Master,
there is no one who has not heard of it.
Now that the people of Lǔ are attacking me and you are leaving me,
why should I protect your dwelling?”
The people of Lǔ did indeed attack Bì and enumerated ten of its crimes,
but nine of these were matters that Zéng Zǐ had argued against.
When the army of Lǔ withdrew,
the Lord of Bì again repaired Zéng Zǐ’s dwelling and then welcomed him back.
8.29 When Sīchéng Zǐhǎn of Sòng held Zǐwéi in high esteem,
he would dine with him when indoors
and share clothes with him when outdoors.
When Sīchéng Zǐhǎn went into exile,
Zǐwéi did not follow him.
When Zǐhǎn returned,
he again summoned Zǐwéi and held him in high esteem.
His attendants said:
“Your Lordship was so good to Zǐwéi,
yet when you went into exile he did not follow;
now that you have returned, you honor him again.
Do you not feel ashamed before your loyal ministers?”
Zǐhǎn said:
“It was precisely because I could not use Zǐwéi’s advice that I came to be exiled.
Now that I have been able to return,
it is still due to the legacy of Zǐwéi’s virtue and teachings.
That is why I honor him.
Furthermore, regarding my exile,
if my ministers had merely followed me, erasing their tracks and pulling up trees,
what benefit would that have been to my exile?”
8.30 Yáng Yīn saw Zhào Jiǎn Zhǔ and said:
“I was expelled from my village three times,
and I have left the service of five rulers.
Hearing that you love worthy men,
I have come running to see you.”
When Jiǎn Zhǔ heard this,
he stopped eating and sighed,
and walked on his knees to greet him.
His attendants came forward to remonstrate, saying:
“Being expelled from his village three times
means he is not tolerated by the masses;
leaving the service of five rulers
means he is not loyal to his superiors.
Now, you have more than eight such 'worthy men' to see.”
Jiǎn Zhǔ said:
“You do not understand.
A beautiful woman
is the enemy of an ugly wife;
a man of great virtue
is shunned by a chaotic age;
and upright conduct
is hated by the crooked and evil.”
He then went out to see him.
Consequently, he appointed Yáng Yīn as Chancellor,
and the state was greatly governed.
Viewing it from this,
people from far and near
cannot but be examined carefully.
8.31 Yìng Hóu was sitting with Jiǎ Yú Zǐ
and heard the sound of him playing the zither.
Yìng Hóu said:
“The zither playing today,
why is it so sad?”
Jiǎ Yú Zǐ said:
“When the strings are pulled tight but the tuning is low,
it inevitably makes it sad!
The strings being pulled tight
represents excellent material;
the tuning being low
represents a low official rank.
To take such excellent material and give it a low rank,
how could it not be sad?”
Yìng Hóu said:
“Excellent!”
8.32 In the thirteenth year,
the feudal lords raised troops to attack Qí.
The King of Qí heard of this,
was startled and afraid,
and summoned his ministers and high officials, saying:
“Those with wisdom should use it for my sake.”
At this, the scholar Chúnyú Kūn looked up to the heavens and laughed loudly but did not respond.
The King asked him again,
and again he laughed loudly and did not respond;
three times he was asked,
and three times he laughed and did not respond.
The King flushed with anger and said displeasedly:
“Does the Master take my words as a joke?”
He replied:
“I would not dare to take the Great King’s words as a joke.
I am laughing at my neighbor’s sacrifice for his fields.
With one basket of rice, one jug of wine, and three carp,
he prayed:
‘May the crab mounds yield fine grain,
may the low-lying fields fill a hundred carts,
and may this be passed down to later generations,
overflowing with abundance.’
I laugh at how thin his offering to the spirits was, yet how thick his request was.”
Thereupon, the King appointed Chúnyú Kūn as a High Minister,
granted him a thousand pieces of gold
and a hundred chariots,
and sent him to settle the affairs with the feudal lords.
When the feudal lords heard of this,
they immediately withdrew their troops
and rested their soldiers,
and thus did not dare to attack Qí.
Was this not the power of Chúnyú Kūn?
8.33 Tián Jì left Qí and fled to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ welcomed him at the outskirts and took him to his lodging,
asking:
“Chǔ
is a state of ten thousand chariots;
Qí
is also a state of ten thousand chariots.
We have always wanted to annex them.
How should we go about it?”
Tián Jì replied:
“It is easy to know!
If Qí sends Shēn Rǔ to lead,
then Chǔ should dispatch fifty thousand men
and have its High General lead them;
they will return after capturing the general’s head.
If Qí sends Tián Jū to lead,
then Chǔ should dispatch two hundred thousand men
and have its High General lead them; they will separate and depart from each other without a clear victory.
If Qí sends Miǎn Zǐ to lead,
then Chǔ must mobilize everyone within its four borders,
the King must personally go out to lead with Jì following him,
and the Chancellor and High General must serve as Left and Right Marshals;
only in this way could the King barely survive.”
At that time, Qí sent Shēn Rǔ to lead,
and Chǔ dispatched fifty thousand men;
they had its High General capture the general’s head and return.
At this, the King of Qí was enraged
and then instead sent Miǎn Zǐ to lead.
Chǔ mobilized everyone within its four borders,
the King personally went out to lead,
Tián Jì followed him,
and the Chancellor and High General served as Left and Right Marshals.
They increased the King’s retinue by nine chariots
and only just managed to escape.
When they reached the lodging,
the King faced north, adjusted his collar and straightened his sleeves,
and asked:
“How did you know this so early, Master?”
Tián Jì said:
“As a man, Shēn Rǔ
insults the worthy and slights the unworthy;
thus both the worthy and the unworthy will not work for him,
and that is why he fell.
As a man, Tián Jū
honors the worthy and despises the unworthy;
the worthy take on responsibilities
while the unworthy withdraw,
and that is why they separate and depart without a decision.
As for Miǎn Zǐ’s character,
he honors the worthy and loves the unworthy;
both the worthy and the unworthy take on responsibilities for him,
and that is why the King only just managed to survive.”
8.34 Wèi Wén Hóu held a banquet for the high officials at Qǔ Yáng.
When the drinking reached its peak,
Wén Hóu let out a deep sigh and said:
"Why is it that I alone do not have a Yù Ràng to serve as my minister?"
Jiǎn Zhòng raised a cup of wine, stepped forward, and said:
"I request that your Lordship drink a penalty cup."
Wén Hóu said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"I have heard it said:
Parents who are within their rights
do not recognize filial sons;
a ruler who follows the Way
does not recognize loyal ministers.
As for the ruler of Yù Ràng,
what kind of ruler was he?"
Wén Hóu said:
"Excellent."
He accepted the penalty cup and drank it,
draining it without hesitation,
and said:
"It is because one lacks a Guǎn Zhòng or a Bǎo Shū to serve as ministers
that the achievements of a Yù Ràng come to be."
8.35 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"I wish to obtain the fine ministers of the Fàn and Zhōng Háng clans."
Shǐ Yǎn said:
"What would you use them for?"
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Fine ministers
are what everyone desires;
why even ask?"
He replied:
"I believe it is precisely because they lacked fine ministers.
For those who serve a ruler,
they remonstrate against errors and recommend what is right,
they make clear what is good and replace what is bad,
they present capability and advance the worthy,
morning and night they recite the causes of success and failure to provide guidance,
if their advice is followed they advance,
if not they retire.
Now the so-called fine ministers of the Fàn and Zhōng Háng clans
were unable to correct and assist their rulers,
leading them to disaster,
causing them to flee abroad,
and they were unable to bring them back,
abandoning them in exile;
how can this be considered fine?
If they had not been abandoned,
how would you, my Lord, be able to obtain them?
A truly fine minister
will manage matters for his ruler
to make him recover his position,
stopping only at death.
Why would they say they have come here to you?
If they could not do this,
then they are not fine ministers."
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Excellent."
8.36 Zǐ Lù asked Kǒng Zǐ:
"What is the way to govern a state?"
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"It lies in honoring the worthy and despising the unworthy."
Zǐ Lù said:
"The Fàn and Zhōng Háng clans honored the worthy and despised the unworthy,
so why did they perish?"
He said:
"The Fàn and Zhōng Háng clans honored the worthy but were unable to use them,
and they despised the unworthy but were unable to remove them.
The worthy knew they were not being used and resented them;
the unworthy knew they were despised and hated them as enemies.
The worthy resenting them,
and the unworthy hating them as enemies—
with resentment and enmity both advancing before them,
even if the Zhōng Háng clan wished not to perish,
how could that be possible?"
8.37 Jìn and Jīng fought at Bì,
and the Jìn army suffered a great defeat.
Xún Lín Fù was the commander,
and upon returning, he requested his own death.
Jǐng Gōng was about to grant it,
but Shì Zhēn Bó said:
"You must not.
At the battle of Chéng Pú,
Jìn was victorious over Jīng,
yet Wén Gōng still had a look of worry.
He said:
'Zǐ Yù still lives;
my worries have not yet ceased.
A cornered beast still fights,
how much more so the chancellor of a state?'
When Jīng killed Zǐ Yù,
the Duke then rejoiced and said:
'No one can harm me now.'
Now Heaven has perhaps given Jìn a great warning.
As for Lín Fù's service to his ruler,
when advancing he thinks of total loyalty,
and when retreating he thinks of making up for his errors;
he is a defender of the state.
To kill him now
would be to double the victory of Jīng."
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Excellent."
He then had him return to his command.
9.1 The Yì says:
"The king's minister is strenuously struggling,
not for the sake of his own person."
The reason why a minister strenuously undergoes difficulties to remonstrate with his ruler
is not for himself,
but wishing to rectify the ruler's errors
and correct the ruler's mistakes.
A ruler's errors and mistakes
are the sprouts of danger and ruin.
To see the ruler's errors and mistakes and not remonstrate
is to treat the ruler's danger and ruin lightly.
Treating the ruler's danger and ruin lightly
is something a loyal minister cannot bear to do.
If one remonstrates three times and is not listened to, then one leaves.
If one does not leave, then one's person is destroyed.
Destroying one's person
is what a humane man does not do.
Therefore, there are five kinds of remonstrance:
the first is called upright remonstrance,
the second is called lowering remonstrance,
the third is called loyal remonstrance,
the fourth is called blunt remonstrance,
and the fifth is called subtle remonstrance.
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"I shall follow subtle remonstrance!"
Not remonstrating endangers the ruler;
stubborn remonstrance endangers oneself.
Rather than endangering the ruler, it is better to endanger oneself,
but if one endangers oneself and is ultimately not listened to,
then the remonstrance has no effect.
A wise man gauges the ruler and assesses the timing,
adjusting the urgency and managing what is appropriate,
so that above he does not dare endanger the ruler,
and below he does not endanger himself.
Thus, being in the state, the state is not endangered,
and regarding his person, his person is not in peril.
Formerly, Chén Líng Gōng did not listen to the remonstrance of Xiè Yě and killed him;
Cáo Jī remonstrated three times with the ruler of Cáo and, not being listened to, he left.
Although the Chūn Qiū's sequence of righteousness considers both to be worthy,
Cáo Jī's actions accord with ritual propriety.
9.2 Qí Jǐng Gōng traveled to the seaside and enjoyed himself there.
He did not return for six months
and ordered his attendants, saying:
"Whoever dares be the first to speak of returning shall be put to death without pardon!"
Yán Zhú Qū hurried forward to remonstrate, saying:
"Your Lordship enjoys governing the sea
but does not enjoy governing the state.
If you do not return for six months,
should there be someone else who governs the state,
how then will Your Lordship be able to enjoy this sea?"
Jǐng Gōng seized a halberd and was about to strike him.
Yán Zhú Qū hurried forward,
smoothed his clothes, and waited for him,
saying:
"Why does Your Lordship not strike?
Formerly, Jié killed Guān Lóng Páng,
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐ Gān.
Your Lordship's worthiness
is not equal to these two rulers;
my talent
is also not equal to these two men.
Why does Your Lordship not strike?
To have me join the ranks of these two men,
would that not also be acceptable?"
Jǐng Gōng was pleased
and finally returned.
Midway on the road,
he heard that the people of the state were plotting not to let him back in.
9.3 When Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng was established as ruler,
for three years he did not attend court.
He then issued an order to the state, saying:
“I loathe those who, as subjects, are quick to remonstrate with their ruler.
Now that I possess the state and the house,
and have established the altars of soil and grain,
anyone who remonstrates shall be put to death without pardon!”
Sū Cóng said:
“To occupy a high rank from the ruler,
to eat the generous stipends of the ruler,
yet to love one’s life and not remonstrate with the ruler,
that is not being a loyal subject.”
He then entered to remonstrate.
Zhuāng Wáng was standing between bells and drums,
with Yáng Jī reclining on his left
and Yuè Jī embraced on his right.
On his left were bedclothes,
and on his right was court attire.
He said:
“I have no time to spare from my bells and drums;
what remonstrance would I listen to?”
Sū Cóng said:
“Your subject has heard that
those who love the Way have many resources,
while those who love music are often deluded;
those who love the Way have much grain,
while those who love music often face ruin.
The day of Jīng’s destruction is near;
even at the cost of death, your subject dares to inform the King.”
The King said:
“Good.”
With his left hand, he took Sū Cóng’s hand;
with his right, he drew a concealed blade
and severed the ropes of the hanging bells and drums.
The next day,
he appointed Sū Cóng as Prime Minister.
9.4 Jìn Píng Gōng loved music;
he increased taxes and levies
and did not repair the city walls.
He said:
“Anyone who dares to remonstrate shall die!”
The people of the state were worried about this.
There was a man named Jiù Fàn
who saw the Gate Official and said:
“Your subject has heard the Lord loves music,
so I wish to see him by means of music.”
The Gate Official went in and said:
“A man of Jìn named Jiù Fàn
wishes to see you by means of music.”
Píng Gōng said:
“Bring him in.”
As the Lord sat upon the palace hall,
bells, lithophones, pipes, and zithers were brought out.
After sitting for a while,
Píng Gōng said:
“Guest, perform some music.”
Jiù Fàn replied:
“Your subject cannot perform music;
your subject is skilled at riddles.”
Píng Gōng summoned twelve riddle-masters.
Jiù Fàn said:
“This riddle-subject takes the liberty of risking death to address you.”
Píng Gōng said:
“Granted.”
Jiù Fàn extended his left arm and bent his five fingers.
Píng Gōng asked the riddle-officials:
“What does this signify?”
The riddle-officials all said:
“We do not know.”
Píng Gōng said:
“Explain it.”
Jiù Fàn then extended his fingers one by one and said:
“This is the first:
wandering for pleasure exhausts the red earth, yet the city towers are built high;
second:
pillars and beams are clothed in embroidery,
but the officers and people have no coarse cloth to wear;
third:
dwarves have surplus wine while the courageous warriors are thirsty;
fourth:
the people have the look of hunger while the horses have fixed rations of grain;
fifth:
near ministers dare not remonstrate,
and distant ministers cannot reach you.”
Píng Gōng said:
“Good.”
He then removed the bells and drums,
did away with the pipes and zithers,
and subsequently governed the state together with Jiù Fàn.
9.5 Mèngshǎng Jūn was about to go west to enter Qín;
his guests and retainers remonstrated with him a hundred times,
but he would not listen.
He said:
“If you remonstrate with me using human affairs,
I know them all;
but if you remonstrate with me using ghostly ways,
I shall kill you.”
The usher entered and said:
