“There is a guest who wishes to be heard regarding ghostly ways.”
He said:
“Please have the guest enter.”
The guest said:
“As your subject was coming here,
I passed by the Zī Shuǐ;
I saw an earthen figurine just then speaking with a wooden figurine.
The wooden figurine said to the earthen figurine:
‘You were originally
earth,
molded into a figurine;
if you encounter heavy rain
and the floods come together,
you will surely be dissolved and destroyed.’
The other replied:
‘If I am dissolved, I simply return to my true nature.
Now you are a peach tree from the eastern garden,
carved into a person;
if you encounter heavy rain
and the floods come together,
you will surely float,
drifting and drifting, not knowing where you will stop.’
Now Qín is a state blocked on four sides,
with the heart of a tiger or wolf;
I fear you will have the disaster of the wooden figurine.”
At this, Mèngshǎng Jūn hesitated and withdrew, having no way to respond;
in the end, he did not dare go west to Qín.
9.6 Wú Wáng wished to attack Jīng;
he told his attendants:
“Anyone who dares to remonstrate shall die!”
Among the retainers was a Shào Rǔ Zi
who wished to remonstrate but did not dare.
He then carried pellets and a slingshot
and wandered in the rear garden,
letting the dew soak his clothes;
he did this for three mornings.
Wú Wáng said:
“Come here!
Why do you suffer the dew soaking your clothes like this?”
He replied:
“In the garden there is a tree,
and upon it is a cicada.
The cicada dwells on high, chirping mournfully and drinking dew,
not knowing that a mantis is behind it.
The mantis crouches and clings, wishing to take the cicada,
not knowing that an oriole is beside it.
The oriole stretches its neck, wishing to peck the mantis, not knowing that a slingshot pellet is beneath it.
These three all strive to obtain the profit before them without considering the disaster that follows behind.”
Wú Wáng said:
“Excellent!”
He then called off his troops.
9.7 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng wished to attack Yángxià;
the campaign lasted a long time and was not ended.
The ministers wished to remonstrate, but none dared.
Zhuāng Wáng was hunting at Yúnmèng,
and Jiāo Jǔ stepped forward to remonstrate, saying:
“The reason the King can obtain many beasts
is because of his horses;
but if the King’s state is lost,
how could the King obtain his horses?”
Zhuāng Wáng said:
“Good.
I (the unworthy one) knew that humbling strong states could make me the leader of the feudal lords,
and I knew that gaining territory could make me wealthy,
but I forgot that my people would no longer be fit for use.”
The next day,
he served wine to the high officials
and made Jiāo Jǔ the guest of honor.
He ended the campaign against Yángxià.
9.8 The Huángtàihòu of Qín Shǐ Huáng-dì was indiscreet,
favoring the Láng Lào Ài,
enfeoffing him as the Chángxìn Hóu,
and bearing him two sons.
Ài monopolized state affairs,
becoming increasingly arrogant and extravagant.
Together with the Shìzhōng and high-ranking officials nearby,
he played board games
and drank wine.
When drunk,
they argued and fought.
He glared and shouted loudly,
saying:
“I am the Huángdì's Jiǎfù!
How dare the son of a pauper contend with me?”
Those with whom he fought fled
and went to inform the Huángdì.
The Huángdì was greatly enraged.
Ài feared execution,
so he started a rebellion
and fought at the Xiányáng Gōng.
Ài was defeated.
Shǐ Huáng then had Ài’s four limbs torn apart by chariots;
he took his two younger brothers, put them in sacks, and beat them to death;
and he took the Huángtàihòu and exiled her to the Fùyáng Gōng.
He issued an order saying:
“Anyone who dares to use the Huángtàihòu’s matter to remonstrate
shall be executed.
Their back flesh shall be pierced with tribulus thorns, and their four limbs shall be dried and piled up below the palace gates.”
Twenty-seven people died from remonstrating.
Máo Jiāo, a guest from Qí, then went there.
He presented his card and said:
“Máo Jiāo, a guest from Qí, wishes to present a remonstrance to the Huángdì.”
The Huángdì sent a messenger to come out and ask:
“Is the guest perhaps going to remonstrate about the matter of the Huángtàihòu?”
Máo Jiāo said:
“Yes.”
The messenger returned and reported:
“He indeed wishes to remonstrate about the matter of the Huángtàihòu.”
The Huángdì said:
“Go back and tell him:
Does he not see the pile of dead people below the gates?”
The messenger asked Máo Jiāo.
Máo Jiāo said:
“I have heard
that heaven has twenty-eight constellations.
Now there are already twenty-seven dead people.
The reason I have come
is that I wish to complete the number.
I am not a man who fears death.
Go in and report this.”
Máo Jiāo's fellow townsmen who ate with him
all carried their clothes and belongings and fled.
The messenger went in and reported this.
The Huángdì was greatly enraged and said:
“This fellow has intentionally come to violate my prohibition.
Quickly heat the boiling cauldron to boil him!
How can he be allowed to be piled below the gates?
Quickly summon him to enter!”
The Huángdì sat pressing his sword,
with foam coming out of his mouth.
The messenger summoned him to enter.
Máo Jiāo refused to walk quickly;
his feet merely followed one after the other.
The messenger urged him.
Máo Jiāo said:
“Once I reach the front, I will die.
Can you not just tolerate me for a moment?”
The messenger felt great pity for him.
Máo Jiāo reached the front.
He bowed twice, rose,
and stated:
“I have heard
that those who possess life do not avoid the topic of death,
and those who possess a state do not avoid the topic of ruin.
Those who avoid death cannot obtain life;
those who avoid ruin cannot obtain preservation.
Life, death, preservation, and ruin
are matters a sagely ruler urgently desires to hear about.
I do not know if Bìxià wishes to hear of them?”
The Huángdì said:
“What do you mean?”
Máo Jiāo replied:
“Bìxià has engaged in mad and perverse conduct.
Does Bìxià not know this yourself?”
The Huángdì said:
“What sort of conduct?
I wish to hear it.”
Máo Jiāo replied:
“Bìxià had your Jiǎfù torn apart by chariots,
showing a heart of jealousy;
you beat your two younger brothers to death in sacks,
gaining a reputation for lack of kindness;
you exiled your mother to the Fùyáng Gōng,
exhibiting unfilial conduct;
you used tribulus thorns on those who remonstrated,
possessing the governance of Jié and Zhòu.
Now, when the world hears of this,
they will all collapse like tiles and none will turn toward Qín.
I privately fear the ruin of Qín
and am distressed for Bìxià because of it.
My words are finished;
I beg to go to the execution block.”
He then untied his clothes and lay on the execution block.
The Huángdì descended from the dais,
took him with his left hand,
and signaled to his attendants with his right hand, saying:
“Pardon him.
Xiānsheng, please rise and put on your clothes.
Now I wish to receive your instruction!”
He then established Máo Jiāo as Zhòngfù
and enfeoffed him as Shàngqīng.
The Huángdì immediately prepared a carriage with a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry,
leaving the left side empty,
and personally went to welcome the Huángtàihòu from the Fùyáng Gōng,
returning to Xiányáng.
The Huángtàihòu was greatly pleased.
She then prepared a great feast for Máo Jiāo.
While drinking,
the Huángtàihòu said:
“Restoring the crooked to straight,
making failure turn back into success,
securing the altars of the soil and grain of Qín,
and allowing this humble woman and her son to meet again,
is entirely due to the efforts of Máo Jūn.”
9.9 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng built Céng Tái,
extending stones for a thousand lǐ,
and extending soil for a hundred lǐ;
there were officers who carried provisions for a three-month return.
The seventy-two high officials who remonstrated had all died.
There was a man named Zhū Yù Jǐ
who was farming a hundred lǐ away from Chǔ.
He said to his farming partner:
“I shall go in to see the King.”
His partner said:
“With your own body?
I have heard
that those who persuade a lord are all people of leisure and ease;
even so, they arrived only to die.
Now you are merely a person of the grass and thatch!”
Zhū Yù Jǐ said:
“If I farm with you, we compare our strength;
but when it comes to persuading a lord, I do not compare my wisdom with yours.”
He left his plow and went in to see Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng.
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng said to him:
“Zhū Yù Jǐ has come;
are you going to remonstrate?”
Zhū Yù Jǐ said:
“A lord makes use of righteousness
and carries out the law;
moreover, I have heard
that when earth supports water, it becomes level;
when wood supports the marking line, it becomes straight;
when a lord accepts remonstrance, he becomes sagely.
The King builds Céng Tái,
extending stones for a thousand lǐ,
extending soil for a hundred lǐ;
the offenses and calamities of the people
make blood flow onto the thoroughfares;
even so, they have not dared to remonstrate;
how would I dare to remonstrate?
Only your servant is foolish;
I have heard that in the past Yú did not use Gōng Zhī Qí, and Jìn annexed it;
Chén did not use Zǐ Jiā Jī, and Chǔ annexed it;
Cáo did not use Xī Fù Jī, and Sòng annexed it;
Lái did not use Zǐ Měng, and Qí annexed it;
Wú did not use Zǐ Xū, and Yuè annexed it;
Qín did not use the words of Jiǎn Shū, and the state of Qín was endangered;
Jié killed Guān Lóng Páng, and Tāng gained the throne;
Zhòu killed Wáng Zǐ Bǐ Gān, and Wǔ Wáng gained the throne;
Xuān Wáng killed Dù Bó, and the Zhōu house became lowly.
These three Sons of Heaven and six feudal lords all could not honor the worthy or use the words of persuasive scholars;
therefore their bodies died and their states perished.”
He then hurried out.
Chǔ Wáng hastily pursued him and said:
“Jǐ,
come back!
I will use your remonstrance.
Those who spoke to me in previous days,
their persuasion
was not enough to move my heart,
and they also brought danger upon me;
therefore they all arrived and died.
Now your persuasion
is enough to move my heart,
and it does not bring danger upon me;
therefore I will use your remonstrance.”
The next day,
he issued an order:
“If there is anyone who can enter and remonstrate,
I will treat him as a brother.”
Thereupon he dismantled Céng Tái and dismissed the people.
The people of Chǔ sang of him:
“Firewood! Weeds!
Without Zhū Yù Jǐ,
would there ultimately be no sons?
Weeds! Firewood!
Without Zhū Yù Jǐ,
would there ultimately be no men?”
9.10 Qí Huán Gōng said to Bǎo Shū:
“I wish to cast a great bell
to manifest my name.
As for my conduct,
how is it inferior to Yáo and Shùn?”
Bǎo Shū said:
“May I venture to ask about my lord’s conduct?”
Huán Gōng said:
“In the past, I besieged Tán for three years;
when I gained it, I did not take it for myself;
this was benevolence.
I campaigned north against Gū Zhú
and returned after leveling Lìng Zhī;
this was martial prowess.
I convened the assembly at Kuí Qiū to halt the wars of the world;
this was civility.
Nine states of the feudal lords brought beautiful jade to pay court;
when I did not accept them,
this was righteousness.
If so, then civility, martial prowess, benevolence, and righteousness
are all possessed by me.
How is my conduct
inferior to Yáo and Shùn?”
Bǎo Shū said:
“The lord speaks directly,
and your servant replies directly.
In the past, when Gōng Zǐ Jiū was in the superior position, you did not yield;
this was not benevolence.
Turning your back on the words of Tài Gōng to invade the borders of Lǔ;
this was not righteousness.
Being intimidated by a single sword upon the ritual altar;
this was not martial prowess.
Nieces and sisters-in-law never leaving your embrace;
this was not civility.
For one whose unvirtuous acts are widespread among all things yet who does not know it,
if there is no calamity from Heaven, there will surely be harm from men.
Heaven dwells very high,
but its hearing is very low.
Remove my lord’s erroneous words,
lest Heaven hears them.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Do I have faults?
I am fortunate that you note them;
this is a blessing to the altars of soil and grain.
If you had not been kind enough to teach me,
I would almost have committed a great crime and shamed the state.”
9.11 Chǔ Zhāo Wáng wished to go to Jīng Tái for pleasure.
Sīmǎ Zǐ Qí entered and remonstrated:
“On a trip to Jīng Tái,
to the left is the marsh of Dòngtíng,
to the right is the water of Pénglí,
looking south toward Liè Shān,
and looking down upon Fāng Huái.
Its pleasure makes one neglect old age and forget death.
Lords who have traveled there have all lost their states;
I hope the Great King will not go there for pleasure.”
The King said:
“Jīng Tái is my land;
since I have the land and would travel there,
why do you stop my travel?”
He was angry and struck him.
Thereupon Lìngyǐn Zǐ Xī drove a comfortable carriage with four horses directly to the palace hall
and said:
“Today’s trip to Jīng Tái
must not be missed.”
The King climbed into the carriage, patted his back, and said:
“On the trip to Jīng Tái,
I shall enjoy the pleasure with you.”
Zǐ Xī walked the horses for ten lǐ,
then pulled the reins and stopped, saying:
“Your servant does not dare to descend from the carriage;
I hope to have a word of the Way;
would the Great King be willing to listen to it?”
The King said:
“Simply speak it.”
Lìngyǐn Zǐ Xī said:
“Your servant has heard
that for one who is a servant and loyal to his lord,
rank and salary are not enough to reward him;
for one who is a servant and flatters his lord,
punishments are not enough to execute him.
One like Sīmǎ Zǐ Qí
is a loyal servant;
one like your servant
is a flattering servant.
I hope the Great King will kill your servant’s body,
punish your servant’s family, and grant salary to Sīmǎ Zǐ Qí.”
The King said:
“If I can stop and listen,
you alone can restrain me from this trip;
but as for future generations traveling there,
there will be no end;
what then?”
Lìngyǐn Zǐ Xī said:
“To restrain future generations is easy;
I hope that when the Great King passes away,
you will make your tomb at Jīng Tái.
There has never been anyone who brings the music of bells, drums, pipes, and strings
to play upon the tombs of their fathers and ancestors.”
Thereupon the King turned the carriage back,
and in the end did not travel to Jīng Tái;
he ordered the dismissal of those sent ahead.
Kǒng Zǐ heard of this in Lǔ and said:
“How beautiful!
Lìngyǐn Zǐ Xī remonstrated ten lǐ before it began,
yet he exerted his influence for a hundred generations after.”
9.12 Jīng Wén Wáng obtained a dog named Rúhuáng,
and tethered arrows made of jùnlù bamboo,
to hunt in Yúnmèng,
and he did not return for three months;
he obtained Zhōu zhī Jī,
and became licentious,
not attending court for a full year.
Bǎo Shēn remonstrated, saying:
“The late king divined that I should serve as Bǎo,
and the result was auspicious.
Now the King has obtained the dog Rúhuáng,
the jùnlù tethered arrows,
and hunts in Yúnmèng,
not returning for three months;
and you have obtained Zhōu zhī Jī,
and become licentious,
not attending court for a full year.
The King’s offense deserves a flogging.”
He prostrated himself and was about to flog the King.
The King said:
“Since I left my swaddling clothes,
I have been entrusted to the feudal lords.
I beg to change my ways and ask that I not be flogged.”
Bǎo Shēn said:
“I have received the command of the late king and dare not abandon it.
If the King does not receive the flogging,
it will be an abandonment of the late king’s command.
I would rather offend the King
than be unfaithful to the late king.”
The King said:
“I respectfully comply.”
Thereupon, a mat was spread for the King,
and the King prostrated himself.
Bǎo Shēn tied fifty thin arrows together,
knelt and placed them on the King’s back,
doing this twice,
then told the King to rise.
The King said:
“The reputation of being flogged
is already established.
You may as well carry it out completely.”
Bǎo Shēn said:
“I have heard
that the Jūnzǐ feels shame
and the petty man feels pain.
If one feels shame but does not change,
what is the benefit of pain?”
Bǎo Shēn hurried out
and intended to go into exile,
so he requested punishment from the King.
The King said:
“This was my fault;
what crime has the Bǎo committed?”
The King then changed his conduct and followed Bǎo Shēn’s advice,
killed the dog Rúhuáng,
broke the jùnlù tethered arrows,
sent away Zhōu zhī Jī,
and devoted himself to governing Jīng.
He annexed thirty states.
That the state of Jīng became as vast as this
was the merit of Bǎo Shēn’s daring to speak the truth to the extreme.
Xiāo Hé and Wáng Líng heard of this and said:
“The sage ruler who could uphold the legacy of his ancestors and achieve success and fame
was surely Jīng Wén Wáng!”
Therefore, the world has praised him until today,
and enlightened rulers, loyal ministers, and filial sons take him as a model.
9.13 Jìn Píng Gōng sent Shū Xiàng on a diplomatic mission to Wú.
The people of Wú scrubbed their boats to welcome him,
with five hundred men on the left
and five hundred on the right.
Some wore embroidered clothes and leopard furs;
some wore brocade clothes and fox furs.
Shū Xiàng returned and reported this to Jìn Píng Gōng.
Jìn Píng Gōng said:
“Will Wú perhaps perish?
Why do they show such respect for boats?
Why do they show such respect for the people?”
Shū Xiàng replied:
“Your Grace built the Chídǐ Terrace;
above it can deploy a thousand soldiers,
and below it can display bells and drums.
When the feudal lords hear of Your Grace, they also say:
‘Why show such respect for a terrace?
Why show such respect for the people?’
What is respected is simply different for each.”
Thereupon, Jìn Píng Gōng discontinued work on the terrace.
9.14 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ raised an army to attack Qí
and ordered that anyone in the army who dared to remonstrate
would be punished with death.
An armored soldier named Gōng Lú
looked at Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ and laughed loudly.
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“Why do you laugh?”
He replied:
“I have a long-standing joke.”
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“If you have an explanation for it, it will be acceptable;
if you have no explanation, you shall die.”
He replied:
“During the mulberry season,
a husband and wife from my neighbor’s house went to the fields together.
The husband saw a woman among the mulberries
and went to pursue her;
he could not catch her,
and when he returned,
his wife was angry and had left him.
I was laughing at his being left alone.”
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“Now if I attack another state and lose my own state,
this would be my being left alone.”
Thereupon, he dismissed the army and returned.
9.15 Jǐng Gōng was building a terrace.
When the terrace was completed,
he also wanted to cast bells.
Yàn Zǐ remonstrated, saying:
“Your Grace’s desires are insatiable.
You have built a terrace,
and now you want to cast bells.
This is heavy taxation on the people,
and the people are in sorrow.
To collect the sorrow of the people and turn it into one's pleasure
is inauspicious.”
Jǐng Gōng then stopped.
9.16 Jǐng Gōng had a horse,
and his stableman killed it.
The Duke was furious
and seized a halberd, intending to strike him himself.
Yàn Zǐ said:
“This man will die without knowing his crimes.
I ask to enumerate them for Your Grace,
so that he may know his crimes before he is killed.”
The Duke said:
“Agreed.”
Yàn Zǐ raised the halberd and stood over him, saying:
“You were raising a horse for our ruler and killed it;
your crime deserves death.
You have caused our ruler to kill a stableman for the sake of a horse;
your crime again deserves death.
You have caused our ruler to kill a man for the sake of a horse,
which will be heard by the neighboring feudal lords;
your crime again deserves death.”
The Duke said:
“Master, release him!
Master, release him!
Do not damage my reputation for benevolence.”
9.17 Jǐng Gōng was fond of hunting with tethered arrows.
He had Zhú Chú in charge of the birds, but he lost one.
Jǐng Gōng was furious and wanted to kill him.
Yàn Zǐ said:
“Zhú Chú has three crimes.
I ask to enumerate his crimes for him
and then kill him.”
Jǐng Gōng said:
“You may.”
Thereupon, he summoned Zhú Chú and enumerated them before Jǐng Gōng,
saying:
“You were in charge of the birds for our ruler and lost one;
this is the first crime.
You have caused our ruler to kill a man for the sake of a bird;
this is the second crime.
You have caused the feudal lords to hear of this
and think our ruler values birds more than scholars;
this is the third crime.”
Having finished enumerating Zhú Chú’s crimes,
he asked to kill him.
Jǐng Gōng said:
“Stop.
Do not kill him.”
And he apologized to him.
9.18 Jǐng Gōng, in broad daylight, had his hair disheveled,
riding in a carriage with six horses,
driving women as he went out of the main gate.
Yuè Guì struck his horses and turned them back,
saying:
“You are not my lord.”
The Duke was ashamed and did not attend court.
Yàn Zǐ saw Yì Áo and asked, saying:
“For what reason does the Lord not attend court?”
He replied:
“Previously, the Lord, in broad daylight,
had his hair disheveled,
rode in a carriage with six horses,
and drove women as he went out of the main gate.
Yuè Guì struck his horses and turned them back,
saying:
‘You are not my lord.’
The Duke was ashamed and returned,
failing to go out;
for this reason, he does not attend court.”
Yàn Zǐ entered to see him.
The Duke said:
“Previously, I committed a transgression:
my hair was disheveled,
I rode in a carriage with six horses
to go out of the main gate.
Yuè Guì struck my horses and turned them back,
saying:
‘You are not my lord.’
Through your kindness, Master,
I was able to lead the people to protect the ancestral temple;
now I have been humiliated by Yuè Guì
and have disgraced the Altars of Earth and Grain.
Can I still stand equal to the regional lords?”
Yàn Zǐ replied, saying:
“Lord, do not be distressed by it.
I have heard
that when those below have no straightforward speech,
those above have a concealed ruler;
when the people avoid speaking the truth,
the ruler has arrogant conduct.
In ancient times, when enlightened rulers were above,
those below had straightforward speech;
when the ruler above loved goodness,
the people did not avoid speaking the truth.
Now the Lord has had a failure in conduct,
and Yuè Guì has used straightforward speech;
this is the Lord’s good fortune.
Therefore, I have come to congratulate you.
Please reward him
to make clear the Lord’s love of goodness;
treat him with ritual
to make clear the Lord’s acceptance of remonstrance.”
The Duke laughed and said:
“Is that possible?”
Yàn Zǐ said:
“It is.”
Thereupon, he ordered that Yuè Guì be given double his resources and exempted from labor,
and the morning court was held as usual.
9.19 Jǐng Gōng was drinking wine.
At night,
he moved to Yàn Zǐ’s house.
The vanguard announced at the gate, saying:
“The Lord has arrived!”
Yàn Zǐ put on his dark formal robe
and stood at the gate, saying:
“Have the regional lords perhaps had some emergency?
Has the state perhaps had some emergency?
Why has the Lord disgraced himself by coming at an improper time during the night?”
The Duke said:
“The flavor of the wine and ale,
the sounds of the bells and stones—
I wish to enjoy them with you, Master.”
Yàn Zǐ replied:
“As for those who lay out the mats and arrange the sacrificial vessels,
there are people for that;
I do not dare to take part in it.”
The Duke said:
“Move to the house of Sīmǎ Rángjū.”
The vanguard announced at the gate, saying:
“The Lord has arrived!”
Sīmǎ Rángjū, wearing armor and helmet and holding a halberd, stood at the gate and said:
“Have the regional lords perhaps raised troops?
Have the high officials perhaps rebelled?
Why has the Lord disgraced himself by coming at an improper time during the night?”
The Duke said:
“The flavor of the wine and ale,
the sounds of the bells and stones—
I wish to enjoy them with you, Master.”
He replied:
“As for those who lay out the mats and arrange the sacrificial vessels,
there are people for that;
I do not dare to take part in it.”
The Duke said:
“Move to the house of Liángqiū Jù.”
The vanguard announced at the gate, saying:
“The Lord has arrived!”
Liángqiū Jù, holding a zither in his left hand
and carrying a mouth organ in his right,
arrived while singing.
The Duke said:
“How joyful!
Tonight I shall drink wine.
Without those two gentlemen,
how could I govern my state?
Without this one minister,
how could I enjoy myself?”
Worthy and sagacious rulers all have beneficial friends
and no ministers of idle pleasure.
Jǐng Gōng was not able to reach that level,
so he used both types,
and barely managed to avoid ruin.
9.20 Wú used the strategies of Wǔ Zǐxū and Sūn Wǔ
to crush the powerful state of Chǔ in the west,
to overawe Qí and Jìn in the north,
and to attack Yuè in the south.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè met them in battle,
defeated Wú at Gū Sū,
and wounded Hé Lǘ in the finger,
causing the army to retreat.
Hé Lǘ's wound became infected and he was about to die,
so he said to Crown Prince Fū Chāi:
"Will you forget that Gōu Jiàn killed your father?"
Fū Chāi replied:
"I do not dare forget."
That evening,
Hé Lǘ died.
After Fū Chāi was established as king,
he appointed Bó Pǐ as Tài Zǎi
and practiced warfare and archery.
In the second year,
he attacked Yuè
and defeated Yuè at Fū Qiū.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè then took his remaining five thousand troops and took refuge on Mount Huì Jī.
He sent Dà Fū Zhǒng with generous gifts to present to Wú’s Tài Zǎi Pǐ to sue for peace,
requesting to surrender the state and serve as subjects and servants.
The King of Wú was about to grant this.
Wǔ Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"The King of Yuè is a man capable of enduring hardship.
If Your Majesty does not destroy him now,
you will surely regret it later."
The King of Wú did not listen,
but followed the plan of Tài Zǎi Pǐ
and made peace with Yuè.
Five years later,
the King of Wú heard that Qí Jǐng Gōng had died and that the high ministers were vying for favor.
The new ruler was weak,
so he raised an army to attack Qí in the north.
Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"This is not permissible.
Gōu Jiàn does not eat food of multiple flavors,
he consoles the bereaved and visits the sick,
and he is capable of employing men.
If this man does not die,
he will certainly become a disaster for Wú.
Currently, Yuè is a disease of the vital organs,
while Qí is merely a skin rash.
Yet Your Majesty does not prioritize Yuè
but instead focuses on attacking Qí—
is this not a grave error?"
The King of Wú did not listen,
attacked Qí,
and heavily defeated the Qí army at Ài Líng.
He then met with the rulers of Zōu and Lǔ before returning,
and he grew even more distant from Zǐxū's words.
Four years after that,
Wú was about to attack Qí in the north again.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè followed the plan of Zǐ Gòng
and led his followers to assist Wú,
while presenting precious treasures to Tài Zǎi Pǐ.
As Tài Zǎi Pǐ had frequently received bribes from Yuè,
his affection and trust for Yuè were extreme,
and day and night he spoke on their behalf to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú trusted and followed Pǐ's plan.
Wǔ Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
"Yuè
is a disease of the vital organs.
Now you believe their wandering words and false deceptions while being greedy for Qí,
which is like a stony field
that is of no use.
The 'Pán Gēng' says:
'The ancients had those who were rebellious and disrespectful;
they cut off their noses or exterminated them,
so that no descendants were left,
ensuring that their seed would not be replanted in this city.'
This is how Shāng flourished.
I wish Your Majesty would set aside Qí and deal with Yuè first;
otherwise,
you will regret it when it is too late."
The King of Wú did not listen
and sent Zǐxū on a mission to Qí.
Zǐxū said to his son:
"I have remonstrated with the King,
but the King will not use my advice.
I now see the destruction of Wú!
For you to perish along with me
would be pointless."
He then entrusted his son to the Bǎo clan in Qí and returned to report to the King of Wú.
Since Tài Zǎi Pǐ already had a rift with Zǐxū,
he slandered him, saying:
"Zǐxū is a man of rigid and violent character with little kindness;
his resentment and suspicion
will bring deep calamity.
Previously, when Your Majesty wished to attack Qí,
Zǐxū thought it was wrong,
yet Your Majesty eventually attacked it and achieved great merit.
Zǐxū was ashamed that his plans were not used,
and so he harbored resentment.
Now that Your Majesty is attacking Qí again,
Zǐxū is obstinate and remonstrates forcefully,
disparaging the state's affairs
and hoping for Wú's defeat to prove his own strategy correct.
Now Your Majesty is setting out in person,
mobilizing all the military strength of the state to attack Qí,
yet because Zǐxū's advice was not taken,
he has withdrawn and declined his duties,
feigning illness so as not to go.
Your Majesty must be prepared;
it would not be difficult for him to start a revolt.
Furthermore, I sent someone to secretly watch him;
when he was on his mission to Qí,
he entrusted his son to the Bǎo clan.
For a minister to be dissatisfied internally
while forming external ties with feudal lords—
he considers himself a strategist for the late king,
and now that he is not being used,
he is constantly disgruntled.
I wish Your Majesty would deal with him early."
The King of Wú said:
"Without your words,
I would also have suspected him."
He then sent an envoy to bestow the Zhǔ Lòu sword upon Zǐxū,
saying:
"You are to die with this."
Zǐxū said:
"Alas!
The slandering minister Pǐ creates chaos,
yet the King turns around and executes me.
I helped your father become hegemon,
and when you were being established,
while the various sons were competing for the throne,
I fought for you at the risk of my life before the late king,
such that you almost failed to be established.
Once you were established,
you wanted to divide the state of Wú with me,
but I did not dare accept it.
Yet how can you listen to a slandering minister and kill your elder!"
He then told his attendants:
"You must plant catalpa trees on my grave
so they can be used to make vessels;
and gouge out my eyes and place them above the eastern gate of Wú,
so that I may watch the Yuè invaders enter and destroy Wú."
He then stabbed himself and died.
When the King of Wú heard of this,
he was furious
and took Zǐxū’s body, placed it in a wine-skin made of leather,
and floated it on the river.
The people of Wú pitied him
and built a shrine for him on the riverbank,
naming it Xū Shān.
More than ten years later,
Yuè attacked Wú.
The King of Wú returned to do battle
but was not victorious.
He sent a Dà Fū to seek peace with Yuè,
but it was not granted.
As the King of Wú was about to die, he said:
"It is because I did not use the words of Zǐxū that I have come to this.
If the dead have no consciousness, then so be it;
but if the dead have consciousness,
with what face can I see Zǐxū?"
He then covered his face with silk cloth and cut his own throat.
9.21 Qí Jiǎn Gōng had a minister named Zhū Yù Yāng,
who remonstrated with Qí Jiǎn Gōng, saying:
"Tián Cháng and Zǎi Yǔ—
these two men hate each other deeply.
I fear they will attack each other.
If they attack each other, even if you try to reverse the situation and end the danger,
it will not be possible.
I wish for Your Lordship to remove one of them."
Qí Jiǎn Gōng said:
"This is not something a person of low rank like you should dare to discuss."
Not long after,
Tián Cháng indeed attacked Zǎi Yǔ in the courtyard
and murdered Qí Jiǎn Gōng in the court.
Qí Jiǎn Gōng sighed deeply and said:
"I did not use the words of Yāng,
and so I have come to this calamity!"
Therefore, the words of a loyal minister
must be examined carefully.
9.22 Lǔ Xiāng Gōng paid court to Jīng.
Upon reaching the Huái River,
he heard that Jīng Kāng Wáng had died.
The Duke wished to return.
Shūzhòng Zhāobó said:
“Your Lordship’s coming
was because of his majesty.
Now that their King is dead,
his majesty has not yet departed.
Why return?”
The grandees all wished to return.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó said:
“Sir, your coming
was for the benefit of the state.
Therefore, you did not dread the toil,
nor the long distance of the road to heed Jīng.
It was not because of Chǔ’s righteousness,
but because you feared its majesty.
Now, as for a righteous person,
one should certainly congratulate their joys and offer condolences for their sorrows;
how much more so for one whom you fear and to whom you are paying a mission?
To go out of fear
and return upon hearing of a death,
who would not say that is an insult?
The Mǐ surname has a successor,
and the King’s Crown Prince is already grown.
The governing officials have not changed;
they serve their lord and manage the government.
If they seek to redress that insult
to stabilize the successor lord and show future generations,
their enmity will grow great.
Using that to wage war against a small state,
who could stop them?
If following the Lord leads to calamity,
it is better to act against the Lord’s wishes to avoid disaster.
Moreover, a gentleman calculates and then acts.
Have you gentlemen calculated?
If you have a method to resist Chǔ
and the preparations to defend the state, then it is fine.
If you have none,
it is better to proceed.”
Thus they proceeded.
9.23 In the time of Xiào Jǐng Huángdì,
Wú Wáng Pì rebelled.
Liáng Xiào Wáng’s Zhōngláng Méi Chéng, courtesy name Shū,
heard of it
and wrote a letter to remonstrate with the King.
The words said:
“Your King’s external servant Chéng
has heard that those who attain wholeness prosper completely,
while those who lose wholeness perish completely.
Shùn had not the ground to stand an awl,
yet he possessed the world.
Yǔ had not a gathering of ten households,
yet he ruled as King over the feudal lords.
The lands of Tāng and Wǔ
were no more than a hundred lǐ square.
Above, they did not block the light of the three luminaries;
below, they did not hurt the hearts of the common people,
because they possessed the art of kingship.
Thus, the way of father and son
is natural disposition.
A loyal minister does not dare to avoid execution to give direct remonstrance,
so that affairs are not abandoned and merit flows for ten thousand generations.
I sincerely wish to bare my heart and offer my humble loyalty,
but I fear Your Greatness cannot use it.
I sincerely wish Your Greatness would slightly apply your thoughts and a heart of compassion to my, Chéng’s, words.
To hang a weight of a thousand jūn by a single thread,
suspended above from an infinite height,
and hanging below into an unfathomable abyss—
even a very foolish person
would still know to lament its impending break.
When a horse is just getting spooked, one startles it further;
when a thread is just about to break, one weights it down further.
Once a thread breaks from heaven, it cannot be tied again;
once fallen into a deep abyss, it is hard to come out again.
Whether it comes out or not
depends on the space of a hair.
If you can sincerely use my, Chéng’s, words,
you will certainly escape in one move.
If you must do what you intend,
it is as precarious as piled eggs
and harder than climbing to heaven;
if you change what you intend to do,
it is easier than turning over your hand
and as stable as Tài Shān.
Now, if you wish to reach the longevity of heaven’s mandate,
exhaust inexhaustible joy,
and preserve the power of ten thousand chariots,
it requires no more than the ease of turning a hand
to dwell in the stability of Tài Shān.
Yet you wish to risk the danger of piled eggs
and pursue the difficulty of climbing to heaven;
this is what greatly confuses your foolish servant.
In human nature, there are those who fear their shadow and hate their tracks.
They turn their backs and run,
but it is of no use;
it is better to go into the shade and stop,
then the shadow vanishes and the tracks are gone.
If you wish people not to hear,
there is nothing better than not speaking;
if you wish people not to know,
there is nothing better than not doing.
If you wish soup to be cold,
and you have one person stoking the fire
while a hundred people stir it,
it is of no use;
it is better to cut off the firewood and stop the fire altogether.
Not cutting it off there,
but trying to save it here,
is like carrying firewood to put out a fire.
Yǎng Yóujī
was a skilled archer of Chǔ.
At a hundred paces from a willow leaf,
he hit the mark a hundred times out of a hundred.
That the willow leaf is small yet he hit it a hundred times,
one can call him a skilled archer.
However, his stopping point was only within a hundred paces.
Compared to me,
I don’t know if he even knew how to hold a bow or arrow.
Good fortune has its foundation;
calamity has its embryo.
If you provide for the foundation
and cut off the embryo,
where could calamity come from?
Dripping water from Tài Shān pierces stone;
pulling a rope for a long time
will saw through wood.
Water is not a drill for stone,
and a rope is not a saw for wood,
but gradual wear makes it so.
If you weigh things zhū by zhū,
by the time you reach a dàn, there will surely be a difference.
If you measure things inch by inch,
by the time you reach a zhàng, there will surely be an excess.
Weighing by the dàn and measuring by the zhàng
is direct and has few errors.
A tree of ten spans
begins as a sprout.
It can be pulled and broken,
or plucked and uprooted.
This is by taking it before it has grown
and acting before it has formed.
Grinding and sharpening on a whetstone,
one does not see it wear away,
yet there comes a time when it is exhausted.
Planting trees and raising livestock,
one does not see them grow,
yet there comes a time when they are large.
Accumulating virtue and practicing conduct,
one does not notice the goodness,
yet there comes a time when it is used.
Doing evil and acting wrongly,
abandoning righteousness and turning against principle,
one does not notice the badness,
yet there comes a time when one perishes.
I sincerely wish Your Greatness would weigh this carefully and practice it yourself.
This is the unchanging way of a hundred kings.”
The King of Wú did not listen,
and he finally died at Dāntú.
9.24 The King of Wú wished to drink wine with the common people.
Wǔ Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
“It cannot be.
Long ago, a white dragon descended to a cool, clear pool and transformed into a fish.
A fisherman named Yùqiě shot it in the eye.
The white dragon ascended to complain to the Heavenly Emperor.
The Heavenly Emperor asked:
‘At that time,
where were you and what was your form?’
The white dragon replied:
‘I descended to a cool, clear pool and transformed into a fish.’
The Heavenly Emperor said:
‘Fish are indeed things that humans shoot.
If it was like this,
what crime did Yùqiě commit?’
Now, the white dragon
is a precious animal of the Heavenly Emperor,
and Yùqiě
was a lowly servant of the state of Sòng.
Had the white dragon not transformed,
Yùqiě would not have shot it.
Now, you are abandoning your position of ten thousand chariots
to drink wine with commoners.
I fear you will have the same trouble as that of Yùqiě.”
The King then stopped.
9.25 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Good medicine is bitter to the mouth but beneficial for illness;
honest words are harsh to the ear but beneficial for conduct."
Thus, Wǔ Wáng prospered by listening to outspoken advice,
while Zhòu perished because of silence and compliance.
If a ruler has no outspoken ministers,
if a father has no outspoken sons,
if an elder brother has no outspoken younger brothers,
if a husband has no outspoken wife,
and if a scholar has no outspoken friends,
their downfall can be expected at any moment.
Therefore it is said:
If the ruler loses it,
the minister gains it;
if the father loses it,
the son gains it;
if the elder brother loses it,
the younger brother gains it;
if the husband loses it,
the wife gains it;
and if the scholar loses it,
the friend gains it.
Consequently, there will be no states that perish or families that are destroyed,
no rebellious fathers or unruly sons,
no banished brothers or abandoned siblings,
no mad husbands or debauched wives,
and no severed ties or ruined friendships.
9.26 Yàn Zǐ reported back to Jǐng Gōng, saying:
"Is the court residence stern?"
The Duke said:
"The court residence is stern.
How does that harm the governance of the state?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"When the court is stern, those below do not speak;
when those below do not speak, the one above hears nothing.
When those below do not speak, it is called muteness;
when the one above hears nothing, it is called deafness.
As for deafness and muteness,
how can they not harm the governance of the state!
Moreover, small amounts of beans and grain are combined to fill the granary;
coarse threads of weft are combined to make curtains.
The height of Tàishān
does not come from a single stone;
it becomes high only after low parts are piled up.
Now, those who govern the world
do not rely on the words of a single scholar.
Indeed, there are those who receive advice but do not use it,
but how could anyone reject it and not let it enter?"
10.1 Survival and ruin, misfortune and fortune,
their essence lies within oneself.
Sages emphasize warnings
and are respectful and cautious regarding what is often neglected.
The *Zhōngyōng* says:
"Nothing is more visible than what is hidden,
and nothing is more manifest than what is subtle.
Therefore, the gentleman is cautious when he is alone."
A proverb says:
"Heed warnings and there will be no disgrace;
reflect and there will be no shame."
To neither heed warnings nor reflect,
yet seek to preserve one's life and the whole country,
is indeed difficult.
The *Shī* says:
"Apprehensive and cautious,
as if approaching a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice."
This is what is meant.
10.2 Formerly, when Chéng Wáng enfeoffed Zhōu Gōng,
Zhōu Gōng declined and would not accept,
so the King enfeoffed Zhōu Gōng’s son, Bó Qín, in Lǔ.
As Bó Qín was about to depart,
Zhōu Gōng cautioned him, saying:
"Go now,
but do not be arrogant toward scholars because of the state of Lǔ!
I am the son of Wén Wáng,
the younger brother of Wǔ Wáng,
and the uncle of the current King.
Furthermore, I am the minister to the Son of Heaven.
My position in the world is not light.
Yet, I have often stopped once while washing my hair to grasp it three times,
and stopped once during a meal to spit out my food three times,
still fearing I might lose the scholars of the world.
I have heard it said:
'One whose virtuous conduct is vast and great, yet maintains it with reverence,
will be honored;
one whose territory is broad and fertile, yet maintains it with frugality,
will be secure;
one whose salary and rank are noble and grand, yet maintains them with humility,
will be noble;
one whose people are numerous and army is strong, yet maintains them with apprehension,
will be victorious;
one who is intelligent and wise, yet maintains it with simplicity,
will benefit;
one who is well-informed and has a good memory, yet maintains it with modesty,
will be broad-minded.
These six ways of maintenance
are all virtues of humility.'
Even if one is as noble as the Son of Heaven
and as wealthy as owning all within the four seas,
if one's virtue is not humble, they will lose the world
and perish,
as was the case with Jié and Zhòu.
Can one not be cautious?
Therefore, the *Yì* has a Way:
at its greatest, it is sufficient to preserve the world;
at its middle, it is sufficient to preserve a state;
and at its smallest, it is sufficient to preserve oneself;
it is called Humility.
The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and increases the humble;
the Way of Earth transforms the full and flows toward the humble;
the spirits harm the full and bless the humble;
the Way of Man dislikes the full and loves the humble.
Therefore, when a robe is finished, its lapel is left incomplete;
when a palace is finished, its corners are left incomplete;
when a house is finished, decorative patterns are added;
these show incompleteness, for such is the Way of Heaven.
The *Yì* says:
'*Qiān* [Humility],
success.
The gentleman carries it through to the end;
good fortune.'
The *Shī* says:
'Tāng's humility was not delayed;
his sage-like reverence ascended daily.' Take heed of this!
Do not be arrogant toward scholars because of the state of Lǔ!"
10.3 When Kǒngzǐ read the *Yì* and reached the hexagrams *Sǔn* and *Yì*,
he sighed deeply.
Zǐxià rose from his seat and asked:
"Why does the Master sigh?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He who diminishes himself is increased,
while he who increases himself is diminished;
this is why I sigh."
Zǐxià said:
"In that case, may a student not seek to increase himself?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No.
By the Way of Heaven,
what is complete has never been able to endure for long.
A student receives knowledge with emptiness;
therefore it is said
he gains it.
If one meets knowledge by maintaining fullness,
then the good words of the world will be unable to enter his ears.
Formerly, when Yáo occupied the position of the Son of Heaven,
he still maintained it with sincere reverence
and treated those below with emptiness and stillness;
thus, after a hundred years, his glory became even greater
and until now has become increasingly manifest.
Kūnwú was self-satisfied and complacent;
he reached the heights without declining;
thus, in his own time, he suffered loss and defeat,
and until now his reputation has grown even worse.
Is this not the proof of decrease and increase?
Therefore, I say:
Humility
is what attains reverence to preserve one's position.
Now, when abundance and brilliance are put into motion, they are able to become great;
but if they become great, they will then suffer loss;
I warn against this.
Therefore it is said:
The good words of the world will be unable to enter his ears.
When the sun reaches the center, it begins to set;
when the moon is full, it begins to wane.
The fullness and emptiness of Heaven and Earth
wax and wane with the seasons.
Therefore, the sage does not dare to remain at the peak of prosperity.
When ascending a carriage, if he meets three people, he descends;
if he meets two people, he leans on the horizontal bar;
he regulates his fullness and emptiness;
thus he is able to endure for a long time."
Zǐxià said:
"Excellent!
I ask to recite this for the rest of my life."
10.4 Kǒngzǐ viewed the temple of Zhōu,
where there was a tilting vessel.
Kǒngzǐ asked the temple caretaker, saying:
“What kind of vessel is this?”
He replied:
“It is likely the vessel for the right side of the seat.”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“I have heard that for the vessel of the right side of the seat,
when full it overturns,
when empty it tilts,
and when halfway full it stands upright;
is this so?”
He replied:
“It is.”
Kǒngzǐ had Zǐlù fetch water to test it;
when full it overturned,
when halfway full it stood upright,
and when empty it tilted.
Kǒngzǐ sighed deeply and said:
“Alas!
How could there be anything that is full and does not overturn!”
Zǐlù said:
“May I ask if there is a way to maintain fullness?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The way to maintain fullness
is to ladle out and diminish it.”
Zǐlù said:
“Is there a way to diminish it?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“To be high and yet able to be humble,
to be full and yet able to be empty,
to be wealthy and yet able to be frugal,
to be noble and yet able to be modest,
to be wise and yet able to be foolish,
to be brave and yet able to be timid,
to be eloquent and yet able to be slow of speech,
to be broad in knowledge and yet able to be shallow,
to be brilliant and yet able to be dim—
this is what is called diminishing without reaching the extreme.
As for being able to practice this way,
only those of perfect virtue can achieve it.
The *Yì* says:
‘To increase it without diminishing it.’
Therefore, by diminishing oneself, one eventually gains increase.
10.5 Cháng Chuāng was ill.
Lǎozǐ went to inquire after him
and said:
“Master, your illness is severe.
Is there no remaining teaching you can speak to your disciples?”
Cháng Chuāng said:
“Even if you had not asked,
I would have spoken to you.”
Cháng Chuāng said:
“One gets down from the carriage when passing through their hometown;
do you know why?”
Lǎozǐ said:
“Getting down from the carriage when passing through one’s hometown,
does it not mean one does not forget their origins?”
Cháng Chuāng said:
“Aha!
That is it.”
Cháng Chuāng said:
“One quickens their pace when passing by tall trees;
do you know why?”
Lǎozǐ said:
“Quickening one’s pace when passing by tall trees,
does it not mean one respects the elderly?”
Cháng Chuāng said:
“Aha!
That is it.”
He then opened his mouth and showed it to Lǎozǐ, saying:
“Is my tongue still there?”
Lǎozǐ said:
“Yes.”
“Are my teeth still there?”
Lǎozǐ said:
“They are gone.”
Cháng Chuāng said:
“Do you know why?”
Lǎozǐ said:
“As for the tongue remaining,
is it not because of its softness?
As for the teeth being gone,
is it not because of their hardness?”
Cháng Chuāng said:
“Aha!
That is it.
The affairs of the world are all contained in this;
what more is there for me to say to you!”
10.6 Hán Píngzǐ asked Shū Xiàng:
“Between hardness and softness, which is more durable?”
He replied:
“I am eighty years old;
my teeth have fallen out twice, yet my tongue still remains.
Lǎo Dān had a saying:
‘The softest thing in the world
gallops over the hardest thing in the world.’
He also said:
‘When humans are born, they are soft and weak;
when they die, they are hard and strong.
When the ten thousand things, the grass and trees, are born, they are soft and brittle;
when they die, they are withered and dried.’
Observing it from this,
‘the soft and weak
are the companions of life;
the hard and strong
are the companions of death.’
That which lives, though damaged, will certainly recover;
that which is dead, once broken, perishes even more.
I therefore know that softness is more durable than hardness.”
Píngzǐ said:
“Excellent!
In that case, what course does your own conduct follow?”
Shū Xiàng said:
“I am also merely soft;
why would I use hardness?”
Píngzǐ said:
“Is softness not brittle?”
Shū Xiàng said:
“That which is soft
can be tied in knots without breaking,
and can have sharp edges without chipping;
how is it brittle?
In the Way of Heaven,
the subtle prevails.
Therefore, when two armies confront each other,
the soft one will overcome;
when two rivals compete for profit,
the weak one will obtain it.
The *Yì* says:
‘The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the humble;
the Way of Earth changes the full and makes the humble flow;
the spirits harm the full and bless the humble;
the Way of Man hates the full and loves the humble.’
If one maintains the softness and weakness of humility and inadequacy, then the four Ways will assist them.
Then where can one go and not achieve their will?”
Píngzǐ said:
“Excellent.”
10.7 Huán Gōng said:
“When metal is hard, it breaks;
when leather is hard, it cracks;
when a ruler is hard, the state perishes;
when a minister is hard, friendships are severed.”
Hardness leads to a lack of harmony,
and a lack of harmony leads to being unusable.
For this reason, if the four horses of a team are not in harmony,
the journey will not be long;
if father and son are not in harmony,
their lineage will be destroyed;
if brothers are not in harmony,
they cannot remain together for long;
if husband and wife are not in harmony,
the household will meet with great misfortune.
The *Yì* says:
“When two people are of one heart,
their sharpness can cut through metal.”
This is because they are not hard.
10.8 Lǎozǐ said:
“When obtaining what is profitable,
one must consider the potential harm;
when rejoicing in what is successful,
one must look toward potential failure.”
When people do good,
Heaven rewards them with blessings;
when people do what is not good,
Heaven rewards them with calamities.
Therefore it is said:
“Calamity is that upon which blessing leans;
blessing is that in which calamity lurks.”
Be cautious of this; be prudent about this.
If a superior man does not apply himself to this,
how can he be prepared?
Above, if one knows Heaven, then one does not miss the seasons;
below, if one knows Earth, then one does not lose wealth;
if one is prudent day and night, then there will be no harmful disasters.
10.9 Céng Zǐ was ill;
Céng Yuán held his head,
Céng Huá held his feet.
Céng Zǐ said:
"I do not have the talent of Yán Shì;
what can I tell you?
Although I lack ability,
a Jūnzǐ must strive for improvement.
That which has many flowers but little fruit
is of Heaven;
those who have many words but few actions
are of man.
Flying birds consider mountains low and build layered nests on their peaks;
fish and turtles consider deep pools shallow and bore holes in their depths;
yet the reason they are caught
is the bait.
If a Jūnzǐ can truly avoid harming themselves for the sake of profit,
then from where can disgrace come?
Negligence in office arises when success is achieved;
illness worsens when one is slightly recovered;
disaster is born from laziness and indolence;
filial piety declines because of wife and children.
Observe these four things
and be as cautious at the end as at the beginning."
The *Shī* says:
"None lack a beginning,
but few are able to have an end."
10.10 Dān Kuài said:
"A state has five 'chills' that are not related to freezing ice.
The first is:
governance focused on the external;
the second is:
female interference;
the third is:
leaking of plans;
the fourth is:
disrespecting the high ministers, leading to the state's ruin;
the fifth is:
being unable to manage internal affairs while striving for external ones.
When these five appear together,
even if sacrifices are performed, there will be no blessings;
efforts to remove disaster will surely result in disaster being obtained;
and as for bringing about blessings, they will be withheld."
10.11 Kǒng Zǐ said:
"Survival or ruin, disaster or blessing,
all lie within oneself.
Calamities from Heaven and omens from Earth cannot kill a person.
Formerly, in the time of the Yīn King Dì Xīn,
a sparrow gave birth to a crow in a corner of the city wall.
The diviner interpreted it, saying:
'Whenever the small gives birth to the great,
the state must prosper,
and the King's name will certainly be redoubled.'
Dì Xīn rejoiced in the 'virtue' of the sparrow,
neglected to govern the state,
and was boundlessly tyrannical.
Foreign invaders then arrived,
and he subsequently lost the state of Yīn.
This was a case of defying Heaven's timing,
where a deceptive blessing turned instead into disaster.
In the time of the Yīn King Wǔ Dǐng,
the Way of the former kings was deficient
and the laws were lax.
A mulberry and a paper mulberry tree grew together in the court;
in seven days, they were so large they required a double arm-span to encircle.
The diviner interpreted it, saying:
'The mulberry and paper mulberry
are wild things;
when wild things grow in the court,
does it mean the court will vanish?'
Wǔ Dǐng was terrified and struck with awe;
he humbled himself and cultivated his conduct,
reflecting on the governance of the former kings.
He restored destroyed states,
continued ended lineages,
promoted neglected men of talent,
and clarified the way of caring for the elderly.
Three years later,
the rulers of distant lands
who came to court through multiple interpreters numbered sixteen states.
This was a case of meeting Heaven's timing,
where disaster was turned instead into blessing.
Therefore, omens
are what Heaven uses to warn the Son of Heaven and the Feudal Lords;
bad dreams
are what it uses to warn the Shì Dàfū.
Thus, omens cannot overcome good governance,
and bad dreams cannot overcome good conduct.
At the height of perfect governance,
disaster turns into blessing."
Therefore, Tài Jiǎ says:
"Calamities sent by Heaven
can still be avoided;
calamities brought on by oneself
cannot be escaped."
10.12 Shí Chóu said:
"In the *Chūn Qiū*, there are those who suddenly fall into ruin;
a ruler of a state cannot be incautious.
Inconsistency toward consorts and concubines is enough to cause ruin;
lack of kinship with the royal clan is enough to cause ruin;
not employing great ministers is enough to cause ruin;
not properly using state ranks is enough to cause ruin;
befriending sycophants and keeping slanderers close is enough to cause ruin;
undertaking many tasks out of season is enough to cause ruin;
using the people without moderation is enough to cause ruin;
punishments that do not hit the mark are enough to cause ruin;
losing the hearts of the masses internally is enough to cause ruin;
being disrespectful to great states externally is enough to cause ruin."
10.13 Blessing is born in times of adversity and restraint,
while disaster is born in times of success and satisfaction;
Qí Qǐng Gōng is an example of this.
Qí Qǐng Gōng
was the grandson of Huán Gōng.
His territory was vast and his people numerous;
his army was strong and his state wealthy.
Furthermore, he enjoyed the lingering prestige of a Hegemon.
Arrogant, stubborn, negligent, and haughty,
he was never willing to go out and meet with the other Feudal Lords.
He then raised an army to attack Lǔ
and subsequently defeated the army of Wèi at Xīn Zhù.
His conduct of slighting the small and being disrespectful to the great was extreme.
Soon after, Jìn and Lǔ went to pay their respects,
and he mocked their envoys.
The two states were angered
and returned to seek allies for assistance;
they gained Wèi and Cǎo,
and the four states supported one another.
They set a time to battle at Ān
and soundly defeated the army of Qí.
They captured Qí Qǐng Gōng
and beheaded Páng Chǒu Fù.
Thereupon, the Duke was startled and greatly terrified.
Relying on the deception of Páng Chǒu Fù,
he fled and managed to return home.
He consoled the dead and inquired after the sick;
for seven years, he did not drink wine or eat meat.
He put aside the sounds of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo
and distanced himself from the charms of women.
He went out to meet and form alliances,
and humbled himself before the Feudal Lords.
Internally, the state practiced righteousness,
and his reputation resonated among the Feudal Lords.
The lands he had lost
came back of their own accord without him seeking them.
He obtained honor and favor without using force.
He can be said to have been able to yield, avoid disaster, and transform himself to achieve this.
Therefore, blessing is born in times of adversity and restraint,
while disaster is born in times of success and satisfaction;
this is the effect of gain and loss.
10.14 The effect of great achievement
lies in employing the worthy and accumulating the Way,
becoming increasingly manifest and increasingly bright;
the fault of decline and destruction
lies in being complacent and negligent upon attaining success,
becoming increasingly obstructed and increasingly lost.
Jìn Wén Gōng is an example of this effect.
When Jìn Wén Gōng went into exile,
he cultivated the Way without ceasing
until he attained the rule of the state.
At the time he ruled the state,
above there was no enlightened Son of Heaven,
and below there were no worthy regional lords.
Powerful Chǔ presided over the meetings
and the feudal lords rebelled.
The Son of Heaven had lost the Way
and had gone out to reside in Zhèng.
Wén Gōng then pitied the weakness of the Central States
and employed Jiù Fàn, Xiān Zhěn, and Yáng Chǔfǔ.
He cherished and loved the common people
and diligently trained his soldiers.
In four years,
domestic governance was settled;
then he raised troops to attack Wèi,
captured Cáo Bó,
and returned to defeat powerful Chǔ,
his prestige shaking the world.
He clarified the laws of the kings
and led the lords to pay court to the Son of Heaven;
none dared not obey.
The world was vastly pacified,
and the Zhōu house became honorable and manifest.
Therefore it is said:
The effect of great achievement
lies in employing the worthy and accumulating the Way,
becoming increasingly manifest and increasingly bright.
Wén Gōng’s hegemonic achievements were thus established;
when his expectations were met and he was satisfied,
the spirit of Tāng and Wǔ arose in him, but he forgot his masses.
In one year he used his army three times
and did not rest.
He then advanced to besiege Xǔ;
the troops were extremely exhausted
and could not subdue them.
He dismissed the lords and returned.
From this point on he neglected government affairs;
for the Covenant of Díquán,
he did not attend in person.
Trust declined and righteousness was lacking,
like a net that is not repaired.
His prestige and martial power were bent and could not be extended;
thus the lords did not pay court,
Zhèng then rebelled,
the Yídí invaded from within,
and Wèi moved to Shāngqiū.
Therefore it is said:
The fault of decline and destruction
lies in being complacent and negligent upon attaining success,
becoming increasingly obstructed and increasingly lost.
10.15 Tián Zǐfāng was sitting in attendance on Wèi Wén Hóu
when Crown Prince Jī hurried in to see them.
The guests and ministers all stood up,
but Tián Zǐfāng alone did not stand.
Wén Hóu had a look of displeasure,
as did the Crown Prince.
Tián Zǐfāng declared:
"Should I stand for you?
That would not accord with the rites!
Should I not stand for you?
That would not accord with the laws regarding offenses!
Please let me recite for you.
When Chǔ Gòng Wáng was Crown Prince,
he was going out to Yúnmèng
and encountered the Grandee Gōngyǐn.
Gōngyǐn then hurried to avoid him inside the gate of a common family.
The Crown Prince got down from his carriage and followed him into the gate of the common family,
saying:
'Grandee, why do you do such a thing?
I have heard
that those who respect the father do not include the son;
to include the son,
no misfortune is greater than this.
Grandee, why do you do such a thing?'
Gōngyǐn said:
'Previously I looked upon your face,
but from now on I will remember your heart.'
If it is truly like this,
what will become of you?"
Wén Hóu said:
"Excellent."
Crown Prince Jī stepped forward,
recited the words of Gòng Wáng
three times, and asked to practice them.
10.16 Zǐgòng was going to Chéng;
someone was on the road,
and he saw by the roadside a man with a worn-out cloth covering his head and wearing mourning clothes;
his name was Zhōu Chuò.
Zǐgòng questioned him,
saying:
"How far is it from here to Chéng?"
The man was silent and did not answer.
Zǐgòng said:
"When someone asks you a question and you do not respond,
why is that?"
Setting aside his head covering, the man spoke:
"One who looks from afar and treats others with contempt,
is he benevolent?
One who sees others but does not recognize them,
is he wise?
One who treats others with slight and insult,
is he righteous?"
Zǐgòng got down from his carriage and said:
"Cì is not benevolent.
I have committed a transgression; concerning those three statements,
may I hear them again?"
The man said:
"These are enough for you;
I will tell you no more."
Thereupon, whenever Zǐgòng met three people together he would lean on the crossbar of his carriage,
and whenever he met five people together he would dismount.
10.17 Sūnshū Áo became the Lìngyǐn of Chǔ.
The officials and people of the whole state all came to congratulate him.
There was an old man wearing coarse clothes
and a white cap
who came later to offer condolences.
Sūnshū Áo adjusted his clothes and hat and went out to see him,
and said to the old man:
"The King of Chǔ did not know I was unworthy
and has made me receive the burdens of the officials and people.
Everyone has come to congratulate me,
but you alone come later to offer condolences;
do you have an explanation?"
The old man said:
"I have an explanation.
One whose person is already noble but treats others with pride,
the people will leave him;
one whose position is already high but usurps power,
the ruler will dislike him;
one whose salary is already generous but does not know contentment,
calamities will dwell with him."
Sūnshū Áo bowed twice and said:
"I respectfully receive your command;
I wish to hear the rest of your teachings."
The old man said:
"When the position is high, let the intent be increasingly humble;
when the office is great, let the heart be increasingly cautious;
when the salary is generous, be cautious and dare not take excess.
If you carefully observe these three things,
it will be sufficient to govern Chǔ."
10.18 In the eleventh year of Wèi Ānlí Wáng,
Qín Zhāo Wáng said to his attendants:
"Currently, between Hán and Wèi versus Qín, which is stronger?"
They replied:
"They are not as strong as Qín."
The King said:
"Currently, between Rú Ěr and Wèi Qí versus Mèng Chǎng and Máng Mǎo, who are more worthy?"
They replied:
"They are not as worthy as Mèng Chǎng and Máng Mǎo."
The King said:
"Even with the worthiness of Mèng Chǎng and Máng Mǎo,
leading the strong forces of Hán and Wèi to attack Qín,
they still could do nothing against me.
Now, with the incompetent Rú Ěr and Wèi Qí leading the weak forces of Hán and Wèi to invade Qín,
that they can do nothing against me
is indeed clear!"
The attendants all said:
"Indeed."
Shēn Qí, leaning over his zither, replied:
"Your Majesty’s assessment of the world
is mistaken.
During the time of the six lineages of Jìn,
the Zhì lineage was the strongest.
They destroyed the Fàn and Zhōngháng lineages.
They then led the troops of Hán and Wèi to surround Zhào Xiāngzǐ at Jìnyáng.
They diverted the Jìn River to flood the city of Jìnyáng,
until the water was short of the top by only three boards.
Zhì Bó inspected the water,
Wèi Xuānzǐ drove his chariot,
and Hán Kāngzǐ served as the outrider.
Zhì Bó said:
'At first, I did not know that water could destroy a person’s state,
but now I know.
The Fén River can flood Ānyì,
and the Jiàng River can flood Píngyáng.'
Wèi Xuānzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
and Kāngzǐ stepped on Wèi Xuānzǐ’s foot.
Elbow and foot met upon the chariot, and the Zhì lineage was partitioned below Jìnyáng.
He himself died and his state perished,
becoming a laughingstock to the world.
Although Qín is now strong,
it does not exceed the Zhì lineage.
Although Hán and Wèi are now weak,
they are still worthier than those beneath the walls of Jìnyáng.
This is precisely the time when they might use the elbow and the foot.
I hope Your Majesty will certainly not take them lightly!"
At this, the King of Qín became afraid.
10.19 When Wèi Gōngzǐ Móu was traveling east,
Ráng Hóu saw him off and said:
"Sir, you are about to leave Rǎn for the east of the mountains.
Do you not have a single word to teach Rǎn?"
Wèi Gōngzǐ Móu said:
"Had you not spoken of it,
Móu would have almost forgotten to tell you.
Do you know that office does not seek power, yet power arrives on its own?
Power does not seek wealth, yet wealth arrives on its own?
Wealth does not seek nobility, yet nobility arrives on its own?
Nobility does not seek arrogance, yet arrogance arrives on its own?
Arrogance does not seek crime, yet crime arrives on its own?
Crime does not seek death, yet death arrives on its own?"
Ráng Hóu said:
"Excellent!
I respectfully receive your enlightened teaching."
10.20 Set high value on honoring the worthy,
and do not be arrogant toward others.
Be discerning, clear-sighted, sagacious, and wise,
and do not use it to corner others.
Be resourceful and swift,
and do not use it to outdo others.
Be firm, resolute, brave, and fierce,
and do not use it to overcome others.
If you do not know, then ask.
If you are unable, then learn.
Even if wise, you must be simple and then argue.
Even if capable, you must be yielding and then act.
Therefore, though a scholar be discerning, clear-sighted, sagacious, and wise,
he guards himself with foolishness.
Though his merit covers the world,
he guards himself with yielding.
Though his courage and strength are unmatched in his generation,
he guards himself with timidity.
Though his wealth encompasses the world,
he guards himself with frugality.
This is what is called being high without being in danger,
and being full without overflowing.
10.21 Qí Huán Gōng prepared wine for his high ministers
and set the time for midday.
Guǎn Zhòng arrived late.
Huán Gōng raised a goblet to make him drink.
Guǎn Zhòng discarded half the wine.
Huán Gōng said:
"You arrived after the appointed time,
and then you drank and discarded the wine.
In terms of ritual, is this permissible?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard that when wine enters the mouth, the tongue comes out.
When the tongue comes out, words are lost.
When words are lost, the person is discarded.
I calculated that discarding the person
is not as good as discarding the wine."
Huán Gōng laughed and said:
"Rise, Zhòngfù,
and take your seat."
10.22 When Chǔ Gòng Wáng and Jìn Lì Gōng fought at Yānlíng,
Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn was thirsty and sought a drink.
The attendant Gǔyáng held out wine and presented it to him.
Zǐfǎn said:
"Retreat!
That is wine."
Gǔyáng said:
"It is not wine."
Zǐfǎn said again:
"Retreat!
It is wine."
Gǔyáng said again:
"It is not wine."
Zǐfǎn accepted and drank it.
He became drunk and fell asleep.
Gòng Wáng wished to fight again
and sent someone to summon Zǐfǎn.
Zǐfǎn declined on the grounds of a heart ailment.
Thereupon, Gòng Wáng rode out to visit him.
Entering the tent,
he smelled the stench of wine
and said:
"In today’s battle,
the one I relied upon was the Sīmǎ.
Yet the Sīmǎ is drunk to this extent.
This is to destroy my state and show no concern for my people.
I have no means to fight again."
Thereupon, he executed Zǐfǎn as a public example
and returned the army.
Now, Gǔyáng’s presentation of wine
was not out of malice toward Zǐfǎn;
he loved him with loyalty, yet it was just enough to kill him.
Therefore it is said:
Small loyalty
is the thief of great loyalty;
small profit
is the ruin of great profit.
10.23 War-loving ministers
must be scrutinized.
They bring about great resentment over small shames,
and they lose the great masses for small gains.
The Chūnqiū contains such warnings,
as in the case of Xiān Zhěn of Jìn.
Xiān Zhěn wished to seek merit and gain fame,
so on the grounds that Qín did not request passage,
he asked to intercept the Qín army.
Xiāng Gōng said:
"It cannot be.
The Lord of Qín had a bond with my late father.
To raise an army and strike them just one day after my father has passed
would be for me to betray my late father,
ruin relations with a neighboring state,
and lose the conduct of a filial son."
Xiān Zhěn said:
"They do not send condolences or gifts when our late lord has passed;
this is to show no grief for our mourning.
They raise an army and pass through our lands without requesting passage;
this is to treat me, the orphaned one, as weak.
Moreover, while the coffin is still under a thatched roof,
they show no grief for our mourning."
When the army was raised,
the divination said:
"The army of a great state is about to arrive;
please strike them."
So the King listened to Xiān Zhěn and raised troops,
intercepting them at Xiáo.
They struck them,
and not a single horse or a single wheel escaped.
This created great resentment and disaster with Qín.
Blades met and blood flowed;
corpses lay prone and skeletons were exposed.
The state was devastated
for more than ten years.
In the end, he lost his troops and the masses,
disaster reached the high officials,
and the sorrow burdened later generations.
Therefore, war-loving ministers
must be scrutinized.
10.24 Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ,
"I have heard that among those who are most forgetful,
some move house and forget their wives.
Does this happen?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"This is not the most forgetful.
The most forgetful
forget themselves."
Āi Gōng said,
"May I hear more about this?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"In the past, Xià Jié was as noble as the Son of Heaven
and as wealthy as owning all under heaven.
He did not cultivate the way of Yǔ,
he destroyed the laws,
cut off the ancestral sacrifices,
abandoned himself to music,
and indulged in wine.
Among his ministers was Zuǒ Shī Chù Lóng,
who flattered him incessantly.
Tāng executed Jié;
as for Zuǒ Shī Chù Lóng,
his body died with his four limbs lying in different places.
This is one who forgot himself."
Āi Gōng looked solemn, changed his expression, and said,
"Excellent."
10.25 Kǒngzǐ went to Zhōu
and observed the Tài Miào.
In front of the right steps,
there was a golden man
whose mouth was sealed thrice,
and on its back was inscribed:
"A person of ancient times who was cautious in speech.
Take heed!
Take heed!
Do not speak much;
much speech leads to much failure.
Do not do many things;
many things lead to much trouble.
In peace and joy, one must be cautious;
do not do what you will regret.
Do not say 'what harm is there?';
the calamity will be long-lasting.
Do not say 'what damage is there?';
the calamity will be great.
Do not say 'what ruin is there?';
the calamity will blaze up.
Do not say 'no one will hear';
heavenly monsters watch over men.
A small spark not extinguished,
what can be done when it becomes a great flame?
A trickling stream not dammed
will become a great river.
A continuous thread not broken
will become a net.
A sprout not cut
will require an axe.
Truly, if one cannot be cautious,
it is the root of calamity.
'How can the mouth cause harm?'
It is the gate of calamity.
The violent and overbearing do not die a natural death;
those who love to win will surely meet their match.
A thief resents the master;
the people harm those in high positions.
The Jūnzǐ knows that all under heaven cannot be covered up;
therefore, he puts himself behind and below,
causing people to admire him.
By holding to the feminine and remaining low,
none can compete with him.
While others rush there,
I alone hold to this.
While the multitude is confused,
I alone do not follow.
I keep my knowledge hidden within
and do not debate skills with others.
Though I am noble and high,
no one harms me.
Now, the reason the Jiāng and Hé are the leaders of the hundred valleys
is because they stay low.
The Way of Heaven has no favorites;
it always stays with the good man.
Take heed!
Take heed!"
Kǒngzǐ looked back and told his disciples,
"Remember this.
These words, though plain, hit the mark of reality.
The Shī says:
'Be fearful and cautious,
as if on the brink of a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice.'
If one conducts oneself like this,
how could one meet calamity through the mouth?"
10.26 Lǔ Āi Hóu abandoned his state and fled to Qí.
The Qí Hóu said,
"How is it that your age is so young, yet you abandoned your state so early?"
Lǔ Āi Hóu said,
"When I first became the Crown Prince,
many people remonstrated with me,
but I accepted their advice and did not use it.
Many people loved me,
but I loved them and did not keep them near.
Thus, inside I heard nothing and outside I had no support.
This is like the autumn tumbleweed;
its roots are poor but its branches and leaves are beautiful.
Once the autumn wind rises,
the roots are pulled out."
10.27 Kǒngzǐ was traveling on the road
when he heard the sound of someone weeping;
the sound was very sorrowful.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Drive on!
Drive on!
There is the voice of an extraordinary person ahead."
Advancing a little further,
he saw him:
it was Qiū Wú Zǐ,
holding a sickle and wearing a rope belt, weeping.
Kǒngzǐ stepped down from his carriage
and asked,
"Sir, you are not in mourning,
why is your weeping so sorrowful?"
Qiū Wú Zǐ replied,
"I have three regrets."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"I wish to hear of these three regrets."
Qiū Wú Zǐ said,
"When I was young, I loved learning
and traveled throughout the world.
When I returned, my parents had passed away;
this is the first regret.
I served a ruler who was extravagant and arrogant;
my remonstrances were not followed;
this is the second regret.
I formed deep friendships but later became estranged;
this is the third regret.
The tree wants to be still, but the wind does not stop;
the child wants to provide for the parents, but the parents do not wait.
That which goes and does not return
is the years;
those whom one cannot see again
are one's parents.
Please let me take my leave here."
Then he cut his own throat and died.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Disciples, remember this;
this is enough to serve as a warning."
Thereupon, thirteen disciples took their leave to return home and care for their parents.
10.28 Kǒngzǐ was discussing the Shī,
and when he reached the sixth stanza of Zhèng Yuè,
he said with alarm,
"A Jūnzǐ who does not meet his time—
is he not in danger?
If he follows his superiors and conforms to the world, he abandons the Way.
If he opposes his superiors and stays away from common customs, he endangers his life.
If the world does not side with goodness
and he alone follows it,
then they say he is either a phantom or a monster.
This is why Jié killed Guān Lóng Páng
and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐ Gān.
Therefore, when a worthy person does not meet his time,
he always fears he will not come to a natural end.
The Shī says:
'Men say the heavens are high,
yet I dare not but stoop.
Men say the earth is thick,
yet I dare not but tread lightly.'
This is what it means."
10.29 Kǒngzǐ saw a man catching birds with a net;
those he caught were all yellow mouths.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"You catch all the yellow mouths,
but the large birds alone you do not catch.
Why is that?"
The netter replied,
"Yellow mouths that follow large birds cannot be caught;
large birds that follow yellow mouths can be caught."
Kǒngzǐ looked back and told his disciples,
"The Jūnzǐ is cautious about whom he follows.
If he does not find the right person,
then he will have the trouble of the net."
10.30 In cultivating the self and rectifying conduct,
one cannot be imprudent.
Desires cause conduct to suffer,
slander and flattery disturb the upright heart,
and the voices of many cause the will to waver.
Anxiety and trouble arise from what is neglected,
and the calamity of anger begins from the minute and subtle.
Disgrace and humiliation are difficult to wash away;
a failed matter cannot be pursued again.
If one does not contemplate deeply or plan far ahead,
how much regret will there be!
Now, those who seek luck
are the axes that cut down nature;
those who follow desires
are the horses that chase after calamity;
those who are boastful and deceitful
are the dwellings of exhaustion and shame;
those who treat others with cruelty
are on the road toward disaster.
Therefore it is said:
Cast away seeking luck,
strive for loyalty and trustworthiness,
moderate your desires,
and do not treat others with cruelty.
Then you will be called a Jūnzǐ,
and your reputation will endure forever.
10.31 Resentment arises from a lack of recompense,
and calamity arises from an excess of fortune.
Safety and danger depend on how one comports oneself;
avoiding distress depends on early preparation;
survival or ruin depends on winning over people.
If one is as cautious at the end as at the beginning,
then one can endure long.
To be able to practice these five things
is sufficient to preserve one's person.
What you do not desire for yourself,
do not do to others;
this is called the essential way.
10.32 When Yán Huí was about to travel west,
he asked Kǒngzǐ:
"How should I cultivate my person?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Reverence, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness
are sufficient for cultivating the person.
Through reverence, one avoids the crowds;
through respect, people love one;
through loyalty, people support one;
through trustworthiness, people rely on one.
He whom people love,
whom people support,
and whom people rely upon
will surely avoid trouble.
One can even preside over a state and family with this,
let alone one's own person!
Therefore, to not stay close to relatives but rather stay close to the distant,
is that not being far off?
To not cultivate the internal but rather cultivate the external,
is that not being perverse?
To not plan for things beforehand
and only deliberate when facing difficulty,
is that not being too late?"
10.33 In all things regarding the management of the person,
one must be prudent with the five roots.
The first is:
gentleness through benevolence;
the second is:
sincerity through trustworthiness;
the third is:
when wealthy and noble,
never dare to be arrogant toward others;
the fourth is:
courtesy through respect;
the fifth is:
magnanimity through tranquility.
By contemplating these five things,
there will be no ill-fated outcomes.
It is said:
