If one can manage respect so as to assist the timing of Heaven,
ill-fated outcomes will not arrive and calamity will not come.
To respect others
is not just respecting others,
but respecting oneself;
to honor others
is not just honoring others,
but honoring oneself.
In the past,
I have seen Heaven rain down gold, stones, and blood;
I have seen the sun and moon come out together on the tenth day of the fourth month,
causing confusion in the heavens;
I have seen high mountains collapse,
deep valleys become blocked,
great capitals and royal palaces destroyed,
and large states extinguished.
I have seen high mountains split apart,
the sands of deep abysses run dry,
and the carriages of noblemen torn asunder.
I have seen dense forests without trees,
level plains become ravines and valleys,
and Jūnzǐ become grooms and servants.
I have seen the Yangtze and the Yellow River dry up into pits,
the picking of elms and mulberries in the middle of winter,
and the raining of snow and frost in mid-summer.
Lords of a thousand chariots and masters of ten thousand chariots
died without being buried.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ uses respect to establish his name,
and the Xiǎorén uses respect to eliminate his punishment.
How can one not be cautious and prudent with the five roots!
10.34 There was a reverent gentleman in Lǔ named Jī Sì;
at the age of seventy,
his reverence became even more profound.
In winter, he walked in the shade;
in summer, he walked in the sun.
Even in the market rows, he did not dare walk without due care;
when walking with others, he always followed behind.
When sitting, he was always upright;
during the course of a single meal, he would rise three times.
He was not ashamed to see those dressed in common cloth and coarse furs;
rather, he treated them with ritual.
The Lord of Lǔ asked:
"Master Jī, your years are quite advanced;
can you not set aside your reverence?"
Jī Sì replied:
"The Jūnzǐ loves reverence to establish his name,
and the Xiǎorén learns reverence to eliminate his punishment.
Sitting before the ruler,
is it not peaceful?
Yet there may still be errors and slips.
Above a single meal,
is it not delicious?
Yet there may still be choking and gagging.
Now, as for what someone like Sì calls luck,
I truly cannot be certain of it myself.
When the swan flies up to pierce the sky,
is it not high?
Yet the tethered arrow can still reach it.
The tiger and leopard are fierce,
yet people still eat their meat
and use their skins as mats.
Those who praise others are few;
those who hate others are many.
At seventy years of age,
I am constantly afraid that the axe and the block might be applied to me;
why should I set aside reverence?"
10.35 Chéng Huí studied under Zǐlù for three years;
Huí’s reverence and respect never ceased.
Zǐlù asked him the reason for this.
Huí replied:
"I have heard that
a traveler is like a bird,
fearing the hawk and the falcon above,
and fearing the nets and snares below.
Now, those who do good are few,
while those who slander are many.
If one has not yet died,
how can one know that calamity and guilt will not be imposed?
At seventy years of age,
I am constantly afraid that my conduct and integrity might fail.
Therefore, I use reverence and respect to await the Great Mandate."
Zǐlù bowed his head and said:
"A true Jūnzǐ!"
11.1 Sūn Qīng said:
“As for the art of persuasion:
Use dignity and solemnity to establish it,
uprightness and sincerity to dwell in it,
firmness and strength to maintain it,
analogies and comparisons to illustrate it,
distinctions and categorizations to clarify it,
and use joy, delight, indignation, and fullness to convey it.
Treasure it and cherish it;
value it and treat it as divine.
If one acts like this, then persuasion will always succeed.
This is what is called being able to value what should be valued.
The *Chuán* says:
‘Only the *Jūnzǐ* is able to value what should be valued.’ ”
The *Shī* says:
“Do not easily give voice to words;
do not say they are of no consequence.”
Guǐgǔzǐ said:
“When a person is not good, to be able to correct them
is difficult.
If persuasion does not work
and words are not followed,
it is because the reasoning is not clear.
If it is clear but still not followed,
it is because it is not maintained firmly.
If it is firm but still not followed,
it has not yet hit upon what the heart considers good.
Reason it out,
clarify it,
maintain it,
and make it firm;
furthermore, hit upon what the person considers good.
Then the words will be divine and cherished,
clear and distinct,
and able to enter a person’s heart.
If persuasion like this still does not work,
the world has never heard of such a thing.”
This is what is called being good at persuasion.
Zǐgòng said:
“Issuing words and presenting speeches
involves the gain or loss of one’s own person
and the safety or peril of the state.”
The *Shī* says:
“When speech is well-ordered,
the people are at rest.”
Now, speech
is the means by which a person communicates.
Zhǔfù Yǎn said:
“If a person lacks speech,
what use is there for them?”
In the past, Zǐchǎn refined his speech and Zhào Wǔ showed him respect;
Wángsūn Mǎn clarified his words and Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng was shamed;
Sū Qín implemented his persuasion and the Six States were secured;
Kuǎi Tōng presented his persuasion and his life was preserved.
Speech
is the means by which one honors the *Jūn* and respects one’s own person,
secures the state and preserves one’s nature.
Therefore, speech must be cultivated,
and persuasion must be practiced skillfully.
11.2 Zhào sent someone to say to the Wèi Wáng:
“For my sake, kill Fàn Cuó,
and I request to offer seventy *lǐ* of land.”
The Wèi Wáng said:
“Agreed.”
He sent officials to arrest him,
and they surrounded him but had not yet killed him.
Fàn Cuó climbed onto the roof, sat on the ridge, and said to the messenger:
“Rather than trading with a dead Fàn Cuó,
it is better to trade with a living Fàn Cuó.
Suppose I, Fàn Cuó, die,
and Zhào does not give the *Wáng* the land;
then what will the *Wáng* do?
Therefore, it is better to first finalize the division of the land with them
and then kill me.”
The Wèi Wáng said:
“Excellent.”
Fàn Cuó then sent a letter to the Xìnlíng Jūn saying:
“I, Fàn Cuó,
am the former dismissed *Xiàng* of Wèi.
Zhào is using land to kill me, and the Wèi Wáng is listening to them.
Suppose powerful Qín also follows Zhào’s desire,
then what will you, my *Jūn*, do?”
The Xìnlíng Jūn spoke to the *Wáng*, and he was released.
11.3 The people of Wú entered Jīng,
and they summoned Chén Huái Gōng.
Chén Huái Gōng summoned the people of the state and said:
“Those who wish to side with Jīng, move to the left;
those who wish to side with Wú, move to the right.”
Féng Huá faced the *Gōng*, stepped forward, and said:
“Wú has not yet had good fortune;
Jīng has not yet had disaster.”
The *Gōng* said:
“The state is defeated and its ruler has fled;
if this is not disaster, what is?”
He replied:
“When a small state has this, it can still recover;
how much more so for a large state?
Although Chǔ lacks virtue,
it has not yet cut down its people.
Wú is daily exhausted by war,
and bones are exposed like weeds;
no virtue has been seen there.
Heaven is perhaps just disciplining Jīng;
as for disaster reaching Wú,
what day will it not happen?”
The Chén Hóu followed his advice.
11.4 Huán Gōng established Zhòngfù and addressed the *Dàfū*, saying:
“Those who think well of me, enter the gate and go to the right;
those who do not think well of me, enter the gate and go to the left.”
There was one who stood in the middle of the gate.
Huán Gōng questioned him,
and he replied:
“Guǎn Zǐ’s wisdom is such that one can plan for the world with him;
his strength is such that one can take the world with him.
If the *Jūn* relies on his trustworthiness,
entrusts him with internal administration,
lets him decide on external affairs,
and drives the people to return to him,
then the state can also be seized.”
Huán Gōng said:
“Excellent.”
He then said to Guǎn Zhòng:
“The administration will ultimately belong to you;
where the administration does not reach,
only you shall rectify it.”
Therefore, Guǎn Zhòng built the Sānguī zhī Tái
to harm his own reputation among the people.
11.5 Qí Xuān Wáng went hunting at Shèshān,
and thirteen elders of Shèshān came together to welcome the *Wáng*.
The *Wáng* said:
“Elders, you have worked hard!”
He told his attendants to grant the elders land without taxes.
The elders all bowed,
but Lǘqiū Xiānshēng alone did not bow.
The *Wáng* said:
“Do the elders think this is too little?”
He told his attendants to further grant the elders exemption from labor service.
The elders all bowed,
and Lǘqiū Xiānshēng again did not bow.
The *Wáng* said:
“Those who bowed may leave;
the one who did not bow, come forward.”
He said:
“I came to observe today,
and the elders fortunately welcomed me.
Therefore, I granted the elders land without taxes;
the elders all bowed,
but you alone did not bow.
I thought it was too little,
so I granted the elders exemption from labor service;
the elders all bowed,
and you again alone did not bow.
Could it be that I have committed some fault?”
Lǘqiū Xiānshēng replied:
“I heard the *Dàwáng* was coming to visit,
and the reason I welcomed the *Dàwáng*
was hoping to receive longevity from the *Dàwáng*,
hoping to receive wealth from the *Dàwáng*,
and hoping to receive honor from the *Dàwáng*.”
The *Wáng* said:
“Heaven’s killing and giving life have their times;
it is not something I can participate in;
I have no means to give you longevity.
Although the granaries are full,
they are to prepare for disasters;
I have no means to give you wealth.
High offices have no vacancies,
and low offices are humble and lowly;
I have no means to give you honor.”
Lǘqiū Xiānshēng replied:
“These are not things a subject dares to hope for.
I wish the *Dàwáng* would select the sons of good and wealthy families who have cultivated conduct to be officials,
and make the laws and standards fair;
in this way, I can obtain a little longevity.
Provide relief in spring, autumn, winter, and summer according to the seasons,
and do not trouble or harass the common people;
in this way, I can obtain a little wealth.
I wish the *Dàwáng* would issue an order
that the young respect their elders
and the elders respect the aged;
in this way, I can obtain a little honor.
Now the *Dàwáng* fortunately grants me land without taxes,
but then the granaries will become empty.
You grant me exemption from labor service,
but then the government offices will have no one to employ.
This is certainly not what a subject dares to hope for.”
The Qí Wáng said:
“Excellent.
I wish to request the *Xiānshēng* to be my *Xiàng*.”
11.6 During the time of Emperor Xiào Wǔ,
a precious tripod was found in Fényīn and presented at Gānquán Palace.
The various ministers offered congratulations
and offered a toast for long life, saying:
“Your Majesty has obtained a Zhōu tripod.”
The Attendant-in-Ordinary Yúqiū Shòuwáng alone said:
“It is not a Zhōu tripod.”
When the Emperor heard this,
he summoned and questioned him, saying:
“Now I have obtained a Zhōu tripod,
and the various ministers all believe it to be a Zhōu tripod,
yet Shòuwáng alone believes it is not;
why is this?
If Shòuwáng has an explanation, he shall live;
if he has no explanation, he shall die.”
He replied:
“How could your servant Shòuwáng dare to have no explanation?
Your servant has heard that the virtue of Zhōu began with Hòujì,
grew with Gōngliú,
became great with Dàwáng,
was completed by Wén and Wǔ,
and became manifest with Zhōugōng.
The moisture of their virtue penetrated the heavens above
and leaked into the springs below;
there was nowhere it did not reach.
Heaven responded,
and the tripod appeared for Zhōu;
therefore it was named a Zhōu tripod.
Now Hàn has succeeded Zhōu since the time of Gāozǔ;
it has also illumined virtue and manifested conduct,
spreading grace and bestowing kindness,
and the six directions are in harmony.
Reaching your Majesty’s person,
merit and virtue have become even more flourishing;
heavenly omens arrive together,
and auspicious signs appear completely.
Formerly, when Emperor Qín Shǐhuángdì personally tried to take a tripod at Péngchéng, he could not obtain it.
Heaven illumines the virtuous and the precious tripod arrives of itself;
this is what Heaven gives to Hàn;
it is a Hàn tripod,
not a Zhōu tripod.”
The Emperor said:
“Excellent.”
The ministers all shouted, “Ten thousand years!”
On that day, Yúqiū Shòuwáng was granted ten catties of gold.
11.7 During the time of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
there was a commoner from the eastern suburbs named Zǔ Cháo
who submitted a memorial to Duke Xiàn, saying:
“I, a commoner of the wild fields from the eastern suburbs named Zǔ Cháo,
desire to ask to hear of the plans of the state.”
Duke Xiàn sent an envoy out to tell him:
“The meat-eaters have already considered them;
what concern is it of those who eat coarse greens?”
Zǔ Cháo replied:
“Has the Great King alone not heard of a general of old called Marshal Huán?
Every morning he would attend his lord;
he set out late,
and the driver called for the carriage to make way;
the outside horse also called for the carriage to make way.
The driver nudged the outside horse with his elbow and said:
‘Why do you overstep your place?
Why do you assist in calling for the carriage?’
The outside horse said to the driver:
‘When it is time to call, calling
is my duty.
You are in charge of driving;
just keep your reins and bits straight.
If you now do not keep the reins and bits straight,
causing the horse to suddenly take fright
and recklessly run over pedestrians on the road,
we will surely encounter a great enemy.
To get down from the carriage and unsheathe the sword,
wading through blood and treading on livers,
is certainly my duty.
Can you perhaps avoid your reins to assist me?
That disaster would also reach my own person;
having deep concern for it,
how could I not call for the carriage?’
Now the Great King says:
‘The meat-eaters have already considered them;
what concern is it of those who eat coarse greens?’
Suppose the meat-eaters were one day to fail in their plans in the ancestral temple;
would those like your servant who eat coarse greens
not have their livers and gall bladders smeared on the ground in the fields of the Central Plain?
That disaster would also reach your servant's person;
your servant shares this deep concern.
How could I not take part in the plans of the state?”
Duke Xiàn summoned and saw him;
for three days,
he spoke with him,
and having no further worries,
he established him as a teacher.
11.8 A guest said to the King of Liáng:
“Huìzǐ is good at using analogies when talking about matters.
If the King makes him not use analogies,
then he will be unable to speak.”
The King said:
“Agreed.”
The next day he saw him
and said to Huìzǐ:
“I wish that when the Master speaks of matters, he would just speak directly,
without using analogies.”
Huìzǐ said:
“Suppose there is a person here who does not know what a pellet-bow is,
and asks:
‘What is the shape of a pellet-bow like?’
If I answer:
‘The shape of a pellet-bow is like a pellet-bow,’
then would he understand?”
The King said:
“He would not understand.”
“Then if I changed the answer to:
‘The shape of a pellet-bow is like a bow,
but with bamboo used for the string,’
then would he know?”
The King said:
“He would know.”
Huìzǐ said:
“In the nature of explanation,
one certainly uses what is known to illustrate what is not known
so as to make people know it.
Now the King says ‘do not use analogies,’
then it is impossible.”
The King said:
“Excellent.”
11.9 Mèngcháng Jūn recommended a guest to the King of Qí.
After three years, he had not been employed.
Therefore, the guest returned
and said to Mèngcháng Jūn:
“When my Lord recommended your servant,
after three years without being employed,
was this your servant’s crime,
or my Lord’s fault?”
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
“I have heard
that the thread enters because of the needle,
but it does not become tight because of the needle;
a daughter’s marriage is completed because of the matchmaker,
but she does not become intimate because of the matchmaker.
The Master’s talent must be meager;
how can you still resent me?”
The guest said:
“It is not so.
I have heard that Zhōu Shì's Kù
and Hán Shì's Lú
were the swift dogs of the world.
If they saw a rabbit and the direction was pointed out,
then they would not lose the rabbit.
If one sees from afar and releases the dog,
then for many generations one could not catch the rabbit.
It is not that the dog is incapable;
the fault lies with the one pointing.”
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
“It is not so.
Formerly, Huà Zhōu and Qǐ Liáng died in battle;
their wives grieved for them
and cried toward the city wall;
a corner collapsed because of it,
and the wall crumbled because of it.
If a gentleman can truly be a model within, then things will respond without.
Even earth and soil can be moved by sincerity,
how much more so a grain-eating ruler?”
The guest said:
“It is not so.
I have seen a wren nest in the reeds,
attaching it to a hair.
Built on the edge of peril,
even a female artisan could not make it;
it can be called complete and firm.
But when a great wind arrives, the reeds break;
why are the eggs broken and the young killed?
It is because of what it relied upon that it is so.
Furthermore, the fox
is what people attack;
the rat
is what people smoke out.
I have never seen a fox of the grain-god shrine being attacked,
nor a rat of the earth-god shrine being smoked out.
Why is this?
It is because of what they rely upon that it is so.”
Thereupon Mèngcháng Jūn again recommended him to the King of Qí,
and the King of Qí made him Prime Minister.
11.10 Chén Zǐ was persuading Liáng Wáng.
Liáng Wáng was pleased but suspicious of him,
and said:
"Why did you leave the state of Chén Hóu
to teach the ruler of a small state here?"
Chén Zǐ said:
"Indeed, goodness has its way,
and an encounter has its time.
Formerly, Fù Yuè wore coarse hemp clothes and a rope belt while building the walls at Bǐchuán.
Wǔ Dīng dreamed of him in the evening and found him in the morning;
this was the time of a King.
Nìng Qī was feeding oxen at Kāngqú,
striking the wheel spokes and singing.
Looking back,
Huán Gōng found him;
this was the time of a Hegemon.
Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself for five sheepskins
and became a captive of the Qín people.
Mù Gōng found him;
this was the time of strength.
Considering the conduct of these three men,
they could not yet be considered Kǒngzǐ's outstanding disciples.
Now Kǒngzǐ managed the world,
suffering distress in Chén and Cài to the south,
and seeking out Jǐng Gōng in the north.
Twice he sat and five times he stood,
never leaving his path.
Kǒngzǐ's time did not come,
and Jǐng Gōng's time was negligent.
With Kǒngzǐ's sagacity,
he could not use his timely conduct to persuade one who was negligent;
what alone could be done about it?"
11.11 Lín Jì wore leather clothing when he attended the court of Qí Jǐng Gōng.
Qí Jǐng Gōng said:
"Is this the clothing of a gentleman,
or the clothing of a lowly man?"
Lín Jì hesitated, his expression changing, and said:
"How can matters of clothing be enough to determine a scholar's conduct?
Formerly, Jīng wore long swords and high caps,
and Lìngyǐn Zǐxī came from there.
Qí wore short clothes and tilted caps,
and Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng came from there.
Yuè tattooed their bodies and cut their hair,
and Fàn Lǐ and Dàfū Zhòng came from there.
The Xīróng fastened their robes on the left and wore their hair in mallets,
and Yóu Yú also came from there.
If it were as you say,
those who wear dog furs should bark like dogs,
and those who wear sheepskins should bleat like sheep.
Moreover, you, My Lord, wear fox furs to court;
one wonders, could you be undergoing a transformation?"
Jǐng Gōng said:
"You are truly brave and bold!
Yet I have not seen your extraordinary eloquence.
Is it for a neighbor's fight,
or for the victory of a thousand chariots?"
Lín Jì said:
"I do not know what you mean.
Now, to climb high and look over a precipice without blinking
and without one's feet trembling,
this is the bravery of a craftsman.
To enter deep pools,
stab flood-dragons,
and come out clutching soft-shelled turtles and crocodiles,
this is the bravery of a fisherman.
To enter deep mountains,
stab tigers and leopards,
and come out clutching bears and brown bears,
this is the bravery of a hunter.
To not find it difficult to have one's head cut off or belly ripped open,
with bones exposed and blood flowing in the middle of a field,
this is the bravery of a warrior.
Now, I stay in this broad court,
changing my expression to speak uprightly,
so as to risk my lord's anger.
Though there may be the reward of a carriage before me,
I am not moved by it.
Though there may be the threat of the axe and block behind me,
I am not afraid of it.
This is what I, Jì, consider bravery."
11.12 Wèi Wén Hóu was drinking wine with his great officers.
He appointed Gōngchéng Bùrén to be the master of the toasts,
saying:
"He who does not drain his cup shall be penalized with a large goblet."
Wén Hóu drank but did not drain his cup.
Gōngchéng Bùrén raised the large goblet to penalize the lord.
The lord looked at him but did not respond.
An attendant said:
"Bùrén, withdraw;
the lord is already drunk."
Gōngchéng Bùrén said:
"The Zhōu Shū says:
'If the front carriage overturns,
the rear carriage should take heed.'
This speaks of danger.
Being a minister is not easy,
and being a lord is also not easy.
Now that the lord has issued an order,
is it acceptable if the order is not carried out?"
The lord said:
"Excellent."
He raised the goblet and drank it.
When he finished drinking, he said:
"Let Gōngchéng Bùrén be treated as an honored guest."
11.13 On the day Xiāngchéng Jūn was first enfeoffed,
he wore kingfisher-feather clothes,
a belt with jade pigs,
a jade-adorned sword,
and white silk shoes,
standing by the flowing water.
A great officer held the bell mallet suspended,
and an official held the drumstick and issued orders,
asking who could ferry the prince across.
Chǔ Dàfū Zhuāng Xīn passed by and was pleased with him.
He approached and paid his respects,
then stood up and said:
"I wish to hold my lord's hand;
may I?"
Xiāngchéng Jūn became indignant and changed his expression without speaking.
Zhuāng Xīn withdrew slightly, clasped his hands, and said:
"Have you alone not heard of È Jūn Zǐxī's boating upon the New Waves?
He rode in a boat with green feathers,
decorated with patterns and plants,
spread a kingfisher-feather canopy,
and held a rhinoceros tail.
Clad in elegant robes and skirts,
when the music of bells and drums had ceased,
a Yuè man holding an oar embraced it and sang.
The lyrics of the song were:
'Làn xī biàn cǎo làn yú,
chāng hù zé yú,
chāng zhōu zhōu,
qì zhōu yān hū,
qín xū xū,
màn yú hū,
zhāo chán qín yú,
shèn tì suí hé hú.'
È Jūn Zǐxī said:
'I do not understand the Yuè song;
please explain it to me in Chǔ.'
Thereupon, a Yuè interpreter was called,
and he explained it in Chǔ, saying:
'What night is this night?
Drifting in the mid-stream.
What day is today?
To be in the same boat as the Prince.
Shamed but favored,
I do not mind the disgrace.
My heart is somewhat stubborn and unending,
because I have known the Prince.
The mountains have trees, and the trees have branches;
my heart is pleased with the lord, but the lord does not know it.'
Thereupon, È Jūn Zǐxī shook his long sleeves, stepped forward and embraced him,
and raised an embroidered quilt to cover him.
È Jūn Zǐxī was the younger brother of the Chǔ Wáng's mother;
his office was Lìngyǐn,
and his rank was Zhíguī.
Even to an oarsman of Yuè,
he still showed such joy and affection.
Now, how are you superior to È Jūn Zǐxī,
and why am I alone not equal to an oarsman?
I wish to hold my lord's hand;
why should it not be allowed?"
Xiāngchéng Jūn then offered his hand and stepped forward, saying:
"When I was young,
I was also praised for my appearance by my elders,
but I have never encountered such an abrupt reproach as this.
From this day forward,
I wish to respectfully receive your instructions with the etiquette due from a youth to an elder."
11.14 Yōngmén Zǐ Zhōu visited Mèng Chǎng Jūn with his zither.
Mèng Chǎng Jūn said:
"Sir, when you play the zither,
can you also make Wén feel sad?"
Yōngmén Zǐ Zhōu said:
"How could I alone make your excellency feel sad!
Those whom I can make sad
are those who were noble but then became lowly,
or those who were wealthy but then became poor.
Or those who, though of refined stature,
happen to encounter a violent and lawless ruler
who wantonly imposes unprincipled logic upon them;
or those who live in isolation,
unreachable by neighbors,
humiliated and rejected,
dwelling in a wretched alleyway
with no one to whom they can appeal;
or those who love each other dearly
but are separated without resentment,
going far away to distant states,
with no hope of meeting again;
or those who lost both parents when young,
are separated from siblings,
have insufficient means for their household,
and are filled with sorrow.
In such times,
they truly cannot bear to hear the sounds of flying birds or rushing winds,
and in their desolation, they find no joy.
For all such as these,
once I adjust the bridge and strings, take up the zither, and heave a long sigh,
then tears will flow and moisten their lapels.
Now, as for your excellency,
you are a lord of a thousand chariots.
You dwell in vast mansions and deep chambers,
with gauze curtains lowered,
where cool breezes come.
Singers, entertainers, and dwarves are before you,
coming forward in turns to flatter.
For amusement, you play chess and watch the dancing of Zhèng girls,
raising the sharp winds of the *Jí Chǔ* melody,
using refined colors to indulge the eyes,
and flowing sounds to please the ears.
For water excursions, you link square-bottomed boats,
bearing feathered banners,
with drums and flutes playing over unfathomable depths.
For field excursions, you gallop and hunt on the plains and vast parks,
capturing fierce beasts.
Upon entering, you strike bells and beat drums within the deep palace.
At such times,
you view heaven and earth as less than a single finger
and forget death and life.
Though there may be those who play the zither well,
they truly cannot make your excellency feel sad."
Mèng Chǎng Jūn said:
"No, no,
Wén truly does not believe this to be so."
Yōngmén Zǐ Zhōu said:
"Indeed,
there is one matter for which I feel sadness for your excellency.
He whose reputation rivaled the Emperor and who troubled Qín
was you, my lord.
He who formed the alliance of five states
to face south and attack Chǔ
was also you, my lord.
The world has never been without trouble;
if not the Vertical Alliance, then the Horizontal Alliance.
If the Vertical Alliance succeeds, the King of Chǔ will rule;
if the Horizontal Alliance succeeds, the King of Qín will be Emperor.
The King of Chǔ or the Emperor of Qín will certainly seek revenge upon Xuē.
With the strength of Qín and Chǔ
taking revenge upon the weak Xuē,
it is like whetting a sharp axe to strike a morning mushroom;
they will certainly not stop in their tracks.
Among the men of knowledge in the world,
there are none who do not feel a chill in their hearts and a sting in their noses for your excellency.
After a thousand years and ten thousand years,
your ancestral temple will surely not receive blood sacrifices.
Once the high terraces have collapsed,
once the winding ponds have been filled in,
once the tombs have been leveled
and covered in green weeds,
infants and youths gathering firewood
will stomp their feet and sing upon them.
When the multitude sees this,
none will not feel distressed and sad for your excellency,
saying:
'With the nobility and honor of Mèng Chǎng Jūn,
how could it come to this!' "
Thereupon, Mèng Chǎng Jūn's tears fell,
hanging from his eyelashes but not yet falling.
Yōngmén Zǐ Zhōu took up the zither and played it.
Slowly he moved the *gōng* and *zhǐ* notes,
subtly strummed the *yǔ* and *jué* notes,
and with a sharp conclusion finished the melody.
Mèng Chǎng Jūn's tears flowed and sweat broke out,
and with a sob, he approached him,
saying:
"Hearing the gentleman play the zither
makes Wén feel instantly like one whose state is broken and whose city is lost."
11.15 Qú Bó Yù was sent on a mission to Chǔ.
He met Gōngzǐ Xī by the Pú Water.
Gōngzǐ Xī was pulling at the grass while waiting
and said:
"May I ask where the honored guest is going?"
Qú Bó Yù leaned on the carriage rail for him.
Gōngzǐ Xī said:
"I have heard that to a superior man one can entrust one's countenance;
to a middle man one can entrust one's words;
and to an inferior man one can entrust one's wealth.
Through these three, can one truly entrust one's person?"
Qú Bó Yù said:
"I respectfully receive your command."
Qú Bó Yù saw the King of Chǔ.
When his diplomatic mission was finished,
they sat and talked,
and the conversation leisurely turned to scholars.
The King of Chǔ said:
"Which state has the most scholars?"
Qú Bó Yù said:
"Chǔ has the most scholars."
The King of Chǔ was greatly pleased.
Qú Bó Yù said:
"Chǔ has the most scholars, yet Chǔ cannot use them."
The King asked in surprise:
"What kind of talk is this?"
Qú Bó Yù said:
"Wǔ Zǐ Xū was born in Chǔ,
but he fled to Wú.
Wú received him and made him Chancellor,
and he raised troops to attack Chǔ,
desecrating the tomb of King Píng.
Wǔ Zǐ Xū was born in Chǔ, but Wú used him well.
Xìn Fén Huáng was born in Chǔ,
but he fled to Jìn.
He governed seventy-two counties;
things dropped on the road were not picked up,
the people did not take things improperly,
the city gates were not closed,
and the state had no thieves or bandits.
Fén Huáng was born in Chǔ, but Jìn used him well.
Now, as I was coming,
I met Gōngzǐ Xī by the Pú Water.
His words were:
'To a superior man one can entrust one's countenance;
to a middle man one can entrust one's words;
and to an inferior man one can entrust one's wealth.
Through these three, can one truly entrust one's person?'
I do not know which state Gōngzǐ Xī will go to govern."
Thereupon, the King of Chǔ dispatched an envoy with a team of four horses
and two assistant envoys in carriages
to pursue Gōngzǐ Xī by the Pú Water.
Gōngzǐ Xī returned
and became important in Chǔ,
which was due to the efforts of Qú Bó Yù.
Therefore, the *Shī* says:
"Who can cook fish?
One must wash the pots and vessels.
Who will return to the west?
Give them good news to cherish."
This is what it means.
The way things find each other
is truly subtle.
11.16 Shū Xiàng's younger brother Yáng Shé Hǔ was friendly with Lè Dá.
Lè Dá committed a crime in Jìn.
Jìn executed Yáng Shé Hǔ,
and Shū Xiàng was made a slave.
Shortly after, Qí Xī said:
"I have heard that when a petty person gains a position
and does not contest what is unrighteous,
it is a worry for the superior man;
and not saving what is auspicious is a misfortune."
He then went to see Fàn Xuān Zǐ and persuaded him,
saying:
"I have heard that those who are good at governing a state are such that rewards do not exceed merit and punishments are not indiscriminate.
If rewards exceed merit, there is fear they will reach the depraved;
if punishments are indiscriminate, there is fear they will reach the superior man.
Rather than being unfortunately excessive,
it is better to be excessive in rewarding the depraved
than to be excessive in punishing the superior man.
Therefore, in the punishments of Yáo,
he executed Gǔn at Yǔ Shān but used Yǔ;
in the punishments of Zhōu,
they executed Guǎn and Cài but used Zhōu Gōng as Chancellor;
this is not punishing indiscriminately."
Xuān Zǐ then ordered the officials to release Shū Xiàng.
When one saves others from trouble,
even if they perform dangerous and bitter deeds without avoiding trouble or humiliation,
they still might not succeed.
Now Qí Xī discussed the virtue of the former kings,
and Shū Xiàng was able to be spared.
How could learning ever be stopped!
11.17 Zhāng Lù, a gatekeeper, went to see Mèng Cháng Jūn and said:
"That clothes remain new and not old,
and that granaries remain full and not empty—
there is a way to achieve this.
Do you, My Lord, also know it?"
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"For clothes to be new and not old,
that is because they are repaired.
For granaries to be full and not empty,
that is because of wealth.
How should one go about it?
May I hear your explanation of it?"
Zhāng Lù said:
"I wish that when My Lord is noble, you promote the worthy,
and when you are wealthy, you relieve the poor.
If it is like this, then clothes will be new and not old,
and granaries will be full and not empty."
Mèng Cháng Jūn considered his words to be correct,
was pleased with his intent,
and admired his eloquence.
The next day, he sent someone to offer one hundred pounds of gold
and one hundred bolts of patterned silk
to present them to Zhāng Xiānsheng.
Zhāng Xiānsheng declined and did not accept them.
Later, Zhāng Xiānsheng went to see Mèng Cháng Jūn again.
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"Previously, Zhāng Xiānsheng favored Wén with his teaching, saying:
'Clothes are new and not old,
and granaries are full and not empty.
There is an explanation for this.
Do you also know it?'
Wén privately delighted in your teaching,
therefore I sent someone to offer one hundred pounds of gold
and one hundred bolts of patterned silk
to present to Zhāng Xiānsheng,
in order to assist those who are not well-off within your gate.
Why did Zhāng Xiānsheng decline and not accept them?"
Zhāng Lù said:
"If My Lord were to dig up your stockpiled coins
and open your granaries of grain to support scholars,
then your clothes would be tattered, your shoes worn through, and you would be insufficient.
What leisure would you have for clothes to be new and not old,
or granaries to be full and not empty?"
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"Then how should one go about it?"
Zhāng Lù said:
"As for Qín,
it is a land blocked on four sides,
where wandering officials cannot enter.
I wish for My Lord to write a short letter for me
to introduce me to the Qín Wáng.
If I go and meet with favor,
it will surely be a gain for My Lord.
If I go and do not meet with favor,
even if someone were seeking a spy or a strategist,
they certainly would not encounter me."
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"I respectfully receive your command."
Thereupon he wrote a letter for him
and sent it to the Qín Wáng.
He went and met with great favor,
and said to the Qín Wáng:
"Since I, Lù, came into Your Majesty’s territory,
the fields have become increasingly cultivated
and the officials and people increasingly well-governed.
However, Your Majesty has one thing that you have not obtained.
Does Your Majesty know what it is?"
The Qín Wáng said:
"I do not know."
He said:
"In Shāndōng there is a chancellor,
the one called Mèng Cháng Jūn.
That man is a worthy person.
If the world has no emergencies, then that is one thing;
but if there is an emergency, he can gather the world's eminent talents and heroic men.
Among those who form alliances and connect friendships with him,
he is likely the only one.
Therefore, why does Your Majesty not become friends with him for my sake?"
The Qín Wáng said:
"I respectfully receive your command."
He offered a thousand pounds of gold to present to Mèng Cháng Jūn.
Mèng Cháng Jūn stopped eating to examine it and realized, saying:
"This is what Zhāng Shēng meant by clothes being new and not old,
and granaries being full and not empty."
11.18 Zhuāng Zhōu was poor
and went to borrow grain from Wèi Wén Hóu.
Wèi Wén Hóu said:
"Wait until the grain from my fief arrives, and then I will give it to you."
Zhōu said:
"Just now as I, Zhōu, was coming,
I saw a goby fish in a wagon rut by the roadside.
It sighed deeply and said to me:
'Can I still live?'
I said:
'Wait for me to go south for you to see the Chǔ Wáng,
and I will divert the Jiāng and Huái rivers to irrigate you.'
The goby said:
'Right now my life is only as if in a tub or a jar.
If you must go see the Chǔ Wáng for me
to divert the Jiāng and Huái rivers to irrigate me,
you might as well look for me in a dried fish shop.'
Now because I, Zhōu, am poor I have come to borrow grain,
and you say wait for the grain from your fief to arrive and then bestow it upon me;
when it comes, you might as well look for me in a shop of hired laborers."
Wèi Wén Hóu then distributed a hundred zhōng of grain
and sent it to Zhuāng Zhōu's house.
11.19 Jìn Píng Gōng asked Shǔ Xiàng:
"In a year of famine the people suffer from pestilence,
and the Dí people attack us.
What shall I do?"
He replied:
"As for a year of famine,
next year things will return to normal.
As for the pestilence,
it will stop.
As for the Dí people,
they are not worth worrying about."
Jìn Píng Gōng said:
"Is there any worry greater than these?"
He replied:
"That high ministers value their salaries and do not offer ultimate remonstrance,
that close attendants fear punishment and do not dare to speak,
and that those on the left and right seek favor from minor officials while the ruler remains unaware—
these are truly the greatest of worries."
Jìn Píng Gōng said:
"Good."
Thereupon he issued an order within the state, saying:
"If anyone wishes to remonstrate, let them do so in secret.
If those on the left or right speak of the state officials,
it is a crime."
11.20 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ attacked Táo.
There were two men who were first to scale the walls,
and they died atop the city wall.
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ wanted their bodies,
but the Táo Jūn would not give them up.
Chéng Pén Jū said to the Táo Jūn:
"Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ is going to dig up your ancestors' graves
to bargain with your common people,
saying:
'Those who leaped over the moats and scaled the city wall will be pardoned;
otherwise,
I will dig up the graves;
for those who have decayed, I will scatter their ashes,
and for those not yet decayed, I will expose their corpses.'"
The Táo Jūn was afraid
and requested to hand over the two men's corpses to make peace.
11.21 Zǐ Gòng went to see Tàizǎi Pǐ.
Tàizǎi Pǐ asked:
"What is Kǒng Zǐ like?"
He replied:
"I am not sufficient to know him."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"If you do not know him,
how can you serve him?"
He replied:
"Precisely because I do not know him,
therefore I serve him.
The Master is like a great mountain forest,
where the common people each find sufficient materials."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"Are you exaggerating the Master?"
He replied:
"The Master cannot be exaggerated.
I, Sì, am like a single basket of earth.
To use a single basket of earth to add to a great mountain
does not increase its height,
and moreover, it would be ignorance."
Tàizǎi Pǐ said:
"Then you have something you can draw from him?"
He replied:
"In the world there is a great sacrificial vessel,
and if you alone do not draw from it,
I do not know whose fault that is."
11.22 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ asked Zǐ Gòng:
"What is Kǒng Zǐ like as a person?"
Zǐ Gòng replied:
"I, Sì, cannot know him."
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ was displeased and said:
"You served Kǒng Zǐ for decades
and completed your studies before leaving him.
When I ask you,
you say:
'I cannot know him.'
Why is that?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"I, Sì, am like a thirsty person drinking from the Jiāng or the sea;
I know when I have had enough and that is all.
Kǒng Zǐ is like the Jiāng or the sea;
how could I, Sì, be sufficient to know him?"
Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Excellent
are the words of Zǐ Gòng."
11.23 Qí Jǐng Gōng said to Zǐgòng:
"Who is your teacher?"
He said:
"My teacher is Zhòngní."
Gōng said:
"Is Zhòngní worthy?"
He replied:
"He is worthy."
Gōng said:
"To what extent is he worthy?"
He replied:
"I do not know."
Gōng said:
"You know his worthiness,
yet you do not know what he is like;
is this possible?"
He replied:
"If we say that the heavens are high,
regardless of whether they are young or old, foolish or wise, all know they are high.
But as for exactly how high they are,
all say they do not know.
This is why I know Zhòngní's worthiness,
yet I do not know what he is like."
11.24 Zhào Xiāngzǐ said to Zhòngní:
"Xiānsheng, you have offered your services to meet with rulers,
seventy of them,
yet you have not had success anywhere.
Do you not realize that either the world has no enlightened rulers,
or perhaps your Way is inherently unsuccessful?"
Zhòngní did not reply.
On another day,
Xiāngzǐ saw Zǐlù and said:
"I once asked the Xiānsheng about the Way,
but the Xiānsheng did not reply.
To know but not reply is to be secretive;
if one is secretive, how can one be considered benevolent?
If he truly does not know,
how can he be considered a sage?"
Zǐlù said:
"If you set up the resonant bell of the world and strike it with a small stick,
how can it produce its sound!
When you questioned the Xiānsheng,
was it not like striking with a stick?"
11.25 Wèi Jiāngjūn Wénzǐ asked Zǐgòng:
"Jì Wénzǐ met with failure three times and success three times;
why is that?"
Zǐgòng said:
"In failure, he served the worthy;
in success, he promoted those in hardship;
in wealth, he shared with the poor;
in high status, he was courteous to the lowly.
Serving the worthy in failure leads to not being insulted;
promoting those in hardship in success shows loyalty to friends;
sharing wealth with the poor when rich makes one's clan close to them;
being courteous to the lowly in high status makes the common people support them.
His gains were naturally due to the Way;
his losses were due to fate."
He said:
"As for those who lose and do not gain back,
why is that?"
He said:
"In failure, they do not serve the worthy;
in success, they do not promote those in hardship;
in wealth, they do not share with the poor;
in high status, they are not courteous to the lowly.
Their gains are due to fate;
their losses are naturally due to the Way."
11.26 Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ:
"What kind of person was Guǎn Zhòng?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A great man."
Zǐlù said:
"In the past, Guǎnzi tried to persuade Xiāng Gōng,
but Xiāng Gōng was not pleased;
this shows he was not eloquent.
He wished to establish Gōngzǐ Jiǔ but could not;
this shows he was without ability.
His family was ruined in Qí, yet he had no look of worry;
this shows he was not compassionate.
He was shackled and sat in a cage-cart without a look of shame;
this shows he was without a sense of disgrace.
He served the ruler he had once shot at;
this shows he was not faithful.
Zhào Hū died for him,
but Guǎn Zhòng did not;
this shows he was without benevolence.
Why does the Fūzǐ consider him great?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Guǎn Zhòng tried to persuade Xiāng Gōng,
and Xiāng Gōng was not pleased;
it was not that Guǎnzi was not eloquent,
but that Xiāng Gōng did not know how to be persuaded.
He wished to establish Gōngzǐ Jiǔ but could not;
it was not that he was without ability,
but that he did not meet the right time.
His family was ruined in Qí, yet he had no look of worry;
it was not that he was not compassionate,
but that he knew fate.
He was shackled and sat in a cage-cart without a look of shame;
it was not that he was without a sense of disgrace,
but that he was taking his own measure.
Serving the ruler he had shot at
was not a lack of faithfulness,
but knowing how to weigh circumstances.
Zhào Hū died for him,
and Guǎn Zhòng did not;
it was not that he was without benevolence,
but that he weighed the importance of things.
As for Zhào Hū,
he was a man of the caliber of a servant;
if he had not died, he would have been a prisoner of the three armies;
by dying for him,
his name was heard throughout the world;
why then should he not have died?
Guǎnzi
was an assistant to the Tiānzǐ
and a minister to the Zhūhóu;
if he had died, he would not have escaped being a corpse in a ditch;
by not dying, his merits were once again used for the world;
why then should he have died?
Yóu,
you do not understand."
11.27 Jìn Píng Gōng asked Shī Kuàng:
"Between Jiù Fàn and Zhào Shuāi, who is worthier?"
He replied:
"Yáng Chǔfù wished to serve Wén Gōng;
through Jiù Fàn, three years passed without him being presented;
through Zhào Shuāi, he was presented in three days.
To have the wisdom but not recognize scholars among the multitude
is to be unwise.
To know them but not speak of them
is to be disloyal.
To wish to speak but not dare to
is to have no courage.
To speak but not be listened to
means one is not worthy."
11.28 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Chéng Tuán:
"I have heard that Yáng Zhí was a worthy Dàfū;
how was his conduct?"
He replied:
"I, Tuán, do not know."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I have heard
that you are close with him as a friend;
yet you do not know,
why is that?"
Tuán said:
"In his character, he changes frequently.
When he was fifteen,
he was upright and did not hide his faults.
At twenty,
he was benevolent and delighted in righteousness.
At thirty,
he served as the Jìn Zhōngjūnwèi;
he was courageous and delighted in benevolence.
When he was fifty,
he was a Jiāngjūn of the border cities;
those far away returned to be close to him.
Now I have not seen him for five years;
I fear he has changed,
and therefore I dare not say I know him."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"He is indeed a worthy Dàfū,
for with every change he rises higher."
12.1 In the phrasing of the Chūnqiū,
there are four contradictions.
It already says that a dàfū has no authority to act on his own initiative
and is not permitted to take it upon himself to initiate matters;
yet it also says that if leaving the border can bring peace to the Shèjì and benefit the country,
then acting on one's own initiative is permissible.
It says that when a dàfū departs on the Wáng's command,
advancing and retreating are up to the dàfū;
yet it also says that when departing on the Wáng's command,
if one hears of a mourning ritual, one should walk slowly and not return.
Why is this?
It is said:
These principles each remain within their own categories
and do not shift.
Not being permitted to take it upon oneself to initiate matters
refers to the constant norms of ordinary life;
that acting on one's own initiative is permissible
refers to rescuing from danger and removing calamities.
That advancing and retreating are up to the dàfū
refers to a jiàngshuài employing troops;
walking slowly and not returning
refers to an envoy hearing of the mourning of his Wáng or parents while on the road.
Gōngzǐ Jié took it upon himself to initiate a matter,
and the Chūnqiū does not criticize him,
because it considered it a rescue of Zhuāng Gōng from danger;
Gōngzǐ Suì took it upon himself to initiate a matter,
and the Chūnqiū ridicules him,
because it considered that Xī Gōng had no dangerous matters.
Therefore, if the Wáng is in danger and one does not act on one's own initiative to save him,
that is disloyalty;
if there is no danger and one takes it upon oneself to initiate matters,
that is failing to be a subject.
The Zhuàn says:
"The Shī has no universal interpretation,
the Yì has no universal auspiciousness,
and the Chūnqiū has no universal principle."
This is what is meant.
12.2 The Zhào Wáng sent an envoy to Chǔ.
He was playing the sè when he sent him off
and cautioned him, saying:
"You must do exactly as I say."
The envoy said:
"When the Wáng plays the sè,
it has never been as sad as this."
The Wáng said:
"The Gōng and Shāng notes were just being tuned."
The envoy said:
"If they are tuned, why not mark the bridges?"
The Wáng said:
"Heaven has dryness and moisture,
and strings have slackness and tension;
the shifting of Gōng and Shāng cannot be known,
therefore they are not marked."
The envoy said:
"When an enlightened ruler employs people,
he entrusts them with tasks
but does not restrict them with words.
If they encounter good fortune, they congratulate them;
if misfortune, they console them.
Now Chǔ and Zhào are more than a thousand lǐ apart;
good fortune, misfortune, worries, and calamities
cannot be known in advance,
just as the bridges cannot be marked."
The Shī says:
"Crowded are the traveling men,
always fearing they will not arrive in time."
12.3 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng raised troops to attack Sòng.
Sòng reported the emergency to Jìn.
Jìn Jǐng Gōng wanted to dispatch troops to save Sòng,
but Bó Zōng remonstrated, saying:
"Heaven is just now favoring Chǔ;
they cannot be attacked yet."
So they sought a brave man
and found a man of Huò named Xiè Yáng,
whose courtesy name was Zǐhǔ,
to go and command Sòng not to surrender.
On his way, he passed through Zhèng.
Zhèng had recently become close with Chǔ,
so they seized Xiè Yáng and presented him to Chǔ.
The Chǔ Wáng gave him generous gifts and made a pact with him,
asking him to reverse his words
and order Sòng to surrender quickly.
Xiè Yáng did not agree.
After being pressured three times,
Xiè Yáng finally agreed.
Thereupon, Chǔ placed Xiè Yáng upon a tower-chariot
and ordered him to shout to Sòng to make them surrender.
He then went back on his pact with Chǔ
and delivered his Jìn ruler's command, saying:
"Jìn is just now mobilizing all the state's troops to save Sòng.
Although Sòng is in an emergency,
be careful not to surrender to Chǔ.
The Jìn troops are arriving now."
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng was greatly enraged
and was about to boil him alive.
Xiè Yáng said:
"A ruler can establish a command to define righteousness,
and a subject can uphold a command to define trustworthiness.
I received my ruler's command to go out;
even unto death, I shall not be of two minds."
The Wáng said:
"You agreed to my request
and then went back on it;
where is your trustworthiness?"
Xiè Yáng said:
"I used my death to agree to the Wáng's request
so that I might fulfill my ruler's command;
I, your subject, have no regrets."
He looked back and said to the Chǔ army:
"As a subject, one should not forget to be fully loyal even if it means death."
The Chǔ Wáng's younger brothers all remonstrated with the Wáng to pardon him.
Thereupon, Zhuāng Wáng ultimately pardoned Xiè Yáng and sent him back.
Jìn granted him the rank of shàngqīng.
Therefore, later generations speak of Huò Hǔ.
12.4 The Qín Wáng wished to exchange five hundred lǐ of land for Yānlíng.
Yānlíng Jūn declined and would not accept.
He sent Táng Jū to apologize to the Qín Wáng.
The Qín Wáng said:
"Qín has broken Hán and destroyed Wèi;
that Yānlíng Jūn alone survives with fifty lǐ of land,
is it because I fear his power?
I simply respect his righteousness.
Now I wish to exchange it for ten times the land,
yet Yānlíng Jūn declines and will not accept;
this is to slight me."
Táng Jū left his mat and replied:
"It is not like that.
Indeed, one who does not take profit or harm as their goal is Yānlíng.
Yānlíng Jūn received the land from the xiānjūn and guards it;
even if it were a thousand lǐ, he would not deem it a fair exchange,
how much less five hundred lǐ?"
The Qín Wáng's face flushed with anger
and he said furiously:
"Have you, sir, ever seen the wrath of the Tiānzǐ?"
Táng Jū said:
"I have not yet seen it."
The Qín Wáng said:
"When the Tiānzǐ is enraged,
a million corpses lie prostrate,
and blood flows for a thousand lǐ."
Táng Jū said:
"Has the Dàwáng ever seen the wrath of a scholar in simple clothes and a leather belt?"
The Qín Wáng said:
"When a scholar in simple clothes and a leather belt is enraged,
he removes his cap and goes barefoot,
and strikes his head against the ground;
what is so difficult to understand about that?"
Táng Jū said:
"That is the wrath of a foolish commoner,
not the wrath of a scholar in simple clothes and a leather belt.
When Zhuān Zhū assassinated Wáng Liáo,
a comet attacked the moon
and a falling star appeared by day.
When Yào Lí assassinated Wángzǐ Qìngjì,
a blue hawk struck upon the terrace.
When Niè Zhèng assassinated the younger uncle of the Hán Wáng,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
These three men were all scholars in simple clothes and leather belts who were enraged;
with me, there will be four.
When a scholar harbors wrath that has not yet broken out,
ominous omens appear in the heavens.
If a scholar has no wrath, that is that;
but if he is once enraged,
two corpses will lie prostrate,
and blood will flow for five paces."
He then grasped his dagger and stood up,
looking at the Qín Wáng and saying:
"Now is that time!"
The Qín Wáng's expression changed, and he knelt tall and said:
"Please be seated, sir.
I understand.
That Qín broke Hán and destroyed Wèi,
yet Yānlíng alone survives with fifty lǐ of land,
is solely because of you, sir."
12.5 Qí attacked Lǔ.
Zǐgòng met with Āi Gōng
and requested to seek help from Wú.
The Gōng said:
"How can we use the treasures of the former rulers?"
Zǐgòng said:
"If we let Wú demand our treasures before granting us an army,
then they cannot be relied upon."
Thereupon, he took six bows of Yánggàn hemp-sinew and went.
Zǐgòng said to the King of Wú:
"Qí is acting without the Way;
they wish to ensure that the descendants of Zhōu Gōng no longer receive blood sacrifices.
Furthermore, Lǔ provides a levy of five hundred,
and Zhū provides a levy of three hundred.
I do not know if adding these to Qí
would be to Wú's advantage or not?"
The King of Wú was afraid
and thus raised an army to save Lǔ.
The feudal lords said:
"Qí attacked the descendants of Zhōu Gōng,
and Wú saved them."
Consequently, they paid court to Wú.
12.6 Wèi Wén Hóu enfeoffed Crown Prince Jī in Zhōngshān.
For three years, he allowed no communication.
The retainer Zhào Cāngtáng stepped forward and said:
"For one who is a son not to hear from his father for three years
cannot be called filial;
for one who is a father not to ask about his son for three years
cannot be called kind.
Why does my Lord not send someone as an envoy to the great state?"
The Crown Prince said:
"I have desired this for a long time,
but have not found anyone suitable to send."
Cāngtáng said:
"I wish to serve as the envoy.
What does the Hóu enjoy?"
The Crown Prince said:
"The Hóu is fond of morning ducks
and likes northern dogs."
Thereupon, he sent Cāngtáng leading northern dogs
and carrying morning ducks
to present them to Wén Hóu.
When Cāngtáng arrived,
he presented himself and said:
"The envoy of the secondary son Jī
does not dare to face the Great Officers at court.
He requests that in a moment of leisure,
he may present morning ducks
to be respectfully offered to the kitchen,
and lead northern dogs
to be respectfully presented to the palace attendants."
Wén Hóu was pleased and said:
"Jī loves me;
he knows what I enjoy
and what I like."
He summoned Cāngtáng and granted him an audience, saying:
"Is Jī without illness?"
Cāngtáng said:
"Yes,
yes."
Having done this three times,
he then said:
"The Lord sent the Crown Prince out to be enfeoffed with a state,
and yet the Lord calls him by name;
this is not in accordance with ritual."
Wén Hóu was startled and his expression changed;
he asked:
"Is your Lord without illness?"
Cāngtáng said:
"When I left,
he bowed and delivered his letter in the courtyard."
Wén Hóu looked and pointed at his attendants, saying:
"Compared to these,
how tall has your Lord grown?"
Cāngtáng said:
"In ritual, one must compare a person with those of his own rank.
Since the feudal lords have no equals,
there is no one to compare him to."
He said:
"Compared to me, how tall has he grown?"
Cāngtáng said:
"If the Lord were to grant him a fur coat from the outer storehouse,
he would be able to fill it;
if you were to grant him an embroidered belt,
he would not need to change its tailoring."
Wén Hóu said:
"In what studies does your Lord engage?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He studies the Shī."
Wén Hóu said:
"In the Shī, what does he like?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He likes 'Chén Fēng' and 'Shǔ Lí'."
Wén Hóu read 'Chén Fēng' himself, saying:
"Swiftly flies that morning falcon,
dense is that northern forest.
Not yet having seen my lord,
my worried heart is full of agitation.
How is it, how is it?
He has truly forgotten me much."
Wén Hóu said:
"Does your Lord think that I have forgotten him?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He does not dare;
he only thinks of you from time to time."
Wén Hóu then read 'Shǔ Lí', saying:
"There the millet is drooping,
there the panicum is sprouting.
Walking along with slow steps,
my heart is agitated within.
Those who know me
say my heart is sorrowful;
those who do not know me
say I am seeking something.
O distant azure Heaven,
what kind of man is this!"
Wén Hóu said:
"Does your Lord
feel resentment?"
Cāngtáng said:
"He does not dare;
he only thinks of you from time to time."
Thereupon, Wén Hóu sent Cāngtáng to present the Crown Prince with a set of robes,
and ordered Cāngtáng to arrive at the time of the cock's crow.
The Crown Prince arose and bowed to receive the gift.
Upon opening the chest and looking at the robes, they were all upside down.
The Crown Prince said:
"Hurry and prepare the carriage;
the Lord Hóu is summoning me."
Cāngtáng said:
"When I came, I received no such command."
The Crown Prince said:
"The Lord Hóu granted me clothes,
not because he thought I was cold.
He wishes to summon me,
but had no one to consult with,
so he sent you with the clothes
and ordered you to arrive at the time of the cock's crow.
The Shī says:
'Before the east is bright,
he puts on his clothes upside down.
Upside down he puts them on,
for the Lord is summoning him.' "
He then went west,
arrived,
and requested an audience with Wén Hóu.
Wén Hóu was greatly pleased
and held a banquet, declaring:
"To keep the worthy at a distance and the beloved close
is not a long-term strategy for the state."
He then sent out his younger son Zhì
to be enfeoffed in Zhōngshān
and restored Crown Prince Jī.
Therefore it is said:
If you wish to know the son,
look at his friends;
if you wish to know the ruler,
look at his envoys.
With one mission from Zhào Cāngtáng,
Wén Hóu became a kind father
and Jī became a filial son.
The Crown Prince then quoted the Shī, saying:
"The phoenixes fly,
their wings rustling.
They settle and rest there.
Numerous are the King's many lucky officers,
to be employed by the Lord,
to be loved by the Son of Heaven."
This refers to retainers.
12.7 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng wanted to attack Jìn
and sent Tún Yǐn to observe them.
Upon returning, he said:
"They cannot be attacked.
Their worries are with those above
and their joy is with those below.
Furthermore, a worthy minister is there,
named Shěn Jū."
The following year,
he again sent Tún Yǐn to observe them.
Upon returning, he said:
"They can be attacked now.
The former worthy man is dead,
and many flatterers are in the Lord's chambers.
The Lord loves music and lacks ritual,
and those below live in danger and resent those above.
Superiors and inferiors are divided in heart.
If we raise an army to attack them,
their people will surely rebel first."
Zhuāng Wáng followed his advice,
and it turned out exactly as he had said.
12.8 The Liáng Wáng gathered his ministers to discuss his faults.
Rèn Zuò came forward to advise him, saying:
"The Zhǔjūn’s state is broad and large,
the people are resilient and numerous,
yet how is it that there are no worthy men or eloquent scholars within the state?"
The Wáng said:
"My state is small and narrow,
the people are weak and the ministers are few.
Since I govern it alone,
for what purpose would I use worthy men or eloquent scholars?"
Rèn Zuò said:
"That is not so.
Formerly, Qí raised troops without cause to attack Lǔ.
The Lǔ Jūn was distressed by this
and summoned his Xiàng, saying:
'What should be done about this?'
The Xiàng replied:
'Liǔ Xià Huì was fond of learning in his youth
and as an adult possesses excellent wisdom.
The Zhǔjūn should try summoning him and sending him as an envoy to Qí.'
The Lǔ Jūn said:
'I am a master of a thousand chariots;
if I personally went as an envoy to Qí
and Qí did not listen,
then Liǔ Xià Huì is merely a scholar in hempen clothes and a leather belt.
What benefit would there be in sending him?'
The Xiàng replied:
'I have heard that
if one seeks fire and does not get it,
one does not expect to roast food.
Now, if you send Liǔ Xià Huì to Qí,
even if he does not disperse the Qí troops,
they certainly will not increase their attack on Lǔ.'
The Lǔ Jūn then said:
'Is that so!'
The Xiàng immediately sent someone to summon Liǔ Xià Huì.
When he arrived,
he entered the gate lifting his robes without rushing.
The Lǔ Jūn rose from his mat and said:
'I am like one who seeks grain only when hungry,
or who digs a well only when thirsty;
I have never been able to see you with joy before.
Now the affairs of the state are urgent
and the common people are terrified.
I wish to rely on you, Dàfū, to serve as an envoy to Qí.'
Liǔ Xià Huì said:
'Very well.'
He then went east to see the Qí Hóu.
The Qí Hóu said:
'Is the Lǔ Jūn afraid?'
Liǔ Xià Huì said:
'My Jūn is not afraid.'
The Qí Hóu said indignantly and with anger:
'I look at your Lǔ city from afar;
it is in such a daze as if it were a lost or ruined state.
The common people are tearing down houses and cutting down trees to save the city walls.
I see the Lǔ Jūn as if he were part of my state.
You say he is not afraid—
why?'
Liǔ Xià Huì said:
'The reason my Jūn is not afraid
is that his ancestors came out of Zhōu
and were enfeoffed in Lǔ,
and your predecessor Jūn also came out of Zhōu
and was enfeoffed in Qí.
They came out of the Zhōu Nán Mén together,
slaughtered a sheep, and made an oath, saying:
"From now on, if any descendants dare to attack one another,
let their crime be like this slaughtered sheep!"
My Jūn certainly remains unafraid because of the slaughtered sheep.
Otherwise,
it is not that the common people are not in an urgent situation.'
The Qí Hóu then withdrew his troops three hundred lǐ.
Liǔ Xià Huì was merely a scholar in hempen clothes and a leather belt,
yet he went so far as to resolve the crisis of Qí and liberate Lǔ.
How can one do without worthy scholars and sages?"
12.9 Lù Jiǎ followed Gāo Zǔ in pacifying the world.
He was known as an eloquent scholar
and stayed by the Emperor's side,
often serving as an envoy to the feudal lords.
During the time of Gāo Zǔ,
when the Central Kingdom was first settled,
Wèi Tuó had pacified Nán Yuè
and consequently ruled as its Wáng.
Gāo Zǔ sent Lù Jiǎ to bestow upon Wèi Tuó the seal of the Nán Yuè Wáng.
When Lù Shēng arrived,
Wèi Tuó received Lù Shēng with his hair in a mallet-shaped bun and squatting like a winnowing basket.
Lù Shēng then persuaded Tuó, saying:
"You are a man of the Central Kingdom,
and your relatives, brothers, and ancestral graves are in Zhēndìng.
Now you have abandoned and turned against your natural character,
cast aside the cap and belt,
and wish to use the tiny region of Yuè to contend with the Tiānzǐ as a rival state;
disaster is about to reach your person!
Moreover, when Qín lost its proper governance,
the feudal lords and heroes rose up together.
Only the Hàn Wáng was the first to enter the Pass
and occupy Xiányáng.
Xiàng Jí broke the agreement
and established himself as the Xī Chǔ Bàwáng.
All the feudal lords were subordinate to him;
he could be called supremely strong.
However, the Hàn Wáng rose from Bā and Shǔ,
whipped the world into submission,
coerced and plundered the feudal lords,
and finally executed Xiàng Yǔ and destroyed him.
Within five years,
the world within the seas was pacified and settled.
This was not by human effort alone,
but was established by Heaven.
The Tiānzǐ heard that you, Great King, are the Wáng of Nán Yuè
and did not assist the world in punishing the violent and rebellious.
The generals and Xiàng wished to move troops to execute the Wáng,
but the Tiānzǐ pitied the common people for their recent toil and suffering
and wished to let them rest.
Thus he sent me to bestow the Wáng’s seal upon you
and to split the tallies for diplomatic exchange.
The Wáng should have welcomed me in the suburbs
and faced north to declare yourself a subject;
yet you wish to use the newly created and unsettled Yuè
to be stubborn and unyielding here.
If Hàn truly hears of this,
they will dig up and burn the Wáng’s ancestors' graves,
exterminate your clan and lineage,
and send a single lieutenant general with a hundred thousand troops to descend upon Yuè.
Then Yuè will kill the Wáng to surrender to Hàn,
as easily as turning over one's hand."
Thereupon, Wèi Tuó sprang up into a sitting position,
apologized to Lù Shēng, and said:
"I have lived among the barbarians for a long time
and have completely lost my sense of ritual and righteousness."
He then asked Lù Shēng:
"Who among me, Xiāo Hé, Cáo Cān, and Hán Xìn is the most worthy?"
Lù Shēng said:
"The Wáng seems worthy."
He asked again:
"Who between me and the Huángdì is more worthy?"
Lù Shēng said:
"The Huángdì rose from Fēng and Pèi,
attacked the violent Qín,
executed the powerful Chǔ,
promoted benefits and removed harms for the world,
continued the legacy of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
and governs the Central Kingdom.
The people of the Central Kingdom are counted by the hundreds of millions,
the territory is ten thousand lǐ,
it occupies the richest land in the world,
the people and carriages are numerous,
and all things are abundant and wealthy.
Governance comes from a single family;
since the heavens and earth were first divided,
there has never been anything like it.
Now, the Wáng's followers do not exceed several hundred thousand,
and they are all barbarians,
cramped between the mountains and the sea.
You are like a single commandery of Hàn;
how could you be compared to the Hàn Wáng!"
Wèi Tuó laughed heartily and said:
"I did not rise in the Central Kingdom,
so I am king here.
If I were to live in the Central Kingdom,
how would I necessarily be inferior to Hàn?"
He was then greatly pleased with Lù Shēng
and kept him to drink for several months.
He said:
"In Yuè, there is no one worth speaking with;
until you arrived,
I did not hear what I have heard daily now."
He gave Lù Shēng gifts in his travel bag worth a thousand pieces of gold,
and Tuó's parting gift was also a thousand gold pieces.
Lù Shēng ultimately formally appointed Wèi Tuó as the Nán Yuè Wáng,
ordering him to declare himself a subject and uphold the Hàn covenant.
Upon returning and reporting,
Gāo Zǔ was greatly pleased
and appointed Lù Jiǎ as a Tàizhōng Dàfū.
12.10 The Jūn of Jìn and Chǔ held a friendly meeting together at Wǎn Qiū.
Sòng sent an envoy to go there.
The Dàfū of Jìn and Chǔ said:
"Hurry and use the ceremony for meeting the Tiānzǐ to meet our Jūn,
then we shall let you see them."
The envoy said:
"Though a cap be worn out,
it should be placed on top;
though shoes be new,
they should remain below.
Though the Zhōu house is weak,
the feudal lords have not been able to replace it.
Even if an army were to scale the walls of Sòng,
I still would not change my official robes."
He bowed and left.
The Dàfū were startled
and consequently used the ceremony for meeting feudal lords to receive him.
12.11 Yuè sent Zhū Fā to present a single plum branch to Liáng Wáng.
A minister of Liáng Wáng named Hán Zǐ
looked at those around him and said:
“How can one present a single plum branch to the ruler of a great state!
Please let me make him feel ashamed for the sake of you all.”
He went out and said to Zhū Fā:
“The Great King has ordered that
if the guest wears a cap, he shall be seen according to the rites;
if he does not wear a cap, then he shall not.”
Zhū Fā said:
“That Yuè was also a fief of the Tiānzǐ,
but we did not obtain the provinces of Jì and Yǎn;
instead, we reside on the edge of the sea,
living as a frontier defense.
There, dragons and serpents contend with us,
and for this reason, we cut our hair and tattoo our bodies,
creating bright patterns
to resemble the sons of dragons
in order to avoid the water spirits.
Now the Great State has issued an order
that if one wears a cap, one is seen with ritual,
and if not, one is not seen.
Suppose an envoy from your Great State
were to pass by my humble town,
and the ruler of my humble town
also issued an order saying:
‘The guest must cut his hair and tattoo his body
before he may be seen.’
How would your Great State feel about that?
If you would be at peace with it,
I would wish to borrow a cap to see him;
if you would not be at peace with it,
I wish that you would not change the customs of our state.”
When Liáng Wáng heard this,
he threw on his clothes and came out to see Zhū Fā,
and ordered that Hán Zǐ be driven away.
The Shī says:
“As the emissary of a superior man,
he is beloved by the Tiānzǐ.”
This is what it refers to.
12.12 Yàn Zǐ went as an envoy to Wú.
Wú Wáng said to the protocol officer:
“I have heard that Yàn Yīng is a person from the north who is eloquent in speech and well-versed in ritual.”
He ordered the usher that when the guest appeared, he should announce that the Tiānzǐ requested an audience.
The next day,
when Yàn Zǐ had business to attend to,
the protocol officer said:
“The Tiānzǐ requests an audience.”
Yàn Zǐ appeared troubled three times
and said:
“I, your servant, received orders from the ruler of my humble town
to serve as an envoy to the place of Wú Wáng.
I am unworthy and have become confused, entering the court of the Tiānzǐ.
May I ask where Wú Wáng is?”
Only then did Wú Wáng say:
“Fū Chāi requests an audience.”
He received him with the rituals of the feudal lords.
12.13 Yàn Zǐ went as an envoy to Wú.
Wú Wáng said:
“I find myself residing in a remote and crude land of barbarians,
and rarely see instructions on the conduct of a superior man.
I request a private word, and let there be no offense taken.”
Yàn Zǐ looked uneasy and moved from his seat.
Wú Wáng said:
“I have heard that the ruler of Qí is cruel and negligent,
rustic and violent.
You, sir, tolerate him;
why is it so extreme?”
Yàn Zǐ withdrew slightly and replied:
“I have heard that
those who cannot understand subtle matters
and cannot perform coarse matters
will surely be exhausted;
those who cannot attain great matters
and will not perform small matters
will surely be poor;
those who on a large scale cannot attract people
and on a small scale cannot go to another’s door
will surely be in distress.
This is the reason why I serve in office.
For someone like me,
how could I be one who uses the Dào to feed others?”
When Yàn Zǐ left,
the King laughed and said:
“Today I mocked Yàn Zǐ,
but it was like a naked man criticizing someone wearing high wooden clogs.”
12.14 Jǐng Gōng sent Yàn Zǐ as an envoy to Chǔ.
Chǔ Wáng presented oranges
and set out a paring knife.
Yàn Zǐ did not peel them but ate them whole.
Chǔ Wáng said:
“Oranges should be peeled.”
Yàn Zǐ replied:
“I have heard that
when a ruler bestows something before one,
melons and peaches are not pared,
and oranges and pomelos are not peeled.
Today, the ruler of ten thousand chariots has given no instruction,
so I did not dare to peel them,
yet it is not that I do not know how.”
12.15 Yàn Zǐ was about to go as an envoy to Jīng.
Jīng Wáng heard of it
and said to those around him:
“Yàn Zǐ
is a worthy man.
Now that he is coming,
I wish to humiliate him;
how shall I do it?”
Those around him replied:
“When he comes,
we ask to bind a man
and walk past the King.
The King shall say:
‘What has he done?’
We will reply:
‘He is a man of Qí.’
The King shall say:
‘What is his crime?’
We will say:
‘The crime of theft.’”
Thereupon, while Jīng Wáng and Yàn Zǐ were standing and talking,
someone bound a man and walked past the King.
The King said:
“What has he done?”
The reply was:
“He is a man of Qí.”
The King said:
“What is his crime?”
The reply was:
“The crime of theft.”
The King looked at Yàn Zǐ and said:
“Are the people of Qí naturally good at stealing?”
Yàn Zǐ looked back and said:
“I, Yīng, have heard that
south of the Jiāng there are oranges;
the King of Qí sent people to take them and plant them north of the Jiāng,
but they grew up to be not oranges but trifoliate oranges.
Why is this so?
It is the soil that makes them so.
Now, the people of Qí live in Qí and do not steal,
but when they come to Jīng they steal;
could it be the soil that makes them so?”
Jīng Wáng said:
“I wished to humiliate you,
but instead I have struck myself.”
12.16 Yàn Zǐ went as an envoy to Chǔ.
Yàn Zǐ was short,
so the people of Chǔ made a small gate at the side of the great gate and invited Yàn Zǐ to enter.
Yàn Zǐ would not enter
and said:
“An envoy to a country of dogs
enters through a dog gate.
Now I am an envoy to Chǔ;
I should not enter through this gate.”
The usher changed the route to enter through the great gate,
and he saw Chǔ Wáng.
The King said:
“Is there no one in Qí?
That they made you the envoy.”
Yàn Zǐ replied:
“Lín Zī of Qí has three hundred neighborhoods;
if people spread their sleeves, they make a canopy;
if they wipe their sweat, it makes a rain;
they stand shoulder to shoulder and heel to toe.
How can you say there is no one?”
The King said:
“Then why did they make you the envoy?”
Yàn Zǐ replied:
“In Qí’s appointments of envoys, each has its specific target:
the worthy are sent to worthy rulers,
and the unworthy are sent to unworthy rulers.
I, Yīng, am the most unworthy of all,
so it is appropriate that I am sent to Chǔ.”
12.17 Qín and Chǔ clashed in battle.
The King of Qín sent a messenger to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ sent someone to mock him, saying:
"Did you also divine this before coming?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"What did the divination say?"
He replied:
"Auspicious."
The man of Chǔ said:
"Alas,
how extreme!
Your state lacks good tortoises.
Our King is about to kill you to smear your blood on a bell;
how is that auspicious?"
The messenger said:
"Qín and Chǔ are clashing in battle.
My King sent me to scout ahead first.
If I die and do not return,
then my King will know to be on alert
and will organize the troops to prepare against Chǔ.
This is what I call auspicious.
Furthermore, if the dead have no consciousness,
then what does smearing blood on a bell matter?
If the dead have consciousness,
would I abandon Qín to help Chǔ?
I will cause the bells and drums of Chǔ to have no sound.
If the bells and drums have no sound,
then there will be no way to organize your soldiers and manage your army.
To kill another's messenger
and cut off another's plans
is not the universal practice of antiquity.
You, Great Officer, should try to consider this carefully."
The messenger reported this to the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ pardoned him.
This is called "creating fate."
12.18 Chǔ sent an envoy to pay respects to Qí.
The King of Qí entertained him at Wǔ Gōng.
The envoy said:
"How grand is this Wǔ tree!"
The King said:
"Fish from the rivers and seas must be large enough to swallow a boat;
trees of a great state must have a massive girth.
Why is the envoy surprised?"
The envoy said:
"Long ago, when Yàn attacked Qí,
they followed the Luò road,
crossed the Jì bridge,
burned the Yōng gate,
struck the left of Qí and emptied its right.
Wáng Chù snapped his neck and died at Dù Shān;
Gōng Sūn Chā was struck down and died at Lóng Mén.
They watered their horses in the Zī and Miǎn rivers
and achieved conquest at Láng Yé.
The King and the Queen Dowager fled to Jǔ
and hid in the mountains of Chéng Yáng.
At that time,
how did the size of this Wǔ tree compare?"
The King said:
"Master Chén, please respond to him."
Chén Zǐ said:
"I am not as good as Diāo Bó."
The King said:
"Master Diāo, please respond to him."
Diāo Bó said:
"Is the envoy asking about the age of the Wǔ tree?
Formerly, King Píng of Jīng acted without the Way,
inflicting cruelty upon the Shēn clan
and killing Zǐ Xū's father and his elder brother.
Zǐ Xū disheveled his hair and begged for food in Wú.
Hé Lǘ made him a general and minister.
After three years,
he led the troops of Wú to take revenge on Chǔ.
They were victorious at Bǎi Jǔ;
a million heads were taken.
Náng Wǎ fled to Zhèng,
and the King sought refuge in Suí.
They led the army into Yǐng,
and the troops moved like clouds in the capital of Yǐng.
Zǐ Xū personally shot arrows at the palace gates,
dug up King Píng's tomb,
and whipped his grave,
counting out his crimes,
saying:
'My ancestors were innocent, yet you killed them.'
Each soldier added a hundred strikes,
and only then did he stop.
At such a time,
the Wǔ tree could have been used to make his coffin lid."
12.19 Cài sent Shī Qiáng and Wáng Jiān as envoys to Chǔ.
When the King of Chǔ heard this, he said:
"Among people's names, there are many illustrious ones;
why are they specifically Shī Qiáng and Wáng Jiān?
Have them presented quickly,
without regard for order."
He looked at their appearance,
doubted their names and found their voices ugly,
and also disliked their forms.
The King of Chǔ was greatly enraged and said:
"Does Cài have no people now?
The state can be attacked.
If they have people but do not send them,
the state can be attacked.
Do they intentionally use these people to warn me?
The state can be attacked."
Thus, because of the dispatching of two envoys,
there appeared three reasons to plan an attack;
this was Cài.
12.20 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ was about to surprise Wèi.
He sent Shǐ Àn to go and observe it,
setting a limit of one month.
He returned only after six months.
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Why were you so long?"
Àn said:
"Seeking benefit yet gaining harm
comes from a lack of observation.
Now Qú Bó Yù is the Prime Minister,
Shǐ Qiú assists him,
Kǒng Zǐ is a guest,
and Zǐ Gòng executes orders before the ruler and is greatly listened to.
The Yì says:
'He disperses his group,
supreme good fortune.'
'Dispersing'
means the worthy;
'group'
means the masses;
'supreme'
is the beginning of good fortune.
'Dispersing his group brings supreme good fortune' means
his assistants are mostly worthy men."
Jiǎn Zǐ held back his troops and did not move.
12.21 Wèi Wén Hóu sent his retainer Wú Zé to present a swan to the Qí Hóu.
Wú Zé lost it on the way
and presented only an empty cage.
He saw the Qí Hóu and said:
"My ruler sent his servant Wú Zé to present a swan.
On the road it was hungry and thirsty,
so I let it out to drink and eat,
and the swan flew up to the sky
and never returned.
I thought about it, and it was not that I lacked the money to buy another swan,
but how can one serve as a messenger for his ruler
and deceitfully replace his tribute?
I thought about it, and it was not that I could not draw my sword and slit my throat,
leaving my rotting flesh and exposed bones in the open fields,
but that would make my ruler value a swan while despising a scholar.
I thought about it, and it was not that I did not dare flee to the lands between Chén and Cài,
but I hated to sever the communication between two rulers.
Therefore, I did not dare treasure my life and flee death,
but came to present an empty cage,
submitting only to your punishment by axe and block."
The Qí Hóu was greatly pleased and said:
"I have now received these three statements,
which are far more worthy than a swan.
I have a capital city
with a hundred lǐ of suburban land;
I wish to present it to you, Great Officer, as your bath-town."
Wú Zé replied:
"How can one serve as a messenger for his ruler,
deceitfully replace his tribute,
and then profit from the land of another feudal lord?"
He then departed and did not return.
13.1 When sage kings undertake an action,
they must first examine it through deliberation and planning,
and only then test it with the milfoil and tortoise.
Scholars from humble cottages
are all involved in their plans;
servants who gather grass and wood
all exhaust their minds in service.
Thus, in ten thousand actions, not a single scheme or plan is lost.
The Chuán says:
"The wisdom of the masses
can gauge the heavens;
to listen broadly but decide alone
rests only with one person."
This is the technique of grand strategy.
Strategy has two levels:
the superior strategy is knowing destiny;
the next is knowing affairs.
Those who know destiny foresee the origins of survival, ruin, misfortune, and fortune;
they know early the beginnings of prosperity, decline, failure, and rise;
they guard against matters before they sprout
and avoid difficulties while they are still formless.
A person like this,
living in a chaotic age,
will not suffer harm to their person;
living in an age of great peace,
they will surely obtain the power of the world.
Those who know affairs are also esteemed;
they see matters and know the distinction between gain, loss, success, and failure,
and they investigate their ultimate ends;
therefore, they have no ruined enterprises or wasted achievements.
Kǒngzǐ said:
