"One may be fit to walk the Way with another,
but not yet fit to exercise strategic discretion with them."
If one is not a person who knows destiny and knows affairs,
who can practice the techniques of strategic discretion?
Strategic discretion has the upright and the evil;
the strategic discretion of a Jūnzǐ is upright,
while the strategic discretion of a Xiǎorén is evil.
As for the upright,
their strategic discretion is for the public good;
therefore, their sincerity in exhausting their hearts for the common people is genuine.
As for the evil,
they love selfishness and value profit;
therefore, they are deceitful toward the common people.
Deceit leads to chaos,
while sincerity leads to peace.
For this reason, the nine ministers of Yáo were sincere and flourished at court,
while his four ministers were deceitful and were executed in the wilderness.
The sincere achieve greatness reaching to later generations;
the deceitful are destroyed within their own lifetimes.
Those who know destiny and know affairs and are capable in strategic discretion
must examine the origins of sincerity and deceit to conduct themselves;
this is also a technique of strategic discretion.
When the wise initiate affairs,
when full, they worry about overflowing;
when level, they worry about danger;
when safe, they worry about peril;
when crooked, they worry about straightness.
They place great weight on preparation
and only fear not doing enough;
thus, in a hundred actions, they do not fall.
13.2 Yáng Zǐ said:
"Matters that can be used to become poor
or can be used to become rich
are those that harm one's conduct;
matters that can be used to live
or can be used to die
are those that harm one's courage."
Pú Zǐ said:
"Yáng Zǐ was wise but did not know destiny,
therefore his knowledge was full of doubt."
The *Yǔ* says:
"One who knows destiny is not confused."
Yàn Yīng is such a person.
13.3 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"Jìn has Zé Míng and Dú Chōu,
and Lǔ has Kǒng Qiū;
if I kill these three people,
then the world can be plotted for."
Thereupon, he summoned Zé Míng and Dú Chōu,
entrusted them with the government, and then killed them.
He sent a person to invite Kǒngzǐ from Lǔ.
When Kǒngzǐ reached the Hé,
he looked at the water and said:
"How beautiful is the water!
How vast!
That Qiū shall not cross here
is destiny!"
Zǐlù hurried forward and said:
"I venture to ask, what do you mean?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Zé Míng and Dú Chōu
were worthy Grand Masters of the state of Jìn.
When Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ had not yet achieved his ambitions,
he shared his views with them;
when he achieved his ambitions,
he killed them and then took over the government.
I, Qiū, have heard:
when the womb is cut open and the young are burned, the Qílín does not come;
when marshes are drained to fish, the Jiāolóng does not swim;
when nests are overturned and eggs destroyed, the Fènghuáng does not soar.
I, Qiū, have heard:
a Jūnzǐ is distressed when those of his kind are harmed."
13.4 Kǒngzǐ was sitting with Qí Jǐng Gōng,
when those to the left and right reported:
"An envoy from Zhōu has come to say that a Zhōu ancestral temple was burned."
Qí Jǐng Gōng went out and asked:
"Which temple was it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is the temple of Lí Wáng."
Jǐng Gōng said:
"How do you know this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'Magnificent is Shàngdì,
His mandates do not err.'
In Heaven's dealings with people,
it must reward those with virtue.
Disaster is also like this.
Lí Wáng changed the systems of Wén and Wǔ,
and built palaces of black and yellow,
with carriages and horses so extravagant
they could not be sustained.
Therefore, Heaven brought disaster to his temple;
this is how I know it."
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Why did Heaven not bring disaster to his person,
but instead to his temple?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Heaven probably did so for the sake of Wén Wáng.
If it had brought disaster to his person,
then the sacrifices to Wén Wáng
would surely have been cut off.
Therefore, it brought disaster to his temple
to make his faults manifest."
Those to the left and right entered and reported:
"It was the temple of Zhōu Lí Wáng."
Jǐng Gōng was greatly astonished;
he rose, bowed twice, and said:
"Excellent!
Is the wisdom of a Sage
not indeed great?"
13.5 `Qí Huán Gōng` and `Guǎn Zhòng` planned to attack `Jǔ`, `
` but before the plan was launched, it was heard of in the capital. `
` `Huán Gōng` wondered at this `
` and asked `Guǎn Zhòng` about it. `
` `Guǎn Zhòng` said: `
` "There must be a sage in the state." `
` `Huán Gōng` sighed and said: `
` Among the laborers the other day, `
` there was one who held a mulberry wood pestle and looked upward at me; `
` could it have been him?" `
` He then ordered the laborers to return to their work `
` and allowed no one to be replaced. `
` After a short while, `
` `Dōngguō Chuí` arrived. `
` `Guǎn Zhòng` said: `
` "It must be this man." `
` He then ordered the usher to invite him in `
` and stand apart on a different level. `
` `Guǎn Zhòng` said: `
` "Was it you who spoke of attacking `Jǔ`?" `
` He replied: `
` "It was." `
` `Guǎn Zhòng` said: `
` "I did not speak of attacking `Jǔ`; `
` for what reason did you speak of attacking `Jǔ`?" `
` He replied: `
` "I have heard that superior men are good at planning, `
` while petty men are good at inferring. `
` I privately inferred it." `
` `Guǎn Zhòng` said: `
` "I did not speak of attacking `Jǔ`; `
` by what means did you infer it?" `
` He replied: `
` "I have heard that a superior man has three countenances: `
` being relaxed and joyful `
` is the countenance of bells and drums; `
` being somber and quiet `
` is the countenance of mourning garments; `
` being vigorous and full of energy `
` is the countenance of weapons and armor. `
` The other day, `
` I looked at my lord on the terrace; `
` he was vigorous and full of energy, `
` which is the countenance of weapons and armor. `
` My lord sighed but did not moan; `
` what he spoke of was `Jǔ`. `
` My lord raised his arm and pointed; `
` what he faced was `Jǔ`. `
` I privately considered which of the small states of the feudal lords have not yet submitted, `
` and thought it must be `Jǔ`. `
` Therefore I spoke of it." `
` The superior man says: `
` Generally, the ear hears by sound; `
` now, without hearing his voice, `
` but by using his appearance and arm, `
` this shows `Dōngguō Chuí` did not use his ears to hear. `
` Even though `Huán Gōng` and `Guǎn Zhòng` were good at planning, `
` they could not hide it. `
` Thus the sage hears the soundless `
` and sees the formless. `
` `Dōngguō Chuí` possessed this. `
` Therefore `Huán Gōng` honored him with rank and salary and treated him with ritual. `
` 13.6 The Grand Historian of `Jìn`, `Tú Yú`, saw the chaos in the state of `Jìn` `
` and saw that `Jìn Píng Gōng` was arrogant and lacked virtue and righteousness; `
` he took his maps and documents and went to `Zhōu`. `
` `Zhōu Wēi Gōng` saw him and asked him, `
` saying: `
` "Among the states of the world, which one will be the first to perish?" `
` He replied: `
` "`Jìn` will be the first to perish." `
` `Wēi Gōng` asked for his explanation. `
` He replied: `
` "When I was in `Jìn`, I did not dare to speak directly. `
` I showed the `Gōng` of `Jìn` heavenly anomalies— `
` that the movements of the sun, moon, and stars were mostly improper— `
` but he said: `
` 'What can these do!' `
` I showed him that human affairs were mostly unrighteous `
` and the common people were mostly resentful, `
` but he said: `
` 'How can these cause harm?' `
` I also showed him that neighboring states did not submit `
` and the worthy and good were not promoted, `
` but he said: `
` 'How can these cause injury?' `
` This is not knowing the reasons for survival or for perishing. `
` Therefore I say: `
` `Jìn` will be the first to perish." `
` After three years, `
` `Jìn` indeed perished. `
` `Wēi Gōng` again saw `Tú Yú` and asked him, `
` saying: `
` "Which will be next?" `
` He replied: `
` "`Zhōngshān` will be next." `
` `Wēi Gōng` asked for the reason. `
` He replied: `
` "Heaven produced the people `
` and ordered them to have distinctions. `
` Having distinctions `
` is the righteousness of humans, `
` which is how they are different from birds, beasts, and deer; `
` it is how ruler and minister, superior and inferior, are established. `
` The customs of `Zhōngshān` `
` involve using day as night `
` and night to continue day; `
` men and women intermingle closely `
` and truly have no rest. `
` They are licentious, confused, and indulge in pleasure; `
` their songs are fond of sadness; `
` their ruler does not know to hate this. `
` These are the airs of a perished state. `
` Therefore I say: `
` `Zhōngshān` will be next." `
` After two years, `
` `Zhōngshān` indeed perished. `
` `Wēi Gōng` again saw `Tú Yú` and asked him, saying: `
` "Which will be next?" `
` `Tú Yú` did not reply. `
` `Wēi Gōng` persisted in asking. `
` `Tú Yú` said: `
` "My lord will be next." `
` `Wēi Gōng` was afraid `
` and sought out the elders of the state. `
` He found `Qí Chóu` and `Tián Yì` and treated them with ritual, `
` and also found `Shǐ Lǐ` and `Zhào Xùn` to be his ministers of remonstrance. `
` He removed thirty-nine items of harsh ordinances `
` and informed `Tú Yú`. `
` `Tú Yú` said: `
` "Will it perhaps last until the end of my lord's life? `
` I have heard that when a state is to rise, `
` Heaven sends it worthy men `
` and gives it scholars who remonstrate to the utmost; `
` when a state is to perish, `
` Heaven gives it chaotic people and those who are good at flattery." `
` When `Wēi Gōng` passed away, `
` his body remained in its temporary coffin for nine months without being buried, `
` and `Zhōu` was then divided into two. `
` Therefore, the words of those who possess the Way `
` cannot be ignored. `
` 13.7 The `Hóu` of `Qí` asked `Yàn Zǐ`, saying: `
` "At the present time, `
` which of the feudal lords is in danger?" `
` He replied: `
` "`Jǔ` will perhaps be the first to perish!" `
` The `Gōng` said: `
` "For what reason?" `
` He replied: `
` "Its land is being encroached upon by `Qí`, `
` and its wealth is being exhausted by `Jìn`. `
` This is why it will perish." `
` 13.8 `Zhì Bó` led the troops of `Hán` and `Wèi` to attack `Zhào`. `
` They besieged the city of `Jìnyáng` and flooded it. `
` The city walls were not yet submerged by only three boards' height. `
` `Chī Cī` said to `Zhì Bó`: `
` "The lords of `Hán` and `Wèi` will surely rebel." `
` `Zhì Bó` said: `
` "How do you know this?" `
` He replied: `
` "They would win against `Zhào` and divide its land into three parts. `
` Now the city walls are not yet submerged by only three boards, `
` frogs are being born in the stoves, `
` and people and horses are eating each other; `
` the day the city surrenders is near. `
` Yet the lords of `Hán` and `Wèi` have no joy in their hearts but instead look worried. `
` If this is not rebellion, what else is it?" `
` The next day, `
` `Zhì Bó` said to the lords of `Hán` and `Wèi`: `
` "`Cī` says that you two are about to rebel." `
` The lords of `Hán` and `Wèi` said: `
` "We will surely defeat `Zhào` and divide its land into three parts. `
` Now the city is about to be conquered. `
` Although our two houses are foolish, `
` we would not abandon such beautiful profit and turn our backs on the treaty `
` to undertake a difficult and impossible task; `
` the logic of the situation is clear. `
` This `Cī` must be advocating for `Zhào` to my lord, `
` and moreover making my lord suspect the hearts of the two rulers `
` so as to slacken the attack on `Zhào`. `
` Now my lord listens to the words of a slandering official `
` and breaks the friendship with the two rulers; `
` we feel regret for my lord." `
` `Zhì Bó` came out `
` and wanted to kill `Chī Cī`. `
` `Chī Cī` fled, `
` and the lords of `Hán` and `Wèi` indeed rebelled.
13.9 The Gōngsuǒ Shì of Lǔ was about to perform a sacrifice but lost his sacrificial animal.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
“The Gōngsuǒ Shì will surely perish within three years.”
After one year, they perished.
A disciple asked, saying:
“Previously, when the Gōngsuǒ Shì lost his animal, the Master said,
‘They will surely perish within three years.’
Now they have perished in exactly one year.
How did the Master know they were going to perish?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The word for sacrifice (jì) implies seeking (suǒ).
Seeking
means exhausting oneself;
it is the means by which a filial son exhausts his heart for his parents.
To arrive at the sacrifice and have lost the animal
means that the other things he has lost are already many.
This is how I knew they were going to perish.”
13.10 The Cài Hóu, the Sòng Gōng, and the Zhèng Bó had an audience in Jìn.
The Cài Hóu said to Shū Xiàng:
“What do you have to say to me?”
He replied:
“In terms of territory and population, Cài
is not the equal of Sòng or Zhèng,
yet your carriages, horses, clothes, and furs
are more extravagant than those of the two states.
Surely some of the feudal lords will plot against Cài!”
After one year had passed,
Jīng attacked Cài and devastated it.
13.11 Bái Guī went to Zhōngshān.
The King of Zhōngshān wanted to keep him,
but he firmly declined and left.
He then went to Qí.
The King of Qí also wanted to keep him,
but he again declined and left.
Someone asked why he declined them.
Bái Guī said:
“The two states are about to perish.
According to what I have learned, a state has five forms of exhaustion:
where none are necessarily loyal,
then speech is exhausted;
where none are necessarily honored,
then reputation is exhausted;
where none are necessarily loved,
then kinship is exhausted;
if travelers have no provisions
and residents have no food,
then wealth is exhausted;
if one cannot employ others
and cannot employ oneself,
then achievement is exhausted.
When a state has these five,
it will surely perish without hope of luck.
Zhōngshān and Qí both fall under this.”
If the King of Zhōngshān and the King of Qí had heard of the five exhaustions and changed their ways,
then they certainly would not have perished.
The trouble is that they did not hear of them,
or even if they heard, they did not believe.
Thus, the duty of a ruler
lies simply in being good at listening.
13.12 Wēi Gōng of Xiàcài closed his doors and wept.
For three days and three nights,
he wept until his tears were gone and were followed by blood.
A neighbor peeking over the wall asked him, saying:
“For what reason do you weep so sorrowfully as this?”
He replied:
“Our state is about to perish.”
The neighbor said:
“How do you know?”
He responded, saying:
“I have heard that when a disease is about to become fatal,
one cannot find a good physician;
when a state is about to perish,
one cannot find a good strategy.
I have repeatedly remonstrated with my lord,
but my lord does not use my advice.
This is how I know the state is about to perish.”
Thereupon, the one who peeked over the wall heard his words,
and he moved his entire clan away to Chǔ.
After several years,
the King of Chǔ indeed raised an army to attack Cài.
The one who had peeked over the wall was a Sīmǎ
and led the army there,
taking a great many captives.
He asked:
“Are there no brothers or old friends here?”
He saw Wēi Gōng bound among the captives
and asked:
“How did you come to this?”
Wēi Gōng responded:
“How could I not come to this?
Moreover, I have heard it said:
those who speak
are the servants of action;
those who act
are the masters of speech.
You could act,
while I could only speak.
You are the master,
and I am the servant.
How could I not come to this?”
The one who peeked over the wall spoke of this to the King of Chǔ,
who then loosened his bonds,
and he went together with them to Chǔ.
Therefore it is said:
Those who can speak are not necessarily able to act,
and those who can act are not necessarily able to speak.
13.13 Guǎn Zhòng was ill.
Huán Gōng went to visit him
and said:
“If you, Zhòngfù, should abandon me,
could Shù Diāo be put in charge of the administration?”
He replied:
“No.
Shù Diāo castrated himself to seek entry to the Lord’s service.
If he is so cruel to his own body,
what regard will he have for the Lord?”
The Lord said:
“In that case, would Yì Yá be acceptable?”
He replied:
“Yì Yá cooked his own son to feed the Lord.
If he is so cruel to his own son,
what regard will he have for the Lord?
If you use them,
you will surely be mocked by the feudal lords.”
When Huán Gōng passed away,
Shù Diāo and Yì Yá indeed caused a rebellion.
Sixty days after Huán Gōng’s death,
maggots crawled out from his door, yet he remained unburied.
13.14 Shí Qǐ was sitting in attendance on Qū Jiàn.
Qū Jiàn said:
“Is Bái Gōng about to start a rebellion?”
Shí Qǐ said:
“What kind of talk is that!
Within Bái Gōng’s household, there are no grand designs.
There are three scholars to whom he humbles himself,
five ministers who are like equals to himself,
and a thousand people with whom he shares food and clothing.
Since Bái Gōng acts like this,
for what reason would he rebel?”
Qū Jiàn said:
“This is exactly why I say he will rebel.
To act as a Jūnzǐ is acceptable,
but if one's actions within the state exceed proper ritual, the state will be suspicious of him.
Furthermore, if he does not find it difficult to humble himself before his subordinates,
he will certainly not find it difficult to place himself above his lord.
This is how I know that man will start a rebellion.”
After ten months,
Bái Gōng indeed rebelled.
13.15 Zhāo Hóu of Hán built a high gate.
Qū Yíjiù said:
“Zhāo Hóu will not pass out of this gate.”
Someone asked:
“Why?”
He said:
“It is not the right time.
What I mean by not being the right time
is not about the day or month.
People naturally have times of fortune and misfortune.
Zhāo Hóu once had fortune
but did not build a high gate then.
Last year, Qín captured Yíyáng;
the next year there was a great drought and the people were starving.
He did not use this time to relieve the urgency of the people,
but instead turned around and increased his extravagance.
This is what is meant by ‘blessings do not come in pairs,
but calamities surely come repeatedly.’”
When the high gate was completed,
Zhāo Hóu died,
and in the end, he never passed out of that gate.
13.16 Tián Zǐyán came from Dàshù to the base of the wall of Pínglíng.
He saw people’s sons and asked about their fathers;
he saw people’s fathers and asked about their sons.
Tián Zǐfāng said:
“Will he use Pínglíng to rebel?
I have heard that one must act within and only then extend it outside.
Zǐyán desires the support of his multitude extremely much.”
Later, he indeed rebelled with Pínglíng.
13.17 The Jìn people had already defeated the Zhì clan,
and upon returning, they repaired their armor and sharpened their weapons.
The King of Chǔ was afraid
and summoned Liáng Gōng Hóng, saying:
"The Jìn people have already defeated the Zhì clan,
and upon returning they are repairing their armor and weapons;
will they target us?"
Liáng Gōng said:
"Do not worry about that;
does the danger not lie with Wú?
The Lord of Wú pities the people and shares in their labor,
making his people respect the orders of their superiors,
and the people treat death lightly in following their superiors' service,
fighting like captives in battle.
I climbed a mountain to observe them
and saw that their reliance on the common people's trust is absolute.
Should we not stop [focusing on Jìn]?
How should we prepare against them?"
He did not listen.
The following year,
Hélǘ attacked Yǐng.
13.18 King Zhuāng of Chǔ wanted to attack Chén
and sent someone to observe it.
The envoy said:
"Chén cannot be attacked."
King Zhuāng said:
"For what reason?"
He replied:
"Their city walls are high,
their moats are deep,
and their stores and accumulations are many."
Níng Guó said:
"Chén can be attacked.
Chén is a small state,
yet its stores and accumulations are many.
When stores and accumulations are many, then taxes and levies are heavy;
when taxes and levies are heavy, then the people resent their superiors.
The city walls are high
and the moats are deep,
which means the people's strength is exhausted.
If you raise troops to attack it,
Chén can be taken."
King Zhuāng listened to him
and subsequently took Chén.
13.19 Shí Yì said to Sūn Bó:
"Wú is about to perish;
do you know this as well?"
Sūn Bó said:
"It is late.
Regarding your knowledge of it,
why should I not know?"
Shí Yì said:
"If so, then why do you not remonstrate?"
Sūn Bó said:
"In the past, Jié punished those who remonstrated,
Zhòu burned the sages
and cut open the heart of Prince Bǐ Gān.
When the wife of the Yuán clan was weaving and lost the lead thread,
her concubine told her of it,
and in anger she cast her away.
Do those who are perishing ever hope for people to know their faults?"
13.20 During the time of Emperor Xiào Xuān,
the Huò clan was extravagant and decadent.
Mr. Xú of Màolíng said:
"The Huò clan will surely perish.
To be superior to others and yet be extravagant
is the way to destruction.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Extravagance leads to lack of humility.'
Those who lack humility
will surely insult their superiors.
Those who insult their superiors
are on the path of rebellion.
When one surpasses others,
others will surely seek to harm them.
Now the Huò clan has held power for a long time,
and there are many in the world who hate and wish them harm.
Since the world seeks to harm them
and they also act with the way of rebellion,
what else is there to wait for but destruction?"
He then submitted a memorial saying:
"The Huò clan is extravagant and decadent.
If Your Majesty loves them,
you should restrain them in time
and not let them reach destruction."
The memorial was submitted three times,
and each time it was acknowledged.
Afterwards, the Huò clan was indeed destroyed.
Dǒng Zhōng and others were enfeoffed for their merit.
Someone submitted a memorial on behalf of Mr. Xú, saying:
"I have heard of a guest who visited a host
and saw that his stove had a straight chimney
with piled firewood beside it.
The guest said to the host:
'Bend the chimney
and move the piled firewood far away;
otherwise, there will be a fire hazard.'
The host remained silent and did not respond.
After a short while,
the house indeed caught fire.
The people of the neighborhood pitied him and saved it,
and fortunately the fire was extinguished.
Thereupon he slaughtered an ox and set out wine;
those with singed hair and scorched skin were in the seats of honor,
and the others were seated according to their merit,
but on the contrary, he did not recognize the one who spoke of bending the chimney.
If the host had previously listened to the guest's words,
he would not have spent on ox and wine,
and ultimately there would have been no fire hazard.
Now Xú Fú of Màolíng several times submitted memorials saying the Huò clan would have a change
and that one should prevent and cut it off.
If Fú's advice had been followed,
then there would have been no expense of dividing land and granting noble titles,
and the state would have been peaceful and secure as usual.
Now that the matter is finished,
Fú alone does not share in the merit.
I hope Your Majesty will examine the guest's strategy of moving the firewood and bending the chimney
and place him above those with singed hair and scorched skin."
The memorial was presented,
and the Emperor then sent someone to grant Xú Fú ten bolts of silk
and appointed him as a Gentleman.
13.21 Duke Huán of Qí was about to attack Shānróng and Gūzhú
and sent someone to request help from Lǔ.
The Lord of Lǔ brought forward his ministers to deliberate,
and they all said:
"The army will travel thousands of miles
and enter the land of the barbarians;
they will surely not return."
Thereupon Lǔ promised to help but did not go.
Qí had already attacked Shānróng and Gūzhú
and wanted to move the troops against Lǔ.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be done.
The feudal lords are not yet close to us.
Now to attack the distant and then return to punish a near neighbor,
neighboring states will not be close;
this is not the way of a Hegemon or King.
The precious vessels the Lord obtained from Shānróng
are rare in the Central States;
can you not present them to the Temple of Zhōu Gōng?"
Duke Huán then divided the treasures of Shānróng
and offered them to the Temple of Zhōu Gōng.
The following year,
he raised troops to attack Jǔ;
Lǔ ordered that all adult males be dispatched,
and even five-foot-tall boys arrived.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Sage turns calamity into fortune
and repays resentment with virtue."
This is what it refers to.
13.22 Zhōngháng Wénzǐ fled into exile and reached the border.
His followers said:
"The one who is the Sèfū here
is your man;
why not rest here
and wait for those in the following carriages?"
Wénzǐ said:
"In the past,
I liked music,
and this person gave me a zither;
I liked pendants,
and he also gave me jade.
This means he does not criticize my faults,
but only seeks to ingratiate himself with me.
I fear he will use me to seek favor with others."
Consequently, he did not enter.
When the following carriages entered the gate,
Wénzǐ asked about the Sèfū's location,
who had seized and killed those inside.
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"Zhōngháng Wénzǐ turned his back on the Way and lost righteousness,
thereby losing his state;
yet afterwards he attained it [the Way]
and thus saved his life.
The Way cannot be abandoned,
even as such."
13.23 Duke Líng of Wèi was loosely dressed in a coverlet while traveling with women.
Zǐgòng saw the Duke,
and the Duke said:
"Will Wèi perish?"
He replied:
"In the past, Jié of Xià and Zhòu of Yīn did not take responsibility for their faults and thus perished.
Chéng Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ knew how to take responsibility for their faults
and thus they rose.
How should Wèi perish?"
13.24 Zhì Bó requested land from Wèi Xuān Zǐ.
Xuān Zǐ would not give it.
Rèn Zēng said:
"Why not give it?"
Xuān Zǐ said:
"He requests land without cause,
and for this reason, I will not give it."
Rèn Zēng said:
"As for those who request land without cause,
if you give it to him without cause,
it will make his greed even more insatiable.
He will be pleased,
and will certainly request land from the other lords.
If the lords do not give it,
he will certainly be enraged and attack them."
Xuān Zǐ said:
"Good."
He then gave him land.
Zhì Bó was pleased
and again requested land from Zhào.
Zhào would not give it.
Zhì Bó was enraged
and besieged Jìnyáng.
Hán and Wèi joined with Zhào and turned against the Zhì clan,
and the Zhì clan was subsequently destroyed.
13.25 King Zhuāng of Chǔ fought with Jìn
and defeated them.
Fearing that the other lords would be afraid of him,
he then built a terrace five rèn high.
When the terrace was completed, he hosted the lords with wine.
The lords requested a treaty.
King Zhuāng said:
"I am a man of meager virtue."
The lords requested to offer a toast,
and then he looked up and said:
"This towering and magnificent terrace,
and its deep and obscure schemes—
if my words are improper,
let the lords attack me."
Because of this, those from afar came to pay court,
and those nearby came to be his guests.
13.26 King Fúchāi of Wú crushed Yuè
and was about to attack Chén.
The grandees of Chǔ were all afraid
and said:
"In the past, Hélǘ was able to employ his masses,
and thus he defeated us at Bǎijǔ.
Now we hear that Fúchāi is even more formidable than he."
Zǐxī said:
"You gentlemen should worry about not being in harmony with each other,
and have no concern about Wú.
In the past, Hélǘ would not eat two different flavors at one meal,
would not sit on double mats,
and in his selections, he did not choose the costly.
When in the capital,
if Heaven sent a disaster,
he would provide for his relatives and the needy.
When in the army,
he would only eat after half of the food was cooked.
Whatever he tasted,
his soldiers and chariot-drivers would certainly share in it.
Because of this, the people did not feel exhausted by labor,
and in death, they knew they would not be neglected.
Now Fúchāi has terraces, pavilions, embankments, and ponds when he stops;
he has concubines, ladies, and consorts when he stays for the night.
In a single day's journey,
whatever he desires must be accomplished,
and his toys and favorites must follow him.
Rare and exotic treasures are gathered there.
Fúchāi has already defeated himself first;
how can he defeat us?"
13.27 Yuè crushed Wú
and requested troops from Chǔ to attack Jìn.
The King of Chǔ and his grandees were all afraid
and were about to grant the request.
Zuǒshǐ Yǐxiàng said:
"This is because they fear we will attack them;
thus they show me they are not exhausted.
I request to provide one thousand chariots
and thirty thousand troops
to divide the land of Wú with them."
King Zhuāng listened to him,
and subsequently took the Dōng Guó.
13.28 Yáng Hǔ caused trouble in Lǔ
and fled to Qí.
He requested troops to attack Lǔ,
and the Lord of Qí was about to grant it.
Bǎo Wén Zǐ said:
"This must not be.
Yáng Hǔ wishes for the army of Qí to be broken.
If the army of Qí is broken,
many of the high ministers will certainly die,
and then he wishes to exert his deceptive schemes.
Now, Hǔ was favored by the Jì Shì,
yet he intended to kill Jì Sūn,
harming the state of Lǔ to accommodate his own demands.
Now you, my Lord, are richer than the Jì Shì
and greater than the state of Lǔ;
this is what Yáng Hǔ wishes to overthrow.
Lǔ has escaped his malady, yet you, my Lord, take him in—
will this not be harmful?"
The Lord of Qí then arrested him;
he escaped and fled to Jìn.
13.29 Tāng wished to attack Jié.
Yī Yǐn said:
"I request that we withhold the tribute and services
to observe his movements."
Jié was enraged
and raised the armies of the Jiǔ Yí to attack them.
Yī Yǐn said:
"It is not yet time.
He is still able to raise the armies of the Jiǔ Yí;
this means the fault lies with us."
Tāng then apologized for his offense and requested to submit,
and resumed the tribute and services.
The following year,
he again withheld the tribute and services.
Jié was enraged and tried to raise the armies of the Jiǔ Yí,
but the armies of the Jiǔ Yí would not rise.
Yī Yǐn said:
"It is time."
Tāng then raised his army,
attacked and ruined him,
and relocated Jié to Náncháo.
13.30 King Wǔ attacked Zhòu.
At dawn he raised fat-candles;
passing through the passes he cut down the banks;
crossing water he broke the boats;
crossing valleys he removed the bridges;
crossing mountains he burned the brush,
to show the people that he had no intention of returning.
When he reached the pass of Yǒuróng,
a great wind broke the banners.
Sǎnyí Shēng remonstrated, saying:
"Is this not an ill omen?"
King Wǔ said:
"No,
it is Heaven bestowing weapons."
When the wind stopped, it was followed by a heavy rain;
the water was level with the ground and gathered.
Sǎnyí Shēng again remonstrated, saying:
"Is this not an ill omen?"
King Wǔ said:
"No,
it is Heaven washing the weapons."
They performed divination, and the tortoise shell crack failed.
Sǎnyí Shēng again remonstrated, saying:
"Is this not an ill omen?"
King Wǔ said:
"It is not favorable for prayers and sacrifices,
but it is favorable for attacking the enemy;
that is all this crack means."
Therefore, King Wǔ followed the ways of Heaven and Earth,
defied the three ill omens, and captured Zhòu at Mùyě.
That which he alone saw was the essence of things.
13.31 Duke Wén of Jìn fought with the people of Jīng at Chéngpú.
The Lord asked Jiù Fàn for advice.
Jiù Fàn replied:
"For a lord who subdues by righteousness,
one cannot have enough trust;
for a lord who subdues by war,
one cannot have enough deception.
You, my Lord, should also just use deception."
The Lord asked Yōng Jì for advice.
Yōng Jì replied:
"If one burns the forest to hunt,
although many animals are obtained,
there will be none left the next year.
If one drains the pond to fish,
although many fish are obtained,
there will be none left the next year.
Deception may still steal a temporary advantage,
but afterward, there will be no repeating it."
He then fought with the army of Jīng
and greatly defeated them.
When it came to awarding rewards,
he put Yōng Jì first and Jiù Fàn second.
The attendants said:
"The battle of Chéngpú
was won by the scheme of Jiù Fàn."
The Lord said:
"The words of Yōng Jì
are a plan for a hundred generations.
The words of Jiù Fàn
are a temporary expediency.
I have already carried them out."
13.32 At the Battle of Chéngpú,
Wén Gōng said to Jiù Fàn:
“I divined regarding the battle and the tortoise shell scorched;
I am facing the Year Star,
while the enemy has their back to it;
a comet has appeared,
and they hold its handle,
while I hold its tail;
I also dreamed of wrestling with the King of Jīng,
and he was on top,
while I was below.
I wish not to fight,
what do you think of this?”
Jiù Fàn replied:
“As for the scorched tortoise shell from the battle divination,
that refers to the people of Jīng;
as for you facing the Year Star
and them having their back to it,
it is because they are departing and we are following them;
as for the comet appearing,
and them holding its handle
while we hold its tail,
if used for sweeping it would favor them,
but if used for striking it favors us;
you dreamed of wrestling with the King of Jīng
and him being on top,
while you were below—
then you were looking up at Heaven while the King of Jīng was prostrate, admitting his guilt.
Furthermore, we have Sòng and Wèi as our main allies,
and Qí and Qín assist us;
we are in accord with the Way of Heaven,
and based on human affairs alone,
we are certain to defeat them.”
Wén Gōng followed his advice,
and the people of Jīng were greatly defeated.
13.33 Yuè suffered a famine,
and Gōu Jiàn was afraid.
Sì Shuǐ stepped forward to advise, saying:
“Famine is a blessing for Yuè
and a disaster for Wú.
The state of Wú is very wealthy and has a surplus of resources,
but its ruler loves fame and does not consider future troubles.
If we use humble words and heavy gifts to request to buy grain from Wú,
Wú will surely give it to us;
if they give it to us, then Wú can be taken.”
The King of Yuè followed this advice.
When Wú was about to give it to them,
Zǐ Xū advised, saying:
“This must not be.
Wú and Yuè share a border and are neighboring territories;
the roads are easy and people pass through.
They are states of bitter enemies and warring rivals.
If Wú does not possess Yuè,
Yuè will surely possess Wú.
Qí and Jìn cannot cross the Three Rivers and Five Lakes to destroy Wú or Yuè.
It would be better to take this opportunity to attack them;
this is how our late King Hé Lǘ achieved hegemony.
Moreover, as for famine,
what of it?
It is like a deep pool.
Defeats and invasions—
which state does not have them?
If Your Majesty does not attack but instead exports grain to them,
then benefit departs and misfortune arrives;
resources will be depleted and the people will be resentful;
then regret will come too late.”
The King of Wú said:
“I have heard
that a righteous army does not attack those who have submitted,
and a humane person does not attack others because of starvation.
Even if I were to gain ten Yuè,
I would not do it.”
He then gave them the grain.
Three years later,
Wú also suffered a famine
and requested to buy grain from Yuè.
The King of Yuè did not give it and instead attacked them,
subsequently destroying Wú.
13.34 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ sent Chéng Hé and Shè Tā to covenant with Wèi Líng Gōng at Zhuān Zé.
Before Líng Gōng had smeared the blood of the covenant,
Chéng Hé and Shè Tā squeezed Líng Gōng’s hand and pushed it down.
Líng Gōng was angry
and wished to rebel against Zhào.
Wáng Sūn Shāng said:
“If Your Lordship wishes to rebel against Zhào,
it would be better to share this hatred with the common people.”
The Duke said:
“How so?”
He replied:
“I ask to order the officials to issue a command to the state saying:
‘Those who have paternal aunts, elder sisters, younger sisters, or daughters,
one person from each household must be sent as a hostage to Zhào.’
The common people will surely be resentful,
and Your Lordship can then rebel against them based on this.”
The Lord said:
“Good.”
He then issued the order.
After three days, he began the conscription,
and after five days, the order was completed.
The people of the state wept in the alleys.
The Lord then summoned the grandees of the state and consulted them, saying:
“Zhào has acted without the Way;
is it permissible to rebel against them?”
The grandees all said:
“It is.”
They then went out through the West Gate
and closed the East Gate.
When the Zhào clan heard of this,
they bound Shè Tā and beheaded him
to apologize to Wèi,
and Chéng Hé fled to Yān.
Zǐ Gòng said:
“Wáng Sūn Shāng can be called skillful in planning!
He hated people and was able to harm them;
he faced trouble and was able to handle it;
he wished to use the people and was able to make them follow him.
With one action, three results were achieved.
He can indeed be called skillful in planning.”
13.35 Chǔ Chéng Wáng gathered the feudal lords together
and made the Lord of Lǔ act as a servant.
The Lord of Lǔ summoned his grandees and consulted them, saying:
“Although I am small,
I am also a state established by Zhōu.
Now Chéng Wáng treats me as a servant;
is this permissible?”
The grandees all said:
“It is not.”
Gōng Yí Xiū said:
“If it is not permissible
and you do not obey the King of Chǔ,
you will die and the state will perish.
Your Lordship's ministers are Your Lordship's property,
but you are the ruler of the people.”
The Lord of Lǔ then served as a servant.
13.36 Qí Jǐng Gōng gave his daughter in marriage to Hé Lǘ.
Seeing her off in the suburbs,
he wept and said:
“I shall not see you again before I die!”
Gāo Mèng Zǐ said:
“Qí has its back to the sea and its mountains are precipitous.
Even if it cannot completely gather the whole world under its control,
who would dare offend my Lord?
If you love her, do not let her go.”
The Duke said:
“I have the security of the state of Qí,
yet I cannot command the feudal lords,
nor can I refuse to listen to them.
This would breed chaos.
I have heard
that if one cannot command, then nothing is better than following.
Moreover, as for Wú,
it is like a wasp or scorpion;
if it does not vent its poison on others, it will not be at rest.
I fear it would vent its poison on me.”
He then sent her away.
13.37 Qí wished to marry a daughter to Zhèng Tàizǐ Hū,
but Tàizǐ Hū declined.
When someone asked for the reason,
the Prince said:
“Every person has their proper match.
Qí is great,
it is not a match for me.
The Shī says:
‘Seek much blessing for oneself.’
It rests with me alone.”
Later, the Róng attacked Qí.
Qí requested troops from Zhèng.
Zhèng Tàizǐ Hū led the army to rescue Qí
and greatly defeated the Róng army.
Qí again wished to marry a daughter to him,
but the Prince firmly declined.
When someone asked for the reason,
he replied:
“When I had done no service for Qí,
I still did not dare.
Now that I have rescued Qí from an emergency by my Lord's command,
if I were to take a wife and return,
people would surely think I used the army to gain a marriage.”
He declined it to the end.
13.38 Kǒngzǐ asked Qīdiāo Mǎrén:
"You served Zāng Wènzhòng, Zāng Wǔzhòng, and Rúzǐ Róng;
of these three Dàfū, who was the most worthy?"
Qīdiāo Mǎrén replied:
"The Zāng family had a divination tortoise
named Cài.
When Wènzhòng held office,
one crack was made every three years;
when Wǔzhòng held office,
two cracks were made every three years;
when Rúzǐ Róng held office,
three cracks were made every three years.
Mǎrén saw this;
as for the worthiness or unworthiness of these three Dàfū,
Mǎrén does not know."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A Jūnzǐ indeed
is this son of the Qīdiāo clan!
When he speaks of people's excellence,
it is subtle yet clear;
when he speaks of people's faults,
it is slight yet manifest.
Therefore, wisdom cannot reach it,
and insight cannot see it;
could it be that he learned this from the frequent divinations?"
13.39 Ānlíng Chán was favored by Chǔ Gòngwáng because of his beautiful and robust appearance.
Jiāng Yǐ went to see Ānlíng Chán and said:
"Did your ancestors have the merit of facing arrows and stones for the King?"
He said:
"They did not."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Do you yourself have such merit?"
He said:
"I do not."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"How did your nobility reach this point?"
He said:
"I do not know the reason."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"I have heard
that those who serve others with wealth
find their connections thinning when the wealth is exhausted;
those who serve others with their appearance
find their love fading when their bloom falls.
Now your bloom has a time to fall;
how will you ensure lasting favor without being neglected by the King?"
Ānlíng Chán said:
"I am young, foolish, and base;
I wish to entrust my wisdom to you, Master."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Only by offering to follow him in death as a sacrificial companion will it suffice."
Ānlíng Chán said:
"I respectfully receive your command."
Jiāng Yǐ left.
After a full year had passed,
he met Ānlíng Chán and said:
"What I explained to you the other day,
have you communicated it to the King?"
He said:
"Not yet possible."
After another full year passed,
Jiāng Yǐ again saw Ānlíng Chán and said:
"Have you explained it to the King?"
Ānlíng Chán said:
"I have not yet found an opening with the King."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"You go out in the same carriage as the King,
you come in and sit with the King;
three years have passed,
and you say you have not found an opening with the King.
You simply think my words are not feasible."
He left in displeasure.
That year,
Gòngwáng hunted in the wilds of the river marshes.
Wildfires rose like clouds and rainbows,
and the howling of tigers and wolves was like thunder.
A frenzied rhinoceros came from the south
and directly struck the King's left outside horse.
The King raised his banners and ordered the skilled archers to shoot it.
With one shot,
the rhinoceros died beneath the carriage.
The King was greatly pleased,
clapped his hands and laughed,
then looked at Ānlíng Chán and said:
"After my ten thousand years,
with whom will you share this joy?"
Ānlíng Chán then hesitated and stepped back,
tears falling and wetting his collar.
He embraced the King and said:
"After your ten thousand years,
I shall follow you in death as a sacrificial companion;
how could I know who would then enjoy this?"
Thereupon, Gòngwáng enfeoffed Ānlíng Chán right there at the carriage with three hundred households.
Therefore it is said:
Jiāng Yǐ was good at plotting,
and Ānlíng Chán knew the right time.
13.40 Tàizǐ Shāngchén resented Lìngyǐn Zǐshàng.
Chu attacked Chén,
and Jìn went to its rescue,
with the armies camping on opposite sides of the Zhì River.
Yáng Chǔfù knew of Shāngchén’s resentment toward Zǐshàng,
so he said to Zǐshàng:
"Withdraw a little,
and I will cross to follow you."
Zǐshàng withdrew.
Yáng then ordered the Jìn army, saying:
"Chu has fled!"
He sent someone to tell Shāngchén:
"Zǐshàng accepted a bribe from Jìn and left."
Shāngchén reported this to King Chéng,
and King Chéng subsequently killed him.
13.41 Zhì Bó wished to launch a surprise attack on Wèi,
so he presented them with a team of four horses
preceded by a jade pi disc.
The Lord of Wèi was greatly pleased
and poured wine for a feast.
All the Dàfū were happy,
but Nán Wénzǐ alone was not pleased
and had a look of worry.
The Lord of Wèi said:
"A great state treats me with ritual;
therefore I pour wine for the Dàfū.
All the Dàfū are happy,
so why are you alone unhappy and worried?"
Nán Wénzǐ said:
"Ritual without precedent
and rewards without merit
are the precursors of calamity.
We have not sent anything there,
yet they have come here with gifts;
this is why I am worried."
Thereupon the Lord of Wèi repaired the bridges and crossings and prepared the border cities.
When Zhì Bó heard that Wèi's troops were at the border,
he returned.
13.42 Zhì Bó wished to launch a surprise attack on Wèi,
so he feigned the exile of his Tàizǐ Yán
and had him flee to Wèi.
Nán Wénzǐ said:
"As for Tàizǐ Yán being the son of his ruler,
he is deeply loved.
He has committed no great crime,
so there must be a reason for his exile.
However, if a person in exile is not received,
it is inauspicious."
He sent an officer to meet him,
saying:
"If the carriages exceed five,
be careful not to let them in."
When Zhì Bó heard of this,
he stopped.
13.43 Regarding Shū Xiàng’s killing of Cháng Hóng,
he had met Cháng Hóng several times in Zhōu.
He then feigned leaving a letter that said:
"Cháng Hóng said to Shū Xiàng:
'You raise the troops of the state of Jìn to attack Zhōu,
and I will depose the Liú clan to establish the Dān clan.'"
The Liú clan petitioned their lord, saying:
"This is Cháng Hóng's doing."
Thereupon they killed him.
13.44 Chǔ Gōngzǐ Wǔ was sent on a mission to Qín,
and Qín imprisoned him.
His younger brother presented three hundred catties of gold to Shū Xiàng.
Shū Xiàng said to Jìn Pínggōng:
"Why not fortify Húqiū?
Qín and Chu are concerned about the fortification of Húqiū.
If Qín is afraid and returns Gōngzǐ Wǔ to stop our fortification,
then you should stop.
Before the conflict even arises,
Chu will surely be grateful to you."
Jìn Pínggōng said:
"Excellent."
So he fortified it.
Qín was afraid
and subsequently returned Gōngzǐ Wǔ,
sending him to Jìn.
The people of Jìn stopped the fortification,
and Chu presented Jìn with a tribute of three hundred chariots.
13.45 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ sent someone with six white-maned carriages,
first with a jade disk,
as a gift for Wèi.
Shū Wén Zǐ of Wèi said:
“To see something unexpected is cause for caution;
this is how the small serve the great.
Now we have not gone to them, yet Jiǎn Zǐ has come to us first;
there must be a reason.”
Thereupon they cleared the forests and removed the obstacles around the walls,
gathered and stored supplies,
and only then sent an envoy.
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
“My action
was intended to be unforeseen;
now that it is already known,
I shall cease the siege of Wèi.”
13.46 Lord Huán of Zhèng intended to surprise the state of Kuài.
First, he inquired about the discerning, wise, brave, and daring men of Kuài,
and wrote down their names and surnames.
He selected the good ministers of Kuài and associated them with rewards,
writing down titles of office and rank for them.
He then set up an altar outside the city gate and buried these documents there,
consecrating it with the blood of a boar as if in a covenant.
The ruler of Kuài thought there was internal rebellion
and killed all his good ministers.
Lord Huán then made a surprise attack
and finally took Kuài.
13.47 Lord Huán of Zhèng went east to a meeting for investiture at Zhèng.
In the evening, he stayed at an inn east of Sòng.
The old man of the inn came from outside and said:
“Where is the guest going?”
He said:
“To the meeting for investiture at Zhèng.”
The old man of the inn said:
“I have heard
that opportunity is hard to find and easy to lose.
Now the guest sleeps peacefully;
this is probably not how to get invested.”
Lord Huán of Zhèng heard this,
grabbed the reins and drove himself.
His servant picked up the rice being washed and loaded it into the carriage,
and they traveled for ten days and ten nights until they arrived.
Lí Hé was competing with him for the investiture.
Therefore, despite the worthiness of Lord Huán of Zhèng,
if not for the old man of the inn,
he would have almost missed the investiture.
13.48 Duke Wén of Jìn attacked Wèi and entered the outer city.
He sat with his officers and ordered them to eat, saying:
“Today we must surely press against the great wall.”
Prince Lǜ lowered his head and laughed at this.
Duke Wén said:
“Why are you laughing?”
He replied:
“When my wife returned home,
I escorted her.
On my return, I saw a woman gathering mulberries and helped her.
But when I looked back at my wife,
there was also someone escorting her.”
Duke Wén became afraid,
turned back his army and returned home.
When he arrived at his state,
the people of Hé were attacking his territory.
14.1 The Shū says:
“Without partiality and without factionalism,
the Kingly Way is broad and vast.”
This speaks of supreme impartiality.
In antiquity, there was one who practiced great impartiality:
Emperor Yáo was the one.
Honorable as the Son of Heaven,
wealthy with all under Heaven,
he found Shùn and passed the throne to him,
not being partial to his own descendants.
He left the world as if discarding a worn-out straw sandal.
If he was like this with all under Heaven,
how much more so with things smaller than all under Heaven!
Who but Emperor Yáo could do this?
Kǒng Zǐ said:
“How sublime!
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yáo took it as his model.”
The Yì says:
“Without a head,
good fortune.”
This refers to the impartiality of a ruler.
For one who gives impartiality to all under Heaven,
his virtue is great indeed.
Extending it here
and modeling it there,
he is supported by the ten thousand surnames
and modeled by later generations.
As for the impartiality of a minister,
in managing official duties, he does not seek personal gain;
in the public gate, he does not speak of goods and profit;
when facing public laws, he does not show favoritism to relatives;
when serving the public and recommending the worthy, he does not avoid his enemies.
He is loyal in serving the ruler,
benevolent in benefiting those below him,
extending himself through the way of empathy,
and acting without factionalism.
Yī and Lǚ were such men.
Therefore their illustrious names remain to this day;
this is what is called impartiality.
The Shī says:
“The way of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
its straightness is like an arrow;
it is what the gentleman treads,
and what the common person gazes upon.”
This is what it refers to.
Impartiality produces clarity;
partiality produces darkness.
Uprightness and sincerity produce far-reaching success;
deception and falsehood produce blockage.
Sincerity and trust produce spirit-like efficacy;
boastfulness and absurdity produce delusion.
These six
are what the gentleman is cautious about
and are what distinguished Yǔ from Jié.
The Shī says:
“Violent and awesome is the High Sovereign;
His commands are full of perversity.”
This refers to being not impartial.
14.2 King Shòu Mèng of Wú had four sons:
the eldest was called Yè,
the next was called Yú Jì,
the next was called Yí Mèi,
and the next was called Jì Zhá,
styled as Jì Zǐ of Yán Líng.
He was the most worthy,
and all three elder brothers knew this.
Thereupon, when King Shòu Mèng died,
Yè yielded the position to Jì Zǐ,
but Jì Zǐ ultimately refused to accept it.
Yè then made a pact, saying:
“Jì Zǐ is worthy;
if we make the state pass to Jì Zǐ,
then Wú can flourish.”
Thus the brothers succeeded each other;
when eating and drinking, they would surely pray, saying:
“Let me die early
to let the state pass to Jì Zǐ.”
Yè died,
and Yú Jì was established;
Yú Jì died,
and Yí Mèi was established.
Yí Mèi died,
and next it was Jì Zǐ’s turn.
At that time, Jì Zǐ had been sent on a mission
and was not present.
A brother by a concubine, Liáo, said:
“I am also a brother.”
Thereupon he established himself as King of Wú.
When Jì Zǐ returned from his mission,
he resumed his service as before.
Yè’s son, Guāng, said:
“According to my father’s intention,
then the state should return to Jì Zǐ;
according to the law of succession,
then I am the legitimate heir
and should succeed the ruler.
What is Liáo doing there?”
Thereupon he sent Zhuān Zhū to assassinate Liáo,
killed him,
and yielded the position to Jì Zǐ.
Jì Zǐ said:
“You killed my ruler;
if I accept the state from you,
then I and you would be co-usurpers.
You killed my brother;
if I were to kill you,
then brothers, fathers, and sons would be killing each other without end.”
Finally, he went away to Yán Líng
and never entered Wú again for the rest of his life.
The gentleman considers his not killing to be benevolence
and his not taking the state to be righteousness.
To not treat the state as a private possession for oneself,
to cast away a thousand chariots without regret,
and to abandon a supreme position without resentment—
this can be considered close to the ideal!
14.3 The righteousness of the feudal lords is to die for the altars of soil and grain.
Dà Wáng abandoned his state and left.
Why?
Sages do not wish to use violence to invade and oppress the common people.
Therefore, they make feudal lords die for their states
to protect their people.
Dà Wáng possessed the grace of supreme benevolence.
He could not bear to let the common people fight.
Therefore, he served the Xūnyù Róng tribe with dogs, horses, and precious silks,
yet the attacks did not stop.
When he asked what they desired,
it was the land.
Thereupon, he assembled his officials and elders and informed them, saying:
“Land
is that which nourishes people.
A gentleman does not use that which nourishes to harm those who are being nourished.
I shall leave it.”
He then resided at the foot of Qí Shān.
The people of Bīn, carrying the young and supporting the elderly, followed him
as if returning to their parents.
After moving three times, the population was five times its original size.
They all promoted matters of benevolence, righteousness, and service to the superior.
A gentleman protects the state and brings peace to the people;
it is not merely about clashing weapons and exhausting the lives of the soldiers.
He does not treat his own person as private property,
but only ensures the people have enough to use.
Protecting the people is indeed the righteousness of abandoning the state;
this is called supreme impartiality.
14.4 Xīn Lì saw Lǔ Mù Gōng and said:
“Zhōu Gōng was not as worthy as Tài Gōng.”
Mù Gōng asked:
“Why do you say so?”
Xīn Lì replied:
“Zhōu Gōng selected land and was enfeoffed at Qǔfù.
Tài Gōng selected land and was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū.
Their ranks and territories were equal,
but the land of Qǔfù was not as beautiful as that of Yíngqiū,
and its population was not as numerous as that of Yíngqiū.
Not only that,
but Yíngqiū also had natural defenses from heaven.”
Mù Gōng felt ashamed in his heart and could not respond.
Xīn Lì hurried out.
Nángōng Biānzǐ entered.
Mù Gōng related Xīn Lì’s words in detail to Nángōng Biānzǐ.
Nángōng Biānzǐ said:
“In the past, when Zhōu Chéng Wáng used divination to dwell at Chéngzhōu,
his command to the tortoise shell said:
‘I, the lone man, possess the whole world.
Seeking to dwell among the common people,
how could I dare not occupy the central land?
If I should commit a crime,
then the four quarters may attack me,
and it will not be difficult for them to reach me.’
When Zhōu Gōng used divination to dwell at Qǔfù,
his command to the tortoise shell said:
‘Let me build a city on the southern side of the mountain.
If I am worthy, then may it flourish and prosper;
if I am not worthy, then may it quickly perish.’
When Jì Sūn Xíngfù cautioned his son,
he said:
‘I wish for our house to be wedged between the two altars,
so that if my descendants are unable to serve their superiors,
their downfall will be all the swifter.’
In such cases, it was said:
‘If worthy, then flourish and prosper;
if not worthy, then quickly perish.’
Where is there any mention of selecting land for enfeoffment
or showing off natural defenses from heaven?
The words of Xīn Lì
are those of a petty man.
You should not speak of them again.”
14.5 After Qín Shǐ Huáng Dì had swallowed the whole world,
he summoned his ministers for a discussion
and said:
“In ancient times, the Five Emperors abdicated to the worthy,
while the Three Kings made succession hereditary.
Which is right?
I shall follow it.”
The seventy Erudites had not yet replied
when Bào Bái Lìngzhī replied:
“To treat the world as a public office and thus yield to the worthy is right.
To treat the world as a family and thus make succession hereditary is right.
Therefore, the Five Emperors treated the world as a public office,
and the Three Kings treated the world as a family.”
Qín Shǐ Huáng Dì looked up to heaven and sighed:
“My virtue issues from the Five Emperors.
I shall treat the world as a public office.
Who can be made to succeed me?”
Bào Bái Lìngzhī replied:
“Your Majesty practices the way of Jié and Zhòu,
yet you wish to perform the abdication of the Five Emperors.
This is not something Your Majesty can do.”
Qín Shǐ Huáng Dì became greatly enraged and said:
“Lìngzhī, come forward!
On what basis do you say I practice the way of Jié and Zhòu?
Hurry and explain it;
if you cannot explain, then you shall die.”
Lìngzhī replied:
“I beg to explain it.
Your Majesty builds terraces that reach the clouds,
and palaces extending for five lǐ.
You have cast bells of a thousand dàn
and erected bell-frames of ten thousand dàn.
Your women are numbered by the hundreds,
and your musicians and performers by the thousands.
You have initiated the construction of the Lí Shān palaces,
reaching all the way to Yōng in an unbroken line.
That which you use for your own maintenance
exhausts the world
and drains the strength of the people.
You are partial and selfish,
unable to extend your concern to others.
Your Majesty is what is called a ruler who only seeks his own gain and barely survives.
How could you have the leisure to compare your virtue to the Five Emperors
and wish to treat the world as a public office?”
Qín Shǐ Huáng was dejected and had no way to respond.
His face showed an expression of shame.
After a long time,
he said:
“The words of Lìngzhī
have made me appear disgraceful before the multitude.”
He then abandoned the plan
and had no further intention of abdicating.
14.6 Qí Jǐng Gōng’s rewards and gifts reached even his inner palace.
Patterned embroideries covered his terraces and pavilions,
while beans and grain were fed to his ducks and geese.
When he went out, he saw a starved corpse.
He said to Àn Zǐ:
“Why did this person die?”
Àn Zǐ replied:
“This person died of hunger.”
The Duke said:
“Alas!
My lack of virtue
is indeed extreme!”
Àn Zǐ replied:
“Your virtue is prominent and manifest.
How can you say you have no virtue?”
Jǐng Gōng asked:
“What do you mean?”
Àn Zǐ replied:
“Your virtue reaches the inner palace and the terraces and pavilions.
Your playthings
are clothed in patterned embroideries.
Your ducks and geese
are fed with beans and grain.
Your internal management and self-enjoyment
extend to the kin of the inner palace.
How can you say you have no virtue?
However, I wish to make a request of you.
Take your intention
and your heart for self-enjoyment,
and extend them to be shared with the common people.
Then how could there be any starved corpses?
If you do not extend this,
and only manage your internal affairs and favor your private interests,
causing wealth and goods to be gathered in one place,
and beans, grain, and silks to rot in the granaries and treasuries,
while your kindness is not spread to the common people,
and your public spirit does not encompass the ten thousand states,
then this is why Jié and Zhòu perished.
The reason the officials and people rebel
is because of this partiality.
If you examine the words of your servant Yīng
and extend your abundant virtue,
spreading it impartially to the world,
then the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ can be achieved.
Why should a single starved corpse be a cause for worry?”
14.7 Chǔ Gòng Wáng went out hunting and lost his bow.
His attendants requested to search for it.
Gòng Wáng said:
“Stop.
A man of Chǔ lost a bow,
and a man of Chǔ will find it.
Why search for it further?”
Zhòng Ní heard of this and said:
“It is a pity that his mind was not greater!
He should have said:
‘A person lost a bow,
and a person will find it,’ and that is all.
Why must it be Chǔ?”
This is what Zhòng Ní called supreme impartiality.
14.8 Wàn Zhāng asked, saying:
“In Wèi, Kǒngzǐ stayed with Yōng Jū,
and in Qí, he stayed with the eunuch Jǐ Huán;
was it so?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“No,
it was not so.
Those who love gossip fabricated this.
In Wèi, he stayed with Yán Chóuyóu.
The wife of Mí Zǐ and the wife of Zǐlù
were sisters.
Mí Zǐ said to Zǐlù:
‘If Kǒngzǐ stays with me,
he can obtain the position of high minister in Wèi.’
Zǐlù reported this.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘There is fate.’
Kǒngzǐ advanced according to ritual
and withdrew according to righteousness;
whether he obtained a position or not,
he said, ‘There is fate.’
But to stay with Yōng Jū and the eunuch Jǐ Huán would be to disregard fate.
Kǒngzǐ was not pleased in Lǔ and Wèi,
and was about to go to Sòng
when he encountered Huán Sīmǎ,
who intended to intercept and kill him.
He passed through Sòng in plain clothes.
This was a time of hardship for Kǒngzǐ.
He stayed with the Sīchéng Zhēn Zǐ while serving as a minister to Zhōu, the Marquis of Chén.
I have heard that
one judges a minister close to the court by the ruler he serves,
and one judges a minister from afar by whom he stays with.
If Kǒngzǐ had stayed with Yōng Jū and the eunuch Jǐ Huán,
how could he be Kǒngzǐ?”
14.9 The Master traveled and spoke to seventy feudal lords without a fixed place to stay,
desiring to let the people of the world each find their proper place,
yet his Way was not practiced.
He retired to compile the *Chūnqiū*,
collecting even the slightest goodness
and censuring even the smallest evil.
Human affairs were fully covered,
and the Kingly Way was made complete.
With refined harmony and sage-like regulations,
he communicated above with Heaven and the Qílín arrived;
this was Heaven’s recognition of the Master.
Thereupon he sighed deeply and said:
“Does Heaven consider supreme brilliance as something that cannot be obscured?
Why then do solar eclipses occur?
Does Earth consider supreme stability as something that cannot be endangered?
Why then do earthquakes happen?
If Heaven and Earth still experience disturbances and obscurations,
it is because worthy sages speak to the world but cannot practice their Way,
and thus calamities and anomalies occur together.”
The Master said:
“I do not resent Heaven,
nor do I blame men.
I study below and reach above.
Is it not Heaven that knows me?”
14.10 Kǒngzǐ was born in a chaotic age,
and no one could accommodate him.
Therefore, if his words were followed by a ruler
and his benevolence reached the people,
only then would he take office;
if his words were not followed by a ruler
and his benevolence did not reach the people, then he remained in retirement.
Kǒngzǐ harbored a heart that covered all like Heaven
and possessed the virtue of benevolence and sageliness.
Pitying the filth of the times and customs,
and grieving over the ruin of the guiding principles,
he took on heavy burdens and traveled far,
wandering around responding to invitations,
waiting for an opportunity to implement the Way to treat the people as his children,
but the feudal lords of that age were unable to employ him.
Thus his virtue accumulated but was not displayed,
and the Great Way was bent and not extended.
Those within the four seas did not receive his transformation,
and the living beings were not covered by his grace.
Therefore he sighed deeply and said:
“If there were someone to employ me,
then might I not make it an Eastern Zhōu?”
Thus Kǒngzǐ traveled and spoke,
not desiring to privately exercise his virtue within a single city,
but wishing to spread it throughout the world
and establish it among all living beings.
14.11 Qín and Jìn were at war,
facing each other as enemies.
Qín sent someone to tell the Jìn general:
“The soldiers of the three armies have not yet rested;
I request to fight again tomorrow.”
Yú Pián said:
“The messenger’s eyes moved and his speech was reckless;
he fears us
and is about to flee.
If we press them toward the river,
we will certainly defeat them.”
Zhào Dùn said:
“To abandon the dead and wounded without collecting them
is not kind;
to not wait for the appointed time and press people into danger
is not courageous.
Please wait.”
The Qín people fled that night.
14.12 Zǐxū was about to go to Wú
and took leave of his friend Shēn Bāoxū, saying:
“After three years,
if Chǔ has not perished,
I shall not see you again.”
Shēn Bāoxū said:
“You should strive for your goal.
I cannot assist you;
to assist you would be to attack my ancestral temple.
To stop you would mean we cannot be friends.
Even so,
if you destroy it,
I shall preserve it.”
Thus one watched Chǔ's destruction and its preservation.
Three years later,
the Wú army attacked Chǔ,
and King Zhāo fled.
Shēn Bāoxū acted without a formal mandate
and went west to see the Earl of Qín, saying:
“Wú lacks the Way;
its army is strong and its people numerous.
It intends to conquer the world,
starting with Chǔ.
My humble ruler has fled
and is staying in Yúnmèng.
He sent me, his subject, to report the emergency.”
Duke Āi said:
“Yes,
I will certainly plan for it.”
Shēn Bāoxū did not leave the court;
he stood in the Qín court
and wept day and night;
for seven days and seven nights his voice did not cease.
Duke Āi said:
“With a minister such as this,
can we not save them?”
He raised an army to save Chǔ.
The Wú people heard of this
and led their troops back.
King Zhāo returned,
and wanted to enfeoff Shēn Bāoxū.
Shēn Bāoxū declined, saying:
“To save from destruction
was not for the sake of fame.
To receive rewards after success is achieved
is to sell one’s courage.”
He declined and did not accept,
then retired into seclusion
and was not seen for the rest of his life.
The *Shī* says:
“Whenever the people have a misfortune,
crawl on hands and knees to save them.”
14.13 The *Chǔ Lìngyǐn Yúqiūzǐ* reported to *Zhuāngwáng*, saying:
"I have heard that by serving the public and following the law,
one may attain honor;
if one's abilities are shallow and conduct is thin,
one should not hope for high position;
if one is not known for benevolence and wisdom,
one should not seek prominence and glory;
where talent is not manifest,
one should not occupy that post.
I have been *Lìngyǐn* for ten years,
yet the state is no better governed,
litigation does not cease,
reclusive scholars are not promoted,
and excessive calamities go unpunished.
To occupy a high position for a long time,
blocking the path of the many worthy,
enjoying the salary while doing nothing,
and being insatiably greedy—
my crimes should be investigated by the authorities.
I have privately selected a talent of the state,
a scholar from the lower villages named *Sūnshū Áo*,
who is lean but multi-talented.
His nature is without desire.
If my Lord raises him and entrusts him with the administration,
then the state can be made orderly,
and the scholars and people can be made to follow."
*Zhuāngwáng* said:
"Since you have assisted me,
I have been able to grow within the Central States,
my orders are carried out in distant lands,
and I have become hegemon over the feudal lords.
Without you, how could this be?"
*Yúqiūzǐ* said:
"To hold onto salary and position for a long time
is greed;
not to advance the worthy and promote the capable
is deception;
not to yield one's position
is a lack of integrity.
To fail in these three
is disloyalty.
If a servant is disloyal,
how can the Lord use him as a servant?
I wish to firmly resign."
*Zhuāngwáng* followed his advice,
granted *Yúqiūzǐ* three hundred units of fief land,
titled him "*Guó lǎo*",
and made *Sūnshū Áo* the *Lìngyǐn*.
Shortly after,
the family of *Yúqiūzǐ* violated the law.
*Sūnshū Áo* seized and executed them.
*Yúqiūzǐ* was pleased
and went in to see the King,
saying:
"I spoke of *Sūnshū Áo*;
indeed he can be made to handle the state administration.
He upholds the state law without being partisan,
and carries out punishments and executions without deviation;
he can be called fair."
*Zhuāngwáng* said:
"It is indeed your gift!"
14.14 *Zhào Xuānzǐ* spoke of *Hán Xiànzǐ* to the Marquis of *Jìn*, saying:
"His character is non-partisan,
he governs the masses without disorder,
and he faces death without fear."
The Marquis of *Jìn* made him the *Zhōngjūn Wèi*.
In the campaign of *Héqu*,
*Zhào Xuānzǐ*'s chariot broke the ranks.
*Hán Xiànzǐ* executed his driver.
Everyone said:
"*Hán Xiànzǐ* will surely die.
His master promoted him in the morning and by evening he executes his master's driver;
who could tolerate that?"
When the campaign was over,
*Zhào Xuānzǐ* hosted a banquet for the Grand Masters.
After the cups had circulated three times,
he said:
"You gentlemen may congratulate me."
The gentlemen said:
"We do not know what to congratulate."
*Xuānzǐ* said:
"I spoke of *Hán Jué* to the Lord;
had my words been inappropriate,
I would certainly have suffered punishment.
Now that my chariot lost its place and he executed my driver,
he can be called non-partisan.
Thus my words were appropriate."
The gentlemen bowed twice and kowtowed, saying:
"Not only does the state of *Jìn* benefit from this,
but even *Tángshǔ* relies on this.
How could we dare not bow twice and kowtow?"
14.15 *Jìn Wéngōng* asked *Jiù Fàn*:
"Who can be made the Governor of *Xīhé*?"
*Jiù Fàn* replied:
"*Yú Zǐgāo* is suitable."
The Duke said:
"Is *Zǐgāo* not your enemy?"
He replied:
"My Lord asked who could be the Governor,
not who is my enemy."
*Zǐgāo* saw *Jiù Fàn* and thanked him,
saying:
"Fortunately you forgave my faults
and recommended me to the Lord
to be the Governor of *Xīhé*."
*Jiù Fàn* said:
"The one who recommended you
did so for the public;
the one who resents you
does so for private reasons.
I do not let private matters harm public righteousness.
You should leave now;
if you look back,
I will shoot you."
14.16 *Chǔ Wénwáng* attacked *Dèng*,
and sent *Wángzǐ Gé* and *Wángzǐ Líng* to gather vegetables together.
As the two went out to pick,
they saw an old man carrying a basket.
They begged for it,
but he would not give it.
They struck him and snatched the basket.
The King heard of this,
ordered both sons to be detained,
and was going to kill them.
The Grand Masters pleaded, saying:
"Taking a basket
is indeed a crime,
but killing them
is not a punishment for such a crime.
Why should my Lord kill them?"
When the words were finished,
the old man reached the army and spoke, saying:
"*Dèng* was attacked because it was unprincipled;
now the sons of the Lord have struck me and snatched my basket,
which is more unprincipled than *Dèng*."
He called out to heaven and wailed.
The King heard this.
The ministers were afraid.
The King saw him
and said:
"To punish the guilty while committing robbery
is not how to stop violence;
to rely on strength to abuse the elderly
is not how to teach the young;
to favor sons and abandon the law
is not how to preserve the state.
To favor the two sons
while destroying the three conducts
is not how to govern.
Old man, let it go.
I shall apologize to you outside the army gates."
14.17 Among the kinsmen of the Chǔ Lìngyǐn Zǐwén,
there was one who violated the law.
The Tínglǐ detained him,
but upon hearing that he was of the Lìngyǐn’s kin, he released him.
Zǐwén summoned the Tínglǐ and rebuked him,
saying:
“Whenever a Tínglǐ is appointed,
it is to oversee those who violate the King’s orders and to investigate those who infringe upon the state’s laws.
An upright man upholds the law;
he is flexible but does not bend,
firm but does not break.
Now you discard the law and betray orders by releasing a lawbreaker;
this is acting as a judge without integrity
and harboring a heart that is not impartial.
Could this be my intention to seek private gain?
Why does the Tínglǐ deviate from the law?
I hold a high position to lead the officers and people.
If the officers and people have grievances
and I cannot exempt them from the law,
now that my kinsman has clearly broken the law,
and you allow the Tínglǐ to release him based on my private interests,
then my lack of impartiality will be clearly manifested in the state.
To hold the power of a whole state
yet be known for private interests—
rather than living without righteousness,
it is better that I die.”
He then delivered his kinsman to the Tínglǐ, saying:
“If this person is not punished,
I shall die for it.”
The Tínglǐ was afraid
and subsequently punished the kinsman.
Chéng Wáng heard of this,
and before he could even put on his shoes, he arrived at Zǐwén’s house, saying:
“I am young
and failed in appointing the right person as Tínglǐ,
thereby going against your intentions, Master.”
Thereupon, he dismissed the Tínglǐ and honored Zǐwén,
putting him in charge of internal affairs.
When the people of the state heard of this, they said:
“With a Lìngyǐn as impartial as this,
what does our community have to worry about!”
They then joined together to sing:
“The kin of Zǐwén
violated the state’s legal code.
The Tínglǐ released him,
but Zǐwén would not allow it.
Caring for the people and watching for the sprouts of grievance,
he is upright, fair, and impartial.”
14.18 Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng had a law regarding the Máomén:
“When the various ministers, high officials, and princes enter the court,
if their horses’ hooves trample the threshold eaves,
the Tínglǐ shall cut their carriage shafts and execute their drivers.”
The Crown Prince entered the court,
and his horses’ hooves trampled the threshold eaves.
The Tínglǐ cut his carriage shaft and executed his driver.
The Crown Prince was greatly enraged
and went in to weep before the King, saying:
“Execute the Tínglǐ for me.”
The King said:
“The law
is that by which we respect the ancestral temple and honor the altars of soil and grain.
Therefore, one who can establish laws and follow orders,
thereby respecting the altars of soil and grain,
is a minister of the state;
how can he be executed?
Now, to violate the law and discard orders,
failing to respect the altars of soil and grain,
is for a minister to override his lord
and for a subordinate to encroach upon his superior.
If a minister overrides his lord, the ruler loses his authority;
if a subordinate encroaches upon his superior, the high position is endangered.
If the altars of soil and grain are not protected,
what shall I leave to my descendants?”
The Crown Prince then withdrew to his quarters,
bowed twice, and requested his own death.
14.19 In the time of Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng,
the Crown Prince’s carriage was standing inside the Máomén,
and Shǎoshī Qìng drove it away.
The Crown Prince was angry,
went in to see the King, and said:
“Shǎoshī Qìng drove my carriage away.”
The King said:
“Leave it be.
He does not overstep when an old ruler is before him,
and he does not show negligence when a young ruler is behind him;
he is a precious minister of the state.”
14.20 Wú Wáng Hélú was going to raise an army for Wǔ Zǐxū to seek revenge against Chǔ.
Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
“A feudal lord does not raise an army for a common man.
Furthermore, serving a ruler is like serving a father;
to diminish the ruler’s righteousness
in order to avenge a father’s grievance
is something I will not do.”
Thereupon, he stopped.
Later, he eventually avenged his father’s grievance through official matters.
One such as Zǐxū can be said to not pursue private ends through public affairs.
14.21 When Kǒngzǐ was the Sīkòu of Lǔ,
in hearing legal cases, he always followed the guidance of the assembly.
They all stood in a solemn and sincere manner,
and then the Master would step forward and ask:
“What does such-and-such a person think?”
Such-and-such a person would state their opinion.
He would also ask:
“What does such-and-such a person think?”
Such-and-such a person would state their opinion.
When the matter was fully debated,
then the Master would say:
“Perhaps we should follow what such-and-such a person said.”
Given the wisdom of a Master,
why would he need to wait for such-and-such a person’s words
before knowing how to decide a case?
It was the Master’s way of being respectful and yielding;
when there is knowledge or wisdom that can be shared with others,
a Master does not keep it solely for himself.
14.22 When Zǐgāo was in charge of the administration of Wèi,
he had a man’s foot amputated.
When the ruler and ministers of Wèi fell into disorder,
Zǐgāo fled to the Guómén.
The Guómén was closed.
The amputee was guarding the gate
and said:
“There is a breach over there.”
Zǐgāo said:
“A gentleman does not climb over walls.”
The man said:
“There is a hole over there.”
Zǐgāo said:
“A gentleman does not crawl through holes.”
The man said:
“There is a room here.”
Zǐgāo went in.
When the pursuers gave up,
and Zǐgāo was about to leave,
he said to the amputee:
“I could not diminish the lord’s laws and orders,
and thus personally ordered your foot amputated.
Now that I am in trouble,
this is your time to seek revenge,
so why did you help me escape?”
The amputee said:
“Having my foot severed was indeed due to my own crime;
there was nothing to be done.
When you judged me,
you examined the laws and orders carefully,
applying the law to me repeatedly from every angle,
wishing for me to be exempted from the law;
I knew this.
When the trial was decided and the crime fixed,
and it was time to pronounce the punishment,
you looked sorrowful and unhappy;
it was visible in your face.
I knew this as well.
Could it be that you were partial to me?
Heaven-born benevolence in a person’s heart
is naturally so;
this is why I helped you escape.”
Kǒngzǐ heard of this
and said:
“One who is good at being an official plants virtue;
one who is not good at being an official plants resentment.
To act with impartiality—
surely this refers to Zǐgāo!”
15.1 The Sīmǎ Fǎ says:
“Though a state may be large,
if it loves war, it will surely perish;
though the world may be at peace,
if it forgets war, it will surely be in danger.”
The Yì says:
“The gentleman repairs his weapons to guard against the unforeseen.”
Weapons are not to be played with;
if played with, they lose their authority.
Weapons are not to be abandoned;
if abandoned, they invite invaders.
In the past, Wú Wáng Fūchāi loved war and perished,
while Xú Yǎnwáng lacked martial strength and was also destroyed.
Therefore, when a wise king governs a state,
those above do not play with weapons,
and those below do not abandon martial readiness.
The Yì says:
“In times of survival, do not forget the possibility of ruin.”
Thus, one’s person is safe and the state can be preserved.
15.2 Qín Zhāo Wáng sighed during a court session and said:
“The swords of Chǔ are sharp,
but their entertainers are unskilled.
When swords are sharp, the soldiers are mostly fierce and brave;
when entertainers are unskilled, then their thoughts and considerations are far-reaching.
I fear that Chǔ is plotting against Qín.”
This is what is called thinking of misfortune when things are auspicious
and not forgetting the possibility of ruin in times of survival;
in the end, he succeeded in achieving hegemony.
15.3 Wángsūn Lì spoke to Chǔ Wén Wáng, saying:
"Xú Yǎn Wáng enjoys practicing the way of benevolence and righteousness.
In Hàndōng, thirty-two vassal states have all submitted to him.
If Your Majesty does not attack him,
Chǔ will surely serve Xú."
The King said:
"If he truly possesses the Way,
he cannot be attacked."
Lì replied:
"The great attacking the small
and the strong attacking the weak
is like a big fish swallowing a small fish,
or like a tiger eating a piglet.
How could there be no justification for it?"
Wén Wáng then raised an army to attack Xú
and destroyed it.
As Xú Yǎn Wáng was about to die,
he said:
"I relied upon civil virtue
but was not clear about military preparation;
I enjoyed practicing the way of benevolence and righteousness
but did not understand the hearts of deceitful men,
and thus I have come to this!"
Indeed, should the kings of old not have preparations!
15.4 Wú Qǐ served as the governor of Yuàn.
While touring the county
and arriving at Xī,
he asked Qū Yíjiù:
"The King did not know that Qǐ was unworthy
and appointed me governor of Yuàn.
What will you, sir, teach me?"
Qū Gōng did not reply.
After one year had passed,
the King appointed him Lìngyǐn.
While touring the county
and arriving at Xī,
he asked Qū Yíjiù:
"Qǐ asked you before,
but you, sir, would not teach me.
Now the King does not know that Qǐ is unworthy
and has made me Lìngyǐn.
Please watch, sir, how Qǐ performs the role."
Qū Gōng asked:
"What do you intend to do?"
Wú Qǐ said:
"I intend to equalize the noble ranks of the state of Chǔ and level their stipends;
