I will reduce those who have a surplus and supplement those who are deficient;
I will sharpen the armor and weapons to contend for the world in a timely manner."
Qū Gōng said:
"I have heard that
in the past, those who were good at governing a state did not change its old ways
and did not alter its constants.
Now you intend to equalize the ranks of Chǔ and level their stipends,
reducing the surplus and supplementing the deficient;
this is changing the old ways and altering the constants.
Furthermore, I have heard that
weapons are ominous tools
and contention is a violation of virtue.
Now you are plotting to violate virtue
and enjoy using ominous tools;
this is something people generally despise
and is the height of perversity.
These are matters of excess and dissipation;
those who practice them will find no advantage.
Moreover, when you used the troops of Lǔ,
you should not have succeeded against Qí,
yet you did succeed.
When you used the troops of Wèi,
you should not have succeeded against Qín,
yet you did succeed.
I have heard it said:
'Unless one is a man of calamity, one cannot bring calamity to fruition.'
I used to wonder why my King frequently violated the Way of Heaven
and yet has suffered no disaster until now.
Alas!
He was simply waiting for you, sir."
Wú Qǐ asked fearfully:
"Can it still be changed?"
Qū Gōng said:
"It cannot!"
Wú Qǐ said:
"I will then plan for myself."
Qū Gōng said:
"One whose form is already set
cannot be changed.
You would be better off dwelling sincerely and acting with earnestness;
in the state of Chǔ, nothing is more valued than promoting the worthy."
15.5 The Chūnqiū records the survival and destruction of states to provide observation for future generations.
Although one may have vast territory and a large population,
sturdy armor and sharp weapons,
and fierce, brave generals,
if the officers and soldiers are not closely attached to their leader,
one cannot achieve victory or success in battle.
Jìn Hóu was captured at Hán;
Chǔ Zǐyù and Déchén were defeated at Chéngpú;
and the people of Cài collapsed without even facing the enemy.
Therefore, the saying goes:
"Wén Wáng could not employ people who were not attached to him;
Xiān Zhěn could not fight with soldiers who were not trained;
Zàofù and Wáng Liáng could not use worn-out chariots and uncooperative horses to travel swiftly and reach distant places;
Yì and Pángméng could not use crooked arrows and weak bows to shoot far and hit a minute target."
Thus, the key to strength or weakness and success or failure
lies solely in attaching the officers and soldiers and training them.
15.6 If internal governance is not achieved,
one cannot rectify the external;
if the fundamental kindness has not been established,
one cannot control the peripheral.
Therefore, the Chūnqiū prioritizes the capital and then the Zhūxià,
prioritizes the Zhūhuá and then the Yídí.
When it came to Zhōu Huì Wáng,
he encountered a chaotic era.
He succeeded to the position of the former kings,
yet the power of Chǔ claimed kingship
and the vassal lords rebelled.
He wished to assert the mandates of the former kings
and unify the world,
but he did not first broadly nurture the capital and then the Zhūxià,
or the Zhūxià and then the Yídí.
His internal governance was not achieved,
and in his anger, he did not estimate his strength
or weigh the gains and losses.
He raised an army to punish the powerful Chǔ,
but his forces were greatly defeated.
His prestige was diminished, his orders were not followed,
and he was greatly mocked by the world.
Fortuitously, he met Qí Huán Gōng,
through whom his dignity was secured.
Therefore, if internal governance is not achieved,
one cannot rectify the external;
if the fundamental kindness has not been established,
one cannot control the peripheral.
15.7 Regarding generals and commanders who receive their mandates:
The general enters,
and the military officers all enter;
they all face north and bow twice, touching their heads to the ground to receive the mandate.
The Son of Heaven faces south and confers the battle-axe to him.
The general moves east,
and the King faces west and bows to him,
showing that he will not command him.
Thus, once he receives the mandate and departs,
he forgets his state;
when he goes to battle,
he forgets his family;
when he hears the sound of the drums and drumsticks,
fearing only that he will not be victorious,
he forgets himself.
Therefore, he is certain to die.
To be certain to die is not as good as being happy to die;
to be happy to die is not as good as finding death sweet;
to find death sweet is not as good as dying for righteousness;
to die for righteousness is not as good as regarding death as a return home.
This is what is meant.
Thus, if one person is certain to die,
ten people cannot withstand him;
if ten people are certain to die,
a hundred people cannot withstand them;
if a hundred people are certain to die,
a thousand people cannot withstand them;
if a thousand people are certain to die,
ten thousand people cannot withstand them;
if ten thousand people are certain to die,
they may march across the world.
When orders are followed and prohibitions are obeyed,
it is the army of a true king.
15.8 Tián Dān was the Senior General of Qí.
Raising an army of one hundred thousand,
he intended to attack Dí.
He went to see Lǔ Zhònglián Zǐ.
Zhònglián Zǐ said:
“General, in your attack on Dí, you will certainly be unable to take it.”
General Tián said:
“I, Dān, with a city of five lǐ
and an outer wall of ten lǐ,
restored the state of Qí.
Why should I be unable to take Dí?”
He left,
boarded his carriage without speaking to him further,
and resolutely attacked Dí.
After three months, he was unable to take it.
The children of Qí sang a nursery rhyme about him, saying:
“Large caps like winnowing baskets,
long swords propping up the chin.
Attacking Dí but unable to take it,
entrenched at Wǔqiū.”
At this, General Tián was struck with fear
and went to see Zhònglián Zǐ, saying:
“How did you, Master, know that my attack on Dí would not succeed?”
Zhònglián Zǐ said:
“When you, General, were in Jímò,
when sitting you would weave straw mats,
and when standing you would lean on a shovel.
You led the soldiers,
saying:
‘There is nowhere else to go!
Our ancestral temples are lost!
Our souls are perished!
To what clan could we return?’
Thus you, General, had the intent to die,
and your soldiers had no desire for life;
this is how you conquered.
Now, General, to the east you have the fief of Yè Yì,
and to the west you have the treasures of the Zī River.
With gold and silver and yellow belts,
you gallop between the Zī and Shèng rivers.
Thus you love life and loathe death.”
The next day, General Tián bound up his hair,
went directly to stand where arrows and stones could reach,
and took up the mallet to beat the drum.
The people of Dí then surrendered to him.
Therefore, the general
is the heart of the soldiers;
the soldiers
are the limbs of the general.
If the heart is hesitant, the limbs will not be used.
Does this not refer to General Tián?
15.9 Zhì Bó of Jìn attacked Zhèng.
Tián Héng of Qí went to rescue it.
If there were canopies to be raised,
he would surely stand there himself.
If there were soldiers or carriages that could not advance,
he would surely order that they be helped.
Only after the ramparts were completed did he dare to rest;
only after the wells and stoves were finished did he dare to eat.
Zhì Bó said:
“I have heard that Tián Héng has newly gained the state and loves its people.
Internally he shares his wealth with them,
and externally he shares their hard labor.
If he governs the army like this,
he has gained the masses;
we cannot wait for them to fail.”
Thereupon he departed.
15.10 The *Tàigōng Bīngfǎ* says:
“Extend a heart of benevolence and love,
establish a battle of martial awe,
to fully engage the masses.
Train the elite,
sharpen their integrity,
to heighten their spirit.
Divide them into five selections,
distinguish their flags and insignia,
and do not let them become confused or disorderly.
Strengthen their formations,
link their squads of ten and five,
to prohibit misconduct.”
The order of the ramparts and ranks,
the positions of carriages and cavalry,
and the disposition of the troops.
The laws and orders of the army,
and the system of rewards and punishments,
which make the soldiers rush into fire and tread on blades,
break through formations and capture generals,
dying without turning back—
these are very different from the generals of today.
15.11 During the time of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
the Imperial Censor supervising the North Army committed a transgression,
piercing the wall of the North Gate to make a marketplace.
Hú Jiàn held the post of Commandant of the North Army.
He was poor and had no carriage or horse.
He often walked and lived among the infantry,
so he comforted and loved the infantry very deeply.
Hú Jiàn wished to execute the Imperial Censor,
so he made an agreement with his infantry, saying:
“I wish to execute someone with you;
when I say to seize him, seize him;
when I say to behead him, behead him.”
Thereupon, on the day for selecting soldiers and horses,
when the various colonels of the Protective Army sat in a row upon the grand hall,
and the Imperial Censor also sat there,
Hú Jiàn followed by his infantry
hurried to the base of the hall and paid his respects.
He then went up to the hall;
the infantry all followed him up.
Hú Jiàn knelt and pointed at the Imperial Censor,
saying:
“Seize him.”
The infantry stepped forward and dragged him down from the hall.
Hú Jiàn said:
“Behead him.”
And so they beheaded the Imperial Censor.
The Protective Army and the various colonels were all shocked and alarmed,
not knowing why.
Hú Jiàn already had a completed memorial in his sleeve,
and so he submitted the memorial to report it,
saying:
“Your servant has heard that in military law,
one establishes martial force to overawe the masses,
and executes the wicked to prohibit evil.
Now the Imperial Censor of the North Army has openly pierced the army's wall to seek profit from trade,
privately buying and selling to market with the soldiers.
He did not establish a heart of resolve and martiality,
or an intent of bravery and fierceness
to lead the officers and men.
This is especially unreasonable and unjust.
Your servant has heard that the *Huángdì Lǐfǎ* says:
‘Once the ramparts and walls are completed,
if one’s movement does not follow the roads,
he is called a person of treachery;
treacherous persons are to be killed.’
Your servant has respectfully beheaded him,
and braving death, I report this.”
The imperial decree said:
“The *Sīmǎ Fǎ* says:
‘The etiquette of the state does not enter the army,
and the etiquette of the army does not enter the state.’
Why should Hú Jiàn have any doubt about this?”
Because of this, Hú Jiàn’s name became famous.
Later he became the Magistrate of Wèichéng
and died.
To this day, Wèichéng has a shrine for him.
15.12 Regarding the sword of Lǔ Shígōng,
it can respond when pressed
and can move when stimulated.
It is infinitely profound and subtle,
its changes have no fixed form.
Gentle and yielding in compliance,
it is like a shadow and an echo.
Like a shaggy dog guarding a door,
like a wheel following a horse,
an echo responding to a sound,
or a shadow resembling a form.
A blink of the eye is not fast enough to reach the impact,
a call is not fast enough for a breath.
The lifting of a foot is not fast enough for its landing,
the distance between them is like a cicada’s wing.
Even in the subtle space above the arm or between the brow and eyelashes,
one cannot use the large to measure the small
or use the small to characterize the large.
Is the way of using troops
not just like this?
This is one who is good at facing an enemy.
Yet it does not reach the level of those who break the enemy’s momentum before it takes shape,
who bow and yield within the ancestral temple,
and bestow benefits upon millions of people.
Therefore, in dwelling there is no upheaval,
and in battle there is no blood on the blades.
Such were the armies of Tāng and Wǔ!
15.13 Kǒngzǐ was traveling in the north
and ascended Mount Nóng in the east;
Zǐlù, Zǐgòng, and Yányuān followed him there.
Kǒngzǐ sighed deeply and said:
"Looking down from a great height
makes one's heart feel sorrowful!
You two or three gentlemen,
each speak your aspirations,
and I, Qiū, shall listen to them."
Zǐlù said:
"I wish to have white feathers like the moon
and red feathers like the sun;
the sound of bells and drums
would be heard up in the heavens,
while flags and banners flutter,
sweeping down to the earth below.
I, Yóu, would lead an army to strike the enemy;
I would surely seize a thousand lǐ of territory,
a feat only I, Yóu, can achieve.
I would have these two gentlemen follow me as my subordinates."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What a brave soldier!
How full of ardor!"
Zǐgòng said:
"I, Cì, wish for Qí and Chǔ to engage in battle in a vast wilderness;
their two fortifications facing each other,
their flags and banners visible to one another,
and the dust of their armies meeting,
as they engage in combat.
I, Cì, wish to wear white robes and a white cap,
to mediate between their sharp blades,
resolving the troubles of the two states;
a feat only I, Cì, can achieve.
I would have these two gentlemen follow me as my subordinates."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What an eloquent soldier!
How graceful!"
Yányuān alone remained silent.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Come, Huí,
why do you alone have no wish?"
Yányuān said:
"Matters of civil and military affairs
have already been spoken of by these two gentlemen;
how would I, Huí, dare to interfere?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If your modest heart does not participate in theirs,
then just speak of it."
Yányuān said:
"I, Huí, have heard that salted fish and fragrant orchids are not stored in the same box,
and that Yáo, Shùn, Jié, and Zhòu do not rule in the same state;
the words of these two gentlemen differ from mine.
I, Huí, wish to find an enlightened king or a sagely ruler to assist,
so that city walls need not be repaired,
moats and ditches need not be crossed,
and swords and halberds are forged into farming tools,
ensuring the world has no troubles of war for a thousand years.
If it were so, why would Yóu need to strike with such ardor,
and why would Cì need to act as an envoy with such grace?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How beautiful is such virtue!
How exalted!"
Zǐlù raised his hand and asked:
"I wish to hear the Master's intention."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What I wish for
is the plan of the Yán family.
I wish to take up my robes and cap and follow the son of the Yán family."
15.14 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zhòngní:
"If I wish to defend when small
and attack when large,
what is the way to do so?"
Zhòngní said:
"If the court possesses ritual,
and those above and below have affection for one another,
then the multitude of people are all the ruler's own;
whom then would the ruler attack?
If the court lacks ritual
and those above and below have no affection,
then the multitude of people are all the ruler's enemies;
with whom then would the ruler defend?"
Thereupon, the Duke abolished the prohibitions on marshes and bridges
and relaxed the taxes on passes and markets
to provide benefits to the people.
15.15 King Wén said:
"I wish to use the military;
whom can I attack?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"The Mìxūshì clan is suspicious of us;
we can go and attack them first."
Guǎnshū said:
"That is not possible;
their ruler is an enlightened ruler of the world;
to attack him would be unrighteous."
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"I have heard
that the former kings attacked the crooked and not the straight,
the treacherous and not the easy,
and those who were excessive rather than those who fell short."
King Wén said:
"Excellent."
He then attacked the Mìxūshì clan
and destroyed them.
15.16 King Wǔ was about to attack Zhòu;
he summoned Tàigōng Wàng and asked him:
"I wish to know of victory without fighting,
and to know of good fortune without divination;
even if I am not the right person,
is there a way to achieve this?"
Tàigōng replied:
"There is a way.
If the King gains the hearts of the people to plan against the unprincipled,
then he will know of victory without fighting;
if he uses the worthy to attack the unworthy,
then he will know of good fortune without divination;
if the enemy harms them
and I benefit them,
even if they are not my people,
I can gain them to serve me."
King Wǔ said:
"Excellent."
He then summoned Zhōugōng and asked him,
saying:
"Those who plan affairs in the world
all regard Yīn as the Son of Heaven
and Zhōu as a vassal lord;
if a vassal lord attacks the Son of Heaven,
is there a way to be victorious?"
Zhōugōng replied:
"If Yīn acts as a true Son of Heaven
and Zhōu acts as a true vassal lord,
then there is no way to be victorious;
how could one attack then?"
King Wǔ said indignantly:
"Is there an explanation for what you say?"
Zhōugōng replied:
"I have heard
that he who attacks ritual is a thief,
and he who attacks righteousness is a bandit.
One who has lost his people
is reduced to a mere commoner.
Your Majesty is attacking one who has lost his people;
how is that attacking the Son of Heaven?"
King Wǔ said:
"Excellent."
He then raised the multitudes and mobilized the army,
fighting the Yīn at the wilds of Mù,
and greatly defeated the Yīn people.
He ascended the hall and saw jade,
saying:
"Whose jade is this?"
It was said:
"The jade of the vassal lords."
He immediately took it and returned it to the vassal lords.
When the world heard this, they said:
"King Wǔ is incorruptible regarding wealth."
He entered the chambers and saw women,
saying:
"Whose daughters are these?"
It was said:
"The daughters of the vassal lords."
He immediately took them and returned them to the vassal lords;
when the world heard this, they said:
"King Wǔ is incorruptible regarding lust."
Thereupon, he distributed the grain from Jùqiáo
and dispersed the gold and money from Lùtái to give to the soldiers and people;
he retired his war chariots and did not ride them,
and laid aside his armor and weapons and did not use them;
he released the horses at Huàshān
and let the oxen go at Táolín,
showing they would not be used again.
All those in the world who heard of it said that King Wǔ practiced righteousness throughout the world;
was it not truly grand!
15.17 King Wén wished to attack Chóng,
so he first made a proclamation saying:
"I have heard that Chónghóu Hǔ treats his father and elder brothers with contempt,
is disrespectful to the elders,
is not impartial in hearing legal cases,
is unfair in the distribution of wealth,
and the common people's strength is exhausted so they cannot get food or clothing.
I am coming to punish him,
solely for the sake of the people."
He then attacked Chóng,
ordering that no one be killed,
no houses be destroyed,
no wells be filled in,
no trees be cut down,
and no livestock be disturbed;
anyone who did not follow the orders would be put to death without pardon.
When the people of Chóng heard this,
they subsequently requested to surrender.
15.18 King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Chén,
and Wú came to its rescue.
It rained for ten days and ten nights.
When it cleared,
the Left Scribe Yǐ Xiàng said:
"Wú will surely arrive tonight.
Our armor is in disarray and the ramparts are ruined;
they will certainly press us.
Why not form ranks with drums and go out to await them?"
When the army of Wú arrived,
they saw the Chǔ army in formation and turned back.
The Left Scribe Yǐ Xiàng said:
"Pursue them."
Wú marched sixty lǐ without success.
When the King's exhausted soldiers were resting,
he indeed struck them
and greatly defeated the army of Wú.
15.19 During the time of Duke Huán of Qí,
there was heavy rain for ten decads.
Duke Huán wanted to attack Chǎo Líng.
Its city walls had not yet been repaired due to the rain.
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng brought the soldiers to the gate.
Duke Huán said:
"What are the troops for?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard that
when there is rain, there are matters to attend to.
Now Chǎo Líng cannot withstand the rain;
I request to attack it."
The Duke said:
"Good."
Thereupon he raised an army to attack it.
When they arrived,
the great army was arrayed outside,
but the soldiers were already within.
Duke Huán said:
"Could there be a sage there!"
Then he turned the banners and departed.
15.20 Sòng besieged Cáo but could not capture it.
Sī Mǎ Zǐ Yú said to the Lord:
"Wén Wáng attacked Chóng.
The army of Chóng fortified its city,
and for three decads did not surrender.
He retreated and cultivated teachings,
then attacked again,
and they surrendered from their ramparts.
Now, is it not possible that your virtue has some deficiency?
Why not retreat and cultivate teachings,
and only after your virtue is without deficiency should you take action?"
15.21 King Hé Lú of Wú fought with the people of Jīng at Bǎi Jǔ
and greatly defeated them.
Reaching the outskirts of Yǐng,
he defeated the people of Jīng five times.
Five of Hé Lú's ministers came forward to remonstrate, saying:
"To penetrate deeply for a far-reaching retribution
is not to Your Majesty's advantage.
Should Your Majesty not return?"
The five generals cut their own throats.
Hé Lú did not respond to them,
and the heads of the five men fell before his horse.
Hé Lú was afraid
and summoned Wǔ Zǐ Xū to ask him about it.
Zǐ Xū said:
"The five ministers were afraid.
But as for those who have been defeated five times,
their fear is even greater.
Your Majesty should advance a little further."
Thereupon he entered Yǐng.
To the south they reached the Jiāng,
to the north they reached Fāng Chéng;
an area of three thousand square lǐ
all submitted to Wú.
15.22 Tián Chéng Zǐ often contended with Zǎi Wǒ.
Zǎi Wǒ ambushed soldiers at night,
intending to attack Tián Chéng Zǐ.
He gave an order among the soldiers, saying:
"Do not rise until you see the pennon-standard."
Chī Yí Zǐ Pí heard of this
and told Tián Chéng Zǐ.
Tián Chéng Zǐ therefore used a pennon-standard to make Zǎi Wǒ's soldiers rise in order to attack him,
and thus he destroyed him.
15.23 Duke Huán of Qí went north to attack the Shān Róng tribe.
He requested troops from Lǔ,
but Lǔ did not provide them.
Duke Huán was angry
and was about to attack them.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"You must not.
We have already punished the northern feudal lords.
Now if we attack Lǔ again,
would that not be impermissible?
Lǔ will certainly serve Chǔ,
and thus with one move we lose two."
Duke Huán said:
"Good."
Thereupon he ceased the attack on Lǔ.
15.24 When sages govern the world,
they put civil virtue first and military force second.
In general, the raising of the military is for the non-submissive.
If cultural transformation does not change them,
only then is punishment applied.
For those whose base ignorance is unmoving,
whom pure virtue cannot transform,
only then is military force applied to them.
Formerly Yáo executed the Four Evils to punish wickedness;
Zhōu Gōng killed Guǎn and Cài to stop rebellion;
Zǐ Chǎn killed Dèng Xī to awe the extravagant;
Kǒng Zǐ beheaded Shào Zhèng Mǎo to change the masses.
If sycophants and thieves are not executed,
it is the way to chaos.
The Yì says:
"If you do not awe the small,
you cannot punish the great;
this is the fortune of the petty man."
15.25 The Five Emperors and Three Kings taught with benevolence and righteousness,
and the world was transformed.
Kǒng Zǐ also taught with benevolence and righteousness,
but why did the world not follow him?
Formerly the enlightened kings had sashes and crowns to honor the worthy,
and had axes and poleaxes to execute the wicked.
Therefore their rewards were most heavy and their punishments most deep,
and the world was transformed.
Kǒng Zǐ considered Yán Yuán worthy but had no means to reward him;
he considered Rǔ Bēi lowly but had no means to punish him.
Therefore the world did not follow.
For this reason, the Way is not established without authority,
and it does not proceed without power.
Only when the Way is respected does it proceed.
15.26 Kǒng Zǐ served as the Minister of Crime in Lǔ.
After seven days, he executed Shào Zhèng Mǎo beneath the Dōng Guān.
When his disciples heard of it, they hurried forward.
Those who arrived did not speak,
but their intent was all the same.
Zǐ Gòng arrived later,
hurried forward and said:
"That Shào Zhèng Mǎo
is a famous man of the state of Lǔ.
Since the Master has just begun to govern,
why have you executed him first?"
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"Cì,
this is beyond your reach.
There are five types of executions by a king,
and theft is not among them:
first, a heart that is discerning but treacherous;
second, speech that is false but eloquent;
third, conduct that is perverse but obstinate;
fourth, ambition that is foolish but broad;
fifth, following what is wrong and making it look attractive.
These five types all have the reputation of being discerning, wise, perceptive, and reaching,
but it is not their reality.
If one acts with falsehood,
then their knowledge is sufficient to move the masses,
and their strength is sufficient to stand alone.
This is the hero of treacherous men,
and they cannot but be executed.
If one possesses even one of these five,
then they cannot escape execution.
Now Shào Zhèng Mǎo possesses all of them,
and that is why I executed him first.
Long ago Tāng executed Zhú Mù,
Tài Gōng executed Pān Zhǐ,
Guǎn Zhòng executed Shǐ Fù Lǐ,
Zǐ Chǎn executed Dèng Xī.
These five men were all surely executed.
What is called executing them is not because they commit robbery by day
or bore through walls by night,
but because they are all people who subvert the state.
This is indeed what the gentleman doubts
and what the fool is confused by.
The Shī says:
'My anxious heart is full of sorrow,
I am hated by the group of petty men.'
This is what it refers to."
15.27 Wáng Mǎnshēng of Qí went to see Zhōugōng.
Zhōugōng came out to meet him
and said:
"Sir, you have come from afar at great cost;
with what will you instruct me?"
Wáng Mǎnshēng said:
"Those who speak of internal matters do so inside;
those who speak of external matters do so outside.
Now, shall we speak of internal matters
or external matters?"
Zhōugōng led him inside.
Wáng Mǎnshēng said:
"I respectfully request that a mat be spread."
Zhōugōng did not yet lead him to sit.
Wáng Mǎnshēng said:
"Those who speak of great matters sit;
those who speak of small matters lean.
Now, shall we speak of great matters
or small matters?"
Zhōugōng led him to sit.
Wáng Mǎnshēng sat down,
and Zhōugōng said:
"With what will you instruct me, Sir?"
Wáng Mǎnshēng said:
"I have heard that a Sage knows without speaking,
while those who are not Sages do not understand even if spoken to.
Now, do you wish for me to speak
or not to speak?"
Zhōugōng lowered his head and thought for a while, but did not respond.
Wáng Mǎnshēng took a brush and tablet and wrote:
"The state is in danger."
He held it against his chest.
Zhōugōng looked up, saw the writing, and said:
"Yes, yes,
I have respectfully heard your command!"
The next day, he executed Guǎn and Cài.
16.1 If a King knows how to preside over those below and govern the masses,
then the various ministers will be in awe and submit;
if he knows how to listen to words and receive affairs,
then he will not be obscured or deceived;
if he knows how to bring peace and benefit to the ten thousand people,
then all within the seas will certainly be settled;
if he knows how to serve those above with loyalty and filial piety,
then the conduct of ministers and sons will be complete.
In all instances where rulers are usurped or killed,
it is because they do not know the Way and its techniques to manage their ministers and subordinates.
16.2 Whenever officials are equal to their duties, affairs are well-governed;
when affairs are well-governed, benefits arise.
If they are not equal to their duties, affairs fall into disorder;
when affairs are in disorder, harm is produced.
16.3 The affairs of a hundred regions
and ten thousand changes emerge like spear points.
Some wish to maintain emptiness;
some wish to maintain substance.
Some like wandering afloat;
some like sincerity and certainty.
Some act with ease and leisure;
some act with the speed of a gust.
Viewed from this perspective,
the world cannot be made uniform,
yet the Sage King presides over the world and is able to unify it.
16.4 Intentions cannot be sharp in two directions at once;
affairs cannot both be at their peak.
That which flourishes there
must decline here;
that which is long on the left
must be short on the right;
one who likes to lie down late
cannot rise early.
16.5 The *luán* bells are set on the bit;
the *hé* bells are set on the crossbar.
When the horse moves, the *luán* bells ring;
when the *luán* bells ring, the *hé* bells respond;
this is the rhythm of travel.
16.6 Without wealth, one has nothing with which to be great;
without giving, one has nothing with which to unite kin.
If kin are distant, there is harm;
if one loses the masses, there is defeat.
To execute without teaching is called cruelty;
to demand completion without warning is called tyranny.
16.7 Water comes from the mountains and enters the sea;
crops grow in the fields and are stored in the granary.
When the Sage sees where something is born,
he then knows where it will return.
16.8 The Way of Heaven distributes in accordance with nature;
human affairs involve taking and giving.
Storing much without using it
is called a "storehouse of resentment";
therefore, things should not be hoarded.
16.9 A tree of one span
can support a house of a thousand *jūn*;
a five-inch bolt
controls opening and closing.
Is it that their material is sufficient for the task?
It is because they occupy the essential position.
16.10 Small pleasures harm righteousness;
small cleverness harms the Way;
small arguments harm governance;
a careless heart damages virtue.
Great governance is not treacherous.
16.11 Although the flood-dragon is divine,
it cannot leave its kind in broad daylight;
although a whirlwind is fast,
it cannot raise dust during cloudy rain.
16.12 Because a town was named Shèngmǔ,
Zéngzǐ would not enter it;
because a spring was named Dàoquán,
Kǒngzǐ would not drink from it.
They detested the names.
16.13 A woman's mouth
can cause one to flee;
a woman's beak
can cause death and defeat.
16.14 Not cultivating oneself
while seeking it from others
is called losing the natural order;
not governing one's interior
while cultivating the exterior
is called a great waste.
16.15 Carrying a heavy load while in danger,
then taking a whip and following it,
is not the way to maintain wholeness.
16.16 If a scholar lies across the road
with his four limbs uncovered,
it is not the scholar's fault;
it is the shame of those who possess the land.
16.17 When the ruler of a state is about to prosper,
Heaven bestows the Way upon him;
when a grand official is about to prosper,
Heaven bestows scholars upon him;
when a commoner is about to prosper,
he must have a good son.
16.18 With worthy teachers and good friends at one's side,
and the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, and *Yuè* displayed before one,
those who would cast them aside and do evil are few.
16.19 A righteous person does not deceive his own heart;
a benevolent person does not harm life.
16.20 If plans are leaked, there will be no success;
if a scheme is not established, the affair will not be completed.
16.21 A worthy scholar does not serve what he considers wrong,
and does not consider wrong that which he serves.
16.22 A fool's conduct becomes even more stubborn through interference;
a vulgar person becomes even more coarse through affected deception.
16.23 No sound is so small as to be unheard;
no conduct is so hidden as to not be manifest.
16.24 There is nothing the utmost divine cannot transform;
there is nothing the utmost worthy cannot shift.
16.25 If the superior is not trusted
and the inferior is not loyal,
and those above and below are not in harmony,
though they may be safe, they will certainly be in danger.
16.26 If one seeks using the proper Way, nothing is not obtained;
if one acts according to the proper time, nothing is not completed.
16.27 If the time has not arrived,
one cannot force growth;
if an affair is not thoroughly investigated,
one cannot force success.
16.28 If the upright and good perish,
it is the remaining calamity of their ancestors;
if the reckless and impulsive survive,
it is the remaining merit of their ancestors.
16.29 Authority takes what is heavy;
grace takes what is long.
16.30 When talent and worthiness are given light responsibilities,
then there is fame;
when the unworthy are given great responsibilities,
they die and their names are ruined.
16.31 A scholar is not moved by profit
and does not change on account of hardship;
when matters of filial piety, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness are established,
he will die without regret.
16.32 To be wise yet use it for private ends
is not as good as being foolish yet using it for public ends;
therefore it is said:
"Skillful falsehood is not as good as clumsy sincerity."
16.33 Studying and questioning without tiring
is the means to govern oneself;
teaching and instructing without weariness
is the means to govern others;
the reason for valuing emptiness and nothingness
is to be able to respond to changes and harmonize with the times.
16.34 Although a cap is old,
it must be placed upon the head;
although shoes are new,
they must be put on the feet.
Between upper and lower there are distinct roles,
which must not be reversed.
16.35 A single heart can serve a hundred lords,
but a hundred hearts cannot serve a single lord.
Therefore it is said:
Be upright, have few desires, and speak little.
16.36 All things that obtain their root will live,
and all matters that obtain their Way (Dào) will succeed.
Where the Way (Dào) resides,
the world turns to it;
where virtue (Dé) resides,
the world prizes it;
where benevolence (Rén) resides,
the world loves it;
where righteousness (Yì) resides,
the world fears it.
When the roof leaks, the people leave it;
when the water is shallow, the fish flee from it;
when the tree is tall, the birds roost in it;
when virtue (Dé) is thick, the scholars flock to it;
when there is ritual propriety (Lǐ), the people revere it;
when there is loyalty (Zhōng) and trustworthiness (Xìn), the scholars would die for it.
16.37 Although clothes are tattered,
conduct must be cultivated;
although the hair is disheveled,
speech must be orderly.
16.38 Timing lies in responding to it;
action lies in following the circumstances.
16.39 If an attack is appropriate,
its blessings are fivefold;
if an attack is inappropriate,
its calamities are tenfold.
16.40 The noble must take the lowly as their root,
and the high must take the low as their foundation.
When Heaven is about to grant to someone,
it must first make them suffer;
when Heaven is about to destroy someone,
it must first burden them.
16.41 Be filial to parents,
and be trustworthy to friends.
In a marsh of ten paces,
there must be fragrant grass;
in a town of ten households,
there must be a loyal scholar.
16.42 When grass and trees die in autumn,
the pine and cypress alone remain;
while water floats all things,
jade and stone stay at the bottom.
16.43 When the hungry and thirsty obtain food,
who could not be joyful?
If one relieves the poor and saves those in emergency,
why worry about having nothing?
16.44 Look at his motives,
observe his methods,
and he can then be known.
16.45 Those who ride in a carriage with horses reach a thousand miles without toil;
those who use a boat and oars cross rivers and seas without swimming.
16.46 Wisdom is no greater than setting aside doubts;
conduct is no greater than being without regret.
16.47 By the arrangement of the residence and the naming of the sons,
one can sufficiently observe a scholar.
16.48 Profit is not doubled,
and rewards are not repeated.
16.49 Plans made in haste and confusion
cannot be carried out;
a heart full of fearful anxiety
must not be allowed to grow.
16.50 If Heaven gives and one does not take,
one will instead receive blame;
if the time arrives and one does not welcome it,
one will instead receive disaster.
16.51 The Way of Heaven (Tiāndào) has no favorites,
but always sides with the good person.
16.52 The Way of Heaven (Tiāndào) is constant;
it did not exist because of Yáo,
nor did it perish because of Jié.
16.53 A family that accumulates goodness
will surely have surplus blessings;
a family that accumulates evil
will surely have surplus calamities.
16.54 Because of one instance of choking,
to give up grain and not eat;
because of one stumble,
to pull back the feet and not walk.
16.55 One whose heart is like Heaven and Earth is enlightened;
one whose conduct is like the plumb line is manifest.
16.56 When the position is high and the Way (Dào) is great, followers come;
when the matter is great but the Way (Dào) is small, it is ominous.
16.57 Those who speak with doubt should not be offended;
those whose actions are doubtful should not be followed.
16.58 Woodworms and larvae topple pillars and beams;
mosquitoes and gadflies make cattle and sheep run.
16.59 Do not respond to inquiries involving hair-splitting words;
do not praise strange talk or empty theories.
16.60 Planning before the matter leads to prosperity;
the matter before planning leads to ruin.
16.61 Do not abandon your occupation for the sake of excessive pleasure,
do not belittle yourself because of poverty or low status,
do not harm your person for the sake of what you love,
do not hinder your life for the sake of desires,
do not seek fame through luxury,
and do not be arrogant or conceited because of wealth and nobility.
16.62 When joy and anger are inappropriate,
it is called a lack of clarity;
if tyranny is not successful,
one will instead suffer its harm;
if resentment arises and is not requited,
calamity will arise from what was good fortune.
16.63 Once a word is wrongly spoken,
a team of four horses cannot chase it back;
once a word is not timely,
a team of four horses cannot catch up to it.
16.64 Flying with the wind
assists one's strength;
soaring while holding a reed in the beak
is to prepare against arrows.
16.65 Because a mirror is clear and bright,
beauty and ugliness reveal themselves;
because a scale is level and impartial,
lightness and heaviness are naturally determined.
16.66 When fleabane grows amidst hemp,
it becomes straight without being propped up;
when white sand is mixed with mud,
it becomes black along with it.
16.67 Oh, the timing! Oh, the timing!
There is no interval for planning;
when the peak of the moment arrives,
there is no room even for a breath.
16.68 If one toils without rest,
one will eventually come to a stop on one's own;
if one has something but does not bestow it,
one will eventually end up with it oneself.
16.69 There is nothing that cannot be done,
and nothing that cannot be achieved;
there is nothing that cannot be desired,
and nothing that cannot be obtained.
16.70 With the accumulation of much righteousness (Yì),
there is no blessing that does not reach;
with the accumulation of much evil,
there is no calamity that does not catch up.
16.71 Diligence overcomes poverty,
prudence overcomes calamity,
caution overcomes harm,
vigilance overcomes disaster.
16.72 To those who do good, Heaven responds with virtue (Dé);
to those who do not do good, Heaven responds with calamity.
16.73 When a gentleman (Jūnzǐ) gains his time, he is like water;
when a petty person (Xiǎorén) gains his time, he is like fire.
16.74 Those who slander those better than themselves
commit a sin of the heart;
those who honor those more worthy than themselves
show the strength of the heart.
16.75 When the heart is gained,
all things are not sufficient to be a concern;
when the heart is lost,
even the heart itself cannot be guarded.
16.76 If a son is not filial,
he is not my son;
if an associate is not trustworthy,
he is not my friend.
16.77 Feed the mouth, and the hundred joints of the body grow fat;
water the root, and the branches and leaves flourish.
When the root is injured, the branches wither;
when the roots are deep, the tips are thick.
16.78 Those who do good obtain the Way (Dào),
those who do evil lose the Way (Dào).
16.79 Evil words should not leave the mouth,
and improper talk should not linger in the ear.
16.80 Practicing falsehood does not last long,
and delighting in emptiness does not endure.
16.81 A man of righteousness (Yì) does not deceive his heart,
and a man of integrity does not take improperly.
16.82 Regard wealth as grass,
and regard one's person as a treasure.
Be compassionate and kind to the young,
and be respectful to the elderly.
16.83 If the barking of dogs causes no alarm,
it is called a "Golden City";
if one constantly avoids danger and peril,
it is called "No Regrets."
16.84 When wealthy, one must think of poverty;
when strong, one must think of old age;
though one's years are few,
one must consider these things early.
16.85 Those who possess ritual decorum will die for one another;
those who lack ritual decorum will also die for one another.
16.86 Nobility does not set a date with arrogance,
yet arrogance comes of itself;
arrogance does not set a date with ruin,
yet ruin arrives of its own accord.
16.87 The lame wish day and night to stand up once;
the blind never forget the desire to see.
16.88 The wise begin with realization
and end in harmony;
the foolish begin with pleasure
and end in sorrow.
16.89 One gazes up at the high mountains;
one follows the great path.
Although one's strength may be insufficient,
the mind must strive toward it.
16.90 Be as cautious at the end as at the beginning,
always taking this as a warning;
trembling with fear and caution,
be careful in one's affairs every day.
16.91 For the rectitude of the sage,
nothing is better than tranquility;
the governance of the worthy
is thus different from that of the masses.
16.92 One who likes to speak of others' evils,
others will also speak of their own evils;
one who likes to hate others
will also be hated by others.
16.93 When food and clothing are sufficient,
one knows honor and shame;
when the granaries are full,
one knows ritual and etiquette.
16.94 The flooding of the Jiāng and Hé Rivers
does not exceed three days;
whirlwinds and rainstorms
conclude in an instant.
16.95 Good fortune arises from the subtle,
while disaster arises from negligence;
fearing day and night,
one only dreads not finishing well.
16.96 Having been carved and polished,
return again to simplicity;
when things reach their opposite,
they return to their origin.
16.97 Following the current downstream makes it easy to arrive;
running with the wind at one's back makes it easy to go far.
16.98 If troops are not prepared in advance,
there is no way to wait for the enemy;
if plans are not considered beforehand,
there is no way to respond to emergencies.
16.99 If the internal is not square,
the reputation will not be manifest;
if the external is not round,
it is a gate to disaster.
One who is straight but cannot bend
cannot move toward greatness;
one who is square but cannot be round
cannot endure for long.
16.100 Be cautious with your person;
do not speak excessively.
16.101 Even from the words of a madman,
the sage makes a selection.
16.102 Those who can endure shame are secure;
those who can endure humiliation survive.
16.103 When the lips are gone, the teeth get cold.
When the river water overflows,
its embrace extends to the mountains.
16.104 Nothing poisons wisdom more than wine;
nothing delays affairs more than music;
nothing destroys integrity more than lust;
nothing breaks the firm more than returning themselves to weakness.
16.105 Wealth lies in knowing contentment;
nobility lies in seeking retirement.
16.106 Those who worry about affairs beforehand will have joy afterward;
those who are arrogant toward affairs beforehand will have worry afterward.
16.107 Good fortune lies in accepting admonition;
this is the means by which one survives.
16.108 Being respectful and yielding,
pure, upright, and without slander;
being compassionate and loving toward others,
one will surely receive rewards for these.
16.109 If admonition is not heard,
there is no use in arguing afterward.
If an undertaking is improper,
it will be slandered by the common people.
Regret lies in recklessness;
trouble lies in being the first to advocate.
16.110 When Pú Qiě readies his arrows and strings,
the wild ducks and geese cry out in sorrow;
when Féng Méng grasps his bow,
tigers and leopards howl at dawn.
16.111 The river is able to go far because it meanders;
the mountain is able to be high because of its gradual slopes.
The Dào is able to transform because it is leisurely;
Dé is able to be heroic because it is pure and thick.
16.112 Speaking of others' good
is more nourishing than ointments and baths;
speaking of others' evil
is more painful than spears and halberds.
16.113 If one does good without being upright,
they will surely end in crookedness;
if one does what is shameful and does not let go,
they will surely end in evil.
16.114 Through a moment of death and a moment of life,
the depth of a friendship is known.
Through a moment of poverty and a moment of wealth,
the attitude of a friendship is known.
Through a moment of nobility and a moment of meanness,
the quality of a friendship is seen.
Through a moment of rising and a moment of sinking,
the reality of a friendship emerges.
16.115 Place virtue and righteousness in the lead;
put the use of military force behind.
16.116 One who has just washed their hair will surely wipe their cap;
one who has just bathed their body will surely shake out their clothes.
16.117 A general of a defeated army cannot speak of courage;
an official of a fallen state cannot speak of wisdom.
16.118 That there are no soft-shelled turtles or crocodiles in a shallow well
is because it is narrow;
that there are no tall forests in a garden
is because it is small.
16.119 Petty loyalty
is the thief of great loyalty;
petty profit
is the ruin of great profit.
16.120 Requesting for oneself to break off is easy;
requesting others to break off is difficult.
16.121 When water is agitated, it becomes fierce;
when an arrow is propelled, it goes far;
when a person is spurred by fame,
they will not allow their reputation to be destroyed.
16.122 A lower-ranking official obtains office and meets death;
a superior official obtains office and finds life.
16.123 Misfortune and good fortune do not emerge from the ground,
nor do they come from heaven;
one produces them from oneself.
16.124 Remote villages have much warped learning;
petty arguments harm great knowledge;
artful words cause trust to be abandoned;
petty favors obstruct great righteousness.
16.125 Not being distressed lies in early consideration;
not being exhausted lies in early preparation.
16.126 If you want others not to know,
there is nothing like not doing it;
if you want others not to hear,
there is nothing like not saying it.
16.127 Do not say what should not be said,
so as to avoid trouble;
do not do what should not be done,
so as to avoid danger;
do not take what should not be taken,
so as to avoid deception;
do not contest what should not be contested,
so as to avoid ill repute.
16.128 The clear-sighted see into the dark;
the wise plan for what has not yet taken shape;
the acute-eared hear where there is no sound;
the thoughtful take precautions against what has not yet happened.
16.129 The world is turbid and I alone am pure;
all the people are drunk and I alone am sober.
16.130 The fault of estrangement
generates everything;
the starting point of ruin and failure
arises from this.
The great breach of the Jiāng and Hé Rivers starts from an ant hole;
a mountain suffers a great collapse because of a small landslide.
16.131 The progression of excess and disorder,
its change becomes a rise;
water, fire, metal, and wood take turns overcoming one another.
16.132 That which is lowly but upright can be increased;
that which is high but leaning will surely collapse.
Those who are as straight as an arrow will die;
those who are as straight as a marking-line will be praised.
16.133 Calamity is born from the desire to gain;
good fortune is born from self-restraint.
16.134 The Shèng-rén uses the heart to guide the ears and eyes;
the petty person uses the ears and eyes to guide the heart.
16.135 For one who is a superior,
the worry lies in a lack of clarity;
for one who is a subordinate,
the worry lies in a lack of loyalty.
16.136 People know how to fertilize fields
but do not know how to fertilize the heart;
by keeping the body upright and conduct correct,
one has preserved oneself until now.
16.137 Seeing destruction, one knows of preservation;
seeing frost, one knows of ice.
16.138 Greatness lies in being fond of benefit;
reverence lies in serving one's parents.
16.139 By following the times, it is easy to practice benevolence;
by following the Dào, it is easy to reach others.
16.140 Those who pursue profit have many worries;
those who promise lightly have little credibility.
16.141 For one who desires to be worthy, nothing is better than humbling oneself before others;
for one who covets wealth, nothing is better than preserving one's life.
Wealth is not as high as righteousness;
power is not as noble as virtue.
16.142 A father cannot love a son who is of no benefit;
a ruler cannot love people who are lawless;
a ruler cannot reward a minister who has no merit;
a minister cannot die for a ruler who has no virtue.
16.143 To ask about good driving, nothing is better than the horse;
to ask about good governance, nothing is better than the people.
16.144 To use the lowly to become noble;
to use submission to achieve expansion.
This is what the Shèng-rén follows,
modeling himself after Heaven above.
16.145 The Jūnzǐ practices virtue to preserve his person;
the petty person practices greed to destroy his person.
16.146 Urge each other with ritual;
strengthen each other with benevolence;
attain the Dào in oneself,
and attain a reputation among others.
16.147 One who knows fate does not resent Heaven;
one who knows oneself does not resent others.
16.148 If a person does not love,
then they cannot be benevolent;
if one is sycophantic and not clever,
then they cannot be trusted.
16.149 When speaking of the good, do not let it involve oneself;
when speaking of the evil, do not let it reach others.
16.150 If the superior is pure and without desire,
then the subordinates will be upright and the people will be simple.
16.151 Future matters can be pursued;
past matters cannot be reached.
16.152 Without a mind of thought and deliberation, one will not be successful;
without the words of conversation and discussion, one will not be joyful.
16.153 Goodness cannot be brought about by pretense;
evil cannot be cast away by words.
16.154 When near the market there are no merchants,
when in the fields there is no wasteland,
then the good do not need to stay in inns.
16.155 Without benevolence, righteousness, firmness, and martial prowess,
there is no way to stabilize the world.
16.156 When water turns its back on its source, the stream dries up;
when a person turns their back on trust, their name will not be known.
16.157 When righteousness overcomes worry, it is auspicious;
when worry overcomes righteousness, it is destruction.
16.158 The plans of the Wǔ Shèng
are not as good as meeting the right time;
eloquence, wisdom, and cleverness
are not as good as encountering the right era.
16.159 To one with a vulgar mind,
one must not grant power or status;
to one with a foolish nature,
one must not give sharp tools.
16.160 Taking things too easily leads to many failures;
speaking too much leads to many mistakes.
16.161 Caps and shoes are not stored together;
the worthy and the unworthy do not occupy the same positions.
16.162 Those with high office have deep worries;
those with many stipends have great responsibilities.
16.163 In accumulating virtue, no amount is too small;
in accumulating resentment, no amount is too great.
Whether much or little, there will surely be a recompense;
such is the certainty of the situation.
16.164 An owl met a dove.
The dove said,
“Where are you going?”
The owl said,
“I am moving to the east.”
The dove said,
“For what reason?”
The owl said,
“The people of the village all hate my call;
therefore, I am moving to the east.”
The dove said,
“If you can change your call,
it will be fine;
if you cannot change your call,
even if you move to the east, they will still hate your voice.”
16.165 The clothing of the Shèng-rén
is convenient for the body to keep the person at ease;
his food
is satisfying to the stomach.
He wears suitable clothes and eats moderately,
and does not listen to the desires of the mouth or eyes.
16.166 Zéng Zǐ said:
“Hawks and vultures consider mountains to be too low,
and so they build their nests even higher;
soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, fish, and turtles consider deep pools to be too shallow,
and so they burrow holes within them.
Yet in the end, what captures them
is the bait.
If the Jūnzǐ does not seek profit or stipend,
then nothing will harm his person.”
16.167 Zéng Zǐ said:
“If intimacy is excessive, then there will be mutual neglect;
if solemnity is excessive, then there will be no closeness.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ’s intimacy is sufficient to share joy,
and his solemnity is sufficient to complete ritual.”
16.168 Zéng Zǐ said:
“When entering this state,
if one's words are trusted by the various ministers,
then staying is acceptable;
if one's loyalty is practiced among the various ministers,
then serving in office is acceptable;
if one's bounty is bestowed upon the common people,
then remaining in peace is acceptable.”
16.169 The mouth is a gate;
the tongue is a trigger.
If one's words are inappropriate,
even a team of four horses cannot catch them.
The mouth is a gate;
the tongue is a weapon.
If one's words are inappropriate,
they return to wound oneself.
Words come from oneself,
but cannot be stopped once they reach others;
actions begin nearby,
but cannot be stopped once they reach far away.
Words and actions
are the pivot and trigger of the Jūnzǐ.
The release of the pivot and trigger
is the root of honor or disgrace.
Can one not be cautious?
Therefore, Kuài Zǐyǔ said:
“Words are like shooting;
once the nock has left the string,
although there may be regret,
it cannot be followed and brought back.”
The *Shī* says:
‘A flaw in a white jade tablet
can still be ground away;
a flaw in these words
cannot be undone.’
16.170 Caterpillars want to be like silkworms;
eels want to be like snakes.
When people see snakes or caterpillars,
everyone shudders with a chill.
Female workers tend to silkworms,
and fishermen hold eels;
why do they not dislike them?
Because they want to get money.
Those who chase fish get wet;
those who chase beasts run fast;
it is not that they enjoy it,
but it is the necessity of the matter.
16.171 Climbing high makes people want to look far;
approaching a deep pool makes people want to peer in.
Why is this?
It is because of the place they are in.
Driving a chariot makes people respectful;
shooting an arrow makes people upright.
Why is this?
It is because the form is convenient for it.
16.172 People have five ways of dying;
the Shèng rén can eliminate three,
but cannot remove the other two.
Those who die of hunger and thirst
can be eliminated;
those who die of freezing and cold
can be eliminated;
those who die by the five weapons
can be eliminated.
Those who die of their allotted life span
cannot be eliminated;
those who die of ulcers and sores
cannot be eliminated.
Those who die of hunger and thirst
have nothing to fill their insides;
those who die of freezing and cold
have the external overcoming the internal;
those who die by the five weapons
have a virtue that is not loyal.
Those who die of their allotted life span
have their years and numbers finished;
those who die of ulcers and sores
have their blood and qì exhausted.
Therefore it is said:
If the internal is not correct,
external excesses arise.
When external excesses arise, there are many resentments and strange things;
when there are many resentments and strange things, diseases are born.
Therefore, through clarity, stillness, and wú wéi,
blood and qì will then be balanced.
16.173 The root of a hundred conducts
is a single word.
If one word is appropriate,
it can repel an enemy;
if one word is fitting,
it can preserve the state.
An echo cannot become a sound on its own;
a shadow cannot turn a curve into a straight line;
things must follow their own kind.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ is cautious about the words that come from himself.
16.174 Carrying a stone and leaping into an abyss
is a difficult action to perform,
yet Shēntú Dí did it,
and the Jūnzǐ does not value it.
Dào Zhí was fierce and greedy,
and his name is like the sun and moon,
being passed down along with Shùn and Yǔ without ceasing,
yet the Jūnzǐ does not value him.
16.175 The Jūnzǐ has five shames:
Not having a seat at court
or being part of the discussion at banquets,
the Jūnzǐ is ashamed of this;
occupying a position
but having no words to offer,
the Jūnzǐ is ashamed of this;
having words to offer
but no actions to match them,
the Jūnzǐ is ashamed of this;
having gained something
and then losing it,
the Jūnzǐ is ashamed of this;
the land having a surplus while the people are in lack,
the Jūnzǐ is ashamed of this.
16.176 Although the Jūnzǐ may be in straits,
he does not dwell in the power of a doomed state;
although he may be poor,
he does not accept the salary of a chaotic ruler.
To be honored in a chaotic age
or to be aligned with a tyrant ruler
is the shame of the Jūnzǐ.
Ordinary people consider the disfigurement of the body a shame;
the Jūnzǐ considers the destruction of righteousness a disgrace.
Ordinary people value profit;
incorruptible scholars value their reputation.
16.177 The system of an enlightened ruler:
rewards follow the heavy,
punishments follow the light.
Feeding people uses their strength as the measure;
serving people uses their age as the standard.
16.178 The words of the Jūnzǐ are few but substantial;
the words of the petty person are many but empty.
16.179 The learning of the Jūnzǐ
enters the ear,
is stored in the heart,
and is practiced by the body.
16.180 The governance of the Jūnzǐ
begins with what is hardly visible
and ends with what cannot be reached.
16.181 The Jūnzǐ considers blessings as though they were insufficient
but considers calamities a hundredfold.
16.182 The Jūnzǐ selects people when taking them in,
but does not select people when giving to them.
16.183 The Jūnzǐ treats fullness as though it were empty
and having as though it were nothing.
16.184 If the Jūnzǐ has his preparations, then he is without trouble.
16.185 The Jūnzǐ does not eat what is gained through shame
and does not obtain things through disgrace.
16.186 The Jūnzǐ rejoices in achieving his will;
the petty person rejoices in achieving his affairs.
16.187 The Jūnzǐ does not allow that which he does not love to affect that which he loves.
16.188 The Jūnzǐ has lifelong concerns
but does not have a single morning's anxiety.
He acts by following the Dào
and speaks by following principle.
Joy does not make him lax,
and anger does not make him difficult.
16.189 The faults of a Jūnzǐ
are like eclipses of the sun and moon;
how do they harm their brightness?
The cleverness of a petty person
is like a dog barking at a thief
or a leopard cat seeing at night;
how does it add to goodness?
16.190 A wise man does not act recklessly;
a brave man does not release his strength recklessly.
16.191 The Jūnzǐ is close to righteousness;
the farmer is close to his grain.
16.192 In serving a ruler, if one cannot advance one's words,
then one resigns the rank;
if one cannot practice one's righteousness,
then one resigns the salary.
16.193 Everyone knows that taking is taking,
but they do not know that giving is taking.
16.194 Governance that invites enemies
and conduct that invites shame—
that such things should arrive on their own without being caused
has never happened in the world.
16.195 A fierce beast that is hesitant
is not as effective as a bee or scorpion's venom;
high-flown discussions that cannot be reached
are not as good as humble theories that have success.
16.196 Qín trusted those of the same surname to rule as kings,
but when it declined,
it was not that those of the same surname had changed,
yet the ruler died and the state perished.
Therefore, a king's governance of the world
lies in the implementation of laws,
not in trusting those of the same surname.
16.197 On the summits of high mountains there are no beautiful trees,
for they are harmed by too much sun;
beneath large trees there are no beautiful grasses,
for they are harmed by too much shade.
16.198 When Zhōng Zǐqī died, Bó Yá cut his strings and broke his zither,
knowing there was no one in the world for whom he could play;
when Huì Shī died, Zhuāngzǐ closed his eyes and would not speak,
seeing there was no one in the world with whom he could converse.
16.199 Self-cultivation
is the storehouse of wisdom;
loving giving
is the beginning of benevolence;
taking and giving
are the marks of righteousness;
shame and disgrace
are the resolution of courage;
establishing a name
is the ultimate of conduct.
16.200 To advance the worthy earns the highest reward;
to obscure the worthy incurs public execution;
this is the universal principle of antiquity.
To rank people at court
and to judge people in the marketplace
is the universal law of antiquity.
16.201 The Dào is subtle yet bright,
bland yet effective.
What is gained not through the Dào
or born not in the right time
is called reckless success;
once gained, it is lost;
once settled, it topples again.
16.202 Blessings
are the gate to calamity;
"right"
is the superior of "wrong";
order
is the precursor to chaos.
That affairs should have a beginning and end without calamities arriving
is something never heard of.
16.203 Let the branches not forget their roots,
let virtue not forget its reciprocity,
and when seeing profit, one must think of the harm to one's person.
Therefore, if the Jūnzǐ keeps his spirit and heart fixed on these three things,
good fortune will reach his descendants.
16.204 Two of high status cannot be weighted equally;
two of great size cannot be accommodated together;
two of equal power cannot coexist;
two of noble rank cannot be paired.
When there is duplication in weight, accommodation, power, or rank,
they will certainly contend for merit.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ moderates his desires,
and each keeps to what is sufficient for him;
only then can he endure for long.
Moderating desires and listening to remonstrance,
respecting the worthy and not being negligent,
employing the capable and not treating them as lowly—
if a ruler of men can practice these three things,
his state will certainly be powerful and his people will not depart or scatter.
16.205 In silence, there are no errors in speech;
in sincerity, there are no errors in action.
A wooden horse cannot walk,
but it also does not consume food;
a Qíjì gallops a thousand lǐ in a day,
but the whip never leaves its back.
16.206 If one measures by the cùn,
by the time one reaches a zhàng, there will certainly be a discrepancy;
if one weighs by the zhū,
by the time one reaches a dàn, there will certainly be an excess.
Weighing by the dàn and measuring by the zhàng
is direct and results in few errors;
sorting silk thread by thread or counting grains of rice
is tedious but does not lead to clarity.
Therefore, broad outlines are easy for the wise to manage,
but intricate arguments are difficult for the intelligent to master.
16.207 A fish large enough to swallow a boat,
if it is tossed out and loses its water,
then it will be controlled by crickets and ants
because it has left its dwelling;
an ape or monkey that loses its tree
and is captured by a fox or raccoon-dog
is in a place not its own.
The Téngshé roams the mist to ascend,
the Yìnglóng mounts the clouds to rise,
the ape finds a tree to leap,
and the fish finds water to gallop;
these are the suitabilities of the places they occupy.
16.208 When the Jūnzǐ learns extensively,
he worries that he might not practice it;
once he has practiced it,
he worries that he might not be able to act upon it;
once he can act upon it,
he worries that he might not be able to yield to others.
16.209 The Jūnzǐ is not ashamed to learn,
and not ashamed to ask.
Inquiring and asking
are the roots of knowledge;
reflection and contemplation
are the ways of knowledge.
These words value adding knowledge by relying on others' knowledge,
rather than valuing the use of one's own knowledge alone to know things.
16.210 The way of Heaven and Earth
is that things reverse when they reach an extreme,
and diminish when they reach fullness.
The five colors dazzle the eyes,
but they have times when they fade;
lush trees and abundant grass
have times when they wither.
All things have their prosperity and decline;
how can they remain the same?
16.211 If the people suffer, they lack benevolence;
if they are exhausted, deceit arises.
When there is peace and security, they can be taught;
when there is danger, they plot.
Extremes lead to reversal,
and fullness lead to loss;
therefore, the Jūnzǐ avoids being full or reaching extremes.
17.1 The worthy and the Jūnzǐ
understand the timing of prosperity and decline,
are clear about the origins of success and failure,
examine the principles of order and chaos,
and scrutinize human nature;
they know what to leave and what to approach.
Therefore, even if they are in straits, they do not occupy a position in a dying state;
even if they are poor, they do not accept the salary of a corrupt ruler.
Thus, Tàigōng did not advance himself until he was seventy years old,
and Sūnshū Áo did not regret leaving the chancellorship three times.
Why?
They would not force a connection with the wrong person.
Tàigōng once connected with Zhōu and his descendants were marquises for seven hundred years;
Sūnshū Áo once connected with Chǔ and his family was enfeoffed for ten generations.
Dàfū Zhǒng preserved Yuè from ruin and made Gōujiàn a hegemon,
but was bestowed death before him.
Lǐ Sī accumulated merit in Qín but ultimately suffered the five punishments.
Being fully loyal and worrying for the ruler,
endangering oneself to stabilize the state—
their merit was the same.
Yet some were enfeoffed without end,
while others were bestowed death or punished.
What they admired and the path they followed were different.
Thus, Jìzǐ abandoned his state and feigned madness;
Fàn Lí left Yuè and changed his name;
Zhìguò left the ruler’s younger brother and changed his surname;
all of them saw the far-reaching and recognized the minute,
and being benevolent, they were able to abandon wealth and power to avoid the disasters that were beginning to sprout.
As for a violent and chaotic ruler,
who would want to be bound to serve him
and participate in his calamities!
Therefore, the worthy do not merely fear death or avoid harm;
they see that sacrificing their lives is of no benefit and only makes manifest the violence of the ruler.
Bǐgān died for Zhòu but could not correct his behavior;
Zǐxū died for Wú but could not preserve its state.
These two men
died for their strong remonstrance,
but they only served to make manifest their rulers’ violence
and were not of benefit even to the tip of an autumn hair.
Thus, the worthy hide their wisdom,
block their ability,
and wait to find the right person before joining them.
Consequently, their words are never ignored,
their actions are never doubted,
ruler and minister harmonize,
and they have no troubles throughout their lives.
Nowadays, people do not find the right time,
nor do they find the right person;
their personal intentions simply cannot be restrained.
Lamenting the chaos of the age
and worrying about the danger of the ruler,
with their common bodies,
they tread upon blocked paths,
pass before slanderers,
approach a ruler of immeasurable temperament,
risk unfathomable crimes,
and injure their innate nature—
how could this not be delusion!
Thus, Wénxìn Hóu and Lǐ Sī
were what the world calls worthy.
In planning for the state,
they gauged the subtle and aimed at the hidden;
these were what are called flawless strategies.
In winning battles and capturing territory,
they had what are called no formidable enemies.
Their accumulated merit was very great,
and their power and profit were very high.
When worthy men were not employed,
and slanderous men held power,
though they knew they were not being used,
their benevolence was not enough to make them leave.
In controlling the enemy and accumulating merit,
they did not lose even an autumn hair;
yet in avoiding trouble and removing harm,
they could not see even a mountain.
They accumulated what they desired
until they reached what they loathed.
Were they not deluded by power and profit!
The Shī says:
"People know one thing,
but do not know the other."
This refers to this situation.
17.2 Zǐshí climbed Wú Shān and looked in the four directions;
he sighed deeply
and said:
"Alas,
how tragic!
In this world, there are those who are clear about the facts of a matter
but do not harmonize with people's hearts;
and there are those who harmonize with people's hearts
but are not clear about the facts of a matter."
A disciple asked:
"What do you mean by that?"
Zǐshí said:
"In the past, King Fūchāi of Wú did not listen to Wǔ Zǐxū's loyal and extreme remonstrance,
causing him to have his eyes gouged out and be executed.
Tàizǎi Pǐ and Gōngsūn Luò dishonestly sought to harmonize and basely accommodated
to follow Fūchāi’s will and attack Qí;
these two men had their bodies submerged in the rivers and lakes,
and their heads hung beneath Yuè banners.
In the past,
Fèizhòng, Èlái, and Jiāogé,
with their long noses and pierced ears,
and Chónghóu Hǔ followed the heart of Zhòu
wanting to harmonize with his intentions.
When Wǔ Wáng attacked Zhòu,
these four men died in the wilds of Mù,
their heads and feet in different places.
Bǐgān showed full loyalty and died with his heart cut out.
Now, if one wishes to be clear about the facts of a matter,
there is fear of the disaster of having eyes gouged out or hearts cut out;
if one wishes to harmonize with people's hearts,
there is the worry of the calamity of having head and feet in different places.
From this perspective,
the path of the Jūnzǐ is narrow indeed.
If one truly does not encounter an enlightened ruler,
within that narrow path,
it will be dangerous, perilous, and blocked,
with no way out."
17.3 Qǐshèzǐ visited King Huì of Qín,
and King Huì was pleased with him.
Thereupon Táng Gū slandered him.
When he visited again,
King Huì harbored anger while waiting for him.
It was not that his persuasion was different,
but that the one listening had changed.
Thus, if one takes the note *zhǐ* to be the note *yǔ*,
it is not the fault of the string;
if one takes sweetness to be bitterness,
it is not the fault of the flavor.
17.4 Mízǐ Xiá was loved by the Ruler of Wèi.
According to the laws of the State of Wèi,
anyone who secretly drove the ruler’s carriage was punished with the amputation of the feet.
Mízǐ Xiá’s mother fell ill,
and someone who heard of it
went at night to inform him.
Mízǐ Xiá took the ruler’s carriage without permission and went out.
When the ruler heard of it, he considered him virtuous, saying,
“How filial!
For his mother’s sake,
he risked the punishment of foot amputation!”
Later, while strolling in an orchard with the ruler,
Mízǐ Xiá ate a peach and found it sweet.
Before finishing it, he offered it to the ruler.
The ruler said,
“He loves me so much that he forgets his own taste!”
When Mízǐ Xiá’s beauty faded and the ruler’s love waned,
he committed an offense against the ruler.
The ruler said,
“This man once falsely claimed my orders to drive my carriage,
and another time fed me a leftover peach.”
Therefore, although Mízǐ Xiá’s conduct
had not necessarily changed from the beginning,
the reason he was first seen as virtuous and later incurred punishment
was that a change had occurred in the ruler’s love and hatred.
17.5 At the time when Shùn was farming,
he was unable to benefit his neighbors;
but when he became the Son of Heaven,
the whole world supported him.
Therefore, the gentleman, when in dire straits, cultivates his own person,
and when successful, he benefits the whole world.
17.6 Kǒngzǐ said,
“Since Jì Sūn gave me a thousand *zhōng* of grain, my friends have become closer;
since Nángōng Jìngshū provided me with a carriage, the Way has been practiced more widely.
Therefore, the Way is valued only after the right time comes,
and it is practiced only after one has power.
Without the gifts of these two gentlemen,
my (Qiū’s) Way would have nearly been discarded.”
17.7 Tàigōng’s farming was not enough to pay for the seeds,
and his fishing was not enough to pay for the nets,
yet he had surplus wisdom for governing the world.
Wén Gōng planted rice,
and Zéngzǐ harnessed a sheep.
When Sūnshū Áo had been the Prime Minister of Chǔ for three years,
he did not know that the yoke was behind the crossbar.
Those who attend to great matters naturally forget small ones.
When the cook of Zhì Bó lost a roasting spit, Zhì Bó knew about it,
but he did not know when Hán and Wèi rebelled against him.
When the gardener of Zǐyáng of Hándān lost a peach, Zǐyáng knew about it,
but he did not know when he was about to perish.
Those who attend to small matters also forget great ones.
17.8 Chúnyú Kūn said to Mèngzǐ,
“Those who put name and reality first
are those who act for others;
those who put name and reality last
are those who act for themselves.
You, Master, were among the three high officials,
yet you left before your name and reality had reached those above or below.
Is a benevolent person naturally like this?”
Mèngzǐ said,
“One who occupies a low position and does not use his worthiness to serve those who are not worthy
is Bóyí;
one who five times went to Tāng and five times went to Jié
is Yī Yǐn;
one who did not detest a corrupt ruler and did not decline a minor office
is Liǔxià Huì.
These three gentlemen followed different paths,
but their goal was one.
What was that one thing?
It was
benevolence.
The gentleman is simply benevolent;
why must they be the same?”
Chúnyú Kūn said,
“In the time of Lǔ Mù Gōng,
Gōngyízǐ was in charge of the government,
and Zǐsī and Zǐgēng were ministers,
yet the diminishment of Lǔ was extreme.
If it is like this,
then worthy men are of no benefit to the state.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“Yú did not use Bǎilǐ Xī and perished,
while Qín Mù Gōng used him and became a hegemon.
Therefore, if one does not use the worthy, one perishes;
how could one even achieve being merely diminished?”
Chúnyú Kūn said,
“In the past, Wáng Bào lived by the Qí River,
and the people west of the Yellow River became good at singing;
Mián Jù lived in Gāotáng,
and the people in the east of Qí became good at singing.
The wives of Huá Zhōu and Qǐ Liáng
were so good at mourning their husbands that they changed the customs of the state.
When something exists within,
it must be manifested without.
As for doing the work but not achieving the result,
I (Kūn) have never seen it.
Therefore, there are no worthy men;
if there were, I (Kūn) would surely recognize them.”
Mèngzǐ said,
“When Kǒngzǐ was the Minister of Justice in Lǔ and was not used,
he participated in the sacrifice,
and when the sacrificial meat did not arrive,
he left without taking off his ceremonial cap.
Those who did not know him thought it was because of the meat;
those who knew him thought it was because of the lack of ritual propriety.
Thus, Kǒngzǐ wished to leave on account of a minor offense
and did not wish to leave for no reason.
Therefore, what a gentleman does
is naturally something the common people cannot understand.”
17.9 When the Prime Minister of Liáng died,
Huìzǐ wanted to go to Liáng.
While crossing the river, he suddenly fell into the water.
A boatman rescued him.
The boatman said,
“Where do you wish to go in such a hurry?”
He said,
“Liáng has no Prime Minister;
I wish to go and be the Prime Minister.”
The boatman said,
“You were in distress just being between the hull and the oars,
and without me, you would have died.
How can you be the Prime Minister of Liáng?”
Huìzǐ said,
“In being between the hull and the oars,
I am not as good as you.
But as for bringing peace to the state and preserving the altars of land and grain,
compared to me,
you are as dim-witted as a puppy that has not yet opened its eyes.”
17.10 Xīlǘ Guò was crossing the river to the east.
In midstream, he began to drown.
A boatman rescued him and pulled him out,
then asked,
“Now, where do you wish to go?”
Xīlǘ Guò said,
“I wish to go east to persuade the feudal lords.”
The boatman covered his mouth and laughed, saying,
“You were drowning in the middle of the river
and could not save yourself.
How can you persuade the lords?”
Xīlǘ Guò said,
“Do not use what you are capable of to disparage others.
Have you not heard of the Jade Disc of Hé?
Its price is worth a thousand pieces of gold,
yet if used as a weight for a spinning wheel,
it is not even as good as a tile or a brick.
The Pearl of Marquis Suí
is a treasure of the state,
yet if used as a pellet to shoot at a magpie,
it is not even as good as a mud ball.
Qíjì and Lù’ěr
can lean against the crossbar and carry the yoke to gallop,
covering a thousand *lǐ* in a day;
this is extreme speed.
Yet if made to catch rats,
they are not even as good as a wildcat worth a hundred coins.
Gānjiàng and Mòyé
can strike a bell without making a sound,
and one would not even know they had tested it on an object;
when the blade is raised, it separates gold;
it can cut feathers and split iron axes.
This is extreme sharpness.
Yet if used to mend shoes,
they are not even as good as an awl worth two coins.
Now you hold the oars and ride a small boat,
dwelling in the midst of vast waters,
facing the waves of Yánghóu and looking into the deep abyss.
This is merely what you are capable of.
If I were truly to take you east to persuade the feudal lords
and meet the ruler of a state,
your dim-wittedness
would be no different from that of a puppy that has not yet opened its eyes.”
17.11 Gān Wù was sent as an envoy to Qí.
While crossing the Dà Hé,
the boatman said:
"The river water
is just a narrow gap;
if you cannot even cross it yourself,
how can you deliver the speeches of a king?"
Gān Wù said:
"Not so;
you do not understand.
Things each have their shortcomings and strengths.
Those who are cautious, sincere, and honest
may serve a master
but cannot be employed in using troops.
Fine horses like Qíjì and Lù'ěr
have feet that can reach a thousand li,
yet if placed in a palace
and made to catch mice,
they are not even equal to a small cat.
Gānjiàng was a sharp sword
whose name was known throughout the world;
yet if a craftsman used it to work wood,
it would be inferior to an axe or a hatchet.
Now, in holding the oar and following the current up and down,
I am not equal to you;
but in speaking to the lords of a thousand chariots and the masters of ten thousand chariots,
you are not equal to Wù."
17.12 Now, when the world differs, affairs change;
when affairs change, the times shift;
when the times shift, customs transform.
Therefore, the gentleman first surveys the land and then fashions the implements;
he observes the customs and then harmonizes the winds;
he gathers the various opinions and then determines the teachings.
There was a fool who learned long-distance archery;
he would aim at the sky and release,
but the arrow would fall within five steps;
yet he would again aim at the sky and release.
The world has already changed,
but if one does not alter their methods,
it is like the fool learning long-distance archery.
One whose eyes observe the tip of an autumn hair
cannot see Tài Shān;
one whose ears listen to the melodies of clear and muddy tones
cannot hear the sound of thunder.
Why is this?
