It is only because their intent has shifted to something else.
If a hundred people handle a bone awl,
it cannot be used to make a firm knot;
if a thousand people slander a legal case,
there can be no straight testimony;
if ten thousand people join in wrongdoing,
there can be no distinguished scholar.
17.13 When deer gather in herds,
tigers and leopards avoid them;
when birds fly in formation,
hawks and eagles do not attack;
when the masses form a gathering,
the sage does not offend them.
The Téngshé travels through mist and dew
and moves by riding the wind and rain,
not stopping until it has traveled a thousand li.
Yet in the evening, it takes shelter in the holes of loaches and eels.
Why is this so?
Because its focus is not singular.
Now, the earthworm lacks the strength of muscles and bones within,
and the sharpness of claws and teeth without;
yet it drinks from the yellow springs below
and tills the dry soil above.
Why is this so?
Because its focus is singular.
Those with keen hearing use their ears to listen;
those with keen vision use their eyes to see.
When hearing and vision are manifested, benevolence and love become prominent, and the distinction between integrity and shame is clear.
Thus, if one travels a path that is not the Way,
though they labor, they will not arrive;
if one seeks what is not theirs,
though they are strong, they will not obtain it.
The wise do not engage in what is not their business;
the upright do not seek what is not their own.
Therefore, they stay far from harm and their names are illustrious.
The Shī says:
"Neither envious nor covetous,
how could anything not be good?"
This is what it means.
17.14 King Zhāo of Chǔ summoned Kǒngzǐ,
intending to have him handle the administration and enfeoff him with seven hundred shūshè.
Zǐxī said to the King of Chǔ:
"Does Your Majesty have a minister who uses troops like Zǐlù?
Or an envoy to the feudal lords like Zǎi Yǔ?
Or an official for the five departments like Zǐgòng?
Formerly, King Wén resided at Fèng
and King Wǔ resided at Hào;
between Fèng and Hào,
with only a territory of a hundred chariots,
they attacked their superiors and killed their masters,
establishing themselves as the Sons of Heaven,
and the world all called them sage kings.
Now, with the worthiness of Kǒngzǐ,
and having a territory of seven hundred li of shūshè,
with those three men assisting him,
it would not be to the benefit of Chǔ."
The King of Chǔ then desisted.
Now, as it is difficult to distinguish between good and evil,
even the sage is met with suspicion;
how much more so for the worthy?
Thus, it is rare for the worthy and the sage to find accord,
while flattery and fawning constantly flourish.
Therefore, there are a thousand years of disorder
and not a hundred years of order.
That Kǒngzǐ was met with suspicion—
is it not painful!
17.15 Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Does the wise man live a long life?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yes.
There are three types of death that are not fated,
but which a person brings upon themselves.
When one is irregular in sleeping and dwelling,
lacks moderation in eating and drinking,
and overextends themselves in leisure or labor,
illness will join to kill them.
When one occupies a low position yet offends their superior,
and is insatiable in their desires and seeks without stopping,
punishments will join to kill them.
When the few offend the many,
and the weak insult the strong,
and one gives way to anger without measuring their strength,
weapons will join to kill them.
These three types of death are not fated
but are brought upon oneself."
The Shī says:
"If a man has no decorum,
why does he not die?"
This is what it means.
17.16 Kǒngzǐ encountered hardship on the border of Chén and Cài.
Their food supply was exhausted,
and the disciples all had hungry looks on their faces,
but Kǒngzǐ sang between the two pillars.
Zǐlù entered to see him and said:
"For the Master to sing,
is that in accordance with ritual?"
Kǒngzǐ did not respond.
When the song ended, he said:
"Yóu,
the noble person loves music
so as to be without arrogance;
the base person loves music
so as to be without fear.
Who knows this?
Could it be that you are one who follows me without knowing me?"
Zǐlù was displeased.
He took up a shield and danced,
and after three rounds, he went out.
When it reached the seventh day,
Kǒngzǐ practiced music without ceasing.
Zǐlù appeared with resentment
and said:
"For the Master to practice music,
is it timely?"
Kǒngzǐ did not respond.
When the music ended, he said:
"Yóu,
in the past, Qí Huán’s ambition for hegemony was born in Jǔ,
Gōujiàn’s ambition for hegemony was born in Huìjī,
and Jìn Wén’s ambition for hegemony was born among the Líshì.
Therefore, if one’s dwelling is not secluded, one’s thoughts will not reach far;
if one’s person is not constrained, one’s wisdom will not be broad.
How can one have wisdom and yet not meet with such circumstances?"
Thereupon he rose.
The next day,
they were freed from the distress.
Zǐgòng held the reins and said:
"We disciples followed the Master and met with this hardship;
it must not be forgotten."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Ah!
What is this you say?
Does the proverb not say:
'Breaking one's arm three times makes one a good physician'?
The time between Chén and Cài
was a blessing for Qiū.
Those of you who followed Qiū
are all blessed.
I have heard that
a ruler of men who is not distressed does not become a king,
and a scholar of rank who is not distressed does not perfect his conduct.
In the past, Tāng was distressed at Lǚ,
Wénwáng was distressed at Yǒulǐ,
Qín Mùgōng was distressed at Xiáo,
Qí Huán was distressed at Chángsháo,
Gōujiàn was distressed at Huìjī,
and Jìn Wén was distressed among the Líshì.
Distress as a Way
is like moving from cold to warmth,
or from warmth to cold.
Only the worthy alone know this, but it is difficult to speak of it to others.
The Yì says:
'Distress.
Success.
Steadfastness.
For the great person, there is good fortune,
and no blame.
There are words, but they are not believed.'
That which the Sage finds difficult to speak about with others
is being believed."
17.17 Kǒngzǐ was distressed between Chén and Cài.
He stayed within a tiny room
and sat on a mat made of three strands of grass.
For seven days he did not eat,
and his goosefoot soup had no grain.
The disciples all had hungry looks on their faces.
He read the Shī and Shū
and cultivated ritual and music without ceasing.
Zǐlù came forward to remonstrate, saying:
"Generally, for those who do good,
Heaven repays them with blessings;
for those who do what is not good,
Heaven repays them with calamities.
Now, Master has accumulated virtue and acted with goodness for a long time.
Could it be that there are still flaws in your conduct?
Why is your dwelling so hidden and distressed?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, come.
You do not understand.
Sit down,
and I will tell you.
Do you think that those who are wise have nothing they do not know?
Then why did Prince Bǐ Gān have his heart cut out and die?
Do you think that those who remonstrate will always be heard?
Then why did Wǔ Zǐxū have his eyes gouged out at the east gate of Wú?
Do you think that those who are upright will always be employed?
Then why did Bó Yí and Shū Qí die of hunger at the foot of Shǒuyáng Shān?
Do you think that those who are loyal will always be employed?
Then why did Bào Zhuāng’s flesh wither away,
why did Prince Gāo of Jīng never become prominent throughout his life,
why did Bào Jiāo embrace a tree and die standing as he withered,
and why did Jiè Zǐtuī climb a mountain and burn to death?
Therefore, many are the noble persons who are broad in learning and deep in planning yet do not meet their time.
Is it only Qiū?
Being worthy or unworthy
is a matter of talent;
acting or not acting
is a matter of the person;
meeting opportunity or not
is a matter of the time;
life and death
are matters of fate.
If one has the talent but does not meet the time,
though talented, one will not be employed.
If one happens to meet the time,
what difficulty is there?
Thus, Shùn plowed at Lìshān and made pottery by the banks of the Hé.
That he was established as the Son of Heaven
was because he met Yáo.
Fù Yuè carried earth
and was released from building walls to be established as a Grand Officer assisting the Son of Heaven;
this was because he met Wǔ Dīng.
Yī Yǐn
was originally a servant of the Yǒu Shīnshì clan.
Carrying tripods and cutting boards,
he blended the five flavors and was established as a Chancellor assisting the Son of Heaven;
this was because he met Chéng Tāng.
Lǚ Wàng at the age of fifty
sold food at Jíjīn,
at seventy
slaughtered cattle at Zhāogē,
and at ninety
became the teacher of the Son of Heaven;
this was because he met Wénwáng.
Guǎn Yīwú was bound and his eyes covered,
confined in a cage-cart.
Rising from the cart, he was made Zhòngfù;
this was because he met Qí Huán Gōng.
Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself for the price of five ram skins
to herd sheep for the Bóshì.
He was raised up to be a high official;
this was because he met Qín Mù Gōng.
Shěn Yǐn’s name was known throughout the world;
he was made Chief Minister,
but he yielded to Sūnshū Áo;
this was because he met Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng.
Wǔ Zǐxū had many successes in the beginning
but was later put to death;
this was not because his wisdom had declined
but because he first met Hélǘ
and later met Fūchāi.
A fine steed (jì) distressed by pulling a salt cart
does not lack the appearance of a fine steed;
it is just that the world cannot recognize it.
If the fine steed found Wáng Liáng or Zào Fù,
would it not have the legs of a thousand-li runner?
Orchids grow in the deep forest
and are not without fragrance just because no one is there to smell them.
Therefore, for the scholar,
study is not for the sake of success;
it is so that when in straits one is not distressed,
and when in sorrow one’s will does not decline.
This is knowing the beginning of disaster and fortune beforehand so that the heart is not confused.
The deep thoughts of the Sage are what he alone knows and alone sees.
Shùn was also a worthy and a sage
and ruled the world facing south
only because he met Yáo.
If Shùn had lived in the age of Jié or Zhòu,
he might have managed to avoid execution,
but what office could he have governed?
Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng and Zhòu killed Prince Bǐ Gān.
At that time,
was it because Guān Lóngpáng lacked knowledge or Bǐ Gān lacked wisdom?
It was because they lived in the unprincipled ages of Jié and Zhòu.
Therefore, the noble person is diligent in learning,
cultivates his person and rectifies his conduct,
in order to wait for his time."
17.18 Kǒngzǐ went to Sòng.
Kuāng Jiǎnzǐ was about to kill Yáng Hǔ.
Kǒngzǐ resembled him,
so armored soldiers surrounded Kǒngzǐ’s lodging.
Zǐlù was angry
and flourished his halberd, about to go down and fight.
Kǒngzǐ stopped him, saying:
"How is it that benevolence and righteousness cannot escape the common lot?
That the Shī and Shū are not studied,
and ritual and music are not cultivated,
that is Qiū’s fault.
But that I resemble Yáng Hǔ
is not Qiū’s crime;
it is fate!
Yóu, sing,
and I will harmonize with you."
Zǐlù sang,
Kǒngzǐ harmonized with him,
and after three rounds, the armored soldiers withdrew.
17.19 Kǒngzǐ said:
"If one does not observe from a high bank,
how can one know the danger of falling?
If one does not look down into a deep abyss,
how can one know the danger of drowning?
If one does not observe upon the sea,
how can one know the danger of wind and waves?
Is not losing oneself found in these?
If a Shì is cautious of these three,
he will not be a burden to others."
17.20 Zēngzǐ said:
"An echo does not refuse a sound,
and a mirror does not refuse a form.
When the Jūnzǐ rectifies the One, then the myriad things are all accomplished.
Walking is not for the sake of the shadow, yet the shadow follows;
shouting is not for the sake of the echo, yet the echo responds.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ's merit is first accomplished, and fame follows it."
17.21 Zǐxià asked Zhòngní:
"As for Yán Yuān's character,
how is it?"
He said:
"Huí's trustworthiness
is superior to mine."
He said:
"As for Zǐgòng's character,
how is it?"
He said:
"Cì's quickness
is superior to mine."
He said:
"As for Zǐlù's character,
how is it?"
He said:
"Yóu's courage
is superior to mine."
He said:
"As for Zǐzhāng's character,
how is it?"
He said:
"Shī's dignity
is superior to mine."
Upon this, Zǐxià withdrew from his mat and asked:
"If so, then why do these four serve you?"
He said:
"Sit down,
I shall tell you.
Huí can be trustworthy but cannot be contrary;
Cì can be quick but cannot be submissive;
Yóu can be courageous but cannot be fearful;
Shī can be dignified but cannot be conforming.
As for combining these four,
I (Qiū) would not do so."
Now, what is called a most sagely man
must be one who sees the benefit of advancing and retreating and the use of bending and stretching.
17.22 Dōngguō Zǐhuì asked Zǐgòng:
"The Master’s gate,
why is it so diverse?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Beside a straightening board, there is much crooked wood;
at a good physician’s gate, there are many sick people;
beside a whetstone, there are many dull objects.
The Master cultivates the Way to await the world,
and those who come do not stop;
this is why it is diverse."
The Shī says:
"Lush are those willows,
the cicadas chirp *huì huì*;
there is a deep pool,
where reeds and rushes grow thick."
This means that beside what is great,
there is nothing that is not accommodated.
17.23 Long ago,
Nánxiázi visited Chéng Běnzǐ,
and Běnzǐ cooked a giant salamander for him.
Nánxiázi said:
"I have heard that a Jūnzǐ does not eat giant salamander."
Chéng Běnzǐ said:
"Is it only a Jūnzǐ who does not eat it?
Why do you concern yourself with this?"
Nánxiázi said:
"I have heard that a Jūnzǐ compares himself upward to broaden his virtue,
and compares himself downward to narrow his conduct.
Comparing oneself to the good
is the stairway to self-advancement;
comparing oneself to the evil
is the source of self-regression.
The Shī says:
'The high mountain, I look up to it;
the great road, I travel it.'
How would I dare to consider myself a Jūnzǐ?
I merely set my will toward it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When you see a worthy person, think of equaling them;
when you see an unworthy person, reflect within yourself."
17.24 Kǒngzǐ was observing at Lǚliáng,
where the waterfall fell forty rèn,
and the swirling current reached ninety lǐ;
fish and turtles could not pass,
and large turtles and crocodiles did not dare to dwell.
There was a man who was just about to cross it.
Kǒngzǐ sent someone along the cliff to stop him, saying:
"This waterfall is forty rèn high,
and the swirling current is ninety lǐ;
fish and turtles dare not pass,
and large turtles and crocodiles do not dare to dwell.
I suspect it would be difficult to cross."
The man did not pay any mind to this
and eventually crossed over and emerged.
Kǒngzǐ asked:
"Are you skillful?
Or do you have some method or art?
What is it by which you were able to enter and emerge?"
The man replied:
"When I first entered,
I first relied on loyalty and trust;
when I emerged,
I again followed with loyalty and trust.
I cast my body into the waves and current,
and I did not dare to use my private will;
this is how I was able to enter and then emerge again."
Kǒngzǐ said to his disciples:
"If even with water one can rely on loyalty and trust and treat it as a close friend,
how much more so with people!"
17.25 Zǐlù dressed in fine robes and went to see Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu,
what is the meaning of this flamboyant attire?
Long ago, the Jiāng river flowed out from Mínshān;
at its beginning,
it was just large enough to float a wine cup.
By the time it reached the river's ferry,
without putting boats side-by-side
and without avoiding the wind,
it could not be crossed.
Is this not merely because of the abundance of many tributary streams below?
Now if your clothing is so grand
and your expression so full of yourself,
who in the world would be willing to add anything to you?"
Zǐlù hurried out,
changed his clothes, and entered again,
appearing natural and easy.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, remember this,
I will tell you.
He who is ornate in speech
is merely flowery;
he who is strenuous in action
is merely boastful.
One who puts on a show of wisdom and ability
is a petty man.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ knows that to know what one knows
and to know what one does not know
is the essential of speech;
to know what one can do
and what one cannot do
is the height of action.
If speech is essential, there is wisdom;
if action is essential, there is benevolence.
Having both wisdom and benevolence,
what more could be added?
Yóu,
the Shī says:
'Tāng's descent was not slow,
his sagely reverence daily ascended.'
This is what it refers to."
17.26 Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Does a Jūnzǐ also have worries?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He does not.
When a Jūnzǐ cultivates his conduct,
before he has attained his goal,
he finds joy in his intent;
once he has attained it,
he again finds joy in his knowledge.
For this reason, he has lifelong joy
and not a single day of worry.
The petty man is not like this.
Before he has attained it,
he worries about not attaining it;
once he has attained it,
he then fears losing it.
For this reason, he has lifelong worry
and not a single day of joy."
17.27 Kǒngzǐ saw Róng Qǐqī wearing a deer-hide robe,
playing the zither and singing.
Kǒngzǐ asked him,
"What makes the Master so happy?"
He replied,
"My joys are very many.
Of all the things heaven has produced,
only humanity is considered precious,
and I have already attained being human;
this is one joy.
People consider being male as precious,
and I have already attained being male;
this is a second joy.
Among those born, there are those who do not see the sun or moon and do not escape their swaddling clothes,
while I have already reached the age of ninety-five;
this is a third joy.
Indeed, poverty
is the constant lot of a scholar;
death
is the end for all people.
Abiding in the constant and awaiting the end,
what should I worry about?"
17.28 Zéngzǐ said,
"I have heard three sayings of the Master,
but I have not yet been able to practice them.
When the Master sees one good point in a person, he forgets their hundred faults;
this is the Master's ease in being served.
When the Master sees others have goodness,
it is as if he possessed it himself;
this is the Master's lack of contention.
Upon hearing of goodness, he must personally practice it
before speaking of it;
this is the Master's ability to be diligent.
The Master's ability to be diligent,
the Master's lack of contention,
and the Master's ease in being served—
I have studied these three sayings of the Master but have not yet been able to practice them."
17.29 Kǒngzǐ said,
"Huí,
you have four of the ways of a gentleman:
strong in self-discipline,
soft in receiving remonstrance,
wary in awaiting official salary,
and cautious in maintaining your character."
17.30 Zhòngní said,
"Shǐ Qiú possessed three of the ways of a gentleman:
not in office yet respecting his superiors,
not performing sacrifices yet respecting the spirits,
and though upright, being able to yield to others."
17.31 Kǒngzǐ said,
"After I, Qiū, have died,
Shāng will make daily progress,
while Cì will suffer daily loss.
Shāng likes to dwell with those more worthy than himself,
while Cì likes to talk with those who are not as good as himself."
17.32 Kǒngzǐ was about to travel,
and it rained but he had no umbrella.
A disciple said,
"Zǐxià has an umbrella;
you can use it."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Shāng's character
is very stingy regarding his wealth.
I have heard that when interacting with people,
one should promote their strengths
and avoid their weaknesses;
in this way, the relationship can be long-lasting."
17.33 Zǐlù was about to travel
and took leave of Zhòngní, saying,
"May I ask how to gain intimacy with new acquaintances?
How to make one's words few but actionable?
How to remain a good man for a long time without causing offense?"
Zhòngní said,
"To gain intimacy with new acquaintances,
is it not through loyalty?
To make words few but actionable,
is it not through trustworthiness?
To remain a good man for a long time without offense,
is it not through ritual propriety?"
17.34 Zǐlù was about to travel
and took leave of Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said,
"Should I gift you a carriage?
Or should I gift you some words?"
Zǐlù said,
"Please give me words."
Zhòngní said,
"Without effort, one cannot go far;
without labor, there is no achievement;
without loyalty, there is no intimacy;
without trustworthiness, there is no return;
without respect, there is no ritual propriety.
Be cautious regarding these five things,
and you can endure for a long time."
17.35 Zéngzǐ followed Kǒngzǐ to Qí.
Duke Jǐng of Qí sought to recruit Zéngzǐ with the ritual treatment of a lower minister,
but Zéngzǐ firmly declined.
As he was about to travel,
Yànzǐ saw him off and said,
"I have heard
that for a gentleman to gift someone wealth
is not as good as gifting words.
Now, take an orchid root:
it takes three years to mature,
but if it is soaked in deer-meat sauce,
once it is finished,
it is easily exchanged for a horse.
It is not that the orchid root itself is beautiful,
but that which it was soaked in is beautiful.
I wish for you to be meticulous about what you are soaked in.
Once you have found what to be soaked in,
seek it out.
I have heard
that a gentleman must choose his place of residence
and choose his direction when traveling.
Choosing his place of residence
is how he seeks worthy men;
choosing his direction when traveling
is how he cultivates the Way.
I have heard that it is desires that subvert constancy and change one's nature;
therefore, one must be cautious."
17.36 Kǒngzǐ said,
"The nature of ordinary people:
if they have an excess, they become extravagant;
if they have a deficiency, they become stingy;
without prohibitions, they become licentious;
without limits, they go astray;
if they indulge their desires, they are ruined.
Having a set measure for food and drink,
moderation in clothing,
limits for dwellings,
fixed numbers for livestock and possessions,
and restrictions on carriages and vessels—
these are the means to block the source of disorder."
Therefore, measures and limits must be made clear,
and good desires must be heeded.
17.37 Kǒngzǐ said,
"Those who are skillful and love measures will surely be expert craftsmen;
those who are brave and love unity will surely be victorious;
those who are wise and love planning will surely succeed.
Fools are the opposite of this.
Occupying high positions and monopolizing favor,
being single-minded in envying the worthy—
these are the dispositions of a fool.
Their ambitions are arrogant, and they take old grudges lightly.
For this reason, if their position is honored, they will surely be in danger;
if their responsibility is heavy, they will surely collapse;
if they monopolize favor, they will surely be disgraced."
17.38 Kǒngzǐ said,
"A child who is whipped
does not follow the father's teaching;
a people who are punished and executed
do not follow the ruler's governance.
This means that harsh words are difficult to put into practice.
Therefore, a gentleman is not hasty in judgment
and does not command with prejudice,
considering such things the sources of disorder."
17.39 Kǒngzǐ said,
"To speak all day without leaving behind personal sorrow
and to act all day without leaving behind personal hardship—
only the wise can do this.
Thus, fear and apprehension are the means to eliminate hardship;
respect and reverence are the means to overcome difficulty.
One may work for them a whole life,
yet a single word can ruin it;
can one not be cautious?"
17.40 Kǒngzǐ said,
"If one uses wealth and status to place oneself below others,
who would not join them?
If one uses wealth and status to respect and love others,
who would not be close to them?
When one does not oppose the words of the masses,
one can be said to understand words.
When one speaks and the masses turn toward them,
one can be said to understand the times."
17.41 Kǒngzǐ said,
"Those who are wealthy and can make others wealthy
will find it impossible to become poor even if they wish;
those who are noble and can make others noble
will find it impossible to become lowly even if they wish;
those who are prominent and can make others prominent
will find it impossible to become destitute even if they wish."
17.42 Zhòngní said:
"If you plant in the wrong soil,
it will not grow;
if you speak to the wrong person,
they will not listen.
Obtaining the right person
is like gathering sand and making it rain;
having the wrong person is like gathering the deaf and drumming for them."
17.43 Kǒngzǐ said:
"A boat cannot travel without water,
but if water enters the boat, it will sink.
A ruler cannot govern without the people,
but if the people rebel against those above, the state will collapse."
Therefore it is said:
A gentleman must not fail to be strict,
and a petty man must not fail to be restrained.
17.44 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Depending on the worthy ensures one is not distressed;
depending on the wealthy ensures one is not impoverished.
Why is it that a millipede can still walk after being cut?
Because the legs that support it are many."
17.45 Kǒngzǐ said:
"If you do not know a son,
look at his friends;
if you do not know a ruler,
look at those he employs."
He also said:
"Living with good people
is like entering a room of orchids and iris;
after a long time one does not smell their fragrance,
for one has been transformed by them;
living with evil people
is like entering a dried-fish market;
after a long time one does not smell the stench,
for one has also been transformed by them."
Therefore it is said:
That which is stored with cinnabar becomes red;
that which is stored with black pigment becomes black.
The gentleman is cautious about what he associates with.
17.46 Zǐgòng asked:
"When a gentleman sees a great body of water, he must observe it;
why is this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The gentleman compares water to virtue.
It gives everywhere and is without selfishness;
this is like virtue.
What it reaches is given life;
this is like benevolence.
Its flow seeks the lower ground, curving and yielding,
yet all according to principle;
this is like righteousness.
In shallow places it flows along;
in deep places it is unfathomable;
this is like wisdom.
It rushes into a hundred-fathom valley without hesitation;
this is like courage.
It is gentle and weak yet reaches everywhere;
this is like discernment.
It receives impurities without refusing them;
this is like encompassing the ignorant.
It enters unclear
and emerges fresh and clean;
this is like being good at transformation.
When filling a measure it must be level;
this is like uprightness.
When full it does not seek the leveling rod;
this is like moderation.
Although it winds a thousand times, it must flow east;
this is like resolve.
This is why a gentleman observes a great body of water."
17.47 Why does the wise man delight in water?
It is said:
Its source gushes forth,
not ceasing day or night;
it is like one who possesses strength.
It follows principle in its movement,
not neglecting even the smallest gap;
it is like one who maintains balance.
It moves and goes downward;
it is like one who possesses ritual propriety.
It rushes into a thousand-fathom gorge without hesitation;
it is like one who possesses courage.
It is dammed up and becomes clear;
it is like one who knows fate.
It enters unclear
and emerges fresh and clean;
it is like one who is good at transformation.
All people use it for leveling,
and all categories are made upright;
the myriad things live when they obtain it
and die when they lose it;
it is like one who possesses virtue.
Pure and deep,
profound and unfathomable;
it is like a sage.
It flows through and moistens everything between heaven and earth,
and the state is thereby established;
this is why the wise man delights in water.
The Shī says:
"Happily thinking of the Pàn Shuǐ,
we gather the water-cress there.
The Lǔ Hóu has arrived,
drinking wine by the Pàn."
This refers to delighting in water.
Why does the benevolent man delight in mountains?
It is said:
Mountains are lofty and majestic,
gazed upon and looked up to by the myriad people.
Grass and trees grow there,
the myriad things stand there,
birds flock there,
beasts rest there,
treasures proliferate there,
and extraordinary men reside there.
It nurtures the myriad things without weariness,
and people from all directions take from it without limit.
It brings forth clouds and wind,
and circulates breath between heaven and earth,
and the state is thereby established;
this is why the benevolent man delights in mountains.
The Shī says:
"Tài Shān is high and rocky,
the Lǔ Hóu gazes upon it."
This refers to delighting in mountains.
17.48 Jade has six beauties,
and the gentleman values it.
Viewed from afar it is warm and moist,
and close up it is firm and textured;
its sound is slow and gentle yet heard from afar;
it may be broken but not bent;
it may be chipped but not made soft;
it has sharp edges but does not cut;
any flaw must be shown on the outside;
this is why it is valued.
That which is warm and moist when viewed from afar,
the gentleman compares to virtue;
that which is firm and textured close up,
the gentleman compares to wisdom;
that whose sound is slow and gentle yet heard from afar,
the gentleman compares to righteousness;
that which is broken but not bent,
or chipped but not made soft,
the gentleman compares to courage;
that which has sharp edges but does not cut,
the gentleman compares to benevolence;
and that which must show its flaws on the outside,
the gentleman compares to genuineness.
17.49 Dàowú said: I heard from the Master:
Between knowing much and knowing nothing,
which is better for one’s person?
He replied:
"One who knows nothing
belongs to the category of the dead;
although not yet dead,
the people they burden must be very many indeed.
However, as for one who knows much,
it depends on how they apply their minds;
if knowing much
stems from benefiting people, then it is good;
if it stems from harming people, then it is not good."
Dàowú said:
"Excellent!"
17.50 Yuè Shífù said:
The unworthy consider themselves worthy,
and the foolish consider themselves great.
As for sycophants, none can judge their hearts;
words come out of their mouths,
and yet they tell others not to speak of it.
It is like digging a well only when thirsty,
or casting weapons only after facing disaster;
though they may follow in haste, they will not be in time.
17.51 One who when facing wealth forgets poverty,
and when facing life forgets death,
can stay far from crime.
The gentleman cherishes his speech,
the peacock cherishes its feathers,
and the tiger and leopard cherish their claws;
these are all methods for managing oneself.
Those who associate with those above do not lose their salaries;
those who associate with those below do not escape from trouble.
Therefore the gentleman chooses the person with whom to associate,
just as the farmer chooses the field to farm.
The gentleman cultivates people,
and the farmer cultivates the field.
The farmer selects the seeds and plants them,
and in a bountiful year he will surely obtain grain;
the scholar selects the person and cultivates them,
and in a fruitful time he will surely obtain a salary.
17.52 Only after the Way is lost in the world do benevolence and righteousness arise;
only after the state is not well-governed do filial sons arise;
only after the people compete and do not share do compassion and kindness arise;
only after the Way is subverted and the seasons are reversed do schemes and stratagems arise.
17.53 Generally, when goodness arises,
it is all due to what is learned.
Within a single household,
there must be a master of the Way,
which refers to the father and mother.
Therefore, if the ruler is upright, the common people will be governed;
if the parents are upright, the children and grandchildren will be filial and compassionate.
This is why the children in the household of Kǒngzǐ did not know how to curse,
and the children in the household of Zéngzǐ did not know how to fight in the road;
the reason it was so
is that they were well taught from birth.
17.54 Now, the benevolent like to bring people together,
while the non-benevolent like to separate people.
Therefore, when a superior man dwells among people, there is order;
when a petty man dwells among people, there is chaos.
A superior man wishes to harmonize people.
It is like water and fire, which are not naturally compatible;
yet if a tripod is placed between them,
the water and fire are not in chaos,
and instead harmonize the hundred flavors.
Thus, a superior man must be cautious in choosing the people who stand between them.
17.55 Qí Jǐng Gōng asked Yànzǐ, saying:
“I myself sit upon the ground,
and you gentlemen all sit upon the ground;
why do you alone pull up grass to sit upon?”
Yànzǐ replied:
“I, Yīng, have heard that
only for funerals and trials does one sit upon the bare ground.
Now, I dare not use the matters of funerals and trials
when I sit in attendance upon my lord.”
17.56 Qí Gāo Tíng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
“I, Tíng, did not seclude myself in the mountains,
nor did I settle on the land;
wearing a straw raincoat
and carrying a staff,
I concentrated my essence and spirit to ask about the way of serving a superior man;
I wish for the Master to tell me.”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Use integrity to manage affairs,
use reverence to assist them,
and be tireless in dealing with others.
If you see a superior man, promote him;
if you see a petty man, dismiss him;
remove the evil from your heart
and give him your loyalty.
Be diligent in your actions,
and cultivate your rituals.
Then, even beyond a thousand lǐ,
people will be as close as brothers.
If your actions are not diligent
and your rituals are not appropriate,
even those facing each other across a gate will not communicate.”
18.1 Yán Yuān asked Zhòngní, saying:
“What are the actions of a complete man like?”
The Master said:
“The actions of a complete man
reach the principles of emotion and nature,
penetrate the changes of various things,
know the causes of the hidden and the manifest,
and observe the source of the wandering ethers.
One who is like this can be called a complete man.
Having known the Way of Heaven,
he conducts himself with benevolence and righteousness
and disciplines himself with ritual and music.
Now, benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music
are the actions of a complete man.
Exhausting the spiritual and knowing transformations
is the peak of virtue.”
18.2 The Yì says:
‘Looking up, one observes the patterns of heaven;
looking down, one examines the principles of the earth.
Therefore, one knows the causes of the hidden and the manifest.’
When the effects of the patterns of heaven, the principles of the earth, and human emotions are stored in the heart,
it is the storehouse of sagehood and wisdom.
Therefore, when the sage kings of old presided over the world,
they necessarily adjusted for the four seasons,
established the laws of the calendar,
investigated the patterns of heaven,
and measured the changes of the times,
ascending the Líng Tái to observe the vapors and atmospheres.
Therefore, Yáo said:
‘Ah, you, Shùn!
The succession of Heaven’s numbers is upon your person.
Sincerely hold to the center,
lest the four seas fall into hardship and poverty.’
The Shū says:
‘Examine the xuánjī and the jade transverse
to regulate the seven governors.’
Xuánjī refers to the Běichén, Gōuchén, and Shū stars;
by following where its dipper points among the twenty-eight mansions,
they determine good and bad fortune, calamity and blessing.
The celestial divisions and mansions,
and the divinations of expansion and contraction,
are each verified by their kind.
The way of divining changes
consists of only two factors.
These two
are the numbers of Yīn and Yáng.
Therefore, the Yì says:
‘One Yīn and one Yáng is called the Way.’
As for the Way,
none of the movements of things are not from the Way.
Therefore, it originates in one,
is completed in two,
is prepared in three,
is perfected in four,
and acts through five.
Thus, among the manifest celestial images,
none are greater than the sun and moon.
In observing the movements of change,
none are more manifest than the five planets.
The five planets of heaven circulate the Qi within the five elements.
Their beginning still originates in Yīn and Yáng,
and their transformations reach eleven thousand five hundred and twenty.
The so-called twenty-eight stars are:
in the east: Jiǎo, Kàng, Dǐ, Fáng, Xīn, Wěi, and Jī;
in the north: Dǒu, Qiānniú, Xūnǚ, Xū, Wēi, Yíngshì, and Dōngbì;
in the west: Kuí, Lóu, Wèi, Mǎo, Bì, Zuīxī, and Shēn;
in the south: Dōngjǐng, Yúguǐ, Liǔ, Qīxīng, Zhāng, Yì, and Zhěn.
The so-called mansions
are where the sun, moon, and five planets lodge.
Their movements within and outside the mansions
are distinguished by official names.
Their roots all originate in the earth
and their flowers take shape in the heavens.
The so-called five planets are:
first, Suìxīng;
second, Yínghuò;
third, Zhènxīng;
fourth, Tàibái;
and fifth, Chénxīng.
Chānqiāng, huìbèi, xúnshǐ, wǎngshǐ, and the flag of Chīyóu
are all produced by the expansion and contraction of the five planets.
The transgressions of the five planets
are each divined by Metal, Wood, Water, Fire, and Earth.
Their hidden or visible appearances in spring, autumn, winter, and summer have their times.
If they lose their constancy
and depart from their season,
then it constitutes an anomaly;
if they keep their season
and dwell in their constancy,
this is called auspicious.
In ancient times, there were those who presided over the four seasons.
The one presiding over spring was Zhāng;
when it was central at dusk,
one could plant grain.
This was reported above to the Son of Heaven
and distributed below to the people.
The one presiding over summer was Dàhuǒ;
when it was central at dusk,
one could plant millet and beans.
This was reported above to the Son of Heaven
and distributed below to the people.
The one presiding over autumn was Xū;
when it was central at dusk,
one could plant wheat.
This was reported above to the Son of Heaven
and distributed below to the people.
The one presiding over winter was Mǎo;
when it was central at dusk,
one could engage in timbering, hunting, and storage.
This was reported to the Son of Heaven
and distributed below to the people.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven faced south to observe the centrality of the four stars,
knowing the urgency or leisure of the people.
In times of urgency, he would not impose taxes
nor raise corvée labor.
The Shū says:
“Reverently grant the people their seasons.” The Shī says:
“When things are present,
it is only because of their season.”
The reason things exist without end
is because of the timing of their movement.
18.3 The *Yì* says:
“Heaven displays symbols,
revealing good and bad fortune,
and the Sage takes them as a model.”
Formerly, Gāo Zōng and Chéng Wáng were moved by the portents of the pheasant's cry and the violent wind;
they cultivated their persons and reformed themselves,
and thus enjoyed the blessings of abundance and prosperity.
When the Qín Emperor ascended the throne,
comets appeared four times,
locusts covered the sky,
there was thunder in winter and ice in summer,
a stone fell in Dōng Jùn,
giants appeared in Lín Táo,
strange omens appeared together,
Yíng Huò occupied the Heart constellation,
a bushy star approached Tài Jiǎo,
and Tài Jiǎo consequently disappeared,
yet in the end he was unable to reform.
When Èr Shì was established,
he redoubled the wickedness.
Upon his accession,
the sun and moon were eclipsed,
mountains and forests were submerged and lost,
Chén Xīng appeared in the four beginning months of the seasons,
Tài Bái crossed the heavens in daytime,
there was thunder without clouds,
a crooked arrow glowed at night,
Yíng Huò invaded the moon,
ominous fires burned the palace,
wild beasts played in the courtyard,
and the inner gates of the capital collapsed.
Portents from Heaven moved above,
the ministers were muddled at court,
and the common people were in chaos below.
He failed to investigate these,
and thus he perished.
18.4 Within the eight wildernesses are the four seas;
within the four seas are the nine provinces.
The Son of Heaven resides in Zhōng Zhōu and governs the eight directions.
The area between the two rivers is called Jì Zhōu;
south of the river is Yù Zhōu;
west of the river is Yōng Zhōu;
south of the Hàn is Jīng Zhōu;
south of the Jiāng is Yáng Zhōu;
between the Jì and the Hé is Yǎn Zhōu;
east of the Jì is Xú Zhōu;
Yàn is Yōu Zhōu;
Qí is Qīng Zhōu.
Rivers, mountains, marshes, and wetlands,
ridges, plains, hills, and mounds—
for the suitability of the five soils,
the sage king followed their natural disposition,
adapted to their conveniences,
and did not lose their nature.
On high ground, broomcorn millet was planted;
on medium ground, foxtail millet;
on low ground, glutinous rice.
The uses of rushes, reeds, and various grasses were not lacking;
hemp, wheat, millet, and sorghum were also not exhausted.
Birds and beasts in the mountains and forests, and fish and turtles in the rivers and marshes multiplied.
The capital of the King was connected in all four directions to attract them.
18.5 In the second year of Zhōu Yōu Wáng,
the three rivers of Western Zhōu all experienced earthquakes.
Bó Yáng Fù said:
“The Zhōu is about to perish!
Now, the Qi of Heaven and Earth
does not lose its order.
If it exceeds its order,
it is because the people have brought chaos to it.
When the Yang is submerged and cannot emerge,
or when the Yin is pressed and cannot rise,
then there is an earthquake.
Now that the three rivers have shaken,
it is because the Yang has lost its place and is suppressed by the Yin.
When the Yang overflows and the Yin becomes strong,
the sources will surely be blocked.
When the sources are blocked,
the state will surely perish.
For when water and soil are moist and flowing, the people's needs are met.
If water and soil have no way to flow,
the people will lack resources for use.
What are they waiting for if not to perish?
Formerly, the Yī and Luò dried up and the Xià perished;
the Hé dried up and the Shāng perished.
Now the virtue of Zhōu is like that of the ends of the two dynasties,
and the sources of its rivers are again blocked.
If they are blocked, they must dry up.
A state must rely on mountains and rivers.
If mountains collapse and rivers dry up,
it is a sign of perishing.
If rivers dry up,
mountains must collapse.
If the state perishes, it will not exceed ten years;
for ten is the limit of numbers.
That which is discarded by Heaven does not exceed its limit.”
In that year,
the three rivers dried up,
and Qí Shān collapsed.
In the eleventh year,
Yōu Wáng was indeed destroyed,
and Zhōu then moved to the east.
18.6 The Five Peaks—
what are they called?
Tài Shān
is the Eastern Peak;
Huò Shān
is the Southern Peak;
Huà Shān
is the Western Peak;
Cháng Shān
is the Northern Peak;
Sōng Gāo Shān
is the Central Peak.
Why are the Five Peaks regarded as equal to the Three Ducal Ministers?
Because they can broadly spread clouds and rain,
and they can broadly gather clouds and rain.
Clouds emerge by brushing against the rocks,
joining together in an instant,
and before a morning is over, they rain upon the whole world.
Because they bestow virtue so extensively,
they are regarded as equal to the Three Ducal Ministers.
18.7 The Four Waterways—
what are they called?
The Jiāng, the Hé, the Huái, and the Jì.
Why are the Four Waterways regarded as equal to the Feudal Lords?
Because they can wash away filth and turbidity,
they can connect a hundred rivers to the sea,
and they can spray clouds and rain over a thousand li.
Because their bestowal is very great,
they are regarded as equal to the Feudal Lords.
18.8 Mountains and rivers—
why are they regarded as equal to the Viscounts and Barons?
Because they can produce things,
they can nourish and moisten things,
they can generate clouds and rain,
and the kindness they provide is much;
however, as their types are numbered in the hundreds,
they are regarded as equal to the Viscounts and Barons.
The *Shū* says:
“Sacrifice to the Liù Zōng,
offer sacrifices in order to the mountains and rivers,
and extend them to the host of spirits.”
18.9 Qí Jǐng Gōng constructed the Lù Qǐn tower.
He heard the hooting of an owl and detested it,
so when it was completed, he did not use it.
Bǎi Chángqiān said:
"The construction of the tower was very urgent;
now that the tower is finished,
why does my Lord not use it?"
The Duke said:
"Indeed,
there was an owl hooting previously;
there was no sound it did not make.
I detested it greatly,
and for this reason I do not use it."
Bǎi Chángqiān said:
"Your servant requests to perform a ritual to remove it."
The Duke said:
"What preparations are needed?"
He replied:
"Construct a new chamber and place white cogon grass within it."
The Duke had the chamber built;
when it was finished,
white cogon grass was placed inside.
Bǎi Chángqiān performed the ritual at night.
The next day he asked the Duke:
"Last night, did you hear the owl's hoot?"
The Duke said:
"It hooted once and was not heard again."
He sent someone to go and look;
the owl was by the steps,
wings spread,
lying dead on the ground.
The Duke said:
"Your Way is so brilliant!
Can you also increase the longevity of my humble self?"
He replied:
"I can."
The Duke said:
"By how much can you increase it?"
He replied:
"Nine years for the Son of Heaven,
seven for the feudal lords,
and five for the grandees."
The Duke said:
"Do you also have an omen to show for it?"
He replied:
"When longevity is obtained,
the earth shall shake."
The Duke was delighted
and ordered the officials to quickly prepare what Chángqiān requested.
Bǎi Chángqiān went out
and met Yànzǐ on the road.
He bowed before the horse
and explained:
"I performed a ritual for the Lord to remove the owl and killed it.
The Lord said to me:
'Your Way is so brilliant,
can you also increase my longevity?'
I said:
'I can.'
Now, a great sacrifice is about to be held to request longevity for the Lord,
so I am going to inform him."
Yànzǐ said:
"Ha,
that is good indeed!
To be able to request longevity for the Lord.
Even so,
I have heard this:
only by means of governance and virtue can one be in harmony with the spirits,
and thereby increase longevity.
Now, if there is only a sacrifice,
can longevity be increased?
Furthermore, was there an omen of blessing to be seen?"
He replied:
"When longevity is obtained,
the earth will shake."
Yànzǐ said:
"Chángqiān,
previously I saw the Wéi star severed
and the Shū star scattered;
the earth will likely shake.
Are you using this?"
Bǎi Chángqiān looked down for a while,
then looked up and replied:
"Yes."
Yànzǐ said:
"Doing this brings no benefit,
and not doing it brings no harm.
You should lighten the taxes,
not burden the people,
and let the Lord know of this."
18.10 Flood and drought are both caused by the Yīn and Yáng of Heaven and Earth.
During a great drought, the Yú sacrifice is performed to request rain;
during a great flood, drums are beaten to threaten the Shè deity.
Why is this?
It is said:
Yáng
is the leader of Yīn.
Among birds, the male is Yáng and the female is Yīn;
among beasts, the male is Yáng and the female is Yīn;
among the people, the husband is Yáng and the wife is Yīn;
in the family, the father is Yáng and the son is Yīn;
in the state, the ruler is Yáng and the subject is Yīn.
Therefore, Yáng is noble and Yīn is lowly,
Yáng is honored and Yīn is base;
this is the Way of Heaven.
Now, a great drought
is Yáng energy being too abundant and suppressing Yīn.
When Yīn is suppressed, Yáng becomes firm;
Yáng fills the void.
Because this filling and suppression is too extreme,
it prevents Yīn from rising.
Thus, one only performs the Yú sacrifice and bows to request rain,
not daring to add anything more.
As for great floods and solar eclipses,
these are cases where Yīn energy is too abundant and rises to diminish the Yáng essence.
This is the lowly riding upon the noble,
the base insulting the honored;
it is a great rebellion and unrighteousness.
Therefore, drums are beaten to frighten it,
and red silk is used to entwine and threaten it.
From this perspective,
the Chūnqiū rectifies the positions within the world,
identifies the failures of Yīn and Yáng,
and directly blames the rebellious,
not avoiding difficulties.
This is also how the Chūnqiū does not fear the strong and aggressive.
Thus, threatening the solemn Shè altar is not considered alarming the spirits;
expelling the Heavenly King is not considered disrespecting the superior;
rejecting the command of Kuài Kuì is not considered not listening to one's father;
cutting off ties with Wén Jiāng is not considered not loving one's mother.
Is this not the ultimate expression of righteousness?
Is this not the ultimate expression of righteousness?
18.11 At the time of a great drought in Qí,
Jǐng Gōng summoned his ministers and asked:
"It has not rained for a long time;
the people have the look of hunger.
I had someone perform divination,
and the misfortune lies in the high mountains and wide waters.
I wish to levy a small tax to sacrifice to Líng Shān;
is this permissible?"
None of the ministers responded.
Yànzǐ stepped forward and said:
"It is not permissible.
Sacrificing to them is of no benefit.
Líng Shān takes stone as its body
and grass and trees as its hair.
When it does not rain for a long time,
the hair will be scorched
and the body will be hot.
Would they alone not desire rain?
Sacrificing to them is of no benefit."
Jǐng Gōng said:
"If not that,
I wish to sacrifice to Hé Bó;
is this permissible?"
Yànzǐ said:
"It is not permissible.
Sacrificing to him is of no benefit.
Hé Bó takes the water as his state
and fish and turtles as his people.
When it does not rain for a long time,
the water level will descend,
the hundred rivers will dry up,
his state will perish,
and his people will be annihilated.
Would he alone not use rain?
What benefit is there in sacrificing to him?"
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Now, what should be done about it?"
Yànzǐ said:
"If my Lord sincerely leaves the palace and exposes yourself to the elements,
sharing the worry with Líng Shān and Hé Bó,
perhaps it will fortunately rain."
Thereupon Jǐng Gōng went out into the wilds and exposed himself;
after three days,
there was indeed a great rain,
and the people were all able to plant.
Jǐng Gōng said:
"Excellent!
Can the words of Yànzǐ be left unused?
Only he possesses virtue."
18.12 Whenever Heaven and Earth have a union of virtue,
then the vital breath possesses essence.
As Yīn and Yáng wax and wane,
then transformations and changes have their seasons.
When the season is attained, there is order;
when the season is attained, there is transformation;
when the season is lost, there is disorder.
For this reason, there are five things that humans are not born possessing:
their eyes cannot see,
they cannot eat,
they cannot walk,
they cannot speak,
and they cannot reproduce.
Therefore, after three months the eyes open and then they can see;
after seven months the teeth grow and then they can eat;
after a full year the kneecaps develop and then they can walk;
after three years the fontanelles close and then they can speak;
and at sixteen the essence flows and then they can reproduce.
When Yīn reaches its limit, it returns to Yáng;
when Yáng reaches its limit, it returns to Yīn;
thus Yīn changes through Yáng,
and Yáng changes through Yīn.
Thus a male grows teeth at eight months
and loses teeth at eight years;
at twice eight, which is sixteen, his essence transforms and begins to flow.
A female grows teeth at seven months
and loses teeth at seven years;
at twice seven, which is fourteen, her essence transforms and begins to flow.
In those who are unworthy, when the transformation of essence first arrives
and the vital breath is stirred,
they act upon their emotions and indulge their desires;
thus they pervert reproduction and bring disorder to transformation.
Thus the Shī says:
"As for that person,
who thinks of marriage,
they are greatly lacking in good faith,
and do not know the decree."
The worthy are not like this;
when their essence and transformation are full and overflowing,
they later grieve that the proper time cannot be met,
and not seeing the beginning of the way,
they then set forth their emotions and desires in song.
The Shī says:
"The quiet girl is beautiful,
she waits for me at the corner of the city wall.
Loving her but not seeing her,
I scratch my head and pace to and fro."
"I look at that sun and moon,
distant is my longing.
The way is said to be far,
how can he come!"
These are words of urgency regarding the season;
they are extreme,
and so they invoke the sun and moon.
18.13 Measures of length, weight, and capacity
are generated from millet grains:
one grain makes one fēn;
ten fēn make one cùn;
ten cùn make one chǐ;
ten chǐ make one zhàng.
Sixteen grains of millet make one dòu;
six dòu make one zhū;
twenty-four zhū weigh one liǎng;
sixteen liǎng make one jīn;
thirty jīn make one jūn;
four jūn weigh one shí.
One thousand two hundred grains of millet make one yuè;
ten yuè make one gě;
ten gě make one shēng;
ten shēng make one dǒu;
ten dǒu make one shí.
18.14 In all the *Liùjīng* written by the emperors and kings,
there are none that do not summon the *Sìlíng*.
When virtue is abundant, they are kept as domestic animals;
when governance is peaceful, the seasonal vapors arrive.
Thus the *Qílín* has the body of a river deer and the tail of an ox,
a rounded forehead and a single horn.
It embodies benevolence and harbors righteousness;
its voice accords with the musical scales.
Its gait accords with the compass,
and its turns accord with the square.
It chooses the ground before treading on it,
and only stays where the site is level.
It does not live in herds
and does not travel in groups.
Resplendent is its substance and pattern.
In seclusion, it is orderly and composed;
when moving, it has a dignified bearing.
When *Huángdì* ascended the throne,
his sagely grace received the mandate of Heaven;
he cultivated the brilliant Way with singular focus
and practiced only benevolence.
Within the universe all was peaceful,
yet the phoenix had not been seen.
He pondered its image
and rose early at dawn.
Thereupon he asked *Tiānlǎo*,
saying:
"What is the phoenix's likeness?"
*Tiānlǎo* said:
"The phoenix
has the front of a swan-goose and the back of a *qílín*,
the neck of a snake and the tail of a fish,
the stature of a crane and the mind of a mandarin duck.
Its will is set upon beautiful transformations and withering branches.
It has the patterns of a dragon and the body of a tortoise,
the beak of a swallow and the bill of a chicken;
its wings are parallel and flow toward the center.
Its head wears virtue,
its crown displays righteousness,
its back carries benevolence,
and its heart holds sincerity and wisdom.
When eating, it has substance;
when drinking, it has ritual;
when going, it has patterns;
and when coming, it has auspiciousness.
Its morning call is named *Fāmíng*,
its daytime call is named *Bǎocháng*,
its flying call is named *Shàngxiáng*,
and its perching call is named *Guīchāng*.
Its wings hold righteousness,
its breast embraces loyalty,
its feet tread on uprightness,
and its tail is tied to martial prowess.
Its soft voice matches the metal bells,
and its loud sound matches the drums.
Stretching its neck and flapping its wings,
the five lights are fully displayed.
Its radiance rouses the eight winds,
and its breath brings down the seasonal rains.
This is what is called the phoenix's likeness.
Only the phoenix can investigate the myriad things,
communicate with Heaven's blessings,
embody a hundred forms,
and reach the Way.
When it leaves, there is disaster;
when it appears, there is fortune.
It surveys the *Jiǔzhōu*,
observes the *Bājí*,
possesses both civil and martial arts,
rectifies the kingly state,
and illuminates the four directions with awe.
The benevolent and sagely all submit.
Therefore, those who obtain one aspect of the phoenix's image,
the phoenix passes by them.
Those who obtain two,
the phoenix descends to them.
Those who obtain three,
it descends during spring and autumn.
Those who obtain four,
it descends during all four seasons.
Those who obtain five,
it stays with them for their whole life."
*Huángdì* said:
"Alas!
How grand!"
Thereupon he prepared a yellow ceremonial crown,
donned a yellow sash,
and fasted in the *Zhōnggōng*.
The phoenix then obscured the sun and descended.
*Huángdì* descended from the eastern steps,
faced west,
and bowed his head, saying:
"August Heaven has sent this down;
how could I dare not receive the mandate!"
Then the phoenix settled in the *Dōngyòu*,
ate the Emperor's bamboo seeds,
perched on the Emperor's paulownia trees,
and did not leave for his entire life.
The *Shī* says:
"The phoenixes cry out,
on that high ridge.
The paulownia trees grow,
on that sun-facing slope.
Luxuriant and dense,
harmonious and shrill."
This is what it refers to.
The numinous tortoise is patterned with five colors,
resembling jade and gold.
Its back is *yīn* and it faces *yáng*.
The upper convexity resembles Heaven,
and the lower flatness models Earth.
Its expansion resembles mountains;
its four toes move in cycle, corresponding to the four seasons.
The patterns displayed resemble the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
It has a snake's head and dragon's wings.
Its left eye represents the Sun,
and its right eye represents the Moon.
In its thousand-year transformation,
the vapor below communicates with the above.
It can know the changes of survival and destruction, fortune and misfortune.
When at rest, it is trustworthy and steadfast;
when moving, it is manifest.
The divine dragon can become high
or low,
large
or small,
hidden
or luminous,
short
or long.
Brilliant is its height;
profound is its depth.
It approaches the celestial light,
and lofty is its manifestation.
Now present, now gone—
how sudden and subtle!
Elegantly forming a pattern,
in void and non-being, it is refined and harmonious;
in movement, it is numinous and transformative.
Alas!
How true!
The gentleman emulates the divine;
observing those dignified bearings
and wandering in seclusion
is like the phoenix.
The *Shū* says:
"The birds and beasts dance in rhythm,
and the phoenixes come to present their bearing."
This is what it refers to.
18.15 At the time of *Chéngwáng*,
there were three rice sprouts that grew through a mulberry tree
and joined together into a single ear of grain.
It was large enough to almost fill a cart
and long enough to almost fill a chest.
The people obtained it and presented it to *Chéngwáng*.
*Chéngwáng* asked *Zhōugōng*, saying:
"What is this?"
*Zhōugōng* said:
"Three sprouts joining as one ear of grain;
does this mean that all under Heaven will harmonize and become one?"
Three years later,
the *Yuèshángshì* people arrived for an audience via multiple translations
and presented a white pheasant to *Zhōugōng*,
saying:
"The roads are distant and far,
and the mountains and rivers are obstructed and deep.
Fearing that a single envoy could not communicate,
we have come to have an audience through triple translation."
*Zhōugōng* said:
"If the bounty of virtue is not applied,
then the gentleman does not enjoy their gifts;
if government orders are not executed,
then the gentleman does not treat their people as subjects."
The translator said:
"I received a command from an elder of my state, who said:
'For a long time, Heaven has been without violent winds or excessive rains.
Does this mean that the *Zhōngguó* has a sage?
If so, why not have an audience with him?'"
Thereupon *Zhōugōng* respectfully accepted the reason for their coming.
18.16 In the fifteenth year of Zhōu Huì Wáng,
a spirit descended at Shēn.
The King asked Nèishǐ Guò:
“What is the reason for this?
Has this happened before?”
He replied:
“It has happened.
When a state is about to rise,
its ruler is devout and enlightened, balanced and upright, refined and pure, kind and harmonious.
His virtue is sufficient to make his fragrant offerings manifest,
and his kindness is sufficient to unite his people.
The spirits accept the offerings and the people listen;
people and spirits have no grievances.
Therefore, the bright spirits descend there,
observing the government's virtue and distributing blessings equally.
When a state is about to perish,
its ruler is greedy and covetous, perverse and evil, licentious and dissolute, idle and negligent, foul and corrupt, cruel and oppressive.
His administration is rank and foul,
and fragrant offerings do not ascend.
His punishments are deceptive and false,
and the common people are divided and disloyal.
The bright spirits do not find it pure, and the people harbor intentions of distancing themselves.
Both people and spirits feel bitter resentment,
with nothing to rely upon or cherish.
Therefore, spirits also go there,
observing the cruelties and vices to bring down calamities.
Thus, some see spirits and rise,
while others see them and perish.
Formerly, when the Xià rose,
Zhùróng descended at Chóng Shān;
when it perished,
Huílù appeared at Tíngsuì.
When the Shāng rose,
Táowù stayed at Pī Shān;
when it perished,
the Yíyáng was seen in Mù.
When the Zhōu rose,
the Yuèzhuó sang on Qí Shān;
when it declined,
Dù Bó shot Xuān Wáng at Gǎo.
These are all the records of the bright spirits.”
The King asked:
“Now, what spirit is this?”
He replied:
“Formerly, Zhāo Wáng took a wife from Fáng,
called Fánghòu.
She had deviant virtue
and was in accord with Dānzhū.
Dānzhū possessed her body to mate with her,
and she gave birth to Mù Wáng.
This spirit watches over the descendants of Zhōu to bring blessings or calamities.
A spirit does not move far away;
looking at it from this perspective,
is it not perhaps Dānzhū?”
The King asked:
“Who will receive it?”
He replied:
“It is in Guó.”
The King asked:
“Then what should be done?”
He replied:
“I have heard:
To follow the Way and receive a spirit
is called abundant blessing;
to be licentious and receive a spirit
is called greedy calamity.
Now Guó is somewhat neglected and desolate;
it will surely perish!”
The King asked:
“What should I do?”
He replied:
“Command the Tàizǎi to lead the Invocators and Scribes along with the Lí clan,
to take sacrificial animals, grains, jade, and silk to offer there,
but do not pray for anything.”
The King asked:
“How long will Guó last?”
He replied:
“Formerly, Yáo oversaw the people in five-year cycles;
now his descendant appears.
When ghosts and spirits appear,
they do not fail to match the proper timing and nature.
Looking at it from this perspective,
it will not exceed five years.”
The King sent Tàizǎi Jǐfù to lead the Fù clan along with the Invocators and Scribes,
bearing sacrificial animals and jade vessels to make the offering.
Nèishǐ Guò followed.
Upon arriving in Guó,
the Guó Gōng also sent Invocators and Scribes to request land from the spirit.
Nèishǐ Guò heard Guó's request for the mandate,
and when he returned,
he told the King:
“Guó will surely perish.
They are not sincere toward the spirit yet seek blessings from it;
the spirit will surely bring calamity upon them.
They are not close to the people yet seek to use them;
the people will surely turn away from them.
To offer with a refined intent
is called sincerity;
to compassionately protect the common people
is called being close.
Now the Guó Gōng acts to exhaust the common people to satisfy his transgressions,
alienating the people and angering the spirit while seeking profit.
Is that not difficult!”
In the nineteenth year,
Jìn took Guó.
18.17 Qí Huán Gōng was campaigning north against Gūzhú.
When he was ten lǐ from the Bēi'ěr Stream,
he suddenly stopped
and stared blankly.
After a while,
he held an arrow but did not dare to shoot.
He sighed deeply and said:
“Will the matter not succeed?
There is a person one foot tall,
wearing a large ceremonial cap and crown,
with all human features complete.
He lifts the left sleeve of his garment
and runs before my horse.”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“The matter will surely succeed.
This person
is the spirit of Zhīdào.
His running before the horse
means he is guiding us.
His lifting the left sleeve
means there is water ahead;
we should cross from the left side.”
After traveling ten lǐ,
there was indeed a river called the Liào Shuǐ.
They marked it;
crossing from the left, it reached the ankles,
but crossing from the right, it reached the knees.
Once they had crossed,
the matter did indeed succeed.
Duke Huán bowed twice before Guǎn Zhòng’s horse and said:
“The sagacity of Zhòngfù reaches such heights!
I have been at fault for a long time.”
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“I, Yíwú, have heard:
A sage knows things before they have taken form;
now that it already had form, I knew it.
This shows that Yíwú is good at following teachings,
but I am no sage.”
18.18 Wú attacked Yuè
and destroyed Huìjī,
obtaining a bone segment that filled a chariot.
They sent an envoy to ask Kǒngzǐ:
“Which bones are the largest?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“When Yǔ summoned his ministers at Mount Huìjī,
the Fángfēng Shì arrived late.
Yǔ killed and executed him;
his bone segment filled a chariot.
This is the largest.”
The envoy asked:
“Who serves as a spirit?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The spirits of the mountains and rivers
who are sufficient to provide order to the world
serve as spirits.
Those of the altars of grain and soil serve as Dukes and Marquises,
and those of the sacrifices to mountains and rivers serve as feudal lords;
all belong to the King.”
He asked:
“What did Fángfēng Shì preside over?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“He was the ruler of the Wāngmáng Shì,
presiding over the mountains of Fēng and Yú.
His spirit belongs to the Lí clan.
During the Yú and Xià dynasties, they were called Fángfēng Shì;
in the Shāng, they were the Wāngmáng Shì;
in the Zhōu, they were the Zhǎngdí Shì;
now they are called the Giants.”
The envoy asked:
“How tall can a person be?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The Jiāojiǎo Shì are three feet tall,
which is the limit of shortness.
The tallest do not exceed ten units,
which is the extreme of the measurement.”
The envoy said:
“Excellent!
You are a sage.”
18.19 When Zhòngní was in Chén,
a falcon alighted in the courtyard of the Marquis of Chén and died.
An arrow of thimbleberry wood was piercing it,
with a stone arrowhead;
its length was a foot and a span.
The Marquis of Chén sent someone to ask Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The falcon has come from afar.
This is an arrow of the Sùshèn clan.
Formerly, when Wǔ Wáng conquered Shāng,
he opened paths to the Jiǔyí and Bǎimán,
making each bring their local goods as tribute,
so that they would not forget their professional duties.
Thereupon, the Sùshèn clan presented arrows of thimbleberry wood and stone arrowheads,
their length being a foot and a span.
The former king wished to illustrate the reach of his illustrious virtue to distant lands,
and to show it to future generations
so they might forever observe it.
Therefore, he inscribed on the nock:
'The Sùshèn clan presented arrows of thimbleberry wood.'
He gave them as a reward to Dà Jī,
when she was married to Yú Hú Gōng and enfeoffed in Chén.
He distributed precious jades to those of the same surname
to manifest familial closeness;
he distributed the tributes from distant lands to those of different surnames
to ensure they did not forget their submission.
Therefore, Chén was given the arrows of the Sùshèn clan.
Try searching for them in the old storehouse."
They were indeed found there.
18.20 When Jì Huánzǐ was digging a well, he found a clay pot;
inside it was a sheep.
He asked Kǒngzǐ about it,
claiming he had found a dog.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"From what I have heard,
it is not a dog
but a sheep.
The monsters of wood and stone
are the Kuí and Wǎngliǎng;
the monsters of water
are the Lóng and Wǎngxiàng;
the monster of earth
is the Fényáng,
not a dog."
Huánzǐ said:
"Excellent!"
18.21 Chǔ Zhāo Wáng was crossing the river
when there was an object as large as a peck measure
that struck the King's boat directly
and stayed inside the boat.
Zhāo Wáng found it very strange
and sent an envoy to ask Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is named Píngshí;
it can be sliced and eaten.
Only a hegemon can obtain it;
this is an auspicious omen."
Afterward, there was a flying bird in Qí
with one leg
that came down
and alighted in front of the palace.
It stretched its wings and hopped.
The Marquis of Qí found it very strange
and also sent an envoy to ask Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is named Shāngyáng.
Quickly tell the people to hurry and repair the ditches and canals;
heaven is about to send a great rain."
Thereupon they did so,
and heaven did indeed send a great rain.
All the various states were flooded,
but Qí alone remained safe.
When Kǒngzǐ returned,
his disciples asked him about it.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the past,
children sang a rhyme:
'The King of Chǔ crossed the river and found a Píngshí;
as large as a fist,
red as the sun,
sliced and eaten, sweet as honey.'
This was the omen for Chǔ.
There were also children who held hands in pairs,
bent one leg and hopped, saying:
'Heaven will send a great rain,
the Shāngyáng begins its dance.'
Now that Qí has obtained it,
it is also its omen.
After such rhymes,
there has never been a time when an omen did not follow."
Therefore, a Sage does not only uphold the Way;
by observing things and recording them,
he grasps the portents.
18.22 Zhèng Jiǎn Gōng sent Gōngsūn Chéngzǐ on a mission to Jìn.
Píng Gōng was ill.
Hán Xuānzǐ assisted him
and assigned a residence to the guest.
The guest asked about the ruler's illness.
He replied:
"The ruler's illness has lasted a long time.
All the spirits of heaven and earth have been petitioned everywhere,
but there has been no relief.
Now he has dreamed of a yellow bear entering the bedroom door;
we do not know if it is a human ghost
or a malevolent spirit."
Zǐchǎn said:
"With your ruler's intelligence
and you conducting the government,
what malevolent spirit could there be?
I, Qiáo, have heard
that when Gǔn formerly disobeyed the Emperor's command,
he was executed at Yǔ Shān.
He transformed into a yellow bear
and entered the Yǔ Yuān.
He became the object of the Xià suburban sacrifice,
which the three dynasties upheld.
As for whom ghosts and spirits reach out to,
if it is not one of their own kin,
then they follow those of the same status.
For this reason, the Son of Heaven sacrifices to the Lord on High,
the Dukes and Marquises sacrifice to the hundred spirits,
and those from high officials down do not go beyond their own kin.
Now the House of Zhōu has slightly declined,
and Jìn has in fact succeeded it.
Perhaps the Xià suburban sacrifice has not been performed?"
Xuānzǐ reported this
and performed the Xià suburban sacrifice,
with Dǒng Bó acting as the personator of the deceased.
In five days, the Duke recovered.
The Duke saw Zǐchǎn
and presented him with the Jǔ Tripod.
18.23 Guó Gōng dreamed he was in the temple.
There was a spirit
with a human face, white fur, and tiger claws,
holding a battle-axe and standing in the western corner.
The Duke was afraid and ran.
The spirit said:
"Do not run!
The Emperor's command says:
'Make Jìn launch a surprise attack at your gates.'"
The Duke bowed and kowtowed.
He woke up
and summoned Shǐ Yǐn to interpret it.
Yǐn said:
"According to your words,
it was Rùshōu,
the divine spirit of Heaven's punishment;
Heaven's affairs are completed through officials."
The Duke had him imprisoned
and ordered the people of the state to celebrate the dream.
Zhōu Zhīqiáo told the other lords:
"Guó will not last long;
I know it now.
The ruler does not reflect but instead celebrates a great state's surprise attack;
how can his malady be cured?
I have heard it said:
'When a great state follows the Way and a small state is surprised by it, it is called submission;
when a small state is arrogant and a great state surprises it, it is called punishment.'
The people hate the ruler's extravagance;
thus he follows a path of disobeying commands.
Now he celebrates this dream;
his extravagance will surely expand.
This is Heaven taking away his discernment and increasing his malady.
The people hate his conduct,
and Heaven has deceived him.
A great state comes to punish him,
yet his issued orders are contrary to reason.
The ancestral state is already debased,
and the feudal lords distance themselves from him.
With no allies inside or out,
who will come to his rescue?
I cannot bear to wait."
He was about to leave
and went to Jìn with his clan.
Three years later,
Guó indeed perished.
18.24 Jìn Píng Gōng built the Chambers of Sī Qí.
A stone spoke.
Píng Gōng asked Shī Kuàng,
"For what reason did the stone speak?"
He replied,
"Stones cannot speak.
A spirit must have possessed it;
if not,
then the people's hearing is deluded.
I have heard:
'When works are undertaken out of season
and resentment and slander move among the people,
then things that do not normally speak will speak.'
Now the palaces and chambers are lofty and extravagant,
the people's strength is exhausted,
the commoners are distressed and resentful,
and none find peace in their nature.
That a stone should speak,
is it not fitting?"
18.25 Jìn Píng Gōng went out to hunt.
He saw a nursing tiger crouching and not moving.
He looked back and said to Shī Kuàng,
"I have heard
that when a lord of hegemons or kings goes out,
then fierce beasts crouch and do not dare to rise.
Now when I go out,
I see a nursing tiger crouching and not moving.
Could this be such a fierce beast?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"Magpies eat hedgehogs;
hedgehogs eat *jùnyí* birds;
*jùnyí* birds eat leopards;
leopards eat *bó*;
and *bó* eat tigers.
The appearance of a *bó* is similar to a *bó* horse.
Today, when my lord went out,
did you not surely hitch a *bó* horse to your carriage to hunt?"
The Duke said,
"Indeed."
Shī Kuàng said,
"I have heard
that one who deceives himself once will be destitute;
one who deceives himself twice will be disgraced;
and one who deceives himself thrice will die.
Now, the reason the tiger did not move
was because of the *bó* horse;
it was certainly not because of my lord’s virtue or righteousness.
Why would you deceive yourself for the first time?"
On another day, Píng Gōng went out to court.
A bird circled Píng Gōng and would not leave.
Píng Gōng looked back and said to Shī Kuàng,
"I have heard
that for a lord of hegemons or kings,
the phoenix descends to him.
Today, when I came out to court,
a bird circled me
and would not leave the whole morning.
Could this be a phoenix?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"In the east, there is a bird named the *jiànkē*.
As a bird,
it has a patterned body and red feet;
it hates other birds but loves foxes.
Today, did my lord not surely wear a fox-fur robe to court?"
Píng Gōng said,
"Indeed."
Shī Kuàng said,
"I have already spoken of this:
one who deceives himself once will be destitute,
one who deceives himself twice will be disgraced,
and one who deceives himself thrice will die.
Now, the bird is here because of the fox-fur robe;
it is not because of my lord's virtue or righteousness.
Why would my lord deceive himself for the second time?"
Píng Gōng was displeased.
On another day, he set out wine at the Tower of Sī Qí.
He ordered the Attendant Mǎ Zhāng to spread caltrops on the stairs.
He then sent someone to summon Shī Kuàng.
Shī Kuàng arrived
and ascended to the hall wearing his shoes.
Píng Gōng said,
"How can a subject wear shoes while ascending the hall of his ruler?"
Shī Kuàng removed his shoes, which pricked his feet.
He crawled on all fours, which pricked his knees.
He looked up to heaven and sighed.
The Duke stood up, led him forward, and said,
"I was just playing a joke on you, old man.
Why are you suddenly so worried?"
He replied,
"I am worried.
Meat breeds worms which then eat it in return;
wood breeds termites which then hollow it in return;
a man brings about his own omens which then destroy him in return.
In the vessels of the five cauldrons,
goosefoot and bean leaves should not grow;
in the halls and temples of a ruler,
caltrops should not grow."
Píng Gōng asked,
"What should be done now?"
Shī Kuàng said,
"The omen is already before us;
nothing can be done!
On the eighth day of the coming month,
after setting the officials in order
and establishing the heir apparent,
you, my lord, will die!"
When the eighth day of the coming month arrived,
at dawn,
the Duke said to Shī Kuàng,
"You set today as the deadline;
how am I doing?"
Shī Kuàng was unhappy
and requested to return home.
Not long after he returned, Píng Gōng died.
Thus it was known that Shī Kuàng's spirit was enlightened.
18.26 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ asked Dí Fēng Tú,
"I have heard that in Dí it rained gadflies and grain for three days.
Is this true?"
He said,
"It is true."
"I also heard it rained blood for three days.
Is this true?"
He said,
"It is true."
"I also heard that horses gave birth to cows,
and cows gave birth to horses.
Is this true?"
He said,
"It is true."
Jiǎn Zǐ said,
"How great!
These omens
are enough to destroy a state!"
He replied,
"As for the rain of gadflies and grain for three days,
it was grain blown by a gadfly-wind.
As for the rain of blood for three days,
it was birds of prey striking above.
As for horses giving birth to cows
and cows giving birth to horses,
it was because they were pastured together.
These are not the omens of Dí."
Jiǎn Zǐ said,
"Then what are the omens of Dí?"
He replied,
"Its state is frequently dispersed;
its ruler is young and weak;
its high ministers take bribes;
its grandees form factions to seek salary and rank;
its officials act willfully without reporting;
its government orders are not completed and frequently changed;
its scholars are clever and greedy and full of resentment.
These are its omens."
18.27 Āi Gōng shot an arrow and hit the God of Millet, Jì.
His mouth became diseased,
and he could not eat meat.
He sacrificed to Jì to seek favor.
He consulted the shaman official through divination.
The shaman official's tone changed as he said,
"Jì carried the five seeds
and leaned on a stalk as he descended from heaven.
Before he reached the ground, the stalk broke.
An old man of Liè Gǔ opened his robe to catch him.
Why do you not announce a sacrifice to him?"
The Duke followed this advice, and his illness went away.
18.28 Biǎn Què passed through Zhào,
and the Crown Prince of the King of Zhào died suddenly of an illness.
Biǎn Què went to the palace gate and said:
"I have heard that in the capital there is suddenly an affair of the burial mounds.
Could it be that there is an emergency?"
A Zhōngshùzǐ who was fond of medical methods came out to answer him, saying:
"It is so.
The King’s Crown Prince has died suddenly of an illness."
Biǎn Què said:
"Go in and say that Qín Yuè rén of Zhèng can revive the Crown Prince."
The Zhōngshùzǐ questioned him, saying:
"I have heard that the one who practiced medicine in high antiquity was named Miáo Fù.
When Miáo Fù practiced medicine,
he used grass for mats
and straw for dogs.
Facing north, he would pray over them.
He would utter only ten words,
and all those who came supported by others
or were carried there
would be restored as they were before.
Can your methods do such a thing?"
Biǎn Què said:
"They cannot."
He continued:
"I have heard that the one who practiced medicine in middle antiquity was named Yú Fù.
When Yú Fù practiced medicine,
he would massage the brain and marrow,
bind the membranes of the organs,
clear the nine orifices by cauterization and fix the meridians,
making the dead become living persons again.
Therefore, he was called Yú Fù.
Can your methods be like this?"
Biǎn Què said:
"They cannot."
The Zhōngshùzǐ said:
"With methods like yours,
it is as if looking at the sky through a tube
or piercing the earth with an awl.
What you look at is very large,
but what you see is very little.
Even if your methods were equal to others,
how could they be enough to change the alarm of a child?"
Biǎn Què said:
"Not so.
