There are indeed those who, in the dark, hit a mosquito’s head with a stick
or distinguish black from white while covering their eyes.
The Crown Prince’s illness
is what is called ‘corpse-syncope.’
If you think it is not so,
try going in and examining him.
The inner thighs of the Crown Prince should be warm,
his ears should be dry and burning,
and there should be a sound as if someone is whistling.
Cases like this
can all be cured."
The Zhōngshùzǐ went in and reported to the King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào rushed out barefoot
and, reaching the gate, said:
"Master, you have come from afar and been troubled;
I am fortunate that you visit me.
If you, Master, are fortunate enough to succeed,
then this offspring of dung and soil
will be able to receive the cover of heaven and tread upon the earth and remain a person for a long time.
If you, Master, do not succeed,
then he will follow the dogs and horses and fill the trenches."
Before he finished speaking,
his tears soaked his lapel.
Biǎn Què then diagnosed him.
He first prepared the brazier of Xuān Guāng
and the broth of eight completions,
and sharpened the needles and stones.
He took the Three Yang and Five Shū points.
Zǐ Róng pounded the medicine,
Zǐ Míng blew into the ears,
Yáng Yí restored the spirit,
Zǐ Yuè supported the form,
and Zǐ Yóu performed massages.
The Crown Prince was then able to come back to life.
When everyone under heaven heard of this, they all said:
"Biǎn Què can bring the dead back to life."
Biǎn Què demurred, saying:
"I am not able to bring the dead back to life;
I only enable those who ought to live to stay alive.
Those who are truly dead still cannot be made to live through medicine."
How sad!
The governance of a chaotic ruler cannot be stopped by medicine.
The *Shī* says:
"With much going on and great heat,
it cannot be saved by medicine."
These are words of the extreme state of things.
18.29 Kǒngzǐ stood in the hall in the morning
and heard the sound of someone weeping very sorrowfully.
Kǒngzǐ took up the qín and played it,
and its tone was the same as the weeping.
Kǒngzǐ went out,
and among his disciples, there was one who sighed.
He asked:
"Who is it?"
The reply was:
"It is Huí."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Huí, why do you sigh?"
Huí said:
"Just now there was someone weeping,
and the sound was very sorrowful.
It was not only weeping for a death,
but also weeping for a separation among the living."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How do you know this?"
Huí said:
"It is like the birds of Wán Shān."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How is that?"
Huí said:
"The birds of Wán Shān
produce four young.
When their wings are fully formed,
they then depart for the four seas.
The mother bird cries mournfully as she sees them off,
because they are going and will not return."
Kǒngzǐ sent someone to question the one weeping.
The one weeping said:
"My father died and the family is poor;
I am selling my son to bury him,
and I am about to part with him."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How excellent!
A sage!"
18.30 Duke Jǐng hunted at Wǔ Qiū.
It was still early in the night.
The Duke sat and dozed off
and dreamed of five men facing north and approaching his lodge,
claiming they were without guilt.
When the Duke woke up,
he summoned Yànzǐ and told him what he had dreamed.
The Duke said:
"Have I perhaps ever killed the innocent or executed those without guilt?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"In the past, the former ruler Duke Líng hunted here.
Five men used nets and startled the beasts,
so he killed them.
He cut off their heads and buried them.
He named the place ‘The Mound of the Five Men.’
Could it be this?"
The Duke ordered people to dig and search for them,
and five heads were found together in one pit.
The Duke said:
"Alas!"
He ordered the officials to bury them.
The people of the state did not know of his dream;
they said:
"The ruler pities even white bones,
how much more the living!
He spares no effort
and leaves no wisdom unused."
Therefore it is said:
"For a ruler of men, doing good is easy."
18.31 Zǐ Gòng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Do the dead have knowledge, or will they have no knowledge?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If I were to say the dead have knowledge,
I fear that filial sons and obedient grandsons would harm the living to see off the dead;
if I were to say they have no knowledge,
I fear that unfilial sons and grandsons would abandon their parents and not bury them.
Cì, if you wish to know whether the dead have knowledge or no knowledge,
once you die you will naturally know it yourself;
it will not be too late then."
18.32 Prince Jiàn went out to guard Chéngfù
and met Chéng Gōng Qián in the fields.
He asked:
"What is this?"
Chéng Gōng Qián said:
"It is a field."
"What is a ‘field’?"
"It is used for growing hemp."
"What is ‘hemp’?"
He said:
"It is used for making clothes."
Chéng Gōng Qián said:
"In the past, King Zhuāng attacked Chén
and stayed at the home of the Yǒu Xiāo Shì.
He said to the people of the roadside house:
‘Is the alley perhaps in poor condition?
Why is the drainage ditch not dredged?’
King Zhuāng even knew if an alley was in poor condition
or if a ditch was not dredged.
Now you do not know that a field grows hemp
or that hemp makes clothes.
You, my lord, will likely not rule the state!"
The Prince indeed did not ascend to the throne.
19.1 When the world possesses the Way (*Dào*),
then rites, music, and punitive expeditions originate from the Son of Heaven (*Tiānzǐ*).
When achievements are completed, one institutes rites;
when order is established, one composes music.
As for rites and music,
they are the greatest means of conducting transformation.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
“For changing customs and transforming habits,
nothing is better than music;
for securing superiors and governing the people,
nothing is better than rites.”
For this reason, the Sage Kings (*Shèngwáng*) cultivated ritual refinements,
established schools (*xiáng* and *xù*),
displayed bells and drums,
the Son of Heaven had the Circular Moat (*Bìyōng*),
and the feudal lords (*Zhūhóu*) had the Semicircular Pool (*Pàngōng*);
these were the means by which they practiced moral transformation.
The *Shī* says:
“In the Circular Moat (*Bìyōng*) of *Hàojīng*,
from the west and from the east,
from the south and from the north,
none thought of not submitting.”
This refers to that.
19.2 Accumulating kindness results in love,
accumulating love results in benevolence (*rén*),
and accumulating benevolence results in the spiritual (*líng*).
The reason why the Spirit Tower (*Língtái*) is called “spiritual”
is because of accumulated benevolence.
Spiritual beings
are the root of Heaven and Earth
and the beginning of the myriad things.
For this reason, King *Wén* (*Wénwáng*) began by treating the people with benevolence,
and there was no one in the world who was not benevolent.
This was the pinnacle of civilizing virtue (*wéndé*);
if virtue is not at its pinnacle, one cannot be civilized.
19.3 *Shāng* means “constant”;
“constant” means “substance”;
substance is governed by Heaven (*Tiān*).
*Xià* means “great”;
“great” means “refinement”;
refinement is governed by Earth (*Dì*).
Therefore, a king alternates between *Shāng* and *Xià*,
repeating every second cycle;
official colors repeat every third cycle.
In flavors, sweetness is esteemed;
in sound, the *gōng* note is esteemed;
these repeat every cycle.
Thus, the methods of the Three Kings (*Sānwáng*) are like a circle.
Therefore, the *Xiàhòu* clan taught through loyalty,
and the superior men (*jūnzi*) were loyal.
The failing of the common people was coarseness;
to remedy coarseness, nothing is better than respect.
Therefore, the people of *Yīn* taught through respect,
and the superior men were respectful.
The failing of the common people was superstition;
to remedy superstition, nothing is better than refinement.
Therefore, the people of *Zhōu* taught through refinement,
and the superior men were refined.
The failing of the common people was superficiality;
to remedy superficiality, nothing is better than loyalty.
Thus, the relation between one sage and another
is like three turns of a carpenter's square
or three turns of a compass;
when the cycle is complete, it begins again;
when it reaches its limit, it returns to the source.
The *Shī* says:
“Carving and polishing its patterns,
like gold and jade is its substance.”
This speaks of the beauty of refinement and substance.
19.4 The *Zhuàn* says:
To be moved by emotions and follow desires
is to be called a beast.
To act whenever it is convenient
is to be called a rustic.
To be content with the old and reluctant to move
is to be called the common masses.
To distinguish right from wrong
and understand the Way (*Dào*) of ancient and modern times
is to be called a scholar (*shì*).
To advance the worthy and promote the capable
is to be called a grand master (*dàfū*).
To respect superiors and love subordinates
is to be called a feudal lord (*zhūhóu*).
To cover like Heaven and support like Earth
is to be called the Son of Heaven (*Tiānzǐ*).
For this reason, the scholar wears the *fǔ* pattern;
the grand master wears the *fú* pattern;
the feudal lord wears the fire pattern;
and the Son of Heaven wears the mountains and dragons.
The more abundant the virtue, the more elaborate the patterns;
the more orderly the inner self, the more manifest the refinement.
19.5 The *Shī* says:
“Moving to the left, moving to the left,
the superior man (*jūnzi*) finds it fitting.
Moving to the right, moving to the right,
the superior man possesses it.”
The *Zhuàn* says:
As for the superior man (*jūnzi*),
there is nothing he does not find fitting.
Therefore, wearing the ceremonial apron and cap with solemnity and caution,
standing in the ancestral hall,
all the officials in charge are nothing but respectful.
Wearing the coarse mourning garments,
carrying the hemp sash and staff,
standing in the mourning place,
all the guests offering condolences are nothing but sorrowful.
Donning armor and lacing the helmet,
standing between the drum and its stand,
all the soldiers are nothing but courageous.
Thus, his benevolence (*rén*) is sufficient to cherish the hundred surnames;
his courage is sufficient to secure a state in peril;
his trustworthiness is sufficient to unite the feudal lords (*zhūhóu*);
his strength is sufficient to repel disasters;
and his majesty is sufficient to lead the three armies.
Therefore it is said:
To be on the left is fitting,
and to be on the right is fitting.
For the superior man, there is nothing that is not fitting.
This refers to that.
19.6 Duke *Jǐng* of *Qí* (*Qí Jǐng Gōng*) ascended to the archery range,
and *Yànzǐ* awaited him while cultivating the rites.
The Duke said:
“As for the rites of the archery selection,
I am weary of them!
I wish to find the brave warriors of the world
and plan for the state with them.”
*Yànzǐ* replied:
“If a superior man (*jūnzi*) lacks rites,
he is a commoner;
if a commoner lacks rites,
he is a beast.
If ministers have much courage, they will assassinate their ruler;
if sons have much strength, they will assassinate their elders.
Yet they do not dare to do so
only because of what is called rites.
Rites are the means by which to control the people,
just as reins are the means by which to control a horse.
That one could govern a state without rites
is something I, *Yīng*, have never heard of.”
Duke *Jǐng* said:
“Excellent.”
He then arranged the archery range and changed the seating,
treated *Yànzǐ* as an honored guest,
and spent the whole day inquiring about the rites.
19.7 The *Shū* says:
“Of the five matters,
the first is called appearance.”
Appearance is
the means by which a man shows reverence and respect,
and a woman shows her beauty and charm.
In walking, one should conform to a square;
in turning, one should conform to a circle.
Standing, one should be bent like a chime-stone;
with folded hands, one should be like embracing a drum.
When entering the ruler's court,
be honorable and dignified;
when entering the ancestral temple,
be respectful and loyal;
when entering the local village,
be harmonious and compliant;
when entering among the clansmen and neighbors,
be harmonious and affectionate.
The *Shī* says:
“The mild and respectful person
is the foundation of virtue.”
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
“Respectfulness nearing the rites
keeps one far from shame and disgrace.”
19.8 Clothing and appearance
are the means to please the eye;
voice and responses
are the means to please the ear;
desires and preferences
are the means to please the heart.
When a *Jūnzǐ*’s clothing is moderate
and his appearance is fitting,
then the eyes of the people are pleased;
when his speech is smooth
and his responses are prompt,
then the ears of the people are pleased;
when he approaches benevolence and rejects what is not benevolent,
then the hearts of the people are pleased.
These three things reside in the heart,
flow through the body,
and manifest in movement and stillness;
even if he is not in office,
this is called his "habitual conduct."
Therefore, with a loyal heart that loves goodness and renews it daily,
he delights in virtue when living alone,
and his inner joy is manifested outwardly.
The *Shī* says:
"How can he stay at ease?
There must be someone with him.
How can he last so long?
There must be a reason."
Only those who have "the reason" are able to live long and see far without being burdened by material things.
19.9 Those who know the *Tiāndào* wear a needle-shaped ornament on their caps;
those who know the *Dìdào* wear cloud-shaped toe-ornaments on their shoes.
Those capable of managing troubles and resolving chaos wear an ivory pick;
those capable of archery and charioteering wear a thumb ring;
those capable of rectifying the *Sānjūn* tuck a ritual tablet into their sash.
Clothing must carry the compass and support the square,
bear the plumb line and be level below.
Therefore, a *Jūnzǐ*’s clothing is moderate and his appearance is fitting;
his dress matches and symbolizes his virtue;
thus, by gazing upon his jade-like appearance, his actions and abilities can be determined.
The *Shī* says:
"On the branches of the *Wán Lán*,
a youth wears an ivory pick."
This refers to one’s actions and abilities.
19.10 Capping is the means to distinguish an adult.
Cultivating virtue and restraining the self,
in order to admonish oneself,
is the means to check one’s heterodox heart
and guard one’s upright intentions.
When a *Jūnzǐ* is first capped, there must be a blessing;
completing the ritual and adding the cap
serves to encourage his heart.
Therefore, when a *Jūnzǐ* becomes an adult, he must wear the cap and sash to conduct affairs,
abandoning the playful and negligent heart of childhood
and finding joy in the aspiration to advance virtue and cultivate his profession.
For this reason, if the clothing does not form a symbol,
the inner heart will not change;
when the inner heart cultivates virtue
and the exterior is covered in ritual refinement,
this is how a prominent and good reputation is established.
Thus, the *píbiàn* and white silk skirt
have not been changed by a hundred kings;
they are used both to cultivate virtue
and to rectify the appearance.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
"When one rectifies his clothes and cap
and makes his gaze respectful,
appearing so dignified that people look upon him with awe—
is this not being majestic without being fierce?"
19.11 When *Chéng Wáng* was about to be capped,
*Zhōugōng* sent *Zhù Yōng* to bless the King,
saying:
"Let the words be expressive but not numerous."
*Zhù Yōng* said:
"May the King be close to the people,
distant from flatterers,
frugal with his time,
generous with wealth,
and employ the worthy and capable."
At this time of his first becoming an adult,
the blessing was repeated four times before he withdrew.
When a *Gōng* is capped,
he acts as the host
and a *Qīng* acts as the guest;
he feasts him with the ritual of three offerings.
The *Gōng* first adds the *xuánduān* robe and the *píbiàn* cap;
all must wear court dress and the *xuánmiǎn* for the four additions.
When the crown prince or sons of *Zhūhóu* are capped,
the *Gōng* acts as the host,
and the ritual is the same as for a *Shì*.
Capping in the ancestral temple, the words are:
"On this auspicious month and lucky day,
we add your adult garments;
cast off your childhood aspirations
and follow your adult virtue."
In the capping ritual, one is seen as correct and capped at nineteen;
this was the universal ritual of ancient times.
19.12 "In summer,
the *Gōng* went to *Qí* to welcome his bride."
"Why was this recorded?
Personally welcoming the bride
is the ritual."
What is that ritual?
It is said:
A *Zhūhóu* uses two pairs of shoes and adds a *cóng* jade.
*Dàfū*, *Shì*, and commoners use two pairs of shoes and add two bundles of *shùxiū*.
He says:
"The lady who is the *Guǎxiǎojūn* of our state
has sent me (*Guǎrén*) to offer this non-precious *cóng* jade
and these non-precious shoes
to show ritual respect to the chaste lady."
The mother says:
"Having a child of the inner chambers who has often brought shame,
and has not yet understood the teachings of the *Fùmǔ*,
if she can be permitted to manage the duties of robes and garments,
how could I dare not to respectfully bow and accept the blessing?"
The *Zhù* returns the bow.
The mother receives the *cóng* jade,
takes one pair of shoes to put on the daughter,
adjusts her hairpins and garments and commands her, saying:
"Go now.
Serve your parents-in-law well.
Use obedience as the rule for your household.
Do not have a divided heart,
and do not dare to be devious."
The daughter bows.
Then she personally leads her by the hand
and hands her to the husband at the door.
The husband leads her by the hand out the door.
The husband walks
and the daughter follows.
She bows in farewell to her father in the hall
and bows to her mothers at the main gate.
The husband first mounts the carriage and holds the reins;
the daughter then mounts the carriage.
After the wheels turn three times,
the husband descends and walks ahead.
*Dàfū*, *Shì*, and commoners address her father, saying:
"The father of So-and-so
and the teachers and friends of So-and-so
have sent me to bring these non-precious shoes
and non-precious *shùxiū*
to respectfully show ritual respect to the chaste lady of such-and-such clan."
The mother says:
"Having a child of the thatched hut
who has not practiced the arts of weaving and spinning,
if she can be permitted to manage the duties of the broom and dustpan,
how could I dare not to respectfully bow?"
19.13 The *Chūnqiū* says:
"On the *Rénshēn* day,
the *Gōng* passed away in the *Gāoqǐn*."
The *Zhuàn* says:
"What is the *Gāoqǐn*?
It is the principal bedchamber.
Why is it sometimes called *Gāoqǐn*
and sometimes called *Lùqǐn*?"
It is said:
"A *Zhūhóu* has three principal bedchambers:
the first is called *Gāoqǐn*,
the second is called Left *Lùqǐn*,
and the third is called Right *Lùqǐn*.
The *Gāoqǐn*
is the bedchamber of the first enfeoffed lord.
The two *Lùqǐn*
are the bedchambers of the successor lords."
"Why two?"
It is said:
"A son does not reside in his father's bedchamber,
so there are two bedchambers.
Successor lords through the generations may not reside in the bedchamber of the *Gāozǔ*,
so there is a *Gāoqǐn*;
it is named 'High'."
"How are the *Lùqǐn* situated?"
"The *Gāoqǐn* is established in the center,
and the *Lùqǐn* are on the left and right.
The *Chūnqiū* says:
"The *Tiānwáng* entered *Chéngzhōu*."
The *Zhuàn* says:
"What is *Chéngzhōu*?
It is Eastern *Zhōu*."
"In that case, how are the bedchambers of the *Tiānzǐ*?"
It is said:
"There are also three.
The bedchambers of a lord who is a *Chéngmíng*, successor of the line, and maintainer of culture
are called the Left and Right *Lùqǐn*."
"Why are they called *Chéngmíng*?"
It is said:
"Because they are situated behind the *Míngtáng*.
Thus, when the three bedchambers of the *Tiānzǐ* and *Zhūhóu* are established, names and realities are rectified,
the righteousness between father and son is manifested,
the affairs of the noble and lowly are distinguished, and
the virtues of the great and small are differentiated."
19.14 The *Tiānzǐ* uses sacrificial ale as a ritual gift.
Sacrificial ale
is the essence of a hundred herbs.
Above, it penetrates to Heaven;
below, it penetrates to Earth;
there is nowhere it does not penetrate.
Therefore, the *Tiānzǐ* uses sacrificial ale as a ritual gift.
The *Zhūhóu* use jade tablets as ritual gifts.
The tablet
is made of jade.
It is thin yet does not bend;
it has sharp edges yet does not cut;
if there are flaws within,
they must be visible on the outside.
Therefore, the *Zhūhóu* use jade as a ritual gift.
The *Qīng* use lambs as ritual gifts.
The lamb
is a sheep.
Sheep flock together but do not form factions.
Therefore, the *Qīng* use sheep as ritual gifts.
The *Dàfū* use wild geese as ritual gifts.
Wild geese
maintain the ritual of seniority in their flight formations.
Therefore, the *Dàfū* use them as ritual gifts.
The *Shì* use pheasants as ritual gifts.
Regarding the pheasant,
they are chosen because they cannot be tamed and made submissive by hand-feeding in a cage.
Therefore, the *Shì* use pheasants as ritual gifts.
The *Shùmín* use domestic ducks as ritual gifts.
The duck
is earth-bound.
Being earth-bound, it has no other heart.
Therefore, the *Shùmín* use ducks as ritual gifts.
Ritual gifts
are the means by which one pledges one's character.
19.15 Every three years, the *Zhūhóu* present recommended scholars.
One successful recommendation is called "loving virtue";
a second is called "honoring the worthy";
a third is called "having merit."
For those with merit,
the *Tiānzǐ* first grants them a chariot, robes, bows, and arrows;
a second time he grants them sacrificial ale;
a third time he grants them one hundred *Hǔbèn* guards,
and they are titled *Mìngzhūhóu*.
*Mìngzhūhóu* are permitted to conduct punitive expeditions on their own authority.
If in a neighboring state a minister murders his ruler
or a son of a concubine murders the head of his lineage,
they may march against them even without requesting permission from the *Tiānzǐ*.
Having completed the expedition, they return the land to the *Tiānzǐ*.
When the *Zhūhóu* recommend scholars,
one failure is called a "fault";
a second failure is called "arrogance";
a third failure is called "deception."
As for those who deceive,
the *Tiānzǐ* demotes them:
first he demotes their rank,
then he demotes their territory,
and after a third time their territory is entirely taken.
If a *Zhūhóu* does not recommend scholars, it is called "not following the correct path."
Regarding those who do not follow the correct path,
the *Tiānzǐ* demotes them:
first he demotes their rank,
then he demotes their territory,
and after a third time their territory is entirely taken.
Afterward, the *Tiānzǐ* annually audits officials who lack refinement and demotes them,
replacing them with the scholars recommended by the *Zhūhóu*.
The *Shī* says:
"Numerous are the many officers,
and through them *Wénwáng* enjoyed peace."
This is what it refers to.
19.16 In ancient times, there were necessarily *mìngmín*.
Among the people, those who were able to respect elders and pity orphans, who were proper in taking and giving and fond of yielding, and who exerted themselves in their duties,
were commissioned by their ruler.
Only after being commissioned could they ride in decorated chariots and teams of horses.
Those not yet commissioned could not ride in them;
those who did were punished.
Thus, even if the people had surplus wealth or extravagant goods,
if they lacked benevolence, righteousness, merit, and virtue,
they would have no use for that surplus wealth or those extravagant goods.
Therefore, the people all rose up in benevolence and righteousness and held material gain in low esteem.
Holding material gain in low esteem, they did not struggle.
Not struggling, the strong did not oppress the weak,
and the many did not violate the few.
This is why *Táng* and *Yú* established symbolic punishments,
yet the people did not dare violate the law,
and disorder thus ceased.
The *Shī* says:
"Advise your people,
be careful of your princely measures,
to guard against the unexpected."
This is what it refers to.
19.17 The travel of the *Tiānzǐ* is called *xúnshǒu*;
the reporting of the *Zhūhóu* is called *shùzhí*.
*Xúnshǒu*
means to inspect what is being guarded;
*shùzhí*
means to recount one's duties.
In spring he inspects the plowing
to assist those with insufficient means;
in autumn he inspects the harvest
to assist those with shortages.
The *Tiānzǐ* conducts an inspection tour once every five years.
In the second month of the year,
he tours the east,
arriving at *Dōngyuè*.
He burns wood in sacrifice and offers distant sacrifices to the mountains and rivers,
receives the *Zhūhóu*,
and inquires after those a hundred years old.
He orders the *Tàishī* to present poems
to observe the customs of the people.
He orders the marketplace to submit prices
to observe the people's likes and dislikes
and whether their wills are licentious or fond of depravity.
He orders the *Diǎnlǐ* to examine the seasons and months,
fix the days,
and unify the pitch-pipes, rituals, music, systems, and clothing,
and correct them.
If the spirits of the mountains and rivers are not sacrificed to, it is called "irreverence."
For those who are irreverent,
the ruler demotes their rank.
If the ancestral temples are not in order, it is called "unfilial."
For those who are unfilial, the ruler reduces their territory.
For those who have merit and benefit the people,
he then adds to their territory.
Entering a territory,
if the land is cleared and cultivated,
and the elderly are respected and the worthy honored, then there is a reward—
his territory is increased.
Entering a territory,
if the land is overgrown and neglected,
the elderly abandoned and the worthy lost,
and oppressive officials are in power, then there is a reprimand—
his territory is reduced.
One failure to attend the court results in demotion of rank;
a second failure results in reduction of territory;
a third failure results in the six armies being moved against them.
In the fifth month of the year,
he tours the south,
arriving at *Nányuè*,
with the same rituals as the eastern tour.
In the eighth month of the year,
he tours the west, arriving at *Xīyuè*,
with the same rituals as the southern tour.
In the eleventh month of the year,
he tours the north,
arriving at *Běiyuè*,
with the same rituals as the western tour.
Upon returning, he goes to the temples of his ancestors and father
and uses a single bull for sacrifice.
19.18 The *Chūnqiū* says:
"In the first month,
the *Gōng* hunted at Láng."
The *Zhuàn* says:
"Spring hunting is called *Sōu*,
summer is called *Miáo*,
autumn is called *Xiǎn*,
winter is called *Shòu*."
"What is the meaning of *Miáo*?"
It says:
"*Miáo* means *Máo* (selection);
taking them without surrounding the marshes,
not ambushing the whole herd,
taking game without killing young deer or taking eggs,
and not killing those heavily pregnant.
In the spring *Sōu*,
one does not kill small fawns or those heavily pregnant;
in the winter *Shòu*, all are taken.
All the common people go out,
not losing their formations while driving,
not striking the game head-on,
not engaging in deceptive encounters,
and not chasing beyond the boundaries;
this is the meaning of *Miáo*, , *Sōu*, and *Shòu*.
Therefore, the rituals of *Miáo*, , *Sōu*, and *Shòu
are to drill the military affairs.
Thus, *Miáo* means to select by the hair,
*Sōu* means to search for them,
and *Shòu* means to stay and wait for them."
"Why is there no hunting in summer?"
It says:
"When the *Yīn* and *Yáng* of Heaven and Earth are in their peak of growth,
fierce beasts do not seize prey,
birds of prey do not strike,
and vipers and scorpions do not sting.
If birds, beasts, insects, and snakes know to respond to Heaven,
then how much more so should humans?
Therefore, the ancients necessarily had pens and stalls for livestock.
Why is it called *Tián* (fielding)?
When a *Shèngrén* (Sage) undertakes an affair, he must return to the root.
The five grains
are used to serve the ancestral temple
and nourish the myriad people;
by removing the birds and beasts that harm the crops,
it is therefore called *Tián*.
When the *Shèngrén* establishes names and titles,
the meaning of the affairs can be known."
19.19 When the *Tiānzǐ* and *Zhūhóu*
have no affairs of state, they hunt three times a year:
first for dried meat offerings,
second for guests,
and third to fill the ruler's kitchen.
To have no affairs and yet not hunt
is called being disrespectful;
to hunt without ritual
is called abusing the products of Heaven.
The *Tiānzǐ* does not completely surround the game,
and the *Zhūhóu* do not ambush the whole herd.
When the *Tiānzǐ* has made a kill, the large tassel is lowered;
when the *Zhūhóu* have made a kill, the small tassel is lowered;
when a *Dàfū* has made a kill, the assistant carriage stops;
when the assistant carriage stops, then the common people may hunt.
Only after the otters have offered fish in sacrifice
do the fishermen enter the marshes and weirs;
only after the jackals have offered beasts in sacrifice
does hunting begin;
only after the pigeons have transformed into hawks
are nets and snares set;
only after the plants and trees have withered and fallen
do people enter the mountains and forests.
If insects have not yet hibernated,
one does not hunt with fire;
do not take fawns or eggs,
do not kill the unborn,
do not cause premature death,
and do not overturn nests.
All of this occurs when a *Shèngrén* is above,
the *Jūnzǐ* is in position,
and the capable are in office;
it is the manifestation of Great Virtue.
Therefore, when Gāoyáo was the *Dàlǐ*,
there was fairness,
and the people each submitted and obtained their due;
when Bóyí presided over ritual,
those above and below were all yielding;
when Chuí was the Master of Works,
the hundred artisans achieved great success;
when Yì presided over the *Yú* office,
the mountains and marshes were opened and developed;
when Qì presided over the *Jì* office,
the hundred grains flourished in their seasons;
when Xiè was the *Sītú*,
the common people were close and harmonious;
when Lóng presided over guests,
people from afar arrived;
the Twelve Shepherds performed their duties and none in the *Jiǔzhōu* dared to be deviant or contrary;
Yǔ diked the nine mountains,
opened the nine marshes,
cleared the nine roads,
and settled the *Jiǔzhōu*;
each came with the tribute of their office,
not losing their proper place.
The territory spanned five thousand *lǐ* square,
reaching as far as the *Huāngfú*.
To the south he pacified Jiāozhǐ, Dàfā, Xīróng, Xīzhī, Qūsōu, Dī, and Qiāng;
to the north he reached the Shānròng, Fā, and Sùshèn;
to the east he reached the Chángyí and Dǎoyí.
Within the four seas,
all honored the achievements of *Dì Shùn*.
Thereupon Yǔ raised the music of the *Jiǔsháo*,
which brought forth extraordinary things,
and the phoenixes came to soar.
The illustrious virtue of the world all began with *Dì Yú*.
19.20 An archer must have a calm mind and a straight body;
holding the bow and arrow,
observing with firmness,
only then can the archer hit the target.
The *Shī* says:
"The great target is set up,
the bows and arrows are drawn,
the archers are all assembled,
show your skill in shooting."
This is what it refers to.
*Hù* (bow) is used to mean *Yù* (precaution).
*Yù* means
to prepare my intentions.
Therefore, in ancient times, when a boy was born for three days,
with a mulberry bow and six mugwort arrows,
they shot at Heaven, Earth, and the four directions.
Heaven, Earth, and the four directions
are where a man has his affairs.
He must have intentions toward his affairs
before he dares to eat grain.
Thus it is said:
"He does not eat the bread of idleness,"
this is what it means.
19.21 Living and interacting with each other,
therefore it is called "staying as guests."
From the Tiānzǐ down to the Shì, each has their rank.
Presenting gifts to the dead that do not reach the coffin or the corpse,
or offering condolences to the living that do not reach the state of sorrow,
is not in accordance with Lǐ.
Therefore, in ancient times, for auspicious journeys, one traveled fifty lǐ,
and for rushing to a funeral, one hundred lǐ.
Presenting fèng while the service is still in progress is called "being on time."
Timing
is the greatest aspect of Lǐ.
The Chūnqiū says:
"The Tiānwáng sent Zǎixuǎn to bring fèng for Huì Gōng and Zhòngzǐ."
What are fèng?
In funeral matters, there are fèng,
which generally consist of teams of horses and bundles of silk.
Chariots and horses are called fèng,
money and goods are called fù,
clothes and quilts are called suì,
objects placed in the mouth are called hán,
and precious playthings are called zèng.
Those who knew the living provide fù and fèng,
while those who knew the deceased provide zèng and suì.
Zèng and suì are used to see off the dead,
while fù and fèng are used to assist the living.
Chariots and horses, bundles of silk, money and goods, clothes and quilts, precious playthings—
what are their numbers?
It is said:
The Tiānzǐ has six horses,
the Zhūhóu have four,
the Dàfū have three,
the Yuánshì have two,
and the Xiàshì have one.
The Tiānzǐ's bundles of silk are five bolts,
three of xuán-black and two of xùn-vermillion,
each fifty feet long;
the Zhūhóu have three xuán and two xùn,
each thirty feet long;
the Dàfū have one xuán and two xùn,
each thirty feet long;
the Yuánshì have one xuán and one xùn,
each twenty feet long;
the Xiàshì have one bolt each of plain colored silk;
the Shùmín have one bolt each of hemp and silk.
For the Tiānzǐ's fèng,
there are six horses
and a team of chariots;
the Zhūhóu have four horses
and a carriage;
the Dàfū have a triple carriage;
the Yuánshì and Xiàshì do not use carriages.
The Tiānzǐ has one set each of embroidered garments,
reaching the ground;
the Zhūhóu's reach the tops of the feet,
the Dàfū's reach the ankles,
and the Shì's reach the thighs.
The Tiānzǐ's hán is a pearl,
the Zhūhóu use jade,
the Dàfū use refined jade beads,
the Shì use cowrie shells,
and the Shùmín use grains.
For those of high rank and great virtue, as well as for close relatives,
the fù, fèng, hán, and suì are generous;
there is also a difference between the poor and the rich.
The numbers of two, three, four, and five
are taken from Heaven and Earth to establish odd and even,
and measured against human emotions to produce moderation and refinement.
This is called having a basis,
and it is the great lineage of Lǐ.
19.22 The Chūnqiū says:
"On the day of Gēngxū,
the Tiānwáng passed away."
The Zhuàn says:
"Why does the Tiānwáng's burial go unrecorded?
For the Tiānzǐ, the death is recorded but not the burial,
as it must occur at its appointed time;
for Zhūhóu, both the death and burial are recorded,
because the Tiānzǐ is present,
so their timing cannot be certain."
"What is meant by 'must occur at its appointed time'?"
"The Tiānzǐ is placed in the coffin after seven days
and buried after seven months;
the Zhūhóu are placed in the coffin after five days
and buried after five months;
the Dàfū are placed in the coffin after three days
and buried after three months;
the Shì and Shùmín are placed in the coffin after two days
and buried after two months."
"Why is it so for all?"
It is said:
"Lǐ does not prepare for calamitous events in advance.
Only after death are the funeral garments prepared,
the mourning clothes donned,
the inner and outer coffins decorated and repaired,
and the grave pit and burial site prepared.
Then the refinements of mourning are completed,
all the maternal and marital relatives arrive,
and the mourners gather at the grave.
The deep grace of filial sons and loyal ministers is then fully provided.
Therefore, the Tiānzǐ is buried after seven months,
when all who follow the same track have arrived;
the Zhūhóu are buried after five months,
when all who are in the same alliance have arrived;
the Dàfū are buried after three months,
when all who belong to the same court have arrived;
the Shì and Shùmín are buried after two months,
when all the distant relatives have arrived."
19.23 Yánlíng Jìzǐ was traveling to Qí.
On his return,
his eldest son died between Yíng and Bó,
and he buried him there.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ
is one of those in Wú who is well-versed in Lǐ."
He sent Zǐgòng to go and observe him.
The depth of the pit did not reach the groundwater,
and the burial was done with the clothes of the season.
After the burial, a mound was raised;
the grave was filled and the mound leveled,
its height being just enough to lean upon.
Once the mound was completed,
he bared his left shoulder,
circled the mound to the right,
and wailed three times,
saying:
"That the bones and flesh should return to the earth
is fate;
as for the soul and spirit, there is nowhere they do not go,
nowhere they do not go!"
And then he departed.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ's actions were in accord with Lǐ."
19.24 A child is born and, after three years,
is then free from the parents' embrace.
Therefore, the mourning period is set at three years,
as a means to repay the grace of the parents.
The one-year mourning period
is practiced among the Zhūhóu,
and the three-year mourning period
is practiced up to the Tiānzǐ;
this is the constant rule of Lǐ.
19.25 When Zǐxià finished his three-year mourning period,
he went to see Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ gave him a qín
and had him play the strings.
He took up the qín and played;
he was harmonious and joyful,
and he rose and said:
"The Xiānwáng established the Lǐ
so that one would not dare fail to reach it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A Jūnzǐ indeed!"
When Mǐn Zǐqiān finished his three-year mourning period,
he went to see Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ gave him a qín
and had him play the strings.
He took up the qín and played;
he was earnest and sorrowful,
and he rose and said:
"The Xiānwáng established the Lǐ
so that one would not dare exceed it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A Jūnzǐ indeed!"
Zǐgòng asked, saying:
"Mǐn Zǐ's sorrow had not yet ended,
yet you said, 'A Jūnzǐ indeed';
Zǐxià's sorrow had already ended,
yet you said, 'A Jūnzǐ indeed.'
I, Sì, am confused,
and venture to ask what this means."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Mǐn Zǐ's sorrow had not yet ended,
but he was able to conclude it according to Lǐ;
therefore, I called him a Jūnzǐ.
Zǐxià's sorrow had already ended,
but he was able to extend it to the limit;
therefore, I called him a Jūnzǐ.
Indeed, the three-year mourning period
is certainly that which those of superior ability restrain themselves for,
and that which those of lesser ability strive toward."
19.26 Qí Xuān Wáng said to Tián Guò:
"I have heard that Rúists mourn their parents for three years
and their lord for three years.
Between the lord and the father, who is more important?"
Tián Guò replied:
"He is likely not as important as the father."
The King, flared up in anger, said:
"If that is so, then why do you leave your parents to serve a lord?"
Tián Guò replied:
"If it were not for the lord's land,
I would have no place to settle my parents;
if it were not for the lord's stipend,
I would have no way to nourish my parents;
if it were not for the lord's rank and position,
I would have no way to honor and distinguish my parents.
What I receive from the lord,
I dedicate to my parents.
In all things, serving the lord
is the means by which I provide for my parents."
Xuān Wáng was dispirited and had nothing with which to respond.
19.27 In ancient times, those who suffered from calamities were called the "afflicted."
For a time, the lord would wear plain white clothing,
and he would send officials to condole with the dead and inquire after the sick,
showing concern through the use of shamans and physicians,
crawling as if to rescue them,
and providing soups and congee as remedies.
Those who do good must put the widowers, widows, orphans, and the solitary first.
When the sick are unable to care for one another,
or when the dead have no means for burial,
then the lord buries them.
For those with a parent's funeral, the lord does not summon them at their gate;
those observing Zīcuī or Dàgōng mourning
are not subject to the labor service tax for five months;
those observing Xiǎogōng mourning
are not subject to the labor service tax
until the burial is complete.
If there is an emergency with many corpses and deaths,
then groups of youths are gathered,
beating drums and carrying torches,
entering government offices and neighborhoods to be of use.
Each beats drums and carries torches,
driving [the plague] from the government offices and neighborhoods.
The master of the house,
wearing his cap,
stands at the eastern steps.
When the ritual is finished,
they exit the neighborhood gate,
exit the city gate,
and go into the wild fields.
This is the way of "crawling to save the afflicted."
It is also thus when an army suffers a great defeat.
19.28 One who fasts
thinks of the deceased's dwelling,
thinks of their laughter and speech,
and thinks of what they used to do.
After fasting for three days,
one then sees the person for whom one is fasting.
On the day of the sacrifice,
as one is about to enter the door,
it seems as if one sees their countenance there;
as one circles back out the door,
one sighs as if one hears the sound of their sighing.
The appearance of the ancestors does not leave the eyes;
the sounds of their voice, coughing, and clearing of the throat
do not leave the ears;
their desires, likes, and dislikes
are not forgotten by the heart.
This is the fasting of a filial son.
19.29 The spring sacrifice is called Cí,
the summer sacrifice is called Yuè,
the autumn sacrifice is called Cháng,
and the winter sacrifice is called Zhēng.
In spring, one offers leeks and eggs;
in summer, wheat and fish;
in autumn, millet and pig;
and in winter, rice and goose.
Every three years there is a Xiá sacrifice,
and every five years there is a Dì sacrifice.
Xiá
means "joining";
Dì
means "examining."
Xiá
is the great collective sacrifice in the ancestral temple;
Dì
is the examination of their virtues and the ranking of their excellence.
When a sage lord is about to sacrifice,
he must purely fast and think with refinement,
as if his parents were present.
Just as he rises but has not yet ascended,
he is solicitous and yearning,
focused solely on imagining the parent's appearance as if it were before him.
This is the sincerity of a filial son.
Those from the four quarters who assist in the sacrifice
come empty and return full;
those who arrive hollow go back substantial,
for all take the lord's model as their law.
19.30 Hán Hézǐ was crossing the Hé when
the ferryman informed him:
"Among those who pass through here,
none fail to make an offering for their use.
Will you not make an offering?"
Hán Hézǐ said:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to the spirits within the seas,
the feudal lords sacrifice to those within their borders,
the Grand Masters sacrifice to their parents,
and the officers sacrifice to their ancestors and deceased fathers.
I, Hé, have not yet obtained the right to serve Hébó."
The ferryman plied the oars,
and the boat took on water and spun around.
The ferryman said:
"Just now this servant certainly told you,
but you, Master, did not listen to this servant's words.
Now the boat is taking on water and spinning;
it is very dangerous.
Will you prepare your garments and swim down?"
Hán Hézǐ said:
"I will not change my will because people dislike me,
nor will I change my righteousness because I am about to die."
Before he had finished speaking,
the boat moved smoothly along.
Hán Hézǐ said:
"The Shī says:
'Lush are the kudzu vines,
spreading over the branches and stems.
The joyful and easy-going gentleman
seeks blessings without deviousness.'
If ghosts and spirits are not devious,
how much more so for men?"
19.31 Kǒngzǐ said:
"Ritual without physical form
is respect;
mourning without garments
is sorrow;
music without sound
is joy.
To be trusted without speaking,
to be majestic without moving,
to be benevolent without bestowing—
this is the will.
As for the sound of bells and drums,
if one strikes them while angry, they are martial;
if one strikes them while grieving, they are sad;
if one strikes them while happy, they are joyful.
When the will changes,
the sound also changes.
If the will is sincere,
it penetrates metal and stone;
how much more so for men?"
19.32 Gōngmèng Zǐgāo saw Zhuān Sūn Zǐmò and asked:
"May I ask what the ritual of a gentleman is like?"
Zhuān Sūn Zǐmò said:
"Cast off your external sternness,
and your inner [unsettledness];
when appearances win out and the heart takes credit for it—
cast off these three things and it will be enough."
Gōngmèng did not understand
and told Zéngzǐ of this.
Zéngzǐ looked solemn, drew back, and said:
"How great are these words!
For those with external sternness will surely collapse within;
those for whom appearances win out and the heart takes credit
will surely be enslaved by others.
Therefore, the gentleman's virtuous conduct is complete, yet his appearance is unassuming;
his learning and knowledge are broad, yet his speech is not contentious;
his wisdom and deliberation are subtle and far-reaching, yet he is capable of appearing simple."
19.33 Zéngzǐ was ill,
and Mèng Yí went to inquire after him.
Zéngzǐ said:
"When a bird is about to die,
its song is surely mournful;
when a gentleman faces the great end,
his words are surely proper.
Ritual has three protocols;
do you know them?"
He replied:
"I do not know them."
Zéngzǐ said:
"Sit,
and I shall tell you.
When a gentleman cultivates ritual to establish his will,
then thoughts of greed and desire do not come;
when a gentleman reflects on ritual to cultivate his person,
then habits of laziness and arrogance do not arrive;
when a gentleman cultivates ritual through benevolence and righteousness,
then words of anger, contention, and violence are kept far away.
As for setting out the wine vessels and platters
or arranging the bamboo baskets and wooden bowls,
these are the duties of the officials;
though a gentleman might not be able to do them,
that is acceptable."
19.34 Kǒngzǐ said:
“He is acceptable,
though lax.”
“Lax”
means being casual and unrefined.
Being casual and unrefined
means lacking ritual refinement.
Kǒngzǐ went to see Zǐ Sāng Bó Zǐ.
Zǐ Sāng Bó Zǐ sat there without wearing his cap or robe.
The disciples said:
“Why did the Master go to see this man?”
He replied:
“His substance is beautiful but he lacks refinement;
I wished to speak with him to refine it.”
Kǒngzǐ left.
Zǐ Sāng Bó Zǐ’s followers were displeased
and asked:
“Why did you see Kǒngzǐ?”
He replied:
“His substance is beautiful but his refinement is excessive;
I wished to speak with him to remove his refinement.”
Therefore it is said:
One whose refinement and substance are both cultivated is called a jūnzǐ;
one who has substance but lacks refinement is called casual and unrefined.
Zǐ Sāng Bó Zǐ was casual and unrefined
and wished to make the way of humans the same as that of cattle and horses.
Therefore Zhòng Gōng said:
“He is too lax.”
Above, there is no enlightened Tiānzǐ;
below, there are no worthy Fāngbó;
the world is without the Way.
If a minister assassinates his lord
or a son assassinates his father,
and one has the power to punish them,
then punishing them is acceptable.
In the time of Kǒngzǐ,
there was no enlightened Tiānzǐ above,
therefore he said, “Yōng could be made to face south.”
One who faces south
is the Tiānzǐ.
The reason Yōng attained the praise of “facing south”
was that when he asked Kǒngzǐ about Zǐ Sāng Bó Zǐ,
Kǒngzǐ said:
“He is acceptable,
though lax.”
Zhòng Gōng said:
“If one dwells in reverence and acts with simplicity to lead the people,
is that not acceptable?
If one dwells in simplicity and acts with simplicity,
is that not being too lax?”
The Master said:
“Yōng’s words are correct.”
Zhòng Gōng was well-versed in the art of transformation,
and Kǒngzǐ was clear about the Kingly Way,
and there was nothing to be added to Zhòng Gōng’s words.
19.35 Kǒngzǐ arrived outside the outer gate of Qí
and met a child carrying a jar.
They walked together;
the child's gaze was focused,
his heart was upright,
and his conduct was proper.
Kǒngzǐ said to his driver:
“Hurry the horses,
hurry the horses!
The Shào music is about to begin.”
Kǒngzǐ arrived there and heard the Shào;
for three months he did not know the taste of meat.
Thus music is not only for one's own enjoyment
but also to bring joy to others;
it is not only for rectifying oneself
but also for rectifying others.
How great it is!
Regarding this music,
he did not expect that making music could reach such a level.
19.36 Huáng Dì ordered Líng Lún to create the musical pitch pipes.
Líng Lún went from the west of Dàxià
to the northern side of Kūnlún.
He took bamboo from Xiègǔ.
Selecting those with a hollow center and even thickness,
he cut a piece between two nodes.
Its length was nine inches, and he blew into it,
making it the Gōng note of the Huángzhōng pitch.
The sun contains the lesser.
Next, he crafted the twelve pipes.
At the foot of Kūnlún,
he listened to the cries of the phoenixes
to distinguish the twelve pitches.
The male cries were six,
and the female cries were also six.
Comparing them to the Gōng note of Huángzhōng,
they perfectly matched the Gōng of Huángzhōng.
All could be generated from it,
and it is the root of the pitches.
Therefore it is said:
Huángzhōng is subtle yet uniform, fresh, complete, and without flaw.
Its position as the Gōng note is uniquely honored,
symbolizing the virtue of a Great Sage,
and it can illuminate the achievements of the most worthy.
Thus it is reverently presented in the ancestral temple
to welcome merit and virtue with song,
never to be forgotten for generations.
For this reason, Huángzhōng generates Línzhōng.
Línzhōng generates Dàlǚ.
Dàlǚ generates Yízé.
Yízé generates Tàicù.
Tàicù generates Nánlǚ.
Nánlǚ generates Jiǎzhōng.
Jiǎzhōng generates Wúshè.
Wúshè generates Gūxiǎn.
Gūxiǎn generates Yìngzhōng.
Yìngzhōng generates Ruíbīn.
By dividing into three parts,
adding one part generates the pitch above;
by dividing into three parts,
removing one part generates the pitch below.
Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Tàicù, Jiǎzhōng, Gūxiǎn, Zhònglǚ, and Ruíbīn are the upper pitches.
Línzhōng, Yízé, Nánlǚ, Wúshè, and Yìngzhōng are the lower pitches.
In the age of a Great Sage's perfect governance,
the Qi of Heaven and Earth combine to produce the winds.
When the solstices arrive, the sun moves with these winds
to generate the twelve pitches.
Thus, at the winter solstice in mid-winter,
Huángzhōng is generated;
in late winter, Dàlǚ is generated;
in early spring, Tàicù is generated;
in mid-spring, Jiǎzhōng is generated;
in late spring, Gūxiǎn is generated;
in early summer, Zhònglǚ is generated;
at the summer solstice in mid-summer,
Ruíbīn is generated;
in late summer, Línzhōng is generated;
in early autumn, Yízé is generated;
in mid-autumn, Nánlǚ is generated;
in late autumn, Wúshè is generated;
and in early winter, Yìngzhōng is generated.
When the Qi of the winds of Heaven and Earth is correct,
the twelve pitches arrive.
19.37 The Sages created the táo drum, the gǔ drum, the kuāng trough, the jié scraper, the xūn ocarina, and the chí flute.
These six
are the sounds of virtuous music.
Then the bells, stone chimes, yú pipes, and sè zithers were used to harmonize with them.
Then the shields, axes, yak-tail banners, and pheasant-feather fans were used in the dances.
This is how sacrifices are made in the temples of former kings,
and how offerings and toasts are made during rituals.
It is how the ranks of officials and the noble and the lowly are ordered, each obtaining their proper place,
and how to show future generations the order of honored and humble, and of old and young.
19.38 The sound of the bell is resonant.
Resonance is used to establish a signal;
the signal is used to establish resolution;
resolution is used to establish martial valor.
When a jūnzǐ hears the sound of the bell, he thinks of his martial ministers.
The sound of the stone chime is clear.
Clarity is used to establish discernment;
discernment is used to lead one to die for a cause.
When a jūnzǐ hears the sound of the stone chime, he thinks of the ministers who die for the borders.
The sound of strings is mournful.
Mournfulness is used to establish integrity;
integrity is used to establish resolve.
When a jūnzǐ hears the sound of the qín and sè, he thinks of ministers of resolve and righteousness.
The sound of bamboo is expansive.
Expansiveness is used to establish assembly;
assembly is used to gather the multitudes.
When a jūnzǐ hears the sound of the yú, shēng, xiāo, and guǎn pipes, he thinks of ministers who gather and provide for the people.
The sound of the drums is vigorous.
Vigor is used to establish movement;
movement is used to advance the multitudes.
When a jūnzǐ hears the sound of the drums, he thinks of his generals and commanders.
When a jūnzǐ listens to music,
he does not merely listen to the resonance and clarity;
he also finds something that resonates within him.
Yuè is
what the Shèngrén delight in, and it can improve the hearts of the people.
Its influence on people is deep,
and it transforms customs and changes traditions;
therefore, the Xiānwáng established its teaching.
Now, the people have a nature of blood, breath, and conscious knowing,
but they have no constant state of sorrow, Lè, joy, or anger;
they are moved in response to the influence of things,
and only then do the pathways of the mind take shape.
Thus, when sounds of distress and emaciation arise,
the people think of sorrow.
When sounds that are easy, slow, elaborate in pattern, and simple in rhythm arise,
the people feel ease and Lè.
When sounds that are coarse, harsh, violently rising, vigorous in movement, and broadly resounding arise,
the people become resolute and bold.
When sounds that are upright, strong, correct, solemn, and sincere arise,
the people become respectful and reverent.
When sounds that are broad, full, smooth, harmonious, and moving arise,
the people become kind and loving.
When sounds that are licentious, perverse, heterodox, scattered, and overflowing arise,
the people become debauched and chaotic.
Therefore, the Xiānwáng rooted it in the emotions and nature,
verified it with measures and numbers,
regulated it with Lǐ and Yì,
infused it with the harmony of the breath of life,
and guided the practice of the Wǔcháng,
causing the Yáng not to scatter
and the Yīn not to be suppressed,
so that the strong breath is not angry
and the soft breath is not fearful.
The four currents flow through the center and manifest on the outside,
all resting in their proper places without encroaching on each other.
Then they established levels of study,
broadened its rhythms,
and refined its patterns
to measure the depth of virtue.
They tuned the proportions of small and large
and ordered the sequence of beginning and end
to symbolize the conduct of affairs,
so that the principles of close and distant, noble and base, elder and younger, and male and female
all take form and appear within Yuè.
Therefore it is said:
"Yuè—
observe its depth!"
When the soil is exhausted, plants and trees do not grow;
when the water is troubled, fish and turtles do not grow large;
when the breath is weak, living things do not flourish;
when the age is in chaos, Lǐ becomes wicked and Yuè becomes licentious.
Thus its sounds are sorrowful but not solemn,
joyful but not peaceful,
negligent so as to violate the rhythm,
and overflowing so as to forget the root.
When broad, they harbor wickedness;
when narrow, they induce desire,
stirring up a turbulent breath and destroying the virtue of peace and harmony.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ despises it.
Whenever wicked sounds influence people, a contrary breath responds;
as the contrary breath takes form, licentious Yuè arises.
When correct sounds influence people, a compliant breath responds;
as the compliant breath takes form, harmonious Yuè arises.
Singing and harmony have their resonance;
perversity and correctness, crookedness and straightness, each returns to its own lot,
and the principles of the myriad things
each move according to their kind.
Thus the Jūnzǐ returns to his emotions to harmonize his will
and compares types to perfect his conduct.
Wicked sounds and chaotic colors do not enter his hearing;
licentious Yuè and wicked Lǐ do not touch the pathways of his mind;
the breath of laziness, negligence, and perversity is not present in his body.
He causes his ears, eyes, nose, mouth, heart, wisdom, and all parts of his body to follow what is compliant and correct to practice Yì.
Then it is expressed through sounds,
patterned with the Qín and Sè,
moved with the shield and battle-axe,
decorated with feathers and yak-tails,
and accompanied by flutes and pipes,
rousing the radiance of supreme virtue
and moving the harmony of the four breaths
to manifest the principles of the myriad things.
Thus, its clarity symbolizes Heaven,
its vastness symbolizes Earth,
its beginning and end symbolize the four seasons,
and its movements symbolize wind and rain;
the five colors form patterns without confusion,
the eight winds follow the pitch-pipes without wickedness,
and the hundred measures obtain their numbers and have constancy;
small and large complete each other,
beginning and end produce each other,
and singing and harmony, clear and turbid,
alternately serve as the warp.
Therefore, when Yuè is practiced, social relations are clarified,
ears and eyes become acute and bright,
blood and breath become harmonious and peaceful,
customs are transformed and traditions changed,
and the whole world is at peace.
Therefore it is said:
"Yuè
is Lè."
The Jūnzǐ rejoices in attaining the Way;
the petty man rejoices in attaining his desires.
When the Way regulates desire,
there is Lè without chaos;
when desire causes the Way to be forgotten,
there is delusion without Lè.
Thus the Jūnzǐ returns to his emotions to harmonize his intent
and broadens Yuè to complete his teaching;
therefore, when Yuè is practiced, the people turn toward the right direction,
and one can observe their virtue.
Virtue
is the beginning of nature;
Yuè
is the flowering of virtue;
metal, stone, silk, and bamboo
are the instruments of Yuè.
Poetry expresses the will;
song chants its sounds;
dance moves its appearance.
These three are rooted in the heart,
and then the breath of Yuè follows them.
Thus, when emotions are deep, the patterns are enlightened;
when the breath is robust, the transformation is spiritual;
when harmony and compliance accumulate within, radiance manifests without.
Only Yuè cannot be faked.
Yuè
is the movement of the heart;
Yīn
are the images of Yuè;
patterns and rhythms
are the decorations of Yīn.
The Jūnzǐ moves the root,
delights in the images,
and then regulates the decorations.
Thus he first drums to sound a warning,
takes three steps to show the direction,
starts again to manifest what has passed,
and repeats the finale to decorate the return;
he is vigorous and swift but not disconnected,
extremely subtle but not hidden.
He alone rejoices in his will
and does not weary of his way;
he fully carries out his way
and does not prioritize his private desires.
Thus emotions are revealed and Yì is established;
Yuè ends and virtue is honored.
The Jūnzǐ uses it to love goodness;
the petty man uses it to gloss over his faults.
Therefore it is said:
"In the way of governing the people,
Yuè is the greatest part of it."
19.40 Of those things in Yuè that can be refined,
the Qín is most suitable.
The Jūnzǐ, because it can be used to cultivate virtue,
therefore keeps it close.
Whenever Yīn arise,
they are generated from the human heart.
The movement of the human heart
is caused by things.
Being influenced by things, it then moves,
and therefore takes form in sound;
sounds respond to each other,
and therefore produce variations;
variations forming a pattern are called Yīn;
combining Yīn and delighting in them,
along with the shield, battle-axe, feathers, and yak-tails, is called Yuè.
Yuè
is that from which Yīn are produced;
its root lies in the human heart being influenced by things.
Thus, when the heart is influenced by sorrow,
its sounds are distressed and fading;
when the heart is influenced by Lè,
its sounds are easy and slow;
when the heart is influenced by joy,
its sounds are expansive and scattered;
when the heart is influenced by anger,
its sounds are powerful and harsh;
when the heart is influenced by reverence,
its sounds are upright and distinct;
when the heart is influenced by love,
its sounds are harmonious and balanced.
A person's goodness or badness
is not their innate nature,
but is a movement after being influenced by things;
therefore, the Xiānwáng were careful about what influenced them.
Thus, Lǐ were used to settle their intent,
Yuè was used to harmonize their nature,
governance was used to unify their conduct,
and punishments were used to prevent their wickedness.
Lǐ, Yuè, punishments, and governance—
their ultimate end is the same:
they are used to unite the hearts of the people and establish the way of order.
19.41 Generally, musical tones arise from the human heart.
When emotions are stirred within, they take shape in sound;
when sounds form a pattern, they are called music.
Therefore, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful;
its government is harmonious.
The music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry;
its government is perverse.
The music of a doomed state is sorrowful and longing;
its people are distressed.
The way of sound and music
is connected with government.
Gōng represents the ruler,
Shāng represents the ministers,
Jué represents the people,
Zhǐ represents affairs,
Yǔ represents objects.
If the five tones are disordered, then there is no law.
Music without law:
If Gōng is disordered, then there is wildness;
its ruler is arrogant.
If Shāng is disordered, then there is deviation;
its officials are corrupt.
If Jué is disordered, then there is anxiety;
its people are resentful.
If Zhǐ is disordered, then there is sorrow;
its affairs are toilsome.
If Yǔ is disordered, then there is peril;
its resources are depleted.
If all five are disordered
and they mutually encroach upon each other, it is called dissoluteness.
In such a case,
the destruction of the state is imminent.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi
is the music of a chaotic age,
and is akin to dissoluteness.
The music of Sāngjiān and Pǔshàng
is the music of a doomed state;
its government is dissipated,
its people are drifting,
and the practice of slandering superiors and pursuing private interests cannot be stopped.
19.42 Generally, the calamities and misfortunes people suffer
arise from excess, indulgence, violence, and negligence.
The root of excess, indulgence, violence, and negligence
arises from drinking wine.
Therefore, the ancients were careful with the rituals of drinking wine,
making the ears listen to elegant music,
the eyes observe correct ceremonies,
the feet move with correct deportment,
and the heart discuss the correct path;
thus, they could drink wine all day without making mistakes.
In the short term for several days,
or in the long term for several months,
all people possessed virtue to increase their goodness.
The *Shī* says:
"Having been intoxicated with wine,
and having been satiated with virtue."
This is what it refers to.
19.43 Of all things that enter from the outside,
none go deeper than sound and music,
and none change a person more profoundly.
Therefore, the Sage follows this and completes it with virtue, calling it music.
Music
is the wind of virtue.
The *Shī* says:
"Dignified and impressive deportment,
virtuous sounds in perfect order."
This refers to ritual and music.
Therefore, the gentleman uses ritual to rectify the external
and music to rectify the internal.
If the internal is separated from music for even a moment,
then evil vital energy will arise;
if the external is separated from ritual for even a moment,
then negligent behavior will start.
Thus, in ancient times, the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords listened to the sound of bells,
never leaving them in the courtyard;
the high officials and grandees listened to the qín and sè,
never leaving them in their presence,
which was the means to cultivate a correct heart and eliminate licentious energy.
When music moves within,
it makes a person follow the Way and love goodness;
when music moves without,
it makes a person gentle, respectful, refined, and elegant.
The sounds of the *Yǎ* and *Sòng* move people, and correct energy responds to them;
harmonious, complete, graceful, and beautiful sounds move people, and harmonious energy responds to them;
coarse, harsh, fierce, and violent sounds move people, and angry energy responds to them;
the sounds of Zhèng and Wèi move people, and licentious energy responds to them.
Therefore, the gentleman is careful about what he uses to move people.
19.44 Zǐlù was playing the sè and it had the sound of the northern frontier.
Kǒngzǐ heard it and said:
"Truly,
Yóu lacks talent."
Rǎn Yǒu was in attendance;
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Qiú, come here.
Why do you not tell Yóu?
When the former kings established music,
they played central sounds
and made central rhythms;
it flowed into the South
and did not return to the North.
The South is the region of birth and growth;
the North is the realm of killing and conquest.
Therefore, the gentleman holds to the center as the root
and strives for life as the foundation.
Thus his music is warm, harmonious, and stays in the center,
symbolizing the energy of birth and growth.
Feelings of worry, sorrow, grief, and pain
do not enter the heart;
movements of violence, harshness, excess, and wildness
do not exist in the body.
Such is the wind of order and survival,
the action of peace and joy.
The petty man is not like this.
He holds to the trivial to discuss the root
and strives for hardness as the foundation.
Thus his music is mournful, harsh, subtle, and trivial,
symbolizing the energy of killing and conquest.
Feelings of harmony, rhythm, and central correctness
do not enter the heart;
movements of warmth, solemnity, respect, and dignity
do not exist in the body.
Killing
is the wind of chaos and destruction,
the action of fleeing to the North.
Long ago, Shùn created the sound of the *Nánfēng*;
its rise was sudden and flourishing,
and to this day kings and dukes transmit it and do not let it go.
Zhòu made the music of the northern frontier;
its downfall was sudden and swift,
and to this day kings and dukes treat it as a joke.
Shùn, as a commoner,
accumulated correctness and conformed to benevolence,
followed the center and practiced goodness, and finally rose to prominence.
Zhòu, as the Son of Heaven,
loved negligence, excess, and wildness,
being hard, harsh, violent, and cruel, and finally faced destruction.
Now Yóu is but a commoner,
one of the likes of those in hempen clothes;
he has no regard for the system of the former kings
and moreover possesses the sounds of a doomed state.
How can he protect his seven-foot body?"
Rǎn Yǒu told this to Zǐlù.
Zǐlù said:
"It is Yóu’s fault.
A petty man lacks ability,
and that I have fallen into this
makes the Master’s words appropriate!"
He then felt remorse,
did not eat,
and after seven days he was as thin as a skeleton.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu's correction
has gone too far."
20.1 Kǒngzǐ performed divination
and the hexagram he obtained was *Bì*.
He heaved a deep sigh
and his mind was uneasy.
Zǐzhāng came forward,
raised his hands, and asked:
"I have heard that *Bì* is an auspicious hexagram; why does the Master sigh over it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"*Bì*
is not a primary color,
and that is why I sigh.
I think of substance
and simplicity.
White should be pure white;
black should be pure black.
What is substance?
I have heard this:
Cinnabar lacquer is not patterned,
white jade is not carved,
and precious pearls are not decorated.
Why is this?
Those who have an abundance of substance
do not accept decoration."
20.2 Those who believe in ghosts and spirits lose their ability to plan;
those who believe in auspicious days lose their sense of timing.
How do we know this is so?
Now, the worthy and the sage have comprehensive knowledge;
they can bring affairs to profit without regard to dates and days.
They respect laws and decrees,
value merit and labor,
and are personally fortunate without divination or stalks;
they are careful with benevolence and righteousness,
follow the principles of the Way,
and receive blessings without prayers or sacrifices.
Therefore, calculating numbers and selecting days,
purifying oneself through fasting,
fattening sacrificial animals,
decorating jade tablets and disks,
and refining sacrifices
ultimately cannot eliminate the calamities of rebellion and perversion.
If one treats the spirits as if they have knowledge and serves them,
yet intends to act recklessly against the Way
and seeks blessings through sacrifices,
the spirits will surely turn away from them.
The *Tiānzǐ* sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the *Wǔyuè*, and the *Sìdú*;
the *Zhūhóu* sacrifice to the *Shèjì*;
the *Dàfū* sacrifice to the *Wǔsì*;
the *Shì* sacrifice to the doors and windows;
the commoners sacrifice to their ancestors.
The Sage Kings inherited the heart of Heaven
and established the distinctions of ritual.
Generally, those who divined the days in ancient times
intended to use them to assist the Way and investigate doubts,
showing that they had something they prioritized and did not dare to act solely on their own authority;
they did not intend to use them to seek the lucky safety of wholeness for the evils of subversion.
*Kǒngzǐ* said:
“To sacrifice to a spirit that is not one’s own
is flattery.”
For this reason, *Tàishān* ultimately did not accept the sacrifice of the *Jì* clan.
The *Yì* states: “The neighbor to the east slaughters an ox,
but it is not as good as the *yuè* sacrifice of the neighbor to the west,”
for it values ritual and does not prize material goods;
it respects reality and does not prize outward show.
If one truly possesses virtue and extends it,
then where could they go and not succeed?
Therefore, when the Sage sees the outward refinement of a person,
he must examine their substance.
20.3 The farmers of *Lìshān* were prone to encroaching on borders,
and *Shùn* farmed there;
the fishermen of *Léizé* were prone to fighting over embankments,
and *Shùn* fished there;
the pottery of the *Dōngyí* was crude and flawed,
and *Shùn* made pottery there.
Thus, farming, fishing, and making pottery were not the proper affairs of *Shùn*,
yet *Shùn* performed them
to rescue them from ruin.
The nature of the people is such that they cannot overcome their desires;
they discard substance and turn to outward show.
Therefore, with crude and flawed vessels,
the troubles of contention and strife arise;
when the troubles of contention and strife arise,
they become evasive and deceitful.
Why
is it so?
It is from departing from sincerity and turning to deception,
discarding simplicity and taking up falsehood,
and pursuing trivialities without rest.
If the Sage suppresses outward refinement and upholds substance,
then the world will return to its proper state.
20.4 The *Shī* says:
“The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree,
its young are seven.
The virtuous gentleman,
his demeanor is one.”
The *Zhuàn* says:
The reason the cuckoo can raise seven young
is by a single mind;
the reason the gentleman can govern the myriad things
is by a single demeanor.
To govern things with a single demeanor
is the heart of Heaven.
When the five are not separated
but are joined as one,
it is called the heart of Heaven.
If I can rely on myself to deeply tie my intent to the One,
then with one mind I can serve a hundred rulers;
with a hundred minds, one cannot serve a single ruler.
Thus, sincerity is not far off.
Now, sincerity
is oneness;
oneness
is substance.
Although the gentleman has outward refinement,
he must not depart from his inner substance.
20.5 In *Wèi*, there were five men
who together carried jars into a well
to irrigate leeks;
at the end of the day, they had finished only one plot.
*Dèng Xī* passed by,
stepped down from his carriage, and taught them, saying:
“Construct a machine,
make it heavy at the back
and light at the front;
it is called a *qiáo*.
If you irrigate the leeks all day with it,
you can do a hundred plots without fatigue.”
The five men said:
“Our teacher said:
‘Wherever there is the ingenuity of machines,
there will surely be the ruin of machine-like minds.’
It is not that we do not know of it,
but that we do not wish to use it.
You should be on your way;
we irrigate with a single mind
and do not intend to change.”
*Dèng Xī* left,
and after traveling several tens of *lǐ*,
his expression was unhappy
and he felt troubled within himself.
A disciple said:
“What kind of people are these that they should cause my master to feel resentment?
Please let me kill them for you.”
*Dèng Xī* said:
“Release them;
these are what are called *Zhēnrén*,
they could be made to guard the state.”
20.6 Qín Gǔ-lí asked Mòzǐ, saying:
"Brocades, embroideries, fine linens, and coarse hemp—
what are they to be used for?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Alas!
This is not what I consider an essential task.
In ancient times, there were those who attained their goals without ornamentation;
Xià Yǔ was one such person.
He made his palaces and rooms low and small,
reduced and thinned his food and drink,
had earthen steps of only three tiers,
and wore clothes of fine cloth.
During this time,
embroidered garments were of no use, and the focus was on completeness and durability.
Pán Gēng of Yīn
enlarged the halls of his former kings,
and relocated the capital to Yīn,
yet the thatched roofs were not trimmed
and the oak rafters were not carved,
in order to change the perspective of all under heaven.
During this time,
patterned and colored silks
had no place to be applied.
Now, the common people do not have a mind of their own;
they take the mind of the ruler as their own.
If the one above does not act,
how would those below use them?
These two kings led all under heaven by their own example;
therefore, transformation flourished in their time,
and their names are established in the present age.
Moreover, brocades, embroideries, fine linens, and coarse hemp
were created by rulers of disorder;
their origins all arose in Qí.
Jǐng Gōng delighted in luxury and forgot frugality;
fortunately, he had Yàn Zǐ to restrain him with frugality,
yet he still almost could not overcome it.
How can luxury ever be exhausted?
Zhòu built the Lù Tái and the Zāo Qiū,
the Jiǔ Chí and the Ròu Lín.
The palace walls were patterned and painted,
carved and engraved.
Brocades and embroideries covered the halls,
with gold, jade, and precious rarities.
There were women, concubines, and entertainers,
with bells, drums, pipes, and strings.
Their indulgence was unrestrained,
and the world became increasingly exhausted.
Consequently, in the end, his person died and his state perished,
and he became the object of the world's execution.
Was it not solely due to the use of brocades, embroideries, fine linens, and coarse hemp?
Now, during a year of famine,
if there were someone who wished to give you the Pearl of Suí Hóu
and said:
'It may not be sold;
it is a treasure to be used as an ornament,'
and also wished to give you a measure of grain,
but the one who receives the pearl cannot have the grain,
and the one who receives the grain cannot have the pearl,
which would you choose?"
Qín Gǔ-lí said:
"I would take the grain,
for it can save one from distress."
Mòzǐ said:
"Indeed, it is so.
Then why bother with luxury?
It increases uselessness
and encourages superficial excesses;
it is not what a Sage considers urgent.
Therefore, one must first be regularly full
before seeking delicious food;
one must first be regularly warm
before seeking beautiful clothing;
one must first be regularly secure
before seeking pleasure.
To act in a way that can be sustained,
to behave in a way that can endure,
putting substance first and ornamentation second—
this is the task of the Sage."
Qín Gǔ-lí said:
"Excellent."
20.7 After Qín Shǐ Huáng had unified the world,
he became greatly extravagant.
Thirty-five years after ascending the throne, he still did not rest,
constructing grand postal roads
from Jiǔyuán to Yúnyáng,
cutting through mountains and filling in valleys
to make them run straight.
Disliking the smallness of the former kings' palaces,
he then, between Fèng and Hào,
at the sites of Wén and Wǔ,
built a court palace within the Shànglín Yuàn south of the Wèi River.
He first built the front hall, Āfáng;
it was five hundred paces from east to west
and fifty zhàng from north to south.
Above, ten thousand people could be seated;
below, flags of five zhàng could be erected.
Around it was an elevated gallery,
running directly from below the hall to Nánshān.
He marked the peaks of Nánshān to serve as gate towers.
He built a double-decked walkway
from Āfáng across the Wèi River
to connect with Xiányáng,
to symbolize the Celestial Pole’s corridor crossing the Milky Way to reach the Yíngshì constellation.
He also began the labor at Líshān,
sealing the bottom of the three springs.
Within the pass, he built three hundred detached palaces.
Outside the pass, there were four hundred,
all equipped with bells, chimes, curtains, and hangings,
as well as women, singers, and entertainers.
He erected stone gate towers in the Qúshān district on the East Sea
to serve as the Eastern Gate of Qín.
Thereupon, the Fāngshì Hán guest Hóu Shēng and the Qí guest Lú Shēng conspired together, saying:
“In the present time, one cannot stay.
The superior delights in using punishment and execution to establish his awe,
while those below fear being blamed and cling to their salaries,
none daring to be fully loyal.
The superior does not hear of his faults and becomes daily more arrogant,
while those below are intimidated into submission, using flattery and deception to gain favor.
Those who offer admonition are not employed,
and the loss of the Way grows ever more severe.
If our group stays for long,
we will eventually be harmed by him.”
Thus, they fled together.
When Shǐ Huáng heard of this,
he was greatly enraged and said:
“In former days, I treated Lú Shēng generously.
I honored him with rank and served him;
now he slanders me.
I hear that many of the scholars speak monstrous words
to confuse the black-headed commoners.”
He then ordered the Imperial Secretary to register all the scholars.
The scholars informed on each other, and those who violated the law numbered more than four hundred and sixty people;
he buried them all alive.
Lú Shēng was not caught, but Hóu Shēng was later captured.
When Shǐ Huáng heard of it,
he summoned him for an audience,
ascending the terrace at Ādōng
overlooking the crossroads
to count his crimes and tear him apart by chariots.
When Shǐ Huáng caught sight of Hóu Shēng,
he was greatly enraged and said:
“Old scoundrel, you are no good!
You slandered your lord,
yet you dare to see me again!”
When Hóu Shēng arrived,
he looked up at the terrace and spoke, saying:
“I have heard that those who know they must die are necessarily brave.
Would Your Majesty be willing to listen to a single word from me?”
Shǐ Huáng said:
“What do you wish to say?
Speak it.”
Hóu Shēng said:
“I have heard that Yǔ established the ‘criticism wood,’
wishing to know his faults.
Now Your Majesty is extravagant and has lost the fundamentals,
indulging in excess and pursuing the trivial.
Palaces, halls, and terraces
are connected and piled high;
pearls, jade, and heavy treasures
are accumulated like mountains;
brocades and embroidered silks
more than fill the storehouses;
women, singers, and entertainers
number in the tens of thousands;
the music of bells and drums
flows without end;
wines, foods, and rare delicacies
are spread out before you;
clothes are light and warm,
and carriages and horses are ornately decorated.
That which you use to provide for yourself
is beautiful, extravagant, and brilliant,
to an extent that cannot be surpassed.
