The black-headed commoners are exhausted,
the people’s strength is depleted,
yet you still do not realize it.
Furthermore, you are quick to punish criticism,
using harsh awe to overcome those below.
Those below are mute and those above are deaf.
That is why we left.
We do not pity our own bodies;
we only pity the coming ruin of Your Majesty’s state!
I have heard that of the enlightened kings of old,
their food was sufficient to satisfy hunger,
their clothes were sufficient to keep warm,
their palaces were sufficient to dwell in,
and their carriages and horses were sufficient for travel.
Therefore, above they were not abandoned by Heaven,
and below they were not abandoned by the commoners.
Yáo’s thatch roof was not trimmed,
his oak rafters were not carved,
and his earthen steps had only three levels;
yet he was happy throughout his life
because his ornate displays were few and his simple substance was plenty.
Dānzhū was arrogant and cruel,
fond of laziness and excess,
and did not cultivate order and transformation;
thus, he did not ascend.
Now Your Majesty’s excess
is ten thousand times that of Dānzhū and a thousand times that of Kūnwú, Jié, and Zhòu.
I fear that Your Majesty has ten reasons to perish and not even one to survive.”
Shǐ Huáng was silent for a long time
and then said:
“Why did you not say this sooner?”
Hóu Shēng said:
“Your Majesty’s intentions
were just then riding the blue clouds,
drifting among the sights of ornate displays,
considering yourself wise and powerful,
above insulting the Five Emperors
and below slighting the Three Kings,
discarding simple substance
and pursuing trivial skills.
The signs of Your Majesty’s downfall have been visible for a long time.
We feared that speaking would be of no use
and would only bring death upon ourselves;
therefore, we fled and did not dare to speak.
Now that I am certain to die,
I have laid this out for Your Majesty;
although I cannot prevent Your Majesty from perishing,
I wish to make Your Majesty aware of yourself.”
Shǐ Huáng said:
“Can I change?”
Hóu Shēng said:
“The situation is already formed;
Your Majesty can only sit and wait for ruin!
If Your Majesty wishes to change it,
can you be like Yáo and Yǔ?
If not,
there is no hope.
Your Majesty’s assistants are also unsuitable;
I fear that even with change, you cannot be saved.”
Shǐ Huáng heaved a sigh
and then released him, not executing him.
Three years later,
Shǐ Huáng died;
Èrshì ascended the throne,
and in three years, Qín perished.
20.8 Wèi Wén Hóu asked Lǐ Kè:
“From where does the source of criminal punishment arise?”
Lǐ Kè said:
“It arises from wicked, evil, and licentious conduct.
Generally, a wicked and evil heart
arises from hunger and cold.
As for licentiousness,
it is the cunning resulting from long-term hunger.
Carvings and engravings
are things that harm agricultural work;
brocades and embroidered silks
are things that damage women’s work.
When agricultural work is harmed,
it is the root of hunger;
when women’s work is damaged,
it is the source of cold.
When hunger and cold both arrive,
that one could not become wicked or evil
has never happened.
When men and women decorate themselves beautifully to boast to one another,
that they could avoid being licentious
has never happened.
Therefore, if the ruler does not forbid clever crafts,
the state will be poor and the people extravagant.
When the state is poor and the people extravagant,
the destitute become wicked and evil,
while the affluent become licentious.
This is driving the people to be evil.
When the people become evil,
the law is then applied to pursue and execute them,
without pardoning their crimes;
this is setting a trap for the people.
The arising of criminal punishment has a source;
if the ruler of men does not block its root but instead punishes its branches,
it is the way to harm the state!”
Wén Hóu said:
“Excellent.”
He took this as the standard for his attire.
20.9 Qín Mù Gōng asked Yóu Yú during a moment of leisure:
"In ancient times, the enlightened kings and sagely emperors
gained or lost their states;
what was the reason for this?"
Yóu Yú said:
"I have heard
that they gained them through frugality
and lost them through extravagance."
Mù Gōng said:
"I wish to hear the specifics of extravagance and frugality."
Yóu Yú said:
"I have heard that when Yáo possessed all under heaven,
he ate from earthen bowls
and drank from earthen jars.
His territory reached Jiāo Zhǐ in the south
and Yōu Dū in the north,
and as far as the rising and setting of the sun and moon in the east and west;
none failed to submit as guests.
When Yáo relinquished all under heaven,
Shùn received it.
He produced eating vessels
by cutting wood and shaping it,
melting copper and iron to sharpen his blades,
and using black lacquer for the vessels.
The feudal lords considered this more extravagant,
and thirteen states did not submit.
Shùn relinquished all under heaven and Yǔ received it.
He produced ritual vessels
that were lacquered on the outside and painted red on the inside.
Silk fabrics were used for cushions and mats,
and wine cups and ladles were decorated with colors.
This was even more extravagant,
and thirty-two states did not submit.
After the Xià Hòu Shì era ended,
Yīn and Zhōu received it.
They produced grand vessels
and built nine prideful structures.
Eating vessels were carved and polished,
and wine cups and ladles were engraved and inlaid.
There were curtains on all four walls,
and cushions and mats had carved patterns.
This was even more extravagant,
and fifty-two states did not submit.
When a ruler loves ornamentation,
those who serve him become even more extravagant.
Therefore it is said:
Frugality is the way."
After Yóu Yú left,
Mù Gōng summoned Nèi Shǐ Liào and told him:
"I have heard that having a sage in a neighboring country
is a source of worry for a rival state.
Now Yóu Yú is a sage,
and I am troubled by him.
What should I do?"
Nèi Shǐ Liào said:
"The Róng are secluded and distant,
and have not heard the music of the Central States.
You should send them music girls
to disrupt their governance,
and generously request a delay for Yóu Yú's return
to alienate the relationship between them.
Once there is a wedge between that ruler and his minister,
then they can be plotted against."
The Prince said:
"Agreed."
He then sent twenty-seven music girls to the Róng king
and requested a delay for Yóu Yú's return.
The Róng king granted the request.
He indeed saw the music girls and delighted in them.
He set out wine and listened to music,
not moving from his place for the rest of the year,
and half of his horses, cattle, and sheep died.
Yóu Yú returned and remonstrated,
but his remonstrance was not heard.
He then left and entered Qín.
Mù Gōng welcomed him and appointed him as an Upper Minister,
asking him about the military strength and the advantages of the terrain.
Having obtained this information,
he raised troops and attacked them,
annexing twelve states
and opening up a thousand lǐ of land.
Although Mù Gōng was an extravagant ruler,
he could listen to the worthy and accept remonstrance;
thus he became the Hegemon of the Xī Róng.
The Xī Róng were licentious in music
and lured by profit,
thereby losing their state;
this was because they departed from simplicity.
20.10 Jīng Hóu went to visit the Crown Prince of Wèi,
wearing a jade-adorned sword on his left
and a jade pendant ring on his right.
The light from the left shone on the right,
and the light from the right shone on the left.
After he had been sitting for a while,
the Crown Prince did not look at them,
nor did he ask about them.
Jīng Hóu said:
"Does the state of Wèi also have treasures?"
The Crown Prince said:
"Yes."
Jīng Hóu said:
"What are its treasures like?"
The Crown Prince said:
"When the ruler is trustworthy and the ministers are loyal,
and the common people support their superiors,
these are the treasures of the state of Wèi."
Jīng Hóu said:
"What I am asking
is not about that;
I am only asking about its objects."
The Crown Prince said:
"We have them.
When Tú Shī Zhǎo governed Wèi,
there was no deceptive pricing in the markets.
When Qiè Xīn governed Yáng,
no one would pick up things lost on the road.
When Máng Mǎo was in the court,
the worthy men of the four neighboring regions all sought to be introduced.
These three Great Officers
are the great treasures of the state of Wèi."
At this, Jīng Hóu remained silent and did not respond.
He untied the jade-adorned sword on the left,
untied the pendant ring on the right,
and left them on the seat.
He stood up in embarrassment,
was silent and did not give thanks,
and hurried out.
He got into his carriage and drove away.
The Crown Prince of Wèi sent a rider carrying the sword and pendant to pursue Jīng Hóu,
and instructed him to tell Jīng Hóu:
"I have no virtue to treasure and cannot be the guardian of pearls and jade.
These cannot clothe one in the cold
and cannot feed one in hunger.
Do not leave me with these sources of harm."
Thereupon Jīng Hóu shut his doors and did not go out,
and eventually died.
20.11 Jìn Píng Gōng made a chariot for racing,
with dragon banners of many colors,
decorated with rhinoceros horn and ivory,
and inlaid with feathers and ornaments.
When the chariot was completed,
worth a thousand gold pieces,
he placed it below the palace hall
and ordered his ministers to view it.
Tián Chāi passed it three times without looking at it once.
Píng Gōng's face changed and he became very angry,
asking Tián Chāi:
"You passed three times and did not look once;
why is that?"
Tián Chāi replied:
"I have heard that those who persuade the Son of Heaven use all under heaven;
those who persuade the feudal lords use the state;
those who persuade the Great Officers use their office;
those who persuade scholars use their service;
those who persuade farmers use food;
and those who persuade women of the household use weaving.
Jié was destroyed because of extravagance,
and Zhòu was defeated because of licentiousness.
Therefore, I did not dare to look."
Píng Gōng said:
"Good."
He then ordered his attendants:
"Remove the chariot."
20．12 The royal granary of Wèi Wén Hóu was destroyed by fire.
Wén Hóu wore plain white clothes
and avoided the main hall
for five days.
All the ministers wore plain clothes and offered their condolences.
Gōngzǐ Chéngfù alone did not offer condolences.
When Wén Hóu returned to the hall,
Gōngzǐ Chéngfù hurried in and offered congratulations, saying:
"It is truly very good,
this fire at the royal granary."
Wén Hóu's face changed and he said unhappily:
"The royal granary
was where I stored my treasures.
Now that there has been a fire,
I wore plain clothes
and avoided the main hall,
and all the ministers wore plain clothes and offered condolences.
Yet you, Grand Officer, did not offer condolences;
and now that I have returned from avoidance,
why do you come in to congratulate me?"
Gōngzǐ Chéngfù said:
"I have heard:
The Son of Heaven stores within the four seas,
the feudal lords store within their borders,
the Grand Officers store within their households,
and the scholars and commoners store within chests and boxes.
If items are not in their proper place of storage,
then if there is no natural disaster from Heaven,
there will surely be human trouble.
Now, fortunately, there is no human trouble,
but instead a natural disaster from Heaven;
is this not good?"
Wén Hóu sighed deeply and said:
"Good."
20．13 Qí Huán Gōng said to Guǎn Zhòng:
"Our state is very small,
and our resources are very few,
yet the clothing, carriages, and horses of the ministers are very extravagant.
I wish to prohibit this;
is it possible?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I have heard:
What the ruler tastes,
the ministers eat;
what the ruler likes,
the ministers wear.
Now, for your lordship’s food,
there must be cinnamon syrup;
you wear clothes of refined purple silk
and furs of white fox.
This is the source of the ministers' extravagance.
The *Shī* says:
'If you do not personally act,
the common people will not believe.'
If your lordship wishes to prohibit it,
why not start with yourself?"
Huán Gōng said:
"Good."
Thereupon he changed to clothes of refined white silk
and a large white cap;
after he had held court for one year, the state of Qí became frugal.
20．14 Jì Wén Zǐ served as the prime minister of Lǔ.
His concubines did not wear silk,
and his horses did not eat grain.
Zhòngsūn Tuō remonstrated, saying:
"You are a high minister of Lǔ,
yet your concubines do not wear silk
and your horses do not eat grain.
People will think you are stingy,
and moreover, it does not bring glory to the state."
Wén Zǐ said:
"Is that so?
I see the fathers and mothers of our countrymen
wearing coarse clothes and eating vegetables;
for this reason I do not dare to do otherwise.
Moreover, I have heard that a gentleman brings glory to the state through virtue,
not through concubines and horses.
As for virtue,
it is attained within myself and also attained by others;
therefore it can be practiced.
If I indulge in extravagance
and immerse myself in outward display
without being able to reflect on myself,
how could I protect the state?"
Zhòngsūn Tuō withdrew in shame.
20．15 Zhào Jiǎn Zǐ rode in a worn carriage with lean horses
and wore a coat of black ram skin.
His steward stepped forward to remonstrate, saying:
"A new carriage is safe,
fat horses make travel swift,
and white fox fur is warm and light.
Your lordship should change these."
Jiǎn Zǐ said:
"It is not that I do not know this.
I have heard:
When a gentleman wears fine clothes, he becomes more respectful;
when a petty person wears fine clothes, he becomes more arrogant.
Now I use these to guard myself,
for I fear having the heart of a petty person."
The *Chuán* says:
"The Zhōu Gōng's position was noble, yet he became more humble;
he defeated enemies, yet became more fearful;
his family was wealthy, yet became more frugal;
therefore the Zhōu clan lasted for over eight hundred years."
This is what that refers to.
20．16 Lǔ built the Láng park.
Jì Píng Zǐ wanted it completed quickly.
Shūsūn Zhāo Zǐ said:
"What is the use of completing it quickly
by being cruel to the people?
Can that be acceptable?
It is better to have no park;
can one do without the people?
Is it not hateful to hear of amusements and games
that exhaust the people under one's rule?"
20．17 Shūsūn Wén Zǐ of Wèi asked Wángsūn Xià:
"The ancestral temple of my late lord is small;
I wish to enlarge it,
is that possible?"
He replied:
"Ancient gentlemen
considered frugality to be ritual;
modern gentlemen
replace it with extravagance.
Although the state of Wèi is poor,
could it be that there is not even a single pair of patterned shoes
that could be traded for the embroidery of ten bushels of millet?
I consider that to be against ritual."
Wén Zǐ then stopped.
20．18 Jìn Wén Gōng gathered the feudal lords and made a covenant, saying:
"I have heard that the disorder of a state
does not come from music and women,
but must come from crafty profit.
Those who love the pleasure of music and women
are licentious;
those who are greedy for crafty profit
are deluded.
A licentious and deluded state,
if it does not perish, it will surely be ruined.
From now on,
do not let beautiful concubines cast doubt upon the wife,
do not let music and song hinder the administration,
do not let personal feelings harm the public interest,
and do not display greed for goods and profit to subordinates.
As for those who do such things,
they are said to be cutting down their roots and foundations
to drift among the flowers and leaves.
For such people, there will be calamities without relief,
and when there are invaders, they shall not be repelled.
Let the covenant show this to those who do not act according to these words."
Thereupon, the gentlemen who heard this said:
"Wén Gōng truly knows the Way;
if he does not become a true King,
it is only because he lacks assistants."
20．19 Yàn Zǐ was drinking wine with Jǐng Gōng.
When dusk fell,
the Duke called for lights.
Yàn Zǐ declined, saying:
"The *Shī* says:
'With the cap set awry,'
referring to the loss of virtue.
'Dancing repeatedly and wildly,'
referring to the loss of dignity.
'Having been made drunk with wine,
having been satiated with virtue.'
'Having drunk and then departing,
both shall receive blessings,'
such is the ritual between guest and host.
'To be drunk and not depart,
is called destroying virtue,'
which is the fault of guest and host.
I, Yīng, have divined for this day,
but I have not divined for this night."
The Duke said:
"Good."
He raised his wine in sacrifice,
bowed twice, and departed.
He said:
"How could he be wrong about me?
I have entrusted the state to Yàn Zǐ.
Even though his family is poor,
he treats me well
and does not wish for me to be licentious or extravagant;
how much more so when he plans the state with me!"
20.20 Yáng Wángsūn fell ill and was approaching death.
He gave instructions to his son, saying:
"When I die, I wish to be buried naked
so as to return to my true state.
You must not change my intention."
Lord Qí heard of this
and went to remonstrate with him, saying:
"I have humbly heard that Wángsūn has ordered his burial
to be done naked into the earth.
If it is indeed as I have heard,
I personally believe it is unacceptable.
If the dead have no consciousness, then that would be one thing,
but if the dead do have consciousness,
then this would be to disgrace your corpse in the underworld.
How would you face your ancestors?
I personally believe it is unacceptable."
Wángsūn said:
"I intend to use this to correct the age.
Lavish burials truly provide no benefit to the dead,
yet the world competes to surpass one another in them,
wasting wealth and exhausting resources
only to let them rot beneath the earth.
Sometimes they go in today and are dug out tomorrow;
how is this truly different from exposing one's bones in the middle of a wilderness?
Furthermore, death
is the transformation at the end of life
and the return of things.
When that which returns reaches its destination
and that which transforms completes its change,
this is each thing returning to its true state.
This true state is dark and obscure,
invisible to the eye,
inaudible to the ear;
it thus accords with the nature of the Dào.
To adorn the exterior to boast to the masses
and use lavish burials to distort the true state,
preventing that which returns from reaching its destination
and that which transforms from completing its change—
this causes all things to lose their natural state.
Moreover, I have heard
that the spirit
belongs to Heaven
and the physical frame
belongs to Earth.
When the spirit leaves the form,
and each returns to its true state,
it is therefore called a ghost (*guǐ*).
The word 'ghost' means 'to return' (*guī*).
When the corpse remains alone like a clod of earth,
how could it have consciousness?
To wrap it thickly in silk fabrics
and provide it with much wealth and goods
is to deprive the living of their resources.
The ancient sages followed human emotions,
unable to bear the loss of their kin,
and thus they established rituals for them.
Nowadays, people exceed these;
therefore, I wish to be buried naked to correct this.
In ancient times, when Yáo was buried,
a hollowed log served as a casket,
and vines served as bindings.
The depth of the excavation did not disturb the springs below,
and the top did not allow odors to leak out.
Therefore, when the sages were alive, they valued simplicity,
and when they died, they were buried simply.
They added nothing useless
and took away nothing that was not beneficial.
To say that wasting wealth on lavish burials today
for the dead who have no knowledge
takes away what the living could use—
how erroneous!
It can be called a profound delusion!"
Lord Qí said:
"Excellent."
And so he was buried naked.
20.21 In Lǔ, there was a frugal person
who cooked food in a clay pot.
Finding the food delicious,
he placed it in an earthenware soup vessel
and presented it to Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ received it
with joy and delight,
as if he were receiving a gift of the *tàiláo* sacrifice.
His disciples said:
"A clay jar
is a lowly vessel,
and cooked food
is a meager meal.
Why is the Master so happy about it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I have heard that those who love to remonstrate think of their ruler,
and those who find food delicious think of their parents.
It is not that I consider the meal to be lavish;
it is because the food was delicious that he thought of my parents."
20.22 When Yànzǐ fell ill
and was about to die,
he hid a document inside a pillar
and said to his wife:
"The pillar has words;
when our son is grown, let him look at them."
When the son grew up and opened the document,
the words of the document said:
"Cloth and silk are not inexhaustible;
once exhausted, they cannot be used for adornment.
Oxen and horses are not inexhaustible;
once exhausted, they cannot be used for service.
Officers are not inexhaustible;
once exhausted, they cannot be given responsibilities.
Exhausted! Exhausted!
Indeed, exhausted!"
20.23 Zhòngní asked Lǎo Dān, saying:
"How extreme it is
that the Dào is so difficult to practice today!
I have prepared myself and offered my services
to seek out the rulers of this age,
but I have not been accepted.
The Dào is truly difficult to practice today!"
Lǎozi said:
"Persuaders are carried away by what they hear,
and speakers are confused by their own rhetoric.
In these two cases,
the Dào cannot be entrusted."
20.24 Zǐgòng asked Zǐshí, saying:
"Do you not study the *Shī*?"
Zǐshí said:
"Do I have any spare time?
My parents expect my filial piety,
my brothers expect my fraternal respect,
and my friends expect my trustworthiness.
Do I have any spare time?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I beg to cast aside my *Shī*
and study under you."
20.25 Gōngmíng Xuān studied under Zēngzǐ;
for three years,
he did not read books.
Zēngzǐ said:
"Xuān, you have stayed at my gate
for three years without studying.
Why is this?"
Gōngmíng Xuān said:
"How would I dare to stay at the Master's gate without studying?
I saw the Master staying in the inner court:
while your parents were present,
the sound of your scolding never reached even the dogs or horses.
I was pleased by this
and have tried to learn it but have not yet been able.
I saw the Master receiving guests:
you were respectful and frugal without being lax or idle.
I was pleased by this
and have tried to learn it but have not yet been able.
I saw the Master attending court:
you were solemn toward those below you without being injurious.
I was pleased by this
and have tried to learn it but have not yet been able.
I was pleased by these three things
and have tried to learn them but have not yet been able.
How would I dare to stay at the Master's gate without studying?"
Zēngzǐ left his mat and apologized to him, saying:
"I, Sān, am not as good as Xuān.
My learning is merely that of books."
20.26 A man of Lǔ was good at weaving straw sandals,
and his wife was good at weaving white silk.
They wanted to move to Yuè.
Someone said to them:
"You will certainly be impoverished."
The man of Lǔ said:
"Why?"
The person said:
"Sandals are for wearing on the feet,
and white silk is for making caps;
yet the people of Yuè go barefoot and cut their hair.
If you travel to a country where your goods are not used,
how could you hope not to be impoverished?"
21.1 Mǐn Zǐqiān and his brother were two.
Their mother died,
and their father remarried,
subsequently having two more sons.
Zǐqiān was driving the carriage for his father
and lost the reins.
The father held his hand
and found his clothing was very thin.
The father then returned,
called his stepmother's children,
and held their hands;
their clothing was very thick and warm.
He immediately said to his wife:
"The reason I married you
was for the sake of my sons.
Now you deceive me.
Leave,
do not stay!"
Zǐqiān came forward and said:
"When mother is here, one son is thinly clad;
if mother leaves, four sons will be cold."
His father fell silent.
Therefore it is said:
"How filial is Mǐn Zǐqiān!
With one word his mother returned;
with further words, the three sons were warm."
Cited from Yìwén Lèijù, Volume 20, Page 369.
21.2 Jìn Líng Gōng built the Jiǔ Céng Tái,
the costs reaching hundreds of billions.
He said to his attendants:
"Anyone who dares to remonstrate shall be beheaded!"
Sūn Xī then remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant can stack thirteen chess pieces
and add nine chicken eggs on top of them."
The Duke said:
"I studied little in my youth
and have never seen this.
Sir, do it for me."
Sūn Xī then placed the chess pieces at the bottom
and added nine chicken eggs on top.
The attendants were terrified.
Líng Gōng prostrated himself,
his breathing uneven.
The Duke said:
"How dangerous!
How dangerous!"
Sūn Xī said:
"Your servant says this is not dangerous;
there is something even more dangerous than this."
The Duke said:
"I wish to see it."
Sūn Xī said:
"The Jiǔ Céng Tái
has not been completed in three years.
Men cannot plow,
women cannot weave,
the national treasury is empty,
the population is decreasing,
officials and commoners are rebelling and fleeing,
and neighboring states are plotting
to raise an army.
When the state is destroyed,
what will my lord have to look forward to?"
Líng Gōng said:
"My mistake
has reached such a point."
He immediately demolished the Jiǔ Céng Tái.
Cited from Lèijù, Volume 24, Page 436.
21.3 Sūn Xī studied sad songs and the Gǔqín.
He then took the qín and played the music of Zhèng and Wèi.
Líng Gōng was greatly moved,
so he composed the piece "Wèi Gōng"
and sang in harmony with it.
Cited from Běitáng Shūchāo, Volume 106, Page 409.
21.4 The King of Qí built the Jiǔ Chóng Tái
and recruited painters from throughout the kingdom, offering them money.
There was a man named Jìng Jūn who usually lived in hunger and cold.
His wife was of wonderful beauty.
Jìng Jūn was skilled in painting,
and coveting the reward, he went to paint the terrace.
Having been away from home for a long time,
he missed his wife,
so he painted her portrait
and would look at it and smile.
Bystanders saw this and reported it to the King.
The King summoned him and questioned him.
He replied:
"I have a wife like this.
Having been away from home for a long time,
my heart constantly thinks of her.
I secretly painted her portrait
to comfort my heart in separation,
not realizing it would reach the ears of my superior."
The King then set out wine
and made merry with Jìng Jūn.
He said to Jìng Jūn:
"The women presented from within the kingdom are none of them beautiful.
I request your wife for a million coins,
is it possible?
If not,
I will kill you."
Terrified, Jìng Jūn listened and consented.
Cited from Lèijù, Volume 32, Page 561, and Tàipíng Yùlǎn, Volume 381, Page 1758.
21.5 When Lǚ Wàng was seventy years old,
he fished at the Wèi Zhǔ.
For three days and three nights,
no fish took the bait.
He spoke with a farmer.
The farmer
was an old sage of ancient times;
he said to Wàng:
"If you are to fish again,
you must thin your line
and make your bait fragrant.
Cast it slowly
so as not to startle the fish."
Wàng did as he said.
First he caught a crucian carp,
then he caught a carp.
Upon cutting open the belly, he found a document.
The text of the document said:
"Lǚ Wàng shall be enfeoffed in Qí."
Wàng knew then that he would become noble.
Cited from Lèijù, Volume 66, Page 1178.
21.6 Qí sent Chún-yú Kūn to Chǔ.
He was short in stature,
and the King of Chǔ looked down upon him greatly,
saying to him:
"Is there no one left in Qí
that they sent you?
What is your stature?"
He replied:
"Your servant has no stature,
but the seven-foot sword at your servant's waist
desires to behead an ill-mannered king."
The King said:
"Stop!
I was only joking with you."
He then drank wine together with Kūn.
The King of Chǔ said to Chún-yú Kūn:
"I have an enemy in Wú;
would you be willing to take revenge for me?"
He replied:
"On my way here, your servant saw a rustic man by the roadside
holding a single fish.
He offered a prayer over his field, saying:
'May the high ground yield ten thousand bundles,
and the low ground yield a thousand bushels.'
Your servant laughed secretly at this,
thinking that the ritual offering was meager while the expectation was great.
Now the King gives me half a day of pleasure but entrusts me with Wú;
the King's plan is not sound."
The King of Chǔ fell silent.
Cited from Yùlǎn, Volume 378, Page 1745; Lèijù, Volume 96, Page 1671; and Yùlǎn, Volume 736, Page 3264.
21.7 Jìn Wén Gōng attacked Chǔ.
Upon returning to the state to distribute rewards,
Hú Yǎn was placed first.
Someone said:
"The affair at Chéngpú
was the strategy of Xiān Zhěn."
Wén Gōng said:
"In the affair at Chéngpú,
Yǎn persuaded me not to lose trust
and not to go back on the agreement of the three retreats.
As for the military matters Xiān Zhěn planned,
I used them to achieve victory.
However, that was a strategy for one occasion,
whereas Yǎn's words established merit for ten thousand generations.
How could I place the benefit of one occasion above merit for ten thousand generations?
This is why I put him first."
Everyone was pleased and convinced.
Cited from Yùlǎn, Volume 279, Page 1302.
21.8 Liáng Jūn went out to hunt,
and saw a flock of white geese.
Liáng Jūn got out of his carriage
and drew his bow, wishing to shoot them.
There was a traveler on the road watching,
who urged Liáng Jūn to stop,
and the flock of geese was startled.
Liáng Jūn was angry
and wished to kill the traveler.
His charioteer Gōngsūn Lóng got out of the carriage and replied:
"In the past, during the time of Qí Jǐng Gōng,
there was a drought for three years.
They divined it, and the answer was:
'One must sacrifice a person
for it to rain.'
Jǐng Gōng said:
'The reason I previously sought rain was for my people.
If I now sacrifice a person to obtain rain,
I myself shall take it upon me.'
Before he had finished speaking,
heavy rain fell for a thousand lǐ.
Now you, my lord, wish to kill a man for the sake of white geese;
this is no different from wolves and tigers."
Liáng Jūn took his hand,
got onto the carriage with him,
and as they entered the outer city gates,
the people shouted "Wànsuì!"
He said:
"How joyful!
In today's hunt,
I have uniquely obtained good words."
Cited in Yùlǎn, volume 390, page 1804.
21.9 Qí sent troops to attack Lǔ
and saw a woman
fleeing with two small children.
She was carrying the smaller one and leading the larger one by the hand.
Seeing that the large army was about to arrive,
she picked up the larger one and led the smaller one by the hand.
The messenger found this very strange
and asked her about it.
The woman said:
"The larger one is my husband's elder brother's son;
the smaller one is my own son.
The husband's brother's son represents public duty;
my own son represents private duty.
Would I rather save the public and abandon the private?"
The messenger was moved,
and considered her words virtuous.
He immediately halted the army and returned,
explaining it to the King of Qí, saying:
"Lǔ cannot yet be attacked.
If the sense of duty of even a common woman is like this,
how much more so that of the ministers of the court?"
Cited in Yùlǎn, volume 422, page 1948.
21.10 In Lǔ, there was a virtuous daughter,
the child of a secondary chamber,
exactly twenty years of age.
She was well-versed in the classics and books,
and would often stand in attendance and chant,
with tears falling like rain.
An acquaintance said to her:
"Do you wish to be married?
Why is your grief so extreme?"
She replied:
"The Lord of Lǔ is old,
and the Crown Prince is still young;
I fear that treacherous ministers will arise."
Cited in Yùlǎn, volume 469, page 2156.
21.11 Zhào Xiāng Zǐ asked Wáng Lí:
"What is the reason a state perishes?"
He replied:
"The ruler is stingy but can be tolerant of evil;
it is because of this that it perishes."
Xiāng Zǐ said:
"Why do you think so?"
He said:
"If stingy, then one cannot reward the worthy;
if tolerant of evil, then one cannot punish crimes.
When the worthy are not rewarded
and the criminals are not punished,
why would it not perish?"
Cited in Yùlǎn, volume 633, page 2840.
21.12 Sū Qín arrived in Qí,
and the King of Qí treated him with great favor.
The various high officials were jealous of him
and sent someone to stab Sū Qín, but he did not die.
The King of Qí offered treasures as a reward to seek the culprit but did not find him.
As Sū Qín was near death,
he said to the King of Qí:
"If the King truly wishes to find the culprit for me,
then after I die,
please tear my corpse apart by chariots in the marketplace
and proclaim it, saying:
'Sū Qín wished to cause chaos in Qí for the sake of Yān.
Today he is dead,
and I am very pleased;
therefore I have torn him apart.
If anyone can be found to have killed the master,
they shall be heavily rewarded.'
In this way,
the one who stabbed me will surely come forward."
The King of Qí followed his words,
tore the corpse, and proclaimed it;
the one who had stabbed Sū Qín indeed came forward to seek the reward.
Cited in Yùlǎn, volume 633, page 2840.
21.13 There was a person at the northern frontier
whose horse escaped into the Hú lands.
Everyone consoled him.
His father said:
"How do you know this will not be a blessing?"
After several months,
the horse returned bringing a fine Hú horse.
Everyone congratulated him.
His father said:
"How do you know this will not be a misfortune?"
The family was wealthy and the horse was fine;
his son loved riding,
but he fell and broke his thigh.
Everyone consoled him.
His father said:
"How do you know this will not be a blessing?"
After one year,
the Hú barbarians invaded in force.
All able-bodied men took up their bows and went to war.
Of the people at the frontier,
nine out of ten died.
This son alone, because he was lame,
survived with his father.
Cited in Yùlǎn, volume 896, page 3980.
21.14 Jìn Píng Gōng asked Zhào Wǔ:
"Zhōngmóu
is the limbs of the three states
and the shoulders and thighs of Hándān.
I wish to obtain a good magistrate for it.
The magistrate's post is vacant;
whom can I send?"
Zhào Wǔ said:
"Xíng Bózǐ will do."
The Duke said:
"Is Xíng Zǐ not your enemy?"
He replied:
"Private enmity does not enter the public gate."
He asked again:
"The magistrate of Zhōngfǔ is vacant;
whom can I send?"
Zhào Wǔ said:
"My son will do."
Thus, in recommending others, he did not avoid an enemy,
and in recommending within, he did not avoid his son.
Cited in Lèijù, volume 50, page 907.
21.15 A turtle a thousand years old
can speak with humans.
Cited in Lèijù, volume 96, page 1668.
21.16 The drum models Heaven;
the bell models Earth.
Cited in Shūchāo, volume 108, page 412.
21.17 The brave warrior Mèng Bēn, when traveling by water, did not avoid flood dragons,
and when traveling by land, did not avoid tigers and wolves.
Cited in Wénxuǎn, "Yǔliè fù" commentary, page 168.
21.18 The music is easy and good, harmonizing with the emotions of the song,
and fully expressing the meaning of the dance.
Cited in Wénxuǎn, "Wǔ fù" commentary, page 320.
21.19 Zǐ Qí was eighteen years old
when the Lord of Qí sent him to govern Dōng'ē.
Dōng'ē was greatly transformed.
Cited in Hòuhànshū, "Biography of Hú Guǎng" commentary, page 1508.
21.20 During the time of Jìn Píng Gōng,
there was parched land for a thousand lǐ.
Cited in Hòuhànshū, "Biography of Zāng Gōng" commentary, page 696.
21.21 Wáng Guózǐ's son by his former wife was Bó Qí,
and his son by his later wife was Bó Fēng.
The later wife wanted her son to be established as the Crown Prince
and said to the King:
"Bó Qí is fond of me."
The King did not believe her.
The mother said:
"Order Bó Qí to be in the back garden;
I will pass by him.
The King should look down from the terrace;
then he will know."
The King did as she said.
Bó Qí entered the garden.
The later wife secretly took a dozen bees and placed them in her unlined garment.
Passing by Bó Qí, she said:
"Bees are stinging me!"
Bó Qí reached into the garment to take the bees and kill them.
The King saw this from afar
and then banished Bó Qí.
Cited in Hòuhànshū, "Biography of Huáng Qióng" commentary, page 2039.
21.22 Jìn Wén Gōng was feasting on roasted meat when a hair was found wrapped around it.
The chef said:
"The carving knife was whetted,
its sharpness equal to Gān Jiàng;
it cut the meat through, yet the hair was not severed—
this is my first fault.
I skewered the pieces of meat but did not see the hair—
this is my second fault.
The coals in the furnace were glowing red, yet the hair was not burned away—
this is my third fault."
Wén Gōng said:
"Ah,
there is a reason for this."
He then summoned the assistant chef to question him,
and indeed he confessed.
Cited from Shū Chāo, Volume 55, page 175.
21.23 When Liǔxià Huì died,
people were going to deliver his eulogy.
His wife said:
"If you are to describe the Master's virtue,
you gentlemen do not know him as well as I do."
She composed the eulogy, saying:
"The Master did not boast,
the Master did not seek favors;
his posthumous title should be Huì."
The disciples heard this and followed her suggestion.
Cited from Shū Chāo, Volume 102, page 391.
21.24 The Master said:
"By judging a person by appearance,
I lost Zǐyǔ;
by judging a person by speech,
I lost Zǎi Yǔ."
Dàntái Zǐyǔ
had the appearance of a superior man,
but after staying with him for a long time,
his words did not live up to his appearance;
Zǎi Yǔ's speech
was elegant and cultured,
but after staying with him for a long time,
his wisdom did not live up to his eloquence.
Cited from Sòng Dynasty Xuē Jù's Kǒngzǐ Jí Yǔ: Chǔ Zhāo Wáng Piān.
21.25 Wèi Líng Gōng was excavating a pond in the cold of winter.
Wǎn Chūn remonstrated, saying:
"Starting a labor project in such cold,
I fear it will exhaust the people."
The Duke said:
"Is it cold?"
Chūn said:
"Your Grace wears a fox fur robe
and sits on a bear skin mat,
and thus you are not cold.
But the people are very cold."
The Duke then stopped the project.
Cited from Yù Lǎn, Volume 27, page 127.
21.26 Chúnyú Kūn offered praise three times,
Zōu Jì understood it three times;
Kūn and the others were at a loss for words and departed.
Therefore, the reason Gān Jiàng and Mò Yé are esteemed is for their ability to cut instantly.
Cited from the commentary to Wén Xuǎn: Dá Dōng Ā Wáng Jiàn, page 750.
21.27 According to Yīn law,
those who discard ashes in the street were punished.
Cited from Shū Chāo, Volume 43, page 121.
21.28 Bìyōng
is the place where the Son of Heaven holds the village drinking ceremony.
Cited from Yù Lǎn, Volume 534, page 2422.
21.29 When Qín Èr Shì ascended the throne,
a crooked arrow star shone at night.
Soon after, the realm fell into great chaos,
and Èr Shì was killed.
Cited from Yù Lǎn, Volume 875, page 3884.
21.30 When Yǔ transformed the world,
he used the five sounds to listen;
he hung a bell, a drum, a wooden-clapper bell, and a lithophone at his gate and placed a hand-drum,
to wait for the scholars from all within the four seas.
Cited from Chū Xué Jì, Volume 9, page 206.
21.31 Wén Gōng liked to eat pickled Chāngběn;
the Běn Cǎo says it is Chāngpú.
Cited from Yù Lǎn, Volume 999, page 4421.
21.32 When Gōngsūn Qiáo was the minister of Zhèng,
items dropped on the road were not picked up;
peaches and plums hung over the streets,
and people did not dare to take them.
Cited from Yù Lǎn, Volume 967, page 4288.
21.33 The rats on the beams are satiated from hearing the discussions of the elders.
Cited from Yù Lǎn, Volume 911, page 4037.
21.34 Chǔ Wén Hóu said:
"The powerful in the town like to conceal good and publicize evil;
you may inquire about it in person."
Cited from the commentary to Wén Xuǎn: Dōng Jīng Fù.
21.35 When Chūlǐ Zǐ was about to die,
he said:
"Bury me to the east of Zhāngtái, south of the Wèi River;
in a hundred years, the palaces of a Son of Heaven will flank my grave."
When the Hàn rose,
the Chánglè Palace was to its east,
the Wèiyāng Palace was to its west,
and the Wǔkù was directly above it.
Shì Wén Xū Jù 56, Gǔ Jīn Hé Bì Shì Lèi Bèi Yào 66.
21.36 Long ago, when Suí Hóu was traveling,
he encountered a large snake cut in two.
Suspecting it was a spiritual being,
he sent someone to seal it with medicine.
The snake was then able to leave.
Thus, the place was named Duànshéqiū.
A year later,
the snake held a bright pearl in its mouth,
an inch in diameter,
perfectly white and radiant;
thus it was called the Suí Zhū.
Shǐ Jì: Lǐ Sī Zhuàn Zhèng Yì.
21.37 When Zǐqí was eighteen years old,
the Lord of Qí sent him to govern Ā.
After he had left,
the Lord of Qí regretted it
and sent a messenger to pursue him.
The pursuer returned and said:
"Zǐqí will surely be capable,
for those riding with him are all white-haired elders."
When Zǐqí arrived in Ā,
he melted down the weapons in the armory to make farming tools.
When Wèi heard that a child was the ruler,
that the armory had no weapons,
and the granaries had no grain,
they raised troops to attack him.
The fathers of Ā led their sons
and brothers led brothers,
fighting with their private weapons,
and they defeated the Wèi army.
Commentary to Wén Xuǎn: Pān Zhèng Shǔ Zèng Hé Yáng Shī.
21.38 The Prince of Gāopíng sent a messenger to borrow grain from Wèi Wén Hóu.
Wén Hóu said:
"Wait until the grain tax from my estates arrives, then you shall have it."
The messenger said:
"When I first came,
I saw a fish in a ditch with its mouth open,
who said to me:
'I am out of water,
my life depends on my next breath;
could I have some water poured on me?'
I said to it:
'Wait until I go south to see the lords of the river dikes,
and I will divert the waters of the Jiāng and Huái to pour into your mouth.'
The fish said:
'My life is a matter of a moment,
yet you speak of needing to divert the waters of the Jiāng and Huái;
by the time you return,
you will surely have to seek me in a dried fish shop.'
Now Gāopíng is in poverty,
so they sent me to Your Lordship to borrow grain,
yet you say to wait for the grain tax to arrive;
Your Greatness will surely have to seek me in a dead man's grave."
Yì Wén Lèi Jù 85, Tài Píng Yù Lǎn 840, Gǔ Jīn Hé Bì Shì Lèi Bèi Yào 57, Tiān Zhōng Jì 45, Yuān Jiàn Lèi Hán 395.
21.39 When Zǐchǎn died,
young maidens wept in their rooms
and farmers wailed in the fields.
Běi Táng Shū Chāo 35.
21.40 When Zǐchǎn died while serving as minister of Zhèng,
women discarded their hairpins and earrings,
and gentlemen loosened the strings of their qín and sè.
Běi Táng Shū Chāo 35.
21.41 The image of vocal music:
the sè is easy and the sè is good, and it accords with the music.
Běi Táng Shū Chāo 109.
21.42 Jìn Líng Gōng liked mournful songs and playing the qín.
Běi Táng Shū Chāo 109, Yuān Jiàn Lèi Hán 188.
21.43 The image of vocal music:
the plucking and striking resembles all things.
Běi Táng Shū Chāo 111.
21.44 The lightning and the yin strike and shine brightly.
Běi Táng Shū Chāo 152.
21.45 Yùzǐ said:
"When Yǔ transformed the world,
he used the five sounds to listen;
he hung a lithophone, bell, and wooden-clapper bell at the gate to wait for the scholars from all within the four seas."
Chū Xué Jì 9.
21.46 Within ten steps, there is fragrant grass.
Hòu Hàn Shū: Wáng Fú Zhuàn, Yuān Jiàn Lèi Hán 408.
21.47 In the past, Zōu Jì served as the Prime Minister of Qí.
Among the seventy-two scholars of the Jìxià Academy, such as Chúnyú Kūn and his peers,
all looked down on Zōu Jì
and devised clever arguments to challenge him.
Chúnyú Kūn made three assertions,
and Zōu Jì understood them all three times,
responding like an echo.
Kūn and the others, their arguments exhausted, departed.
Thus, the reason people value Gānjiàng and Mòyé
is for their ability to cut through things instantly;
the reason people value Qíjì
is for its ability to arrive at a destination immediately.
If it must take many days and a long duration,
even a silk thread or a fine hair can carve stone,
and a slow horse can also reach a great distance.
Therefore, intelligence and swiftness
are the beautiful talents of a person.
*Hòuhànshū: Cuī Yīn Zhuàn* commentary; *Wénxuǎn: Chén Kǒngzhāng dáp Dōng'é Wáng Jiàn* commentary; *Tàipíng Yùlǎn* 432.
21.48 Bào Jiāo wore tree bark for clothing
and ate tree fruit for food.
*Hòuhànshū: Cuī Yīn Zhuàn* commentary.
21.49 Nìng Qì was feeding oxen at Kāngqú,
striking the carriage wheel hub while singing "Shuò Shǔ";
Fù Yuè, standing in for a convict laborer, was building at the wilds of Fùyán
when Gāozōng saw him in a dream and obtained his service.
*Hòuhànshū: Mǎ Róng Zhuàn* commentary.
21.50 Indiscriminate talk,
uncircumspect conduct,
and unpraised speech—
the gentleman is cautious regarding these.
*Xúnzǐ: Zhèngmíng Piān*, Yáng Jìng's commentary.
21.51 When starving horses fill the stable
and starving dogs are in the palace,
upon seeing fodder or bones,
their movement cannot be restrained.
*Shìlèi Fù* 23.
21.52 Serving Zhòngní
is like holding a cup and going to the rivers and seas to drink;
one cannot know the depth.
*Tàipíng Yùlǎn* 2; *Jìzuǎn Yuānhǎi* 43.
21.53 Wèi Wénhóu's teacher Lǐ Kuī wrote six chapters of legal books.
*Gǔjīn Hébiì Shìlèi Bèiyào Wàijí* 17.
21.54 Tián Yīng said:
"Those who die for righteousness do not avoid the power of the axe and hatchet;
those who are destitute for righteousness do not accept the gift of high rank and carriage.
To live without righteousness
is not as good as dying with righteousness."
*Jìzuǎn Yuānhǎi* 54.
21.55 To associate with those below oneself for the sake of profit
without even a look of shame;
for a profit of a mere fraction,
to know it and yet insist on competing for it.
*Jìzuǎn Yuānhǎi* 54.
21.56 To take the zhǐ note as the yǔ note
is not the fault of the strings;
to take sweetness for bitterness
is not the fault of the flavor.
*Jìzuǎn Yuānhǎi* 55.
21.57 Yègōng Zhūliáng asked Lè Wángfù:
"What kind of man is the Jìn Grand Master Zhào Wénzǐ?"
He replied:
"He loves learning and accepts correction and admonition."
Yègōng said:
"I suspect that this is not comprehensive."
He replied:
"One who loves learning is wise;
one who accepts correction and admonition is humane.
When the Jiāng River flows out from Wènshān,
its source is as small as the mouth of a jar;
by the time it reaches the State of Chǔ,
its width is ten lǐ.
There is no other reason for this
than that its lower reaches receive many tributaries.
For a person who loves learning and accepts correction and admonition,
how fitting it is that he should be established!"
*Tiānzhōng Jì* 9.
21.58 Wǔ Wáng asked Tàigōng:
"Are poverty and wealth determined by fate?"
Tàigōng said:
"If one's actions are not diligent,
or if one is diligent but not wealthy,
then there is a thief in the house."
Wǔ Wáng asked:
"What constitutes a thief?"
Tàigōng said:
"Failure to plan thoroughly
is the first thief.
Harvesting and planting at the improper time
is the second thief.
Marrying an incompetent wife
is the third thief.
Raising too many daughters
is the fourth thief.
Abandoning work for wine
is the fifth thief.
Extravagance in clothing
is the sixth thief.
Lack of caution in storage
is the seventh thief.
If the well and stove are not functional
is the eighth thief.
Taking loans with interest to perform rites
is the ninth thief.
Burning lamps when there is nothing to do
is the tenth thief.
With such drains, how can one be wealthy?"
Wǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent."
*Tiānzhōng Jì* 39.
21.59 Two noble honors cannot coexist;
two powerful forces cannot be paired.
Yáng Shèn's *Yìlín Fáshān* 17.
21.60 Lǔ Xiànzǐ paid a diplomatic visit to Jìn.
Xuānzǐ hosted him with wine.
The feast was moved to three different locations,
and each time the sets of hanging bells and stone chimes were ready without being moved.
Xiànzǐ said:
"How wealthy is your house!"
Xuānzǐ said:
"Is your house as wealthy as mine?"
Xiànzǐ said:
"My house is very poor.
I only have two scholars named Yán Huí and Zī Wúlíng,
who keep my state and house peaceful and stable
and the common people in harmony and cooperation.
With only these two,
my wealth is exhausted by this!"
After the guest left,
Xuānzǐ said:
"He is a gentleman,
for he considers nurturing the worthy as wealth;
I am a base person,
for I consider bells and stones as wealth."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The wealth of Mèng Xiànzǐ is worthy of being recorded in the *Chūnqiū*."
*Jiāo Shì Lèilín*, Volume 1, Part 2.
21.61 Mǐn Zǐqiān lost his mother early
and suffered under his stepmother.
In the winter months, she dressed him in clothes stuffed with reed blossoms,
while she dressed her own two biological sons in clothes stuffed with cotton.
His father ordered Mǐn Zǐ to drive the carriage.
Because his body was cold, he dropped the reins.
His father scolded him,
but Mǐn Zǐ did not explain himself.
His father investigated and realized the truth.
Returning home, he said to his wife:
"The reason I married you
was for the sake of my sons;
now you have deceived me.
Leave and do not stay."
Zǐqiān came forward and said:
"If Mother stays, only one son is cold;
if Mother leaves, three sons will be bereft."
His father remained silent.
Therefore it is said:
"How filial was Mǐn Zǐqiān!
With one word his mother remained;
with another word the three sons were warm."
*Yuānjiàn Lèihán* 271.
21.62 The Lord of Lí lost his state
and lived for a long time in Wèi.
Wèi did not come to his aid.
His ministers urged him to return
and composed "Zhōnglù."
*Yuānjiàn Lèihán* 10.
21.63 Sāng Jūn took medicine from his bosom and gave it to Biǎn Què,
telling him to drink it with water from an upper pool;
before it touched the ground,
catch the dew water from upon the bamboo and trees.
*Yuānjiàn Lèihán* 10.
21.64 Zhōu Chéng Wáng was playing with his younger brother.
He picked up a leaf from the ground
and gave it to his brother, saying:
"I enfeoff you with Táng with this."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Please select an auspicious day."
The King said:
"It was just a joke;
I will not enfeoff him."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"A ruler's words are weighty;
to enfeoff someone and then regret it is to be untrustworthy."
Thereupon, he finally enfeoffed him.
*Yuānjiàn Lèihán* 118.
21.65 Wáng Zhāng was a scholar
studying in Cháng'ān,
living alone with his wife.
Zhāng was ill and had no quilt,
so he lay in a cattle-cloth.
He bid farewell to his wife,
weeping.
His wife scolded him angrily, saying:
"Zhòngqīng,
among the honored and noble of the capital at the imperial court,
who is there that surpasses Zhòngqīng?
Now that you are ill and in distress,
you do not rouse yourself
but instead weep;
how base!"
Yuānjiàn Lèihán 267.
21.66 Zhū Yún died at home at over seventy years of age.
When ill, he did not call for a physician or drink medicine.
His final instructions were to be shrouded in his everyday clothes,
with a coffin just large enough for his body
and the earth just filling the outer coffin pit.
Yuānjiàn Lèihán 267.
21.67 Xí Sīmí visited Tián Chéngzǐ.
Tián Chéngzǐ climbed a terrace with him to look out in four directions;
three sides were all unobstructed,
but when looking south,
the trees of Xízǐ's house blocked the view.
Tián Chéngzǐ also said nothing.
Xízǐ returned home
and had men cut them down.
After the axes had made several gashes,
Xízǐ stopped them.
His steward said:
"Why this sudden change?"
Xízǐ said:
"An ancient proverb says,
'To know the fish in the depths is inauspicious.'
Now Tiánzǐ is about to undertake a matter.
The matter is great, yet I have shown him that I notice the subtle;
I will certainly be in danger.
If I do not cut down the trees,
I have not yet committed an offense;
but to know that which a man does not speak of,
that offense is great indeed."
Thus he did not cut them down.
Yuānjiàn Lèihán 276.
21.68 Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was hunting on the sunny side of Jìnshān;
he stroked the reins and sighed, saying:
"I have several thousand grain-eating horses
and several hundred strong warriors
with which I wish to hunt wild beasts,
yet I fear that neighboring states are nurturing worthy men to hunt me."
How wise!
Jiǎnzǐ was good at reflecting upon himself.
Yuānjiàn Lèihán 277.
